[3] Butts (2008). A relational event framework for social action. Sociological Methodology, 38(1). [4] Lillo & Rizzini (2024). Modelling shock propagation in financial temporal networks. arXiv :2407.09340. [5] Jord` a (2005). Estimation and inference of impulse responses by local projections. AER, 95(1).

column9: Synchronization Enhancement by Phase Lag in Coupled Oscillators with Inertia
column11: Yi, Sudo*; Kim, Cook Hyun; Kim, Heetae; Kahng, B.
column13: Coupled-oscillator systems with inertia offer a realistic framework for describing many physical systems, including electrical power grids. Although inertia is essential to capture realistic dynamical behavior, it suppresses global synchronization, so the system can be synchronized only at relatively large coupling strengths and in a discontinuous manner, often accompanied by the formation of several clusters locked in frequency [1–3]. The effect of phase lag has been extensively explored in the first-order Kuramoto model—most notably in the Sakaguchi–Kuramoto variant—where it is typically observed to suppress synchronization and modify the critical coupling threshold [4]. In this study, we demonstrate that introducing a phase lag to only a subset of oscillators can, conversely, promote synchronization in the second-order Kuramoto model with inertia.  We consider a heterogeneous population comprising oscillators with no phase lag and those with a uniform, nonzero phase lag. The dynamics are investigated using a post-lag protocol, in which the phase lag is imposed only after the initially lag-free system has relaxed to a steady state. Figure 1 shows that introducing a phase lag in only part of the population alters the structure of the primary frequency-entrained cluster. For large inertia, numerical results indicate that the phase lag displaces the left boundary of the primary entrained cluster in the intrinsic-frequency domain toward more negative values. As a result, oscillators with negative natural frequencies—both drifting units and those originally forming secondary or higher-order clusters—are recruited into the synchronized state [2,3]. In contrast, oscillators with sufficiently large positive natural frequencies do not depinning, so the right boundary of the primary cluster stays fixed, yielding a net expansion of the primary synchronized cluster.  These findings demonstrate that introducing a partial phase lag can qualitatively alter the configuration of synchronized clusters in inertia-oscillator systems, leading to an expansion of the central frequency-locked cluster in the large-inertia regime. By revealing how phase lag reshapes cluster boundaries without triggering depinning on the positive-frequency side, this work clarifies the impact of partial phase lag on synchronized cluster organization in the second-order Kuramoto model, providing guidance on synchronization control for inertial systems, such as power grids.

column9: Operational time and criticality in physics co-authorship networks
column13: Many real-world complex networks display either fractal or small-world structure, but rarely both. Prior work explains this incompatibility through static architectural constraints: fractality emerges from critical branching trees, whereas small-world structure requires supercritical expansion supported by long-range shortcuts. Here we show that this dichotomy is not merely structural but dynamical. Using more than a century of APS co-authorship data, we construct a sequence of network time slices by tuning aggregation to the percolation transition. Measuring a set of macro-level parameters -- including percolation observables and small-world indicators -- we find that all scale as power laws with the networks’ distance from criticality. Networks remain fractal near criticality but acquire small-world shortcuts only when aggregated beyond the critical point. We further show that the critical time scale emerging from this aggregation procedure constitutes an operational time to which the system self-organizes: citation avalanches obey dynamical scaling theory only when defined in this intrinsic time. These results indicate that static analyses are insufficient whenever the evolutionary time scale of a network is empirically accessible. A dynamical scaling framework is required to correctly identify and characterize critical and supercritical network states.

column9: Cortical Topology emerges from a Multi-scale Cellular Potts Model
column11: Laasch, Niklas*; Hilgetag, Claus; Hadaeghi, Fatemeh
column13: The mammalian cerebral cortex displays a complex network architecture that supports high-level cognition, yet the developmental rules driving its formation remain poorly understood. Current computational models often rely on static templates or global optimization, failing to capture the physical morphogenesis of the neural tissue. Here, we present a multi-scale generative model that integrates tissue-level mechanics with local wiring rules to simulate the emergence of the cortical connectome. Our approach combines a Cellular Potts Model (CPM) for tissue dynamics with a biologically grounded connectivity algorithm. We simulate the ”inside-out” cortical developmental program, where early-born neurons settle in deep layers and later-born neurons migrate past them to superficial positions [1]. This spatiotemporal process naturally creates distinct distance constraints and cytoarchitectonic profiles (e.g., layer thickness variations) without a priori prescription. As neurons settle, they form connections based on spatially constrained preferential attachment and lineage-based microcolumnar biases [2]. We demonstrate that realistic macro-scale network topology emerges solely from these local developmental interactions. The simulated networks exhibit heavy-tailed degree distributions, hierarchical modularity, and realistic reciprocal clustering coefficients. Crucially, we reproduce the Architectonic Type Principle [3], where connectivity profiles are predicted by the similarity of laminar cytoarchitecture between areas. This finding suggests that the complex topology of brain networks is not necessarily the result of a global optimization of the trade-off between wiring cost and topological value, but may be an emergent property of simple physical migration and wiring rules. This framework offers a bridge between developmental biology and network science, providing a new platform to investigate how perturbations in physical growth leads to altered network phenotypes in neurodevelopmental disorders. column9: Disruptions in constrained optimal transport networks
column13: Over the past decades, a variety of transportation systems have been successfully modelled using optimal transport (OT), from biological networks as leaf venation and blood vessels, to engineering networks as urban transportation or communication networks. In this context, adaptation equations (or dynamical formulation of OT) that describe how conductivities, flows and pressure potentials evolve interdependently to consolidate into an optimal network structure. This have been used extensively to study a variety of transportation scenarios, and it has been shown to explain with a high degree of similarity observed on real networks.  However, current approaches based on adaptation equations suffer from not considering constraints (beyond standard ones like conservation of mass and positivity) as part of the general framework. As a result, networks output from these models can be unrealistic in practice, without incorporation of relevant constraints, such as constraints on the network global infrastructure or capacity constraints.  This work, first, propose a general framework powerful enough to accommodate nonlinear and nonconvex constraints in OT problems. Our approach follows a physics-based perspective on including constraints by leveraging the principle of d’Alembert-Lagrange from classical mechanics. This leads to a sparse, local and linear approximation of the feasible set, leading in many cases to closed-form updates. Next, we study the impact of disruptions in these OT dynamics. We propose two scenarios for trajectory extraction, and relevant metrics to evaluate and quantify disruptions within optimal transport networks.

column9: Mid-point Rule for Community Detection
column13: In this paper, we derive and demonstrate the empirical efficiency of a simple and practical rule for detecting the boundaries of disjoint communities in a network based on shortest path lengths. Our approach is founded on a network communication game, a member of the family of cheap talk games, that defines how audiences for public messages are formed. The method requires only a table of shortest path lengths and a ranking of nodes according to their closeness centrality, as defined by Freeman (1978), which is itself based on shortest paths. The mainstream game-theoretical approach to community detection focuses on allocating nodes across communities in a modularity maximising manner. Jonnalagadda and Kuppusamy (2016) provide an overview of this approach. Our framework is inspired by the network formation game of Galeotti et al. (2013). In their model, a receiver node decides whether to communicate with a sender, assumed to be more central, based on whether the interaction is perceived as trustworthy. A collection of such communication links forms a network shaped by agents’ biases and the amount of information they possess, both of which are unobservable in practice. If a real-world social network emerge from such trustworthy communication, it is natural to ask whether this property can be exploited to partition an observed network into communities that reveal underlying personal biases. To address this question, we develop a game on networks in which shortest path lengths are interpreted as indicators of trustworthy communication. The most influential senders form communities consisting of nodes that are close to them along an unobservable attribute, such as personal preferences. A sender’s utility increases with the size of their audience, while a receiver’s utility increases the closer they are to their preferred sender. Any node may act as a sender or a follower. A Nash equilibrium is reached when no sender, or community centre, can be replaced by another node in the network in a way that increases the size of the corresponding community. In the case of multiple equilibria (they may have different numbers of communities), the equilibrium with the largest number of allocated nodes is selected. By optimising this game, we obtain an empirically validated rule that partitions the network into disjoint communities: Midpoint Rule: A community consists of the nodes whose shortest path to its community centre is shorter than their shortest path to any other community centre. To evaluate efficiency of the Mid-point Rule, we applied it to three real-world networks with known ground-truth communities: the Zachary Karate Club network (two communities), a political blog network from the 2004 U.S. election (two communities), and an email network from a large European research institution (calculated for five large communities). The first two datasets were obtained from the Koblenz Network Collection, while the email network was downloaded from the Stanford Large Network Dataset Collection. The results demonstrate about 90% level of detection of community nodes. We measured the efficiency of the rule by comparing its output with ground truth communities, although it can also be validated using modularity. Only a small number of nodes in each network were assigned to incorrect communities. The method tends to omit nodes rather than assign them to the wrong community, which may be a desirable property in applications that require high accuracy. Our approach also selects nodes with high closeness centrality as community centres, which can be approximated by out-degree centrality at high values. Restricting the set of nodes that can play the sender role in this way makes the method more computationally efficient when applied to large networks.

column9: The Political Reorganization of Everyday Life? Uncovering Latent Lifestyle Structures via Digital Traces
column13: A common claim in polarization research is that everyday life is increasingly organized along partisan lines: from what we consume online to how we understand ourselves, even non-political content is thought to reinforce political identity [1,2]. We treat this “political reorganization of everyday life” as an empirical hypothesis and test it using network models of online lifestyles inferred from large-scale digital traces. We use a decade-long panel of U.S. Twitter users with linked demographic and voter-registration information (2011–2022)[3]. For each year, we build a weighted bipartite network between demographic groups and web domains, where groups are defined by race, age, gender, region, and party, and edges encode how often a group shares a domain. Excluding news and mega-platform sites allows us to focus on everyday, lifestyle-oriented content (entertainment, shopping, local services, hobbies).  From the group–domain matrices we apply non-negative matrix factorization to obtain K latent “lifestyle bundles,” and represent each group as a point in this bundle space. We then construct a yearly group–group lifestyle similarity network, whose edges reflect normalized correlations between bundle profiles. On these networks, we compute assortativity for race, age, gender, region, and party to compare how strongly each attribute structures lifestyle similarity. Regression models complement this by asking (1) how much variance in bundle memberships partisanship explains relative to other demographics, and (2)how strongly ideology predicts similarity ties once other features are controlled for. We also track these statistics over time to relate changes in sorting to major events such as elections and the COVID-19 pandemic. Conceptually, we treat online lifestyles as a networked object—a temporal stack of lifestyle similarity layers grounded in a demographic–domain bipartite graph—to scrutinize the “political reorganization” thesis. Methodologically, our combination of factor models, similarity networks, assortativity, and regression provides a template for extracting meso-scale lifestyle structure from digital traces. Substantively, preliminary results show that race often generates stronger assortativity than party, that sorting is not monotonic over time, and that cross-cutting lifestyle ties persist, suggesting that while politics matters, everyday online life does not always consolidate primarily along partisan lines. Nature, 620(7972), 137-144. [3] Yang, K. C., Goel, P., Quintana-Math´ e, A., Horgan, L., McCabe, S. D., Grinberg, N., ... & Lazer, D. (2025). DomainDemo: a dataset of domain-sharing activities among different demographic groups on Twitter. Scientific data, 12(1), 1251.

column9: On the Structure of China's High-Speed Rail-Aviation Composite Network
column13: This study constructs China’s high-speed rail(CRH)-aviation composite network. By analyzing its topological properties and comparing them with those of the single-modal CRH and aviation networks, we identify the multiple network roles of transportation hubs and reveal the hub-periphery structural pattern.  We collected schedule data from China’s CRH timetables and flight plans to construct the aviation and CRH networks. Nodes are cities with CRH stations, airports, or both; edges mean direct CRH or flight connectivity, directed and unweighted. Railway stations and airports within the same city are considered interconnected in the composite network,   Topological analysis shows CRH network and aviation network both have scale-free and small-world features—key for efficient transport. Differences exist: The CRH network has extremely high clustering, ensuring high local efficiency. The aviation network has a lower clustering, and no clear communities, supporting long-distance travel. The composite network expands coverage by leveraging the complementary advantages of these two transportation modes.  We then assigned multiple network roles to nodes based on their multiplex degrees and distributions. From a multiplex network perspective, we identified four distinct roles of national transportation hubs: Focused nodes (R1), Multiplex nodes (R2), Focused hubs (R3), and Multiplex hubs (R4). This analysis reveals the uneven distribution of these hub types across geographical space and network hierarchical structures. We further explored the different roles of air and rail transportation in organizing passenger network structures; the inherent differences between the two modes have led to the structural differentiation of China’s CRH-aviation composite network, forming a fundamental pattern consisting of a hub core and peripheral clusters.  This study addresses the limitations of single-modal transportation network research. It uncovers the hub-peripheral structural pattern and uneven distribution characteristics of the composite network, providing theoretical support for the optimization of comprehensive transportation planning and the precise layout of hub systems.  Future research will further explore the weighted properties of the composite network and the influencing factors of regional differences.

column9: The mesoscopic structure of the Carbon Trade Network across the last twenty years
column13: As emissions from burning fossil fuels are the primary cause of global warming~[1], the last decades have witnessed a considerable effort to mitigate carbon emissions. At country level, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change attributes emissions to countries producing goods and services~[2]; recent literature has, however, advocated the adoption of a consumption-aware accounting, that re-distributes the responsibility for the emissions between producers and users~[3]. Studies have attempted to understand to what extent a `consumption principle' may help reducing disparities in carbon accounting, estimating the amount of traded carbon via Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) tables. As noticed by Caro et al.~[4], MRIO tables are very sensitive to the accuracy of the available data on trading sectors; interestingly enough, data requirements can be relaxed by considering aggregate measures: specifically, the amount of carbon embedded into a country export can be simply quantified by multiplying it by the related \emph{GDP-induced carbon intensity}, measuring the kilograms of carbon per dollar of GDP released by a given country during a given year.  Inspired by the work of Caro and co-authors, we have constructed the Carbon Trade Network (CTN), i.e. the graph induced by the trade-embedded carbon exchanges between world countries, with the aim of investigating it over the past two decades. More specifically, we have limited ourselves to analyze the mesoscopic organization of the CTN Strongly Connected Component (SCC), by optimizing the binary, weighted, and enhanced variants of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) on it. In all cases, the SCC is characterized by an additional, nested structure constituted of a core and a periphery - the core (periphery) subgraph being characterized by the highest (lowest) level of reciprocity (see fig.~1).  In the purely binary case, the core block gathers the $84$ richest, and more polluting, countries (among which Brazil, Canada, China, Europe, India, Japan, South-Africa, USA); if, instead, we leave the BIC instantiated with the directed, binary variant of the Stochastic Block Model (bSBM) free to find the optimal number of groups, we recover ten modules - only five of which are assembled in the aforementioned core. Optimizing BIC instantiated with the directed, weighted variant of the Stochastic Block Model (wSBM) confirms the results obtained by running the bSBM, the subset of core-nodes concentrating the highest percentage of the total weight ($\simeq 10\%$) now including China, India, South-Africa, USA: an important exception is represented by Russia, no longer part of this subset - as the year considered for the present analysis is $2023$, this may be due to the sanctions suffered by Russia in consequence of the war with Ukraine. As a last exercise, we have instantiated BIC with the directed, enhanced variant of the Stochastic Block Model (eSBM), constraining both binary and weighted properties in a block-wise fashion: in such a case, the algorithm recovers China, India, Russia, USA as the nodes constituting the subgraph summing up $\simeq 10\%$ of the total weight (see fig.~1).  As an additional exercise, we have individuated the countries playing the role of hubs (top exporters) and authorities (top importers) by running both the binary and weighted versions of the HITS algorithm: accounting for weights reveals that \emph{i)} China is becoming increasingly central in the category of authorities as well, closely followed by India; \emph{ii)} Vietnam is becoming the second most central country in the category of hubs.

column9: Polarization and echo chambers in Reddit’s political discourse
column11: Cirulli, Daniele*; Cimini, Giulio; Saracco, Fabio; Desiderio, Antonio
column13: Online social networks have become key arenas for political debate, with elections often serving as an epicenter of political discourse. Understanding how these online interactions evolve is key to uncovering the formation of polarization and echo chambers, which have resounding effects in the offline world. Among these platforms, Reddit is often considered less prone to polarization and echo-chamber dynamics than timeline-based platforms such as Facebook or X. We analyze the evolution of political discourse on Reddit from 2013 to 2017, jointly considering user interactions and news dissemination. Our method involves constructing two distinct weighted bipartite networks: one linking users to subreddits based on comment activity, and another associating subreddits with the domains of shared URLs. By applying maximum- entropy statistical validation grounded in information theory to both networks, we identify significant co-occurrences among subreddits. Validated links are used to construct subreddit networks encoding both topic-based and interaction- based communities, explicitly accounting for the role of external information. This analysis reveals how communities align with specific political orientations or topics over time. We observe a significant rise in Democratic and Conservative subreddits during elections, as well as an increase in users who engage with both types of subreddits. During the 2016 elections, Democrats and Conservatives form distinct clusters, with heightened antagonistic feedback between opposing groups and increasing yet tense cross-group interactions. Polarization emerges across both interaction-based and topic- based communities, particularly within Democratic, Conservative, and Banned subreddits. During election periods, we note the close alignment between Conservative and Banned groups, with the latter significantly influencing Conservative discourse. Additionally, we observe limited variability in the language used within the same groups. By analyzing overlaps in user bases and information consumption patterns, we indicate that the mechanisms underlying community formation through interactions also govern the dissemination of external news sources. Overall, this dual perspective underscores Reddit’s role as a polarized environment, revealing clear patterns in political discourse, shedding new light on the presence of echo chambers, and positioning network validation as a key tool to decipher patterns critical to the healthy functioning of our society.

column9: How Large Language Models play humans in online conversations: a simulated study of the 2016 US politics on Reddit
column11: Cirulli, Daniele*; Cimini, Giulio; Palermo, Giovanni
column13: Large Language Models (LLMs) have captured unprecedented public and academic attention in recent years, especially after the release of GPT-3.5, which is capable of generating complex texts from a prompt. Within the field of complex systems, LLMs have sparked a lot of interest in complex networks and agent-based models, with a broad spectrum of applications. Indeed, they have been applied to explain several emergent phenomena, such as preferential attachment in networks or the creation of fake social networks. The ability of these generative models to mimic human behavior opens new avenues for scientific discovery, but also raises concerns about their potential use for covert manipulation in online political discussions (e.g., fake news, polarization, and divisive content). Since the importance of these topics, in this work, we want to assess the performances of LLMs when used for these kinds of purposes. We use GPT-4 in a real, divisive setting for our tests, namely the conversations on Reddit about the 2016 US presidential election. After collecting two subreddits supporting Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, we simulate three prompting scenarios: user impersonation based on real comment histories, and custom pro- or anti-candidate histories consisting of synthetic comments. The first one aims to test whether a LLM can act as a real user and sneak into conversations. In the second and third case, we test if bots designed to, respectively, endorse and weaken the candidate can actually do it effectively. After generating the comments, we classify them using GPT itself, asking the model to identify their party alignment, sentiment and violence content. Our findings reveal that GPT-4 is more prone to produce agreement rather than dissent, as the party alignment of the generated comments tends to be the same as the subreddit’s dominant political orientation (and hardly opposed to it), even when prompted with a custom user history clearly against the candidate. However, the classification of the output also strongly depends on the context, as highlighted by previous works. Furthermore, while LLM- generated comments seem indistinguishable from real ones, we show they actually cluster in semantic embedding space and separate from human-written texts, suggesting a potential approach to identify LLM-generated content in social networks.

column9: A Mechanistic Model of Network Connectivity
column13: The manifold hypothesis, which posits that high-dimensional datasets reside on low-dimensional structures, constitutes an important observation in modern data-driven science. One can reformulate this hypothesis within the context of network science, asserting that numerous real-world networks may be characterized as sampled random geometric graphs (RGGs). [1] Under this framework, we assume the existence of a low-dimensional manifold Mequipped with a Riemannian metric g, which induces a distance metric, and a probability distribution µ. Nodes x1,...,xN ∈Mare sampled according to µ, with connection probabilities defined as pij∼exp(−distg (xi,xj )/epsilon), where epsilon is a scaling factor. Such random geometric constructions encompass a broad class of complex networks; for instance, uniform sampling on a hyperbolic half-plane effectively yields scale-free networks. [3] We introduce the Mechanistic Model of Network Connectivity (MMoNCy), a computational framework designed for the generation and analysis of complex networks. A primary challenge addressed herein is the inverse problem: reconstructing the latent manifold and its associated distribution from an observed network topology. The graph Laplacian is central to this inquiry, as it converges to the manifold’s diffusion operator (the Laplace-Beltrami operator) in the limit N →∞. [4] Rather than merely identifying a low-dimensional embedding, we seek a coordinate representation of the nodes that optimizes the sparsity of the reconstructed Riemannian metric. This pursuit of structural parsimony allows for a more interpretable geometric characterization of the network. We evaluate several methodological approaches to this reconstruction task, suggesting that the MMoNCy framework provides a robust mechanism for elucidating the global organizational principles governing large-scale complex systems.

column9: Quantifying the Robustness of Network Medicine Algorithms to Interactome Incompleteness and Noise
column13: Network medicine relies on the hypothesis that disease-associated proteins localize in specific topological neighborhoods, or ”disease modules”, within the interactome. However, current protein-protein interaction networks are both incomplete and prone to false positives [1,2]. The sensitivity of network-based prioritization algorithms to such structural noise remains under-characterized, limiting our ability to assess the confidence of computational predictions.  In this study we assess algorithmic robustness by simulating varying degrees of network noise. Starting with the baseline interactome, we generate perturbed networks by randomly removing (simulating missing data) and adding (simulating experimental noise) links.  To quantify robustness, we evaluate the performance of widely used prioritization methods (e.g. Random Walk with Restart). We compare the identified disease modules in perturbed networks against those from the baseline interactome using metrics such as Jaccard similarity. Our analysis suggests that while neighborhoods remain stable under minor perturbations, they diverge significantly beyond specific noise thresholds.  By analyzing these ”breakdown points” of common algorithms, we provide guidelines for selecting robust methods and interpreting in silico findings in the context of an imperfect interactome.

column9: Across-Visit Consensus Community Detection in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) Gene Co-expression Temporal Network Data
column13: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by strong heterogeneity and time-varying immune dysregulation. While gene co-expression network analysis has proven useful for identifying disease-associated modules, most existing approaches rely on static or cross-sectional representations and do not explicitly leverage longitudinal structure.  Here, we propose a time-aware multilayer network framework to identify stable gene communities and underexplored hub genes in longitudinal whole-blood transcriptomic data from SLE patients (GSE65391). GSE65391 is a publicly available longitudinal whole-blood gene expression dataset in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), where patients are profiled repeatedly across multiple clinical visits (i.e., the same individuals contribute samples at different time points), alongside healthy controls. This longitudinal design enables constructing visit-specific co-expression layers and then identifying time-stable communities by aggregating evidence across visits rather than relying on a single static network [1,2].  Gene co-expression networks are constructed independently for each clinical visit, yielding a sequence of visit-specific network layers defined over a shared set of genes. Instead of optimizing a coupled multislice modularity with explicit inter-layer identity edges [3], we adopt a consensus-across-time strategy [4]: communities are detected separately within each visit layer using the Leiden algorithm [5], and a weighted consensus graph is subsequently built based on gene–gene co-assignment fractions across layers. Re-clustering this consensus graph produces time-stable gene communities that summarize recurrent co-expression patterns across visits.  Applying this framework, we identify eight robust communities corresponding to major immune processes, including interferon signaling, neutrophil activation, plasmablast-related programs, and platelet-associated pathways. Beyond these well-characterized structures, our approach highlights unexpected hub genes that exhibit high within-community centrality, despite having a limited prior association with SLE. To systematically assess novelty, we integrate automated literature and GWAS-based screening to quantify existing disease-specific evidence for each candidate hub, revealing several highly ranked genes with minimal representation in prior SLE studies [6,7].  We further verify that the identified hub genes remain highly central when analyses are restricted to female samples, which constitute the majority of the cohort, indicating that hub detection is not driven by a small subset of subjects. Together, these results demonstrate that time-aware consensus community detection provides a robust and interpretable alternative to identity-coupled multislice methods for longitudinal omics data, enabling the discovery of stable network structure and novel candidate regulators in complex autoimmune diseases. This abstract also aligns with our prior RA study in which network community structure was leveraged to prioritize underexplored hub genes via systematic evidence screening [8].

column9: Simulating prosocial content delivery on social media by manipulating algorithms and architecture
column11: Saeed, Mohammad; Broniatowski, David; Simons, Joseph; Gralla, Erica; Suri, Manan; Al-Rashid, Haneen; Ciampaglia, Giovanni Luca*
column12: ms190@email.gwu.edu; broniatowski@gwu.edu; jsimons09@gmail.com; egralla@gwu.edu; manans@umd.edu; haneenr@email.gwu.edu; gciampag@umd.edu*
column13: Due to the astounding ability of social media platforms to disseminate a wide variety of content at scale with little oversight, concerns have grown over their impact in society, especially given their over-reliance on engagement-maximizing algorithms. These concerns have prompted interest in novel governance models and alternative recommendation approaches, however, research in these areas is limited to studying individual platforms, leading to a lack of generalizable knowledge across different platforms and designs. Building on Moses' theory of flexibility in system design, here we develop a generic model of a social media platform that captures two essential characteristics of these designed spaces: the architecture of the network (determining the type of entities and their interactions) and the ranking algorithm (determining the flow of information between interacting entities). We use our generic model to investigate the spread of positive messages on four prototypical platform designs. We find that architectures dominated by algorithmic choices (à la TikTok) show the fastest and widest information spread, while more traditional designs (similar to e.g. Twitter/X, Reddit, or Facebook) spread content more slowly. On top of architectures, the choice of the algorithm further shapes outcomes, with popularity-based rankings amplifying virality and producing long-tail popularity effects. These findings have strong implications for technologists and policymakers, highlighting the interacting nature of two fundamental design components behind social media.

column9: Renormalization and Modularity in Bipartite Networks
column13: Renormalization group techniques provide a powerful framework for analyzing the multiscale architecture of complex networks. In this work, we extend the Laplacian Renormalization Group (LRG) to bipartite networks, leveraging Laplacian diffusion dynamics to define a distance metric that uncovers the network's multiscale structure and modular organization.  We validate the method on Random Bipartite Networks (RBNs), focusing on their critical properties. We construct these networks as a function of the balancing parameter α (alpha), which allows us to tune the ratio between the two node sets. This analysis reveals that while the critical percolation threshold ⟨kc⟩ shifts towards lower values due to the emergence of star-like structures, the critical exponents consistently align with the mean-field isotropic percolation universality class. Notably, we observe a second susceptibility peak at low α, suggesting a potential localization–delocalization transition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the renormalization procedure preserves both the scale-free topology and the spectral properties of the RBNs.  Finally, we apply the framework to real-world datasets, effectively revealing the hierarchical modular organization of empirical bipartite architectures.

column9: Social compensation strategies in response to individual loss in natural populations
column11: Newman, Eloise*; Abraham, Adelaide; Firth, Josh; Knowles, Sarah; Sheldon, Ben
column13: Societies across natural populations can be represented as social networks. Beyond intrinsic drivers such as disease and demography, many species face escalating pressures from climate change and anthropogenic activity, leading to population decline. Individuals adjust their own social position in response to the impact of individual loss on a population. Despite the key role of social structure for various populations, we currently have limited knowledge of how animal social networks compensate for individual loss, which behavioural strategies are used, or how social responses might vary across diverse real-world network structures.   To address this, we draw upon 268 real-world animal networks to simulate different types of individual loss and different mechanisms of compensation responses, to investigate how animal social structures may mitigate against loss of social associates as populations decline. We show that social responses to loss are important, and that the effects of node loss vary depending on whether random, central or peripheral nodes are removed. Our findings show that compensation is important, yet the specific compensation method used within a population may be less important than the existence of compensation strategy. As such, when predicting the impact of population decline on the social structure of natural populations, it would be useful to know the types of individuals that are likely to be lost, and whether the remaining individuals will compensate for loss, but the precise mechanisms of how they compensate may not be entirely necessary. These findings show how comparative analyses of animal social networks can provide fundamental insights into the robustness of real-world networks, with applied implications for population management and biodiversity.

column9: Transformers for network based drug repurposing
column13: Network medicine leverages protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks for disease gene identification and drug repurposing, but these networks are typically unweighted. Transformer models pretrained on single-cell transcriptomes can extract complex gene interaction patterns from large datasets. We investigate whether the learned representations within transformers—specifically their attention weights and gene embeddings—can effectively capture protein interactions and improve network medicine predictions.  We extracted weighted edges from three pretrained models (Geneformer, scFoundation, scBERT) using cosine similarity between gene embeddings and attention weights between gene pairs, constructing weighted PPI networks for evaluation on drug repurposing across 27 diseases.   Weighting PPI networks with transformer attention weights improved drug repurposing accuracy compared to unweighted networks and traditional weighting methods, with consistent improvements across diseases. Our results demonstrate that transformers implicitly learn biologically meaningful gene interactions that enhance graph-based predictions, suggesting a promising integration of deep learning representations with network medicine algorithms for advancing drug discovery.

column9: Explosive synchronization in networks of Type-I neurons with electrical synapses
column13: Explosive or abrupt transitions to synchronization have implications for several brain processes, such as epileptic seizure and switching between conscious states. Such transitions have been studied extensively in the abstract Kuramoto oscillator networks. Although previous studies have reported explosive synchronization (ES) in neuronal networks, they are model-dependent and lack the generality to extend to other neuron models. Our work bridges this gap by demonstrating ES in a class of neurons. We achieve this by establishing ES in the normal form of Type-I neurons — the QIF model, and further affirming it in a Biophysical model exhibiting Type-I behavior - the Morris-Lecar model. The neurons are coupled through electrical synapses and placed on scale-free (SF) and star networks with complete and partial degree-frequency correlation conditions. Our simulations show ES in networks of both QIF and Morris-Lecar neurons, under weak heterogeneity. Leveraging the mapping between Type-I neurons and the Kuramoto model, we realize theoretical predictions of ES for different conditions on neuronal networks. We can realize various scenarios that are known to induce ES in the Kuramoto model on these networks of Type-I neurons.  Thus, this work establishes a set of universal conditions that allows ES to arise in Type-I neurons. The generality of these results across a class of neurons, together with their origin in the Kuramoto framework, takes us a step closer to understanding abrupt transitions in the brain.

column9: Multilayer Network Architecture of Global Politics: Combining Diplomatic Connectivity and Historical Sentiment
column13: ------ SEE ATTACHED PDF ------ Global political structure emerges from multiple, overlapping relational layers, including formal diplomatic ties and his- torical relationships. Here, we construct two global networks spanning all 195 UN sovereign nations: a diplomatic network based on mutual embassy representation and common diplomatic membership, and a historical network derived from sentiment-weighted bilateral mentions in narrative foreign-relations texts - both based of the respective nations Foreign Relations Wiki-page. Under Louvain community detection the diplomatic layer produces fewer, more integrated communities, reflecting the unifying role of formal representation, whereas the historical layer yields a more fragmented partition, consistent with persistent geopolitical divisions encoded in historical sentiment. These partitions are used as reference structures to validate a multilayer integration model defined on a weighted, undirected graph, with edge weights formulated as:  wij = σ(α · Eij + β · (Sij − 0.5)) where: Eij ∈ {0, 1} represents embassy connection. Sij ∈ [0, 1] represents sentiment score (0.5 if no sentiment link exists). σ(x) = 1/(1+e^{−x}) represents the sigmoid function. A systematic grid search over (α, β) reveals a smooth modularity landscape in which the degree of geopolitical division varies predictably with layer dominance. Emphasis on historical sentiment reinforces fragmented community structure, while increasing diplomatic weight collapses these divisions into more unified partitions - concluded on the basis of modularity-measures. All parameter configurations were evaluated across three independent runs with fixed random seed, yielding identical results and demonstrating robustness. Together, these results showcase a quantitative framework for integrating and weighting multiple network layers, enabling the unification of historical and diplomatic relations within a single model that captures contrasting geopolitical structures.

column9: Forecasting Shipping Schedule Network Changes Using Link Prediction
column13: Maritime logistics networks face significant, largely unsolved challenges in predicting vessel schedule changes (such as port omissions and blank sailings) due to the complex interdependencies between ports, vessels, and voyages. Traditional approaches forecast the arrival times of vessels using a combination of historical time-series of vessel positions, speed, and arrival times.This forecast is extrapolated to incorporate any delays to a pre-computed shipping schedule and dependencies between vessels are rarely considered, each vessel voyage pair is assumed to be independent.  In this work, we formulate vessel schedule evolution as a temporal link prediction task utilising windowed historical data to predict changes in vessel itineraries. We model maritime vessel movements as a heterogeneous multi-layer network of edges between ports, voyages, legs and vessels. Each vessel is connected to the voyages it runs on, which are decomposed into multiple legs, linking pairs of ports. This hierarchical representation captures the complex structural and temporal dependencies between 6,697 vessels, 87,041 voyages, and 1,050 port nodes. For prediction, we investigate the effectiveness of three state-of-the-art graph neural network architectures: a Temporal Graph Transformer, a Continuous-Time Graph Neural Network, and a spatially-aware Graph Transformer extended to encode rich temporal edge features across node types. Unlike traditional time-series forecasting methods, our link prediction framework encodes graph structure through message passing and attention mechanisms. By concatenating source and destination embeddings, the models predict the probability of future edge formation.  Our comparative evaluation demonstrates the strengths and trade-offs of each architecture in modelling large-scale, dynamic maritime traffic networks.  This work represents a significant advancement in applying deep learning to maritime operations, providing a foundation for proactive maritime logistics planning.

column9: Characterizing Open-Ended Evolution Through Undecidability Mechanisms in Random Boolean Networks
column11: Lopez-Diaz, Amahury*; Rivera Torres, Pedro Juan; Febres, Gerardo; Gershenson, Carlos
column13: Open-ended evolution (OEE) is the sustained production of novel phenotypes rather than convergence to a fixed repertoire. In finite-state network dynamics, novelty is easily confounded with noise, while asymptotic diagnostics are often computationally intractable. We introduce a simple, substrate-agnostic metric, $\Omega$, that scores a trajectory by the residence-time-weighted contribution of each distinct attractor’s cycle length, rewarding persistent new cyclic phenotypes while penalizing both single-attractor dynamics and fleeting random jumps. Using Random Boolean Networks (RBNs) as a unifying testbed, we compare classical Boolean dynamics with biologically motivated non-classical mechanisms (probabilistic context switching, annealed rule mutation, paraconsistent logic, modal necessary/possible gating, and quantum-inspired superposition/entanglement) under deterministic homogeneous and stochastic heterogeneous updating schemes. As Figure 1 shows, in homogeneous structures PBN stochastic switching dominates in the sparse/near-critical regime, while modal gating supports sustained novelty at higher connectivity. These results suggest that OEE-relevant dynamics in networked regulatory models are promoted not by noise alone, but by structured, state-dependent uncertainty that continually creates new, persistent attractor families, supporting recent theoretical results showing that only self-referential mechanisms enable authentic OEE.

column9: Understanding Urban-Rural Disparities in Mobility Inefficiency for Colombia, Mexico, and India
column11: Iyer, Nandini*; Luca, Massimiliano; Di Clemente, Riccardo
column13: As urbanisation accelerates globally, understanding mobility disparities between urban and rural areas becomes crucial for equitable development. Previous approaches to defining urban-rural boundaries rely on population density thresholds [1] or built environment contiguity [2], yet these static methods fail to capture functional interdependencies between regions. This critical gap leaves policymakers without actionable insights about where and how mobility infrastructure fails to serve rural communities, particularly in Low and Middle-Income Countries where informal employment and multi-purpose trips shape travel patterns differently than in Global North contexts. We address this gap by investigating mobility inefficiency inequalities across Colombia, India, and Mexico using aggregated Location-Based Services data from November-December 2019 [3]. We develop a novel framework that defines urban-rural boundaries through network percolation of mobility patterns rather than static characteristics, capturing functional integration of settlements. Our classification shows strong agreement with established Global Urban Rural Settlement datasets, validating our mobility-based approach. We introduce mobility inefficiency as a metric measuring deviation between actual trip lengths and optimal shortest paths. Importantly, high inefficiency values do not imply poor individual routing choices but reveal aggregated systemic constraints such as congestion, limited infrastructure, geographic barriers, or trip chaining patterns. Our analysis reveals that rural areas consistently exhibit higher mobility inefficiency than urban areas, particularly for longer trips (>5km) and later in the day (Figure 1A visualises the case of Colombia). These disparities only emerge when analysing both trip distance and time of day simultaneously, while aggregate analyses mask important inequalities.   For urban areas, we construct vector fields to analyse transit-efficiency alignment. We calculate public transit accessibility scores combining coverage area (convex hull of transit stops) and stop density from OpenStreetMap data, then create spatial gradient vectors showing how transit access and mobility efficiency vary across neighbouring areas. Our transit metric was validated against General Transit Feed Specification data in Bogotá and Mexico City, showing strong correlations during operational hours. Comparing angular differences between these vector fields reveals four distinct urban patterns, with Colombian cities showing stronger alignment likely due to Bus Rapid Transit systems (Figure 1B). For rural areas, we analyse all rural geohashes within 256km of major cities, linking each to its nearest urban centre. Using OLS regression, we examine how distance from city centre, population, directional orientation (east-west and north-south positioning), and proximity to alternative cities relate to inefficiency. Results reveal context-specific patterns: distance matters in Bogotá, population in New Delhi (Figure 1C), while directional patterns in all three cities align with documented geographic barriers and socioeconomic distributions. Our framework demonstrates that measuring mobility inequality requires both consistent metrics and context-appropriate analytical methods, providing actionable insights for targeted infrastructure investment.

column9: A toolkit to construct synthetic temporal networks in schools
column11: Calmon, Lucille*; Colosi, Elisabetta; Colizza, Vittoria
column13: High-resolution temporal contact networks provide crucial information on the mixing patterns underlying infectious disease transmission in a host population. Publicly available data sets of contacts in school populations have been gathered in few instances [1,2], but remain limited in their collection window, and the school features where data was collected (grade structure, timetable, school size...). Such school features vary by country which have different school systems, timetable organisations, and class sizes, as well as within countries, e.g. depending on urbanity and population density.  Here, we present a toolkit to generate synthetic temporal contact networks in schools of varying size, grade structure, and timetable organisation in order to match school features determined by local (urbanity, population density) and global (countrywide school system) contexts. Our method preserves characteristic features of empirical face-to-face school contacts such as the balance of casual and repeated contacts due to friendships between children [3], the community structure induced by class membership, characterised by increased mixing within class, and between classes of the same grade, the distributions of contact durations, and empirical temporal contact dynamics. This method provides school contact networks of flexible structure which can then be extended longitudinally [3], accounting for a tailored timetable to provide infectious disease model inputs.  This method contributes to a growing toolkit [3,4] allowing modellers to leverage existing temporal network data for tailored infectious disease modelling needs.  [1] Stehlé et al. Plos One (2011) [2] Mastrandrea et al. Plos One (2016) [3] Calmon et al. Plos Comp Bio (2024) [4] Calmon et al. in preparation.

column9: Parallelizing Visibility Graph Construction
column13: The Visibility Graph (VG) is a powerful tool for time series analysis that maps temporal data to complex networks while remaining robust to additive and multiplicative noise. However, VG construction remains a major computational bottleneck in large-scale applications of network science to time series data. The naive algorithm requires O(N^2) time, while state-of-the-art Divide-and-Conquer (DC) and Binary Search Tree (BST) approaches achieve O(N log N) average-case complexity but still exhibit O(N^2) worst-case behavior. Moreover, these methods rely on serial CPU execution, limiting their applicability to massive datasets (N > 10^6).  In this work, we present a high-performance parallel algorithm for constructing Normal Visibility Graphs using General-Purpose Graphics Processing Units (GPGPUs) with CUDA. Our approach modifies the original DC algorithm by incorporating a Sparse Table data structure, enabling constant-time Range Maximum Queries (RMQs). Importantly, the modifed approach has a key subproblem, viz. determination of visibility bounds for all nodes, which can be parallelized efficiently. We implement our GPU accelerated algorithm and further introduce a hybrid task-partitioning strategy that dynamically classifies nodes based on the size of their visibility domains: "small'' tasks are assigned to individual threads, while "large'' tasks are processed using thread blocks with parallel reduction to improve GPU occupancy and load balancing.  We evaluated our implementation against CPU baselines (Naive, DC, and BST) on synthetic datasets including Random Walks, Logistic Maps, and Conway series. The results demonstrate that the proposed GPU-accelerated algorithm achieves atleast an order-of-magnitude speedup, constructing visibility graphs for time series with up to 10^7 points comfortably within our defined experimental window of 15 seconds even on consumer hardware, while CPU-based methods are timed out. This level of scalability enables the application of visibility graph analysis to massive-scale time series data.

column9: The Specialization of Interdisciplinary Innovators in Science and Technology
column13: Interdisciplinary research is widely recognized as essential for science and society, yet our quantitative understanding of who drives such work remains limited. Funding agencies have traditionally emphasized assembling teams of disciplinary specialists, while recent studies point to the importance of individual generalists. Analyzing 52 million publications and 7 million patents, we uncover a striking regularity: the timing of a researcher’s most interdisciplinary work follows a uniform distribution across the career, implying that interdisciplinarity is best understood as a persistent, individual-level trait. Building on this universal pattern, we derive a quantitative index, Λ that captures each researcher’s interdisciplinary specialization. Λ remains stable across careers and fields, is strongly associated with the production of highly interdisciplinary works across team sizes, and sharply predicts the quantity and impact of future interdisciplinary work. Large-scale analyses leveraging Λ further reveal that interdisciplinary output is specialized at the individual level: a small set of high-Λ innovators disproportionately drive boundary-spanning contributions; impact peaks when the interdisciplinarity of work aligns with individual Λ; and collaboration networks exhibit strong homophily in Λ, reinforcing this specialization. Together, these findings demonstrate that interdisciplinarity is not only a collective property of teams but also a measurable, persistent individual trait, offering a new framework for understanding how interdisciplinary knowledge is produced, evaluated, and rewarded.

column9: The influence of preferential mixing assumptions on Monkeypox virus outbreak projections
column11: Rosenblatt, Samuel*; Manuelpillai, Bevin; Mistry, Dina; Vega Yon, George; Miller, Paige; Spicknall, Ian; Clay, Patrick; Pollock, Emily
column12: samfrosenblatt@gmail.com*; bevinmanuelpillai@gmail.com; uqx8@cdc.gov; xrd4@cdc.gov; yub1@cdc.gov; xfu0@cdc.gov; ruq9@cdc.gov; ruu7@cdc.gov
column13: Projections of clade Ib Monkeypox virus outbreaks were generated with a previously developed network-and-agent-based model of transmission via sexual partnerships among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) in select United States counties. The networks represent main, casual, and one-time partners using dynamic exponential random graph models (ERGMs), with partnership formation influenced by age, activity, and role preference. In addition to tracking infection, diagnosis, and vaccination status of the agents, the model also included agents who would never get diagnosed to reflect differences in healthcare access and assumed proportional mixing between men who would or would not seek diagnosis. However, related health behaviors like PrEP use or HIV/STI screening can influence partner selection, and assortativity can generate complex outbreak phenomena like reduced outbreak reach due to clustering. In this study, we evaluate how increasing assortativity between diagnosis-seekers and non-seekers influences short-term Monkeypox virus outbreak projections.  We extended this model to include assortativity by diagnosis-seeking status in the ERGM-based network dynamics, generating a range of scenarios from proportional to highly preferential mixing. We replicated a previous analysis introducing clade Ib cases into a county with a GBMSM population of size 25,800, with varying clade Ib transmissibility: equivalent to clade IIb (“baseline”), 10%, and 20% more transmissible. We simulated each assortativity and transmissibility scenario for 365 days with 10,000 replicates. In the higher transmissibility scenario, outbreak sizes and probability of sustained transmission increased with increasing assortativity until a peak was reached, after which these measures declined (Figure 1). In the lower transmissibility scenario, increasing assortativity relative to proportionate mixing only led to reductions in these measures.  Our results indicate that assortative mixing by healthcare-related behaviors in GBMSM networks can influence outbreak dynamics in potentially in non-monotonic ways. Further research should document how changing assortativity influences features like clustering and infection reservoirs, how these properties scale with population size, and other finite size effects. Incorporating assortativity into future models may improve our projections of possible outbreak trajectories, especially if accompanied by additional data on healthcare-associated mixing patterns in this population.

column9: Hypergraph Representation Improves Cell Clustering in Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Data
column13: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data analysis is often performed using network projections that produce co-expression networks. These network-based algorithms are attractive because regulatory interactions are fundamentally network-based and there are many tools available for downstream analysis. However, most network-based approaches have two major limitations. First, they are typically unipartite and therefore fail to capture higher-order information. Second, scRNA-seq data are often sparse, so most algorithms for constructing unipartite network projections are inefficient and may overestimate co-expression relationships, or may under-utilize the sparsity when clustering (e.g., with cosine distance. To address these limitations, we propose representing scRNA-seq expression data as hypergraphs, which are generalized graphs where a hyperedge can connect more than two vertices. In this context, hypergraph nodes represent cells, and hyperedges represent genes. Each hyperedge connects all cells in which its corresponding gene is actively expressed, indicating the expression of that gene across different cells. The resulting hypergraph can capture higher-order information and appropriately handle varying levels of data sparsity. This representation enables clustering algorithms to leverage higher-order relationships for improved cell-type differentiation.  To distinguish cell types using hypergraph representations of scRNA-seq data, we introduce two novel clustering algorithms: (1) Dual-Importance Preference Hypergraph Walk (DIPHW) and (2) Coexpression and Memory-Integrated Dual-Importance Preference Hypergraph Walk (CoMem-DIPHW) [1]. DIPHW is a new hypergraph-based random walk algorithm that computes cell embeddings by considering the relative importance of genes to cells and cells to genes, incorporating a preference exponent to facilitate clustering. CoMem-DIPHW integrates two unipartite projections, the gene coexpression and cell coexpression networks, along with the cell-gene expression hypergraph derived from single-cell abundance count data into the random walk model. The advantage of CoMem-DIPHW is that it accounts for both local information from single-cell gene expression and global information from pairwise similarity in the two coexpression networks.  We benchmark the performance of our algorithms against established and state-of-the-art deep learning approaches using both real-world and simulated scRNA-seq data. Real-world datasets include cells from human pancreas, mouse pancreas, human brain, and mouse brain tissues. We also use a ground-truth labeled cell-type annotation dataset based on human lung adenocarcinoma cell lines. Quantitative evaluation using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) shows that CoMem-DIPHW consistently outperforms established algorithms and state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms for cell-type clustering. Our proposed algorithms show the greatest improvement on scRNA-seq data with weak modularity. Moreoever, CoMem-DIPHW successfully annotates clusters with biologically relevant cell types. Our results highlight the utility of hypergraph representations in the analysis of scRNA-seq data. Our algorithms are implemented in Python and are available at https://github.com/wanhe13/CoMem-DIPHW.

column9: A Hierarchical Multipartite Graph Approach to Macro-level Analysis of Discourse Networks
column13: Discourse structural analysis has a long history [1] in the linguistic network literature [2]. Network science offers a systematic way to map the complex, often latent structures and interactions within discourse systems. With a system-level perspective on discourse networks, researchers can identify emergent properties, trace generative mechanisms, track discursive shifts (including regime changes and phase transitions), and monitor the evolution of overall structure and configuration—ultimately deepening our understanding of language use. Yet macro-level discourse networks remain largely underexplored. To address this gap, an approach is proposed that synthesizes document–term matrix with hierarchical multipartite graphs using a lexical–frame–actor framework. This approach can be used to evaluate the morphology (in its biological sense) and anatomy of a wide range of discourse networks [3]. In this approach, the discourse’s conceptual boundary is defined by the subject or topic around which the discourse forms, and the temporal boundary is determined by the timing and sequence of actor activity [3]. The top layer is the agent/actor layer, comprising individuals, organizations, and other entities that contribute to the discourse through dialogues, monologues, and polylogues. The middle layer(s) comprise frames—or other units of analysis—selected based on what constitutes a meaningful textual unit along the discourse continuum (e.g., tweets, paragraphs, pages, chapters, books, scenes, responses to questions, article sections). The bottom layer is the lexical layer, operationalized as a projected term co-occurrence graph.  A tripartite graph of X handles posting tourism- and entrepreneurship-related content using the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) hashtag is used to demonstrate the approach proposed in this study. To assess the network at the macro level, the analysis examines the graph’s degree distribution, estimates node fitness and preferential attachment, and slices the system into weekly snapshots using two methods: segregated and aggregated slicing [3]. For each slicing method, five measures are analyzed: graph order, graph size, the power-law degree exponent, structural complexity (defined as the product of normalized entropy and negentropy), and fractal dimension (approximated using the correlation dimension) [4]. Under aggregated slicing, the five measures are analyzed for scaling properties; under segregated slicing, they are examined for long-range dependence (i.e., persistent memory). The results suggest various scaling regimes and a strong memory effect in the network’s configuration, respectively. In addition, multifractal analysis [5] is applied to eight time intervals (every two years, i.e., 104 weeks) to evaluate structural evolution, self-similarity, and configurational complexity within the discourse system. The conceptualization proposed in this study can be applied to a wide range of discourse analyses—traditional or digital—including speeches, interviews, artworks, scientific articles, books, social media posts, and other forms of user-generated content. More broadly, it can be used with any collection of communication artifacts in any multimedia format, provided the content can be rendered as written text or transcribed speech.
