(Eds.). (2016). Towards a theoretical framework for analyzing complex linguistic networks. Berlin: Springer. [3] Khalilzadeh, J., Kromidha, E., & Taheri, B. (2025). Anatomy of a CSR discourse system: Entrepreneurship and tourism domains. Tourism Management, 110, 105195. [4] Moore, J. M., Wang, H., Small, M., Yan, G., Yang, H., & Gu, C. (2023). Correlation dimension in empirical networks. Physical Review E, 107(3), 034310. [5] Xiao, X., Chen, H., & Bogdan, P. (2021). Deciphering the generating rules and functionalities of complex networks. Scientific reports, 11(1), 22964.

column9: Philanthropic Influence of Art Collectors on U.S. Art Museums
column13: Art museum collections evolve through complex social relationships [1]. In particular, art collectors play a key role: their philanthropic donations sustain many museum holdings [2], yet their influence on artists’ institutional careers remains poorly quantified. Here, we compile a large-scale dataset of historical museum acquisitions from 15 major publicly funded art museums in the United States, selected to balance institutional prestige and geographic diversity. We extract artists and collectors names from unstructured text through an AI-human name disambiguation pipeline. The final data comprise 1,341,762 artworks linked to 100,686 artists, 47,123 collectors, and 3,640 organizations. Each artwork in the data includes its acquisition year, title of the artwork, artist name, and name of the collector, who donated or provided resources for the respective museum acquisition. From these data, we map the network of collectors linking artists with museums over time through philanthropic donations. We characterize connectivity in the museum network along two general dimensions: scope and frequency. Scope captures whether connections remain local, concentrated within a single museum, or global, spanning multiple institutions. Frequency captures whether these connections occur one-time, or repeat over time. Together, these dimensions define four connectivity types: local one-time, local repeat, global one-time, and global repeat. Applied jointly to collectors and artists, these dimensions describe how relationships between artists and museums are established and sustained. We find that 20% are local repeat collectors, who act as institutional anchors, supporting 56% of the long-term growth of museum collections. A 69% are one-time donors (local or global) who contribute occasionally with a 12% of total donations. In contrast, 11% are global repeat collectors responsible for 32% of total donations, who emerge as cultural connectors by linking museums and introducing artists into multiple institutional contexts. On the artist side, 75% of artists are distributed in only one museum, whereas 25% of artists achieve global institutional presence. We observe that wider artists’ visibility is closely associated with the giving patterns by global repeat collectors, who enable the circulation of artworks across institutions. Interestingly, global repeat collectors form connections with artists and institutions through mixed selective patterns (Fig. 1a), demonstrating that collectors’ donation choices can significantly influence artists’ institutional career success (Fig. 1b). Collectors’ selective connectivity evidences that they function as bridges, or gatekeepers, for artists’ visibility across institutions, forming or reinforcing the artists-museum connection. Overall, our network-based framework captures fundamental dimensions of collector-mediated connectivity, offering a quantitative lens on how artistic visibility is gained and why artists’ careers diverge within museum systems shaped by philanthropic giving. More broadly, this work points to new ways of turning cultural data into structured knowledge, creating building blocks that can feed into future AI systems, data science tools, and new forms of computational art.

column9: Recurrent visitations expose the paradox of human mobility in the 15-Minute City vision
column11: Zhang, Xiuning*; Poliakov, Alexei; Tenkanen, Henrikki; Arcaute, Elsa
column13: In the transition towards sustainability and equity, proximity-centred planning has been adopted in cities worldwide. Exemplified by the 15-Minute City (15mC), this emerging planning paradigm assumes that proximate amenity provision translates into localised utilisation, yet evidence on actual mobility behaviour remains limited. We advance a behaviourally grounded assessment by introducing the K-Visitation framework, which identifies the minimal set of distinct visitations needed to cover essential amenities under two orderings: one based on observed visitation frequency (K-freq), and the other based on proximity to home (K-dist). Applying it to an 18-month, anonymised mobility data from Finland containing 720 thousand users, we directly compared local mobility potentials with recurrent destination choices, revealing a paradox of human mobility within the 15mC framework. A clear misalignment is observed between proximity and recurrent behaviour, most pronounced in urban cores–areas boast with amenities and traditionally viewed as ideal settings for local living–where residents voluntarily overshoot nearest options, while peripheral routines remain more locally constrained. The paradox further revealed asymmetric functions influences, as compared with everyday amenities, individual travels significantly further for to encounter specialised functions. Furthermore, the social consequences of localism are spatially contingent: increased reliance on local options reduces experienced segregation in central districts but can exacerbate it elsewhere. Our findings stress that proximity is therefore necessary but insufficient for achieving the proximity living ideal; implementation of the 15mC should be behaviourally informed and place-sensitive, coupling abundant local provision of routine needs with access enhancement to specialised amenities to avoid unintended equity trade-offs.

column9: Organizations, teams, and job mobility: A social microdynamics approach inspired by a large US organization
column13: Most of the modeling approaches used to understand organizational worker mobility are highly stylized, using idealizations such as structureless organizations, indistinguishable workers, and a lack of social bonding of the workers. Aided by a decade of precise, temporally resolved data of a large civilian organization of the US Army in which employees can change jobs in a similar way to many private organizations, we introduce a new framework to describe organizations as composites of teams within which individuals perform specific tasks and where social connections develop.   Personnel mobility among teams comes in two forms: members transition between teams on their own (which we characterize as uncoordinated moves) or in groups of team members (labeled as coordinated moves. The first type of move is much more driven by individual agency than the second type, which usually reflects managerial intervention. Here, we focus on uncoordinated moves because they are much more prevalent and can be more clearly connected to individual-level variables. Using this methodology, we track the evolving personnel composition of organizational teams, finding that workers who change jobs are strongly influenced by preferring to reunite with past coworkers.   In this organization, 34% of all uncoordinated moves across temporally stable teams (and 32% of the totality of moves) reunite previous co-workers, percentages that have not been reported and are well-above intuitive expectation. To assess the importance of worker reunions in determining job moves, we define a consistency index y_m, where m is a chosen combination of constraints applied to a random network model of job mobility. We mix constraints in several ways. Comparing the mixtures shows that the most consistent information about job change is provided by reuniting moves. We further find that the greater the time workers spend together or the smaller the team they share both increase their likelihood to reunite, supporting the notion that increased familiarity and trust drives such reunions and that social capital plays a dominant role in the personnel evolution of large organizations. Our study of this organization supports the idea that to correctly forecast job mobility inside large organizations, their teams structure and the social ties formed in those teams play a key role in shaping internal job change.

column9: Graph evolution rules meet communities: assessing global and local patterns in the evolution of dynamic networks
column11: Galdeman, Alessia*; Zignani, Matteo; Gaito, Sabrina
column13: Dynamic networks often exhibit modular structure, yet the mechanisms driving the evolution of their communities remain poorly understood. Graph evolution rules (GERs) capture recurrent local transformations in evolving networks in a data-driven and interpretable way. In this work, we combine GER mining with community detection to analyze network evolution at both global and mesoscopic scales. Using EvoMine and the Leiden algorithm, we derive evolutionary profiles that characterize networks and their communities. Our results show that communities may follow heterogeneous or uniform evolutionary patterns depending on the system, and that structurally connected communities tend to evolve similarly. This approach provides a fine-grained perspective on how local temporal processes shape community evolution.

column9: Community Detection in Labeled Growing Hypergraphs
column13: We consider a model of growing hypergraphs in which in which hyperedges form as noisy copies of prior hyperedges. Our model extends prior work [1] by incorporating binary community node labels. The formation of new edges is affected by homophily with respect to these labels. Unlike standard generative community detection methods which assume that edges form independently conditioned on node labels, our model instead explicitly assumes that new interactions are most likely to arrive between similar nodes which have previously iteracted. This generative model is thus well-suited for community-detection for higher-order data sets collected from systems which may be reasonably believed to exhibit path-dependence, in which which interactions happen in the future are causally influenced by which interactions occurred in the past. This setting is common in many higher-order social and information systems; for example, in a network of scientific collaborations, whether a group of researchers collaborates on a new paper depends strongly on whether or not that same group, or some variant thereof, has collaborated in the past. The community structures which result from this model are very different from those than which would be generated by standard stochastic blockmodel variants.  To perform community detection under this model, we develop a likelihood-based inference method. Due to the computational complexity of computing the likelihood, we develop an approximation based on edge intersection sizes, which we show to have good empirical performance. We perform the maximization via simulated annealing. This approximated likelihood is highly correlated with the true labels of the graph, allowing the maximization of the approximate likelihood to yield an effective approximation of the true labels. The latent-variable structure of this model also allows us to estimate the genealogy of edges, giving an approximate branching process describing the emergence of new interactions represented in the data.  On synthetic data, we find that likelihood maximization in this model can result in much higher-fidelity reconstruction of ground-truth communities than standard methods such as Louvain modularity maximization (Fig. 1(a)-(b)). We also apply our methods to two classes of node-labeled data sets which do not obey standard community detection assumptions: legislate cosponsorship in the US congress (tagged by party aﬀiliation) and co-authorship data from arXiv (tagged by inferred author gender). In sum, our results indicate that methods for community detection in edge-dependent hypergraphs can outperform standard methods for some systems, and suggest future work for modeling and inference in such systems.

column9: Modeling the Effect of Social Contagion in Solar Adoption through Commuter and Socioeconomic Networks
column13: The widespread adoption of residential solar panels is critical for the global energy transition, but its progress is hindered by challenges such as high customer acquisition costs and slowing demand, with a market contraction of 31% in 2024, the first contraction since 2017. While social contagion is known to be a powerful driver of increasing solar adoption, the exact mechanisms within this “peer effect” remain poorly distinguished. Specifically, a gap exists in understanding whether influence spreads primarily through Information Flow – that is, through interaction and connections – or through Socioeconomic Similarity (Homophily), where influence is stronger within groups of more similar socioeconomic characteristics, such as income, race, and education levels.  This study aims to quantitatively distinguish between these two competing mechanisms for solar adoption, hypothesizing that if the principle of homophily – as opposed to information flow – was the dominant mechanism in social contagion for solar adoption, then a network model built on socioeconomic similarity would produce communities with more uniform solar adoption rates and correlate more strongly with real adoption data.  Three networks were created at a U.S. county level to compare adoption: a Socioeconomic Similarity Network connecting geographically proximate counties based on a multi-dimensional Jenson-Shannon Divergence similarity score from socioeconomic profiles; an Information Flow Network from county-to-county commuter flows; and a State-Level Network for a geographic baseline. Then, a static analysis using the Louvain algorithm identified community structures and measured their homogeneity, and then a Susceptible-Infected-Resistant (SIR) epidemiological model was used to test which network structure's diffusion patterns best correlate with the real-world solar adoption data. Rather than designating beta as a global constant, the probability of transmission between two counties is made proportional to the strength of their connection and calculated as:  P(transmission) = base_beta * (edge_weight / max(network_weight).  Static analysis showed that the Socioeconomic Similarity network produced highly homogeneous clusters (lower intra-cluster standard deviation of adoption rates), confirming that adoption concentrates within specific socioeconomic groups. However, dynamic SIR simulations revealed that the Commuter Network was the only model to yield a strong, statistically significant positive correlation with real-world adoption rates, with the Commuter Network having correlation r = 0.18 (p < 0.01) to real-world results while the Socioeconomic Network had correlation r = -0.24.  These findings suggest that while socioeconomic homophily dictates receptivity, information flow via commuter ties drives propagation. Commuter routes act as “weak ties” bridging distinct communities, while socioeconomic similarity represents “strong ties” required for validation. Policy interventions must therefore be hybrid: leveraging high-mobility commuter corridors for broad information dissemination while tailoring incentives to specific socioeconomic peer groups to ensure local uptake.

column9: NetzWerkStatt - NetWorkShop
column13: In a scientific era defined by complex global challenges, the ability to understand networked systems is an underrated fundamental skill. However, network science remains largely absent from primary and secondary school curricula. The project "NetzWerkStatt" makes modern science accessible for schools kids aged 8 to 16 by providing a workshop program designed explicitly for early access to complex systems thinking. The Ludwig Boltzmann Gesellschaft prides itself upon providing "Science for Society", ensuring that network science is not an elite pursuit but a tool for all. The project "NetzWerkStatt" also encompasses this guideline as a principal motivation. "NetzWerkStatt" is a pilot initiative (running February 2026 to December 2027) teaching the students how networks shape our everyday life, our environment and our bodies. We are building three age-appropriate workshops translating complex theories from graph theory, systems biology, and data science into interactive and gamified formats for three distinct groups: primary school (ages 8–9), lower secondary (ages 12–14), and upper secondary (ages 15–16). There is an educational gap which disproportionately affects students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds or those who have a mother thongue other than German, who often have limited or no access to the world of research. The workshops are developed in a cooperation with three Viennese schools and Prof. Beatrice Müller from the KPH Wien/Niederösterreich and designed to be linguistically low-threshold and inclusive. The schools have been chosen to represent a broad spectrum of social realities, including high linguistic diversity and varied socioeconomic backgrounds.\\ One workshop will focus on encouraging girls in the upper grades to pursue MINT (STEM) fields where they still remain underrepresented. Beyond the initial pilot phase, NetzWerkStatt is designed for long-term institutional anchoring. A digital platform will make workshops and materials accessible in the long term and supports sustainable use. This creates a future-oriented educational offering that promotes curiosity, strengthens networked thinking and shows young people that science is for everyone. This project combines scientific excellence, pedagogical expertise and the perspective of a diverse student body. By empowering young people to critically engage with the networked nature of their environment, from social media to biological processes, NetzWerkStatt contributes to a more scientifically literate and equitable society.

column9: Asymmetric Reciprocity in Cortical Networks Is Shaped by Functional Modules and Cytoarchitectonic Gradients
column11: Hadaeghi, Fatemeh*; Atapour, Nafiseh; Majka, Piotr; G. P. Rosa, Marcello ; Hilgetag, Claus C.
column13: Recurrent connectivity in the cerebral cortex is neither random nor symmetric, but instead shows graded asymmetries in reciprocal coupling across cortical areas. Motivated by the no-strong-loop hypothesis and our prior computational work [1], we examine how asymmetric reciprocity is organized in primate cortical networks.  Using weighted inter-areal connectomes from marmoset cortex and data on neuronal distribution [2], we quantified pairwise reciprocity and directional bias while controlling for spatial distance and neuron density. We tested whether asymmetric reciprocity is structured by functional organization, cytoarchitectonic differentiation, or relative neurodevelopmental timing (as indexed by neuron density). Reciprocity and directional asymmetry were analyzed at the area level, and further decomposed into within-module and between-module components.  Reciprocity differed strongly across functional modules and was expressed primarily in between-module interactions, whereas within-module reciprocity was comparable across modules. In contrast, directional asymmetry did not vary systematically across functional modules but was associated with cytoarchitectonic differentiation: more differentiated areas showed more feedforward-like asymmetry and reduced reciprocity. Multiple laminar metrics converged on a shared differentiation axis, and directional asymmetry did not show an independent dependence on this axis after accounting for module identity. Neuron density showed a modest association with directional bias but did not explain additional variance beyond cytoarchitectonic differentiation. Together, these results dissociate reciprocity, which reflects functional modular architecture, from directional asymmetry, which aligns with continuous gradients of cortical differentiation. This dissociation suggests a general network principle balancing recurrent coupling with directional information flow.

column9: The Structure of Spreading in Temporal Networks
column13: Understanding how spreading takes place on a network is important for developing mitigation strategies. In static networks, the outcome of an epidemic spreading process can be predicted through analysis of the underlying network's structure. However, real world epidemics take place on temporal networks, for which such solutions are not readily available. Our solution to this problem is to map temporal networks to temporal event graphs, a static graph representation that encodes the relevant temporal information and enables the use of tools from static network theory.  The temporal event graph [1,2] is constructed by mapping temporal events into nodes and connecting them via links directed forward in time if they represent temporally adjacent event pairs. Weights denoting time difference between events are also assigned to the links of the event graph. The result is a causal directed acyclic graph (DAG), which encodes all time-respecting paths in the network. Since these time respecting paths form the structural backbone for any epidemic process, this means that there exists a unique structure for any spreading process on a temporal network, (see Fig 1). In order to recover these structures, one must prune the unused links from the event graph. The challenge - and opportunity - lies in how one can recover these structures in a manner which is both cost effective and analytically tractable, without explicitly simulating the epidemic process.  For spreading processes with recovery, a weight thresholded event graph can be used to identify the reachable event sets, with waiting-time as a control parameter [3]. We demonstrate that this constrained reachability maps to a reinforcing susceptible-infected-susceptible (rSIS) model, where each contact between two infectious nodes will re-infect an already infected node, thus restarting its recovery clock. This model forms an upper bound for a conventional SIS process in the supercritical regime, while the threshold of these processes map directly on to each other in random directed temporal networks. Crucially, this method allows us to measure the outcome of an epidemic process through analysis of the event graph structure.  This approach to modelling spreading on temporal networks allows us to uncover the interplay between temporal dynamics and static structure in a single analytical framework, paving the way to greater understanding of spreading process on temporal networks.

column9: FORGE: Foundational Optimization Representations from Graph Embeddings
column13:
Combinatorial optimization (CO) problems are fundamental across science and engineering, yet learning-based approaches face critical limitations: they require extensive training data from solving numerous difficult instances, demand dedicated models for each problem distribution and task, and depend on the very solvers they aim to accelerate. These constraints severely limit scalability and generalization to new domains. We therefore introduce 	extsc{Forge}: 	extbf{F}oundational 	extbf{O}ptimization 	extbf{R}epresentations from 	extbf{G}raph 	extbf{E}mbeddings, a framework that addresses these limitations through unsupervised pre-training on diverse mixed-integer programming (MIP) instances. Unlike existing methods, 	extsc{Forge} does not require optimization solvers or optimal solutions during training.  
oindent	extbf{Core Innovation}: 	extsc{Forge} employs a vector-quantized graph autoencoder that learns structural representations at the instance level. Drawing inspiration from foundational models in NLP and computer vision, we introduce two key concepts to optimization: (1) a discrete vocabulary for representing MIP instances through vector quantization, and (2) preservation of global information that traditional GNN approaches fail to capture due to their inherent locality bias.  
oindent	extbf{Evaluation}: We demonstrate 	extsc{Forge}'s versatility in both unsupervised and supervised settings:  egin{itemize}     \item 	extbf{Unsupervised}: 	extsc{Forge} embeddings effectively cluster unseen instances across diverse problem domains and sizes without any task-specific training.     \item 	extbf{Supervised}: A single pre-trained 	extsc{Forge} model can be fine-tuned for multiple downstream tasks using minimal additional data. We evaluate on two distinct tasks: (1) predicting integrality gaps for cut generation, and (2) predicting variable hints for search guidance. Critically, the same pre-trained model with $\approx 3.25$M parameters generalizes across varied problem types and instance sizes. \end{itemize}  
oindent	extbf{Results}: Integrating 	extsc{Forge} predictions into Gurobi, a state-of-the-art commercial solver, consistently reduces primal gaps across both tasks and multiple problem domains. 	extsc{Forge} can also augment existing learning-based methods, improving their performance on instances these methods were specifically trained on but unseen by 	extsc{Forge}.  
oindent	extbf{Contributions}: We provide: (1) a general-purpose foundational model producing multi-level embeddings (instance, variable, and constraint), (2) unsupervised generalization across problem types, (3) supervised adaptability with minimal fine-tuning, (4) improved solver performance through integration, and (5) open-source code, pre-trained weights, and embeddings to foster further research.

column9: Uncovering excitatory and inhibitory associations across nodes via stochastic generalization of Markov chains
column11: Okamoto, Hiroshi*; Yamano, Hiroko; Sakata, Ichiro
column13: Markov chains are widely recognized as a fundamental framework for analysing complex networks. The most representative example is Google’s PageRank algorithm, which evaluates node importance using the stationary distribution of a Markov chain. Similarly, the circulation of goods, services and money in economic networks—such as supply chains, input–output tables and international trade—can be represented as probability flows in Markov chains. Conventional Markov chains converge to a stationary state over time. However, actual circulations, for instance monetary flows in economic networks, are dynamic rather than static. To capture the dynamism of real-world flows, we propose a stochastic generalization of Markov chain (SGMC). We show that SGMC uncovers hidden patterns of associations across nodes at any distance, which are intrinsically related to community structure.

column9: Skill–Technology Dependencies and Wage Premium in a Polarized Labor Market
column11: Jeong, Dawoon*; Hosseinioun, Moh; Youn, Hyejin
column13: Humans have historically applied technologies as extensions of their internal skills to undertake increasingly complex tasks. The literature has studied the consequences of isolated technologies, such as computers or spinning mills, for labor markets. Yet, a systematic examination of how the interdependent organization of human skills and technologies emerges remains scarce. We provide such a systematic perspective by developing a network framework based on empirically derived dependencies between human skills and technologies.  We proceed in two steps. First, using O*NET data, we construct an occupation–skill network (879 occupations and 120 skills) and an occupation–technology network (879 occupations and 172 standardized technology families). To operate based on statistically significant information, we extract the backbone of each network using the disparity filter. This transformation preserves degree ranks on both sides of the network, yielding backbones that retain the distinction between high- versus low-skilled occupations (for example, managers versus plumbers), general versus specialized skills (for example, reading versus programming), and general-purpose versus narrowly applicable technologies (for example, software versus medical devices). Such distinctions are vital for wage analysis. High-skilled occupations, such as Natural Science Managers, earn substantially higher wages than occupations with few skills, such as Amusement Attendants (Figure 1a). Studying the joint distribution of skills and technologies, however, reveals that low-skill occupations compensate for their limited skill capacity through technologies: among these occupations, additional technologies are associated with wage premia up to roughly 25 skills (Figure 1b).  We then construct a skill–technology dependency network by defining directed links between technologies and skills (A to B) based on conditional co-occurrence probabilities P(A given B) across occupations (Figure 1c). When P(A given B) exceeds P(B given A), element A (for example, Physics skill) can be interpreted as a prerequisite for B (for example, Scientific equipment technology). To focus on balanced interdependencies, we construct a human skill–technology network using the minimum of the two directional dependencies (Figure 1d). In this network, skills form a polarized backbone separating cognitive and physical clusters. A small set of general-purpose technologies—such as computers, software, and scientific instruments—bridge distant skill clusters, while most other technologies reside at the periphery of the skill space.  Building on this network, we define the machine reliance of a skill as the share of its outgoing ties to technologies, indicating the fraction of its prerequisites that are technologies rather than other skills. For instance, management of financial resources primarily depends on other skills, while explosive strength has a much higher share of prerequisites that are technologies (Figure 1e). Machine-reliant skills require low levels of education and experience to apply (Figures 1g and 1h) and instead appear to be learned through training (Figure 1i). Aggregating to occupations and weighting by skill importance, higher occupational machine reliance predicts wage premia among jobs with a comparable number of salient skills (Figure 1f).  Such wage premia for low-skilled workers highlight clear policy and decision implications for job polarization and automation, showcasing the utility of our systematic framework that jointly considers applied skills and technologies. The dependency and machine-reliance metrics, for instance, allow the study of how new technologies, including generative AI, may reconfigure the human–technology ecosystem by determining which skills remain central, which are pushed to the periphery, and how pathways into high-value occupations are opened or closed.

column9: Discovering Semi-Private Social Networks: Structural Bias from Private--Private Edge Censoring
column13: Network data are often incomplete; methodological literature shows that how edges go missing can bias structural inference as much as, or more than, the number of missing edges. Some online social networks now exhibit a specific, privacy-driven observation regime when users ``lock'' their accounts: they remain reachable via public neighbors, but the edges among ``private'' users may be unobservable, creating a correlated pattern of missingness that differs from classic random-edge loss and from full actor nonresponse. Related work on mixed public/private profiles emphasizes that privacy can still permit substantial inference from visible structure, motivating a discoverability-oriented perspective on partial observation.  We operationalize network discoverability by comparing two edge-loss mechanisms on a large real-world social network (~10,000 nodes, ~95,000 edges), holding the total number of removed edges fixed at each sparsification level. In a baseline condition, edges are removed uniformly at random. In a privacy-realistic condition, a random subset of nodes is designated private, and only private--private edges are censored, modeling platforms in which private users can still be encountered via public edges, but their mutual edges are hidden. We track local cohesion (global clustering/transitivity), global reachability (giant component size and diameter), degree-distribution shape (power-law exponent), fragmentation (number of connected components), and mesoscale structure (Louvain community count and Newman modularity).  Despite identical edge-loss budgets, the two mechanisms produce sharply different trajectories: random edge removal preserves the degree-shape parameter and delays fragmentation, but rapidly inflates distances within a still-large giant component; privacy-driven censoring accelerates the loss of clustering, increases fragmentation, shrinks the giant component more quickly, and substantially shifts the fitted degree exponent. These results align with prior findings that measurement error and non-random missingness can systematically distort topology and inference. We conclude that discoverability in partially private social networks depends crucially on privacy semantics, not merely missingness rates, and we discuss implications for robust measurement and reconstruction under correlated edge censoring.

column9: Gene Co-expression Network Rewiring Explains Variation in Immune-Mediated Fibrosis in wild Stickleback
column13: Fibrosis is a complex, multigenic phenotype driven by sustained immune activation and tissue remodeling, making it well suited to network-based and machine-learning analyses that capture non-linear gene interactions. Rather than focusing on individual genes, understanding fibrosis requires identifying coordinated transcriptional programs and network structures that differentiate mild and severe outcomes across populations. We integrate head–kidney and liver transcriptomic data with fibrosis severity, parasite infection status, and ecological metadata from wild threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus). Fibrosis was framed as a binary classification problem, enabling systematic comparison of linear and non-linear supervised models, including logistic regression with L1 and L2 regularization, random forests, and gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost). Models were evaluated with and without parasite load to assess robustness to infection-related confounding. XGBoost achieved the highest predictive performance (AUC = 0.748 with parasite load; 0.727 without), demonstrating that gene expression alone captures substantial fibrosis-related signal. Using XGBoost feature importance, we selected the top 50 genes for downstream analysis and resolved gene identities via BLAST alignment and Ensembl orthology mapping. To characterize higher-order organization, we constructed phenotype-specific gene co-expression networks and per- formed differential network analysis, identifying 1,748 statistically significant edges distinguishing high- and low-fibrosis states. Community detection revealed 13 densely connected gene modules, highlighting coordinated network rewiring associated with fibrosis severity. These results show that fibrosis variation in natural populations is governed by structured, gene network dynamics. Newly discovered genes from this analysis can uncover novel gene regulatory dynamics underlying immune responses to inflammatory diseases for various species.

column9: The Extended Community of Diet Culture Around Eating Disorders: A Network Analysis of Reddit Forums
column11: Qiu, Jiaxing*; Levinson, Cheri; Kropko, Jonathan; Henry, Teague; Gates, Alexander
column13: Clinical studies suggest a history of dieting is a known risk factor for eating disorders (ED), yet the relationship between diet culture and ED in online spaces remains underexplored. While ED online communities offer insight into psychological and behavioral experiences about the illness, broader dieting culture---often shaped by restrictive eating norms and body hierarchies---may inadvertently promote disordered behaviors.  We investigate the structural and thematic connections between ED and diet-culture online communities by combining network analyses with large language model (LLM)-assisted topic modeling. We analyzed posts and comments from 12 ED and 105 dieting or body-image forums on Reddit. We constructed two forum-level networks: a semantic similarity network, where edge weights are defined as the average cosine similarity between Sentence-BERT embeddings of posts across forum pairs, and a co-engagement intensity network, where edge weights capture normalized cross-posting and co-commenting activity from shared users based on each forum’s newest posts and associated comments. To identify clusters of forums with dense semantic or behavioral connectivity, we detected communities by optimizing the modularity objective function using the Louvain method, selecting the resolution parameter that maximized modularity. We further quantified between-group connectivity using average edge weight and assessed statistical significance via a resampling-based null model. To interpret these clusters, we examined the prevalence of 13 topics using annotations by advanced LLMs, aggregated into forum-level prevalences.   Results show significantly higher semantic similarity and co-engagement intensity between ED and dieting forums than random topics. The detected community structures on both networks revealed extended communities in which a subset of dieting forums consistently clustered with ED forums. Within these communities, ED and ED-adjacent dieting forums shared elevated discussions of 'nutritional restriction', 'food cravings', 'body dissatisfaction', and 'family or social relationships'. These findings highlight the entanglement of ED and diet culture in online discourse and underscore the need for nuanced public health approaches to monitoring not only ED but general dieting discussions in digital spaces.

column9: Global Supply Chain Resilience and Geopolitical Uncertainty
column13: The ongoing tensions worldwide have generated unprecedented uncertainty and introduced new challenges to the resilience of global supply chains. We study the evolution of a global network of firm-level supplier-customer relationships between July 2024 and July 2025. In particular, we systematically examine the structural properties of the network and measures of its resilience under intensifying geopolitical uncertainty. A novel aspect of our analysis is the use of ``network motifs'' - recurring and statistically significant sub-graphs within networks - as building blocks underpinning notions of resilience (Figure \ref{fig:image} illustrates possible 4-node undirected motifs in the global supply chain network). Rather than focusing on global network characteristics, the concentration of network motifs measures the local robustness of a network and provides a basis to assess how long a network can preserve its geometry to different types of shocks \cite{dey2019network}. Comparing two snapshots of the global supply chain network, we find that global supply chains appear to have become more fragmented and less robust to a variety of shocks. Our results indicate that the global supply chain network has become significantly less robust to various disruptions, especially those targeting firms with the highest connectivity or intermediation effects. We also provide formal statistical methods for the analysis of differences in the robustness properties of supply chain networks.  By integrating network theory with economic analysis, our study presents an alternative and competitive pathway for understanding the resilience of global supply chains. Moving beyond traditional approaches that focus solely on binary relationships, the introduction of network motifs underscores the significance of higher-order interactions in economics. Our results also provide valuable insights for policymakers seeking to mitigate instabilities and build a more resilient economy.

column9: The Diffusion of Causal Language in Social Networks
column13: Causal reasoning plays a central role in human cognition. It facilitates the ability to infer, predict, and manipulate outcomes within the environment, which in turn lays the foundation for a uniquely adaptive decision-making framework that is crucial in navigating complex problem-solving contexts. With the pervasive influence of social media platforms, these online social networks have become critical for disseminating information, shaping public beliefs, and influencing daily life. However, no study has examined the propagation of causal language within social networks. In this work, we analyze the dispersion of messages containing causal language against those without, within the milieu of a large online social network. With the entirety of messages over one complete day on Twitter along with two additional days for validation, and with our validated ensemble method for identifying causal language, our findings reveal that messages with causal language exhibit a more extensive reach than those without. Furthermore, our counterfactual analysis demonstrates that the effect of causal language on information diffusion is truly \textit{causal}. Moreover, our findings indicate that messages incorporating causal language manifest a higher ability to spread to out-groups compared to those without. These novel insights reveal the unique diffusion pattern of causal language within social networks, and suggest a potential to mitigate the echo chamber effect, while causal language could serve as a bridge for diverse perspectives.

column9: Cascade Processes in Directed Hypergraphs and the Architecture of the Chemical Space
column11: Medina, Sofia*; LaRock, Timothy; Lambiotte, Renaud
column13: Directed hypergraphs allow us to capture multi-way interactions, and the development of methodologies on directed hypergraphs is an active area of investigation within network science. In this work, we develop a methodology for the analysis of connectivity in directed hypergraphs with an emphasis on the propagation of local connectivity and influence. This methodology is motivated by the logic of chemical reactions and captures how reactivity amongst nodes and hyperedges flows and accumulates. We note that this methodology may also be applied in general to hypergraphs beyond chemically-derived hypergraphs, in particular those that model system interactions which require specific prerequisite configurations or orderings before influence can propagate. We further introduce graph-theoretic metrics on the nodes and hyperedges of the hypergraph based on the application of our methodology, which unveil key drivers of the hypergraph system. Our metrics develop the reactive capital of nodes and hyperedges in relation to their capacity for production, the ease with which they can be produced, and their general association to other nodes and hyperedges in the directed hypergraph.  As a playground, we extend our investigation to the application of modelling of chemical reactions, capturing the properties of organisation within the chemical space. We compare the results of our methodology, and in particular the metrics derived for nodes and hyperedges, between a chemical reaction dataset and a randomised null model of this data. This analysis illustrates how our method can be applied and also allows us to outline properties of the chemical space and its connectivity.   The method we develop introduces an approach to modelling connectivity in directed hypergraphs, as well as offers a perspective of the organisation and traversal of directed hypergraph systems. Our methodology is a system-wide, exploratory method that captures the growth of possibilities in a system. Our method further quantifies how richly a system can be expanded in its inherent connectivity via selected subsets of nodes or hyperedges and in what depth, breadth, and ordering this can be done.

column9: Untapped Innovation Potential of University Research
column11: Qian, Yifan*; Wang, Binglu; Lin, Zihang; Erkol, Sirag; Wen, Zhe; Gao, Jian; Loffler, Alicia; Jones, Benjamin; Wang, Dashun
column12: yifan.qian1@kellogg.northwestern.edu*; binglu.wang@kellogg.northwestern.edu; zihang.lin@northwestern.edu; sirag.erkol@kellogg.northwestern.edu; zhe.wen@kellogg.northwestern.edu; gaojian@hku.hk; a-loffler@northwestern.edu; bjones@kellogg.northwestern.edu; dashun.wang@kellogg.northwestern.edu
column13: Innovations that advance economic prosperity and human health are regularly rooted in scientific advances that emerge from university research. Yet much of the innovation potential from university research may remain untapped, reflecting frictions in technology transfer that undermine societal progress and the returns on public investment in university research. From a network science perspective, this raises a fundamental question about the structure of the science–technology system: how many potentially valuable connections between research and real-world application exist but remain unrealized? Here we present analyses to quantify, predict, and activate the untapped innovation potential of university research. Methodologically, we combine large-scale datasets, network science, AI models, and randomized controlled trials to test how human–AI partnerships can translate scientific research into new inventions. We conceptualize the university innovation system as a heterogeneous network linking faculty, publications, invention disclosures, patents, and commercialization outcomes. We integrate 23 large-scale datasets from both confidential and public sources—including census-level rosters, publications, disclosures, patents, licenses, and career attributes—to measure the translation of university research into real-world outcomes. These confidential data are obtained through the Bridge initiative, a multi-institutional collaboration with US university Technology Transfer Offices convened by the Northwestern Innovation Institute, which provides record-level visibility into invention disclosures, patenting, licensing, and startup outcomes. This integrated data infrastructure allows us to observe both realized and unrealized nodes and edges in the heterogeneous network connecting science to technology. We find that most faculty never disclose inventions, patent, or generate licenses, even in technology-proximate fields, and that realized innovation outcomes exhibit large disparities by gender, career stage, and institutional rank. However, these disparities are not mirrored in the underlying potential for innovation, as measured by patent–paper linkages and AI-predicted patentability of research. In network terms, many faculty occupy structurally promising positions—producing research strongly connected to downstream invention—yet remain disconnected from commercialization pathways. This gap between innovation potential and innovation realization is both large and structured. We then conduct a pre-registered randomized field experiment using AI models and low-cost human outreach. The intervention more than doubled the rate of new disclosures comparing treatment and control faculty. Overall, this study reframes innovation research to consider not only realized inventions but also those that remained unrealized. By treating innovation as a problem of missing links and edge activation in a heterogeneous network, our results highlight how data-driven identification and targeted intervention can reshape the connectivity of the science–technology system and expand the societal impact of scientific research.

column9: Mapping Innovation: Geometrics of the Adjacent Possible
column13: The adjacent possible captures how new configurations arise from existing components [1], yet its underlying geometry has remained implicit. We argue that this implicit geometry is central to understanding innovation in sociotechnical systems, where recombination occurs within institutions, conventions, and infrastructures accumulated through past collective action, distorting the space of possibilities into regions of differing feasibility and value. Here, we develop a network-based framework that makes this geometry explicit by formalizing the adjacent possible as a recombination network, building on prior views of innovation as recombination search [2]. Within this framework, we conceptualize technological innovation as a network of technology codes, where historically typical assemblies–frequently co-used components–can form dense clusters that compress effective distances, distort shortest paths, and may give rise to curvature in the surrounding possibility space. We operationalize curvature by comparing least-resistance paths between newly combined components, weighted by past co-use, to their expected distances in the absence of typicality (Fig. 1a), capturing sociotechnical inertia as a measurable mesoscopic network property. Using U.S. patent data, we illustrate curvature with Edison’s 1881 electric lighting system, where accumulated precedents compress the adjacent possible and lengthen least-resistance paths relative to expected paths (Fig. 1b); at the inventor level, iconic cases reveal systematic differences in structural contexts, with Edison’s inventions more often observed in high-curvature regions and Tesla’s in flatter regions of the possibility space (Fig. 1c–d). At scale, curvature is consistently associated with innovation outcomes: inventions observed in higher-curvature regions are more likely to be high-impact “hit” patents, defined as those in the top 5% of ten-year forward citations (Fig. 1e), and to exhibit greater market value (Fig. 1f). Together, these findings highlight curvature as a unifying network concept linking typicality, search, and value, offering a network-science perspective on where successful innovations are more likely to be observed, at curved peripheries of institutionalized knowledge.  [1] Kauffman, S. A. (1993). The Origins of Order. Oxford University Press. [2] Fleming, L. (2001). Recombinant uncertainty in technological search. Management Science, 47(1), 117–132.

column9: Balancer: Temporal knowledge graph embedding for novel events reasoning with contrastive learning
column11: Kuang, Zhenyu; Qu, Bo*; Li, Xiang; Li, Cong
column13: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) provide a dynamic framework for analyzing real-world scenarios by integrating a temporal dimension into traditional knowledge graph structures. While the task of extrapolation—predicting future events based on historical sequences—has seen significant advancements, existing models typically rely heavily on historical regularities to forecast behavior. As a result, these models often struggle to predict "novel events," such as unprecedented disasters or emerging human behaviors, which lack established patterns in the historical data. This paper introduces Balancer, a novel TKG reasoning framework designed to ensure accurate prediction of repetitive historical events while significantly enhancing the model's ability to uncover potential novel events.  The Balancer architecture consists of three primary components: a history regularity learning module, a contrastive learning module, and a T-convKB decoder. The history regularity module employs graph attention networks (GAT) to capture structural dependencies and single-gated recurrent units (GRU) to model temporal evolution. To further enrich embeddings, a time information embedding module captures periodic and cumulative features within the dataset, such as cyclical global crises. Central to the model’s success is the supervised contrastive learning module, which learns comparative representations of query vectors to differentiate between historical and novel events. This module trains a binary classifier to generate an auxiliary vector that is integrated directly into the decoding process, ensuring the final prediction is guided by both structural-temporal reasoning and explicit novelty detection. Experimental results on benchmark datasets YAGO, ICEWS14, and ICEWS18 demonstrate Balancer’s superiority, with Hits@1 improvements over baselines of 21.12%, 23.21%, and 51.40%, respectively.

column9: Structurally Equivalent to Truth: A Stochastic Blockmodeling Analysis of Misinformation Publishers in Mainstream Networks
column13: This article examines a critical paradox in the digital media ecosystem: given that misinformation constitutes a minor fraction of online information diets [1], how do specific misinformation publishers achieve a level of legitimacy and engagement that rivals established news organizations? By analyzing the audience co-consumption network of mainstream and misinformation publishers using Stochastic Blockmodeling (SBM), this research reveals that legitimacy derives from structural equivalence rather than media prestige or content resonance. Using a large repository of COVID-19 tweets [2,3], I identify a structural inversion of the media hierarchy. First, contrary to the "echo chamber" hypothesis, high-engagement misinformation publishers are not segregated into distinct communities. Instead, they are structurally equivalent to legitimate news—occupying the same network blocks as major mainstream outlets. Second, displacing the traditional center, the network is anchored by a “Populist Core” and a “Partisan Broadcast Bridge”, where misinformation is fully integrated. In a stark departure from assumptions of elite centrality, prestigious non-conservative outlets constitute a segregated "Elite Mainstream Silo" that is structurally isolated from this new core. Third, negative binomial regressions focusing on misinformation virality find that tweets linking to publishers in integrated core blocks generate significantly higher engagement than those from isolated blocks, adjusting for media and tweet factors. By contrast, misinformation outlets co-located in the "Elite Mainstream Silo" suffer the same viral stagnation as the radical right fringe and the misinformation echo chamber. Ultimately, misinformation succeeds not by operating in the shadows, but by capturing the network’s integrated core, leaving the structurally isolated elite mainstream unable to compete for viral reach.

column9: Identifying disturbances in power grids using reservoir computing
column13: SEE PDF ATTACHED  Power grids are large, complex networks in which generators must remain synchronized to maintain stable energy flow. Disturbances such as generator failures or power surges can quickly escalate into widespread outages if not promptly addressed, as demonstrated by the blackout across Spain and Portugal in April 2025. This project focuses on the identification and characterization of such disturbances using only prior observations of system dynamics. Although various methods exist for detecting these events, accurately identifying and responding to them remains a significant challenge due to the grid's size, speed, complexity, and inherently dynamic behavior.  We model the grid using the second-order Kuramoto model, which captures the coupled dynamics of synchronous generators. To simulate disturbances, we apply sinusoidal functions to the frequency of selected generators, altering the behavior of the network. The Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) 240-bus dataset, provided by NREL, serves as our test system, containing 146 generators and realistic network connectivity. Using reservoir computing, we can identify which generators are disturbed as well as the nature of the disturbances. Reservoir computing is a recurrent neural network based framework consisting of three layers: an input layer, a high-dimensional nonlinear “reservoir,” and a trainable readout layer. In our application, the input is the phase and frequency data from a system of N synchronous generators. The reservoir then transforms this data into a higher-dimensional space, and finally the readout layer is trained to learn a mapping from the reservoir states to the desired output, the underlying disturbances applied to each generator.   Preliminary results demonstrate that our method can successfully identify disturbances in the WECC power grid. Using a delayed control scheme, we can not only identify but also suppress the disturbances. Current efforts focus on testing robustness under limited observability and reflecting realistic operating conditions. This project addresses a pressing challenge in contemporary energy systems through the integration of rigorous modeling, data-driven methods, and realistic test cases. The results not only confirm the feasibility of this approach but also point to numerous avenues for future research, underscoring its potential to make a substantial and enduring impact on the field.

column9: Measuring Gendered Access Costs to the Philosophical Canon via Steiner Trees and Path Analysis
column11: Suda, Towa*; Takedomi, Yuka; Hashimoto, Susumu
column13: Background. The history of philosophy has often been narrated as an intellectual network centered on “Great Men” [1]. Feminist philosophy argues that core values such as reason and universality have been historically constructed around implicitly male subjects, topologically marginalizing female philosophers [2,3]. While recent quantitative studies show that articles about females generally exhibit lower centrality in hyperlink networks [4], philosophy’s intellectual system is uniquely shaped by a privileged core: the “canon.” In this system, what matters is not overall network centrality, but rather connectivity to the privileged core—access to authenticity. This study analyzes gender bias in access to the canon by simulating access through graph structures representing connectivity, using Steiner trees and shortest paths.  Methodology. We constructed a cross-lingual intersection graph using Wikipedia and Wikidata [5], capturing the 1-hop neighborhood of 130 canonical 20th-century philosophers and the lateral connections among them. We ensured cross-lingual comparability by retaining only entities present in four target languages (EN, FR, DE, JA). We model the network as a directed graph and compute two substructures: (1) approximate minimum directed Steiner trees rooted at philosopher nodes to the canonical set, representing the minimal knowledge set required to reach the canon; and (2) unweighted shortest paths. We define a centrality score C(v, l) for a node v regarding a gender label l ∈ {f,m} based on the proportion of shortest paths from gendered sources s ∈ Vl to canonical targets t ∈ T that pass through v.  Results. Contrary to the hypothesis that female philosophers incur higher access costs, our Steiner Tree analysis reveals that connectivity costs are nearly identical between genders across all datasets. Females do not suffer from lower network efficiency; they achieve canonical access through equally efficient but separate subnetworks. However, path composition differs drastically. Shortest paths originating from female philosophers contain other female entities at a rate 3.4 to 4.4 times higher than paths from males (Fig. 1). Permutation tests confirm this homophily is statistically significant (p < 0.01). Ranking analysis further identifies that female engagement is routed through specific hubs (e.g., “Feminism”, “Simone de Beauvoir”) that are peripheral in male paths.  Contribution. By focusing on connectivity to the canon, we elucidate the structural dimension of gender bias. Bias in the history of philosophy manifests not as a disparity in efficiency, but as a structural segregation of pathways. Female philosophers rely on a distinct female genealogy to bridge the topological gap to the canon.  [1] R. Collins. The sociology of philosophies. Belknap Press (1998). [2] M. Le Doeuff. The philosophical imaginary. Stanford Univ. Press (1989). [3] M. E. Waithe. In Methodological reflections on women’s contribution..., Springer (2020). [4] C. Wagner et al. ICWSM ’15, 454–463 (2015). [5] T. Suda, S. Hashimoto, Y. Takedomi. IPSJ Symp. Ser. Jinmoncom, 117–122 (2025).

column9: Rising Dispersion in Country-Level Academic Mobility Rankings from ORCID-Derived Flow Networks
column13: We study whether the global academic mobility system has become more stratified in recent years by constructing country-to-country mobility flow networks from longitudinal affiliation episodes in the ORCID Public Data File (2025 release). From ORCID affiliation transitions, we build directed weighted networks where edge weights represent cross-border mobility volume between countries (country codes normalized via ISO 3166-1 mappings). To quantify structural position in these mobility networks, we compute country scores using SpringRank, a generative, flow-based ranking method for directed networks. We then perform a temporal analysis using centered sliding windows (e.g., 3-year windows centered at each year) to obtain yearly distributions of country SpringRank scores. To summarize system-level inequality, we track the weighted dispersion (weighted standard deviation) of country scores in each window, using total mobility volume as weights.  Across the observation period (2007--2025), we observe a marked increase in score dispersion beginning around 2020, indicating a widening separation between countries that consistently occupy high-ranked positions in global mobility flows and those that remain peripheral. Because the dispersion metric aggregates over all countries, it provides a compact view of system-level stratification beyond individual country trajectories. These findings are consistent with an increasingly uneven mobility landscape, where a smaller set of countries concentrates a growing share of high-rank positions and mobility influence. Our dataset release and end-to-end pipeline enable independent verification and extension of the analysis.

column9: When Complexity Simplifies: The Paradox of More Random, More Tractable
column13: Heterogeneity is intrinsic to real networked systems but fundamentally challenges the classical Master Stability Function (MSF) [1], which relies on identical node dynamics and modal decoupling. When local dynamics vary across nodes, instabilities may emerge without a clear identification of which node is responsible. We introduce a localization-based generalized MSF that restores interpretability in heterogeneous networks. The approach exploits the tendency of Laplacian eigenvectors in large random networks to localize on small subsets of nodes [2, 3]. Each non-uniform mode can then be approximated by a reduced Jacobian governed by the local dynamics of the node on which the eigenvector is concentrated, yielding a heterogeneous MSF that predicts instability onsets while preserving a modal viewpoint. The uniform mode, which is not localized, is treated conservatively by evaluating node-wise Jacobians across the network. Crucially, the framework enables node-level attribution: when a small number of nodes are modified, the heterogeneous MSF identifies which specific node drives the instability. For a simple illustration, we demonstrate this in a heterogeneous Brusselator network, where three perturbed nodes coexist with a large homogeneous background. Although all perturbed nodes contribute to spectral splitting, only one is correctly identified as responsible for the instability, in agreement with direct numerical simulations (Fig. 1).

column9: Universal Subtree-Size Scaling in Hyperbolic Minimum Spanning Trees
column13:
Hyperbolic random graphs provide a geometric model for complex networks with hierarchical organization and scale-free degree statistics. A single parameter $\alpha$, $0.5 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, controls how strongly nodes deviate from a uniform distribution on the hyperbolic disk; varying $\alpha$ changes the degree exponent by reshaping how much mass concentrates near the origin [1]. From such graphs we extract the \emph{hyperbolic minimum spanning tree} (HMST): each node connects to its nearest neighbor with smaller radial coordinate (except the node of minimal radius). The HMST retains the scale-free signature of the ambient network: the CCDF of HMST degrees follows a power law proportional to $k^{-2\alpha}$, hence it is strongly $\alpha$-dependent [2,3].  In contrast, we observe a universality phenomenon: the HMST { f subtree size} distribution is remarkably insensitive to $\alpha$. Across a broad range of $\alpha$ values, the decay exponent stays confined to a narrow interval, approximately $	au\in[1,1.09]$, despite substantial changes in degree heterogeneity. This suggests that while $\alpha$ tunes local connectivity, the hierarchical decomposition induced by the HMST rule is governed by a robust geometric mechanism.  A stochastic geometric description yields an equation for the expected subtree size. Let $S(r)$ denote the expected size of the entire subtree rooted at a node of radius $r$, including the node itself. Each direct child at radius $s>r$ contributes its own expected subtree $S(s)$, giving  egin{equation} S(r)=1+\int_{u=r}^{R} K(r,u)\,S(u)\,du,\qquad K(r,u)=\kappa_{\alpha}\,e^{-r/2}e^{u/2}, \label{eq:Volterra_subtree} \end{equation} which is a linear Volterra equation of the second kind with a separable kernel. Its solution implies an asymptotic power-law tail for the \emph{subtree size distribution}: if $\mathcal{S}$ denotes the (random) subtree size of a uniformly sampled node in the HMST, then $\Pr\{\mathcal{S}>s\}\propto s^{-	au(\alpha)}$ for large $s$, where $	au(\alpha) = \alpha/(\alpha^2-0.5 \alpha+0.5)$ .  Numerical simulations for $\alpha=0.6,0.7,0.8,$ and $0.9$ confirm the theoretical prediction, showing close agreement between measured subtree size distributions and the analytical exponents $	au(\alpha)$. These findings suggest that HMST hierarchies obey a robust, nearly parameter-invariant scaling law, and highlight geometry-derived trees as promising backbones for navigation and robustness studies [3].   igskip {\small

column9: Signed percolation in neuronal-network models
column11: Wang, Annie*; Litwin-Kumar, Ashok; Porter, Mason
column13: Percolation, which was first introduced by Broadbent and Hammersley [5], has been studied widely in diverse applications [3, 4]. One can examine a percolation process to determine when a system is connected in a macroscopic way. Percolation has been generalized to many scenarios, including epidemic spreading on networks [6], urban traffic and transportation [7], and cascading failures in power grids [8]. However, in many physical systems, interactions between sites can either promote or inhibit spread. Signed percolation processes that capture such phenomena are understudied. Due to the existence of negative edge weights, the growth of the giant-cluster size is not monotonic in such processes.  Based on the Watts threshold model [1] and the work of Gleeson et al. [2], we study a two-state model with 0 and 1 as the states of nodes, where 0 stands for being inactive and 1 stands for being active. We suppose that all nodes have the same threshold, and we update each node to be active if the input signal from its neighbors is at least the threshold. If not, we set the state of the node to be inactive. We first study possible phase transitions of our model on a configuration model with a Poisson degree distribution. We choose the edge weights uniformly at random from 1 and −1. We then update the states of nodes asynchronously and observe a very sharp phase transition in the giant-cluster size as we vary the threshold, the Poisson parameter, and the initial fraction of active nodes. To then consider a more realistic model, we examine a stochastic block model with different Gaussian weight distributions within and between its blocks. However, we do not observe any phase transitions.  To gain further insights, we examine our threshold model on tree networks in which the top layer is the root and only the bottom layer has edges with negative weights. We observe oscillations in the giant-cluster size for synchronous state updates but not for asynchronous updates. Our theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that these oscillations depend on the number of active nodes in the bottom few layers, rather than on the number of active layers, which are layers with at least one active node. We also observe these oscillations in the stochastic block model with synchronous updates but not in our configuration model (for both synchronous and asynchronous updates). We never observe such oscillations when we consider asynchronous updates.  With our simulations as a guide, we are working on a theoretical explanation of our observations and how activity propagates from one part of a neuronal network to another. column9: From Large Language Models to Large Communication Models: A Network Architecture for Dyadic and Adaptive Human-AI Interaction
column13: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable fluency, yet they fundamentally lack the prerequisites for communication: they do not maintain an explicit model of their interlocutor, cannot infer pragmatic intent, and operate without temporally coherent experience or internal quality control (Bender & Koller, 2020; Shanahan et al., 2023). In contrast, human communication is inherently dyadic, temporally patterned, and adaptively coordinated (Solomon et al., 2021). We propose a network-communication architecture, the Large Communication Model (LCM), which conceptualizes human-AI dialogue as a coupled, multilayer, adaptive network system. Building on communication theory (Solomon et al., 2021) and cognitive emergence principles (Tyler, 2020), the LCM consists of two interacting network layers:  (1) a User Model Network encoding inferred goals, affective states, and interactional intentions, and (2) an Agent State Network comprising semantic, pragmatic, and experiential nodes.  Edges within and between these networks evolve over time via experience-based updating, implemented through an Experience Store that captures dialogue episodes as temporally ordered subgraphs. This dynamic structure supports iterativity, context renewal, and self-referential reassessment, all properties associated with adaptive cognitive systems (Tyler, 2020). A Communicative Reasoning Layer monitors coherence and alignment across layers by evaluating network-level consistency in turn sequences, sentiment transitions, and intent prediction paths.   We present a proof-of-concept simulation that implements the architectural components via specialized agents. These agents are realized using various AI technologies, including LLMs and Knowledge Graphs. The simulation environment models dynamic communication and validates the system's core functionalities, showing that experience-based updates significantly enhance dialogue quality relative to baseline LLMs, which is in line with evi-dence found in neural systems that long-term memory improves downstream performance (Wang et al., 2023).  Our findings suggest that communicative competence emerges from the interaction of two coupled adaptive network layers whose structure evolves through recurring dyadic exchanges, and which is constantly monitored for quality purposes by a third one, the Communicative Reasoning Layer. This points toward a new generation of AI systems capable of stable, reciprocal, and socially intelligible communication – an important frontier for science and industry working at the forefront of responsible human-AI interaction, or adaptive multilayer systems more generally. column9: Benchmarking hyperbolic network embedders for link prediction
column11: Jankowski, Robert*; Celińska-Kopczyńska, Dorota; Kitsak, Maksim
column13: Link prediction is a fundamental task in network analysis, aiming to infer missing or future edges from incomplete data. Hyperbolic geometry provides a natural latent space for this problem, as it captures both hierarchical organization and degree heterogeneity typical of real networks. We present a unified benchmark of hyperbolic network embedding methods for link prediction, comparing approaches from network science, machine learning, and algorithmic graph theory. Using a common evaluation protocol, we test all methods on synthetic networks from the S1/H2 model and real-world graphs. Our results reveal regime-dependent performance, with different embedders excelling under different levels of clustering, sparsity, and degree heterogeneity.

column9: Identifying Multi-Layer Networks via their Motif Fingerprint
column11: Hövel, Philipp*; Sharma, Deepak; Renz, Matthias
column13: Motif discovery is a powerful approach for quantifying network structure related to functional organization. In this work, we apply a motif-discovery algorithm for network analysis, the Efficient Subgraph Counting Algorithmic PackagE (ESCAPE) [1].  As a case study, the algorithm is applied to the multilayer connectome of Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) [2]. We analyze motifs comprising three, four, and five nodes. The resulting motif occurrence analysis reveals several key findings. First, the high abundance of wedge motifs indicates the widespread presence of shared regulators across different network layers corresponding to distinct molecular entities (neurotransmitters), suggesting conserved regulatory mechanisms. Furthermore, the prevalence of motifs containing closed paths – such as triangles, 4-cycles, and 5-cycles, as well  as their extended variants – provides evidence for the existence of regulatory feedback loops.  To identify statistically significant motifs, we compare the original network with an ensemble of 1,000 random networks that preserve the same number of nodes and links, i.e., the same link  density. For almost all layers and motif classes, we find that motif frequencies cannot be explained by a random network model. Notably, 3-path and 4-path motifs constitute an exception, as they are not statistically significant in the electrical and GABAergic layers and therefore do not adequately characterize these network layers.   In contrast, the frequent occurrence of 4-cycles and diamond motifs across multiple layers indicates recurrent regulatory patterns and interconnected information pathways. Conversely, 4- and 5-clique motifs are comparatively rare, suggesting that fully interconnected regulatory clusters are less prevalent in the network.  The proposed approach can be readily extended in several directions, e.g., to the characterization of significant and insignificant motifs in other empirical networks across diverse domains. While random networks are used here as a reference model, the analysis pipeline readily accommodates alternative network ensembles. In this way, networks derived from empirical data can be fingerprinted and uniquely characterized by their composition of small-scale substructures. column9: Beyond pairwise interactions: Hypergraph and stoichiometry representation improve prediction of gene essentiality and drug targets
column11: Applegarth, Anita*; Klimm, Florian; Toledo, Enrique; Mulnaes, Daniel Liao; Imrie, Fergus; Reinert, Gesine
column12: anita.applegarth@reuben.ox.ac.uk*; f.klimm@gmail.com; enriquetoledo@gmail.com; qdm@novonordisk.com; fergus.imrie@stats.ox.ac.uk; reinert@stats.ox.ac.uk
column13: Biological systems operate through vast webs of higher-order interactions, yet conventional network approaches simplify these complex systems to pairwise graphs, losing important information about multi-way simultaneous relationships. Stable protein complexes consist of multiple proteins physically joined together to function as a complete unit, with stoichiometry ratios (the number of copies of each protein within the complex) traditionally ignored in network representations.   Research by [1] demonstrated that hypergraph degree—the number of complexes in which a protein participates—can be a stronger predictor of gene essentiality than its degree in a pairwise network. Also, their analysis showed that projecting hypergraphs to pairwise graphs can lead to spurious conclusions. Building on this foundation, we constructed hypergraph and pairwise graph representations from the same protein complex data (EMBL-EBI Complex Portal [2], 2266 human complexes, 3394 proteins). In the hypergraph, proteins are nodes and hyperedges represent complete complexes; in the pairwise graph, proteins are nodes with edges connecting any two proteins co-occurring in the same complex. We extracted features at node level for both representations, including custom stoichiometry-based metrics for the hypergraph that quantify copy number relationships within complexes.   Using traditional machine-learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM), we rigorously evaluated predictive performance across different train-test splits for two clinically relevant contexts: gene essentiality and drug target identification. Stoichiometry-based features were both statistically significant and ranked amongst the most important predictive features, aligning with recent findings on the functional significance of stoichiometric balance [3].  Beyond structural fidelity, we show that hypergraphs can encode quantitative relationships such as stoichiometric ratios, transforming them into multidimensional objects capable of representing concurrent or co-dependent biological events. This work hopes to advance both biomedical network science and the trustworthy use of machine learning in systems biology.
