Johnson. “Stoichiometric balance of protein copy numbers is measurable and functionally significant in a protein-protein interaction network for yeast endocytosis”.  PLOS Computational Biology 14.3 (Mar. 2018).

column9: Hyperlink Prediction on Hypergraphs of Text
column11: De Vinco, Daniele; Antelmi, Alessia; Polato, Mirko; Di Pasquale, Valerio; De Maio, Dario; Citro, Tiziano; Spagnuolo, Carmine*
column12: ddevinco@unisa.it; alessia.antelmi@unito.it; mirko.polato@unito.it; vadipasquale@unisa.it; d.demaio16@studenti.unisa.it; tcitro@unisa.it; cspagnuolo@unisa.it*
column13: Hypergraphs are powerful tools for modeling high-order relationships, but most hyperlink prediction methods focus only on structural connectivity and ignore the rich textual information often available on nodes and hyperedges. We address this by proposing a framework for hyperlink prediction on Hypergraphs of Text (HoTs), where both nodes and hyperedges are equipped with textual attributes. Our model combines hypergraph convolutional operators with cross-attention mechanisms to jointly exploit structural and semantic signals, iteratively refining node and hyperedge representations. We (i) formulate the hyperlink prediction problem on HoTs, (ii) introduce a learning framework that integrates structure and text, and (iii) show on four benchmark hypergraph datasets that leveraging textual context substantially improves performance over topology-only baselines, underscoring the value of semantic-aware hypergraph learning.

column9: Robustness of interdependent scele-free onion networks
column13: We present the theoretical analysis of the robustness of interdependent scale-free onion networks, which is the most robust network structure against both random failure and targeted attacks with extremely assortative degree correlation between nearby node connections. The functioning fraction of nodes of interdependent networks at each step of the cascading failure and the final giant component fraction are calculated by numerically solving the exact analytical equations governing the behavior of the system.  Various important quantities such as the critical values of the initial remaining node fraction at which the first-order collapse of the giant components occurs, the critical values of interdependency between the networks at which the first-order (abrupt) collapse of the giant component becomes the second-order (continuous), and the values of the critical exponents are also calculated.

column9: Exploring Contact Patterns Among Students via Social Network Analysis: A Cohort Study in Istanbul, Turkiye
column11: Güçlü, Hasan*; Yaylalı, Emine; Hasanniazi, Tanya
column13: Given the vital role school students play in the transmission of infection, this study delves into the contact patterns based on proximity of a Turkish middle school, a high school, a medical school of a university and a regional directorate of the Ministry National Education analyzing various grades and subunits in separate days using Social Network Analysis (SNA), in Istanbul, Turkiye. [1] We have collected face-to-face contact data by handing the students wireless sensors to wear throughout the deployment days, in order to bridge gaps, by presenting a novel study, in the understanding of different factors impacting social mixing of students and individuals at different settings. [2,3]  In general, it is noticeable that students of the same class tend to have both larger number of proximal contacts and greater duration of interactions compared to students from different classes. What deserves particular attention is that as the grade level goes up, the modularity of the network in each grade decreases, conveying that senior students tend to have more mixed connections across different classes. Additionally, it is also observed that spatially closer classrooms tend to have more interactions with each other, highlighting the importance of physical layout of schools in contact patterns of students. In the regional directorate, the contact patterns resemble any other office settings but it is remarkable that some of the individuals later to be identified as managers and service-staff members tend to create too many but short contacts, which has a crucial role in transmission of infections as well as in parameterizing the models of infection. [4]  These findings along with social contact statistics are highly relevant and significant to be considered in infectious disease transmission models; thus, they are useful in designing interventions in schools and institutions to be implemented during pandemics. Our study contributes to the literature with more detailed quantitative metrics of social interactions with fine-grained collected data diverging from conventional methods such as surveys and diaries that were previously employed. column9: Using Spatial Networks to Encode the Geometry of Deep Learning-based Black Hole Accretion Simulations
column11: Tan, Chester*; Bös, Cedric; Fromm, Christian; Scholtes, Ingo
column13:
General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations are fundamental for interpreting horizon-scale images of supermassive black holes, such as those captured by the Event Horizon Telescope [0]. However, these simulations, performed by codes like the Black Hole Accretion Code (BHAC) [1], are computationally intensive, often requiring millions of CPU hours to resolve the complex dynamics of the accreted plasma and magnetic fields. A significant barrier to developing fast neural surrogates for these systems is the complex geometry of the data: BHAC employs block-based Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) [2] to dynamically concentrate resolution where needed, resulting in highly irregular, non-Euclidean data structures that defy standard grid-based deep learning approaches.  We describe ongoing work to bridge this gap by fundamentally treating the simulation domain as a spatial network, which represents the irregular AMR mesh points as nodes in a network, This network representation allows us to use the Geometry-Informed Neural Operator (GINO) [3], an architecture that utilizes Graph Neural Operators (GNO) to perform kernel integration via message passing within local neighborhoods (Figure 1). This network-based encoding allows the model to process BHAC's native adaptive grids directly, maintaining discretization invariance -- the ability to learn the underlying solution operator independent of the specific mesh resolution. The GNO encoder transforms the physical network into a latent regular grid where efficient Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) compute global interactions, before a graph-based decoder projects the solution back onto the target geometry. We demonstrate the suitability of this network-centric approach for learning the temporal evolution of black hole accretion flows, offering a path toward accelerating parameter space exploration by orders of magnitude compared to traditional numerical solvers.   igskip {\small

column9: Absence-aware surprisal for interpretable anomaly detection in temporal networked systems
column13: A central challenge in networked complex systems lies in analyzing high-dimensional temporal data, where the number of measured variables (nodes, features, or layers) vastly exceeds available samples. This is common in temporal and multilayer networks~\cite{multi}, where the ambient space grows exponentially while observations grow only polynomially, leading to sparsity and the breakdown of classical asymptotic guarantees~\cite{wainwright2019high}.  Quantitative analysis of complex and networked systems typically assumes that meaningful patterns arise from correlations among present features alone. This overlooks a critical insight: structure emerges not only from what is present, but also from patterns of absence. When expected patterns are missing in a specific datum, this carries diagnostic information that most methods ignore. We term these absent population-prevalent elements \textit{missing commonalities (MCs)}.   \textbf{Learning via Surprisability (LvS)} is an absence-aware surprisal method designed to identify MCs~\cite{mokryn2025interpretable}. LvS operates on data where each time bin or datum is a discrete probability distribution over features. In temporal networks, each bin can be viewed as a distribution over node, edge, or motif features, so LvS defines an interpretable transformation of dynamics on/of the network into surprisal-based profiles. First, LvS constructs a population-wide reference model (a ``timeline center’’) over all features. Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) then quantifies how much each time bin’s state deviates from this expected network state and remains well defined even under extreme sparsity. Crucially, JSD decomposes per feature, allowing LvS to attribute divergence to specific overrepresented or missing elements and to construct a compact surprisal signature for each time bin.   \noindent\textbf{Empirical results on temporal networked systems.} On the SWaT industrial control system, a water‑treatment sensor–actuator network with 450{,}000 time‑stamped records, LvS clearly outperforms standard unsupervised detectors such as Isolation Forest, LOF, LSTM, and an autoencoder in AUC while offering competitive $F_1$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:swat}). Beyond performance, LvS provides interpretable, feature‑level explanations of attacks on the network by highlighting unusual activations and missing commonalities in the evolving system state. Additional experiments on global mortality and historical text, viewed as temporal population and communication networks, indicate that absence‑aware surprisal profiles generalize across domains, enabling interpretable anomaly detection and change‑point discovery in high‑dimensional temporal networks.

column9: From Hub Amplification to Periphery Dominance: Regime Shifts Under Trust–Uncertainty Gated Networks
column11: Masoumi, Razieh*; Lin, Yuru; Biswas, Ahana
column13: Authors/Affiliation Razieh Masoumi, Ahana Biswas, and Yuru Lin School of Computing and Information, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, USA  Abstract In this work, we model collective belief evolution under simulated radicalization in social networks where trust and distrust toward the same source can coexist. Going beyond influence mechanisms based solely on reinforcing trust, we formalize this ambivalence—trust in information/competence alongside distrust in motives—which reveals a pathway to polarization and extremism that standard opinion-dynamics models miss, since distrust is not simply a lack of trust (Zhang et al., 2022).  We introduce Gated Network Credence, a network-dynamics framework for belief evolution. Each directed tie maps coexisting trust and distrust to net trust and uncertainty, capturing willingness to rely on a source and tolerance for contradictions between trust and distrust as distinct drivers of social influence. Dual thresholds on net trust and uncertainty gate social influence, yielding a directed, nonsymmetric influence graph whose belief evolution follows continuous-time Laplacian consensus. We show that multiple zero eigenvalues indicate fragmentation, and that the left nullspace determines which nodes dominate the final belief, linking network filtering to long-run outcomes via spectral structure.  To test belief evolution across radicalization scenarios, we vary four empirically grounded mechanisms: trust–distrust coupling (rho; co-variation of trust and distrust on ties), prestige bias (p_s; trust toward highly connected nodes), promoter prevalence (x; fraction of high-degree nodes that promote a belief), and polarization degree (psi; initial belief gap between communities). We study these mechanisms across Erdős–Rényi, Barabási–Albert, and modular networks, and across three trust datasets: Bitcoin-OTC reputation, Wikipedia voting, and a political actor network derived from U.S. legislators’ ideology and interactions on X.  Exploring the trust–uncertainty threshold space (T_T, U_T) identifies three credence regimes characterized by trust propensity (Open vs. Guarded) and uncertainty screening strictness (Rigid vs. Fluid). Regimes F (Guarded–Fluid) and G (Open–Rigid) yield sharply different radicalization outcomes. Under regime F, promoter prevalence and prestige bias push influence toward the promoted belief values; stronger hub structure amplifies radicalization, weaker coupling further increases hub dominance, and modularity limits but does not reverse this effect. In contrast, under regime G, strict uncertainty screening prunes hub-supporting ties and shifts dominance to the periphery; modular networks are more resistant than other topologies. Results for Bitcoin-OTC and Wikipedia match these patterns. The political actor network is richer: ideology scores and interactions yield net trust, uncertainty, and polarization. Party-varying prestige bias and promoter prevalence reproduce the regime contrast: under regime F, hubs dominate; under regime G, influence shifts to non-hubs in the targeted community, even when the promoted belief comes from the opposing party.  Overall, our results show that belief formation depends not only on extremists, prestige, or topology, but also on how influence is gated. Trust and uncertainty thresholds induce distinct credence regimes with sharply different outcomes, and their spectral structure reveals how topology amplifies or constrains polarization and radicalization.

column9: Beyond Retweets: Contrasting User–User and User–Content in Bow-Tie Decomposition
column11: Guarino, Stefano; Mounin, Ayoub; Caldarelli, Guido; Saracco, Fabio*
column13: Most research on online social media focuses on interactions among users, with limited attention on the interactions between users and content. Indeed, ignoring content popularity when studying user interactions may lead to misleading conclusions: viral posts are far less informative than “standard” ones, since their diffusion does not necessarily reflect users’ preferences but rather the dynamics of virality itself. In this paper, we compare the insights coming when online debates on X/Twitter are described either considering only user–user interactions or including user–content interactions. Our main focus is the statistical significance of the bow-tie decomposition of the retweet network. The bow-tie decompositionof directed networks was first introduced by Broder et al. to describe the structure of the early WWW [1].  In Ref. [2], it was shown that in nearly all discursive communities across online debates in different languages, bow-tie structures are both informative (i.e. involving almost all accounts) and statistically significant (i.e. not simply due to random noise). We analyse three Italian political debates on X/Twitter collected in 2022. We compare results obtained studying the retweet network, i.e. a directed network of reposting where nodes represent accounts, and the user–content bipartite network. Using these two frameworks, we evaluate the statistical significance of quantities involved in the bow-tie decomposition. As a benchmark, we rely on maximum-entropy null models for complex networks, which have proven versatile in many contexts [3]. Our results show that in several relevant cases, significance patterns are reversed: quantities that are significantly larger than expected in one representation are significantly smaller in the other. This finding has several non-trivial implications. Among the most relevant ones, the statistical significance of bow-tie components depends on the chosen representation, meaning that interpretation hinges on the interaction type under consideration. Since social platforms inherently involve both user–user and user–content dynamics, neglecting either dimension risks producing a distorted view.  References [1] Andrei Broder et al., Computer Networks (2000). [2] Mattia Mattei et al., Scientific Reports 2022 12:1 (2022). [3] Giulio Cimini et al., Nature Reviews Physics (2019).

column9: Embracing the geometric and topological natures of spatial networks via incomplete linking
column13: Many networks in nature and engineering are not abstract graphs but physical, spatially embedded structures, such as roads, vessels, fibers, and conduits, whose function depends jointly on geometry and topology. Over recent years, a growing body of work has begun to address edge-level organization by examining relationships between cycles, loops, or higher-order connectivity patterns, which naturally capture how edges interact beyond pairwise adjacency. In particular, Kramer and Modes [1] have developed the ensnarlment operator to characterize the complexity of unraveling two spatial networks via the linking number between the cycle bases. However, identifying cycle bases is computationally demanding, and more critically, real-world spatial networks are often incompletely observed, leading to a research gap in characterizing the edge-level information in spatial networks.   To address this gap, we propose an operator that directly quantifies incomplete linking between edges, bypassing explicit cycle enumeration while maintaining computational efficiency by simplifying the edges to line segments. One distinctive feature of the proposed operator is that it naturally takes both positive and negative values, reflecting the relative orientation of edges in space. This property situates our framework at the intersection of spatial and signed network analysis [2], opening a new avenue for studying spatial organization through the lens of edge polarity. We show that, despite the orientation dependence at the local level, the operator’s eigenvalues constitute intrinsic characteristics of the spatial network and remain invariant under changes in edge orientation. Building on this structure, we introduce an associated unbalance score that provides a principled and interpretable measure of edge-level complexity in spatial networks. Finally, by performing signed bi-clustering on the operator, we identify patterns of intrinsic negative linking that reveal distinct functional roles played by edges within the spatial network. We validate our framework on both synthetic regular lattices and real spatial networks, specifically the mouse brain vasculature. Our findings are further supported by biological interpretations and validations.   [1] F. Kramer, and C. Modes. (2023). Ensnarled: Topological linkage of spatially embedded network pairs. Physical Review Research, 5(3), 033203. [2] Y. Tian, and R. Lambiotte. (2024). Spreading and Structural Balance on Signed Networks. SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems 2024 23:1, 50-80. [3] J. Paetzold,  J. McGinnis, S. Shit, I. Ezhov, P. Büschl, C. Prabhakar, ... and S. Günnemann. (2021). Whole brain vessel graphs: A dataset and benchmark for graph learning and neuroscience. In 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

column9: Revisiting fractional stochastic processes through the lens of spreading processes on networks
column13: Motivated by empirical observations of epidemic dynamics, where infection and recovery times rarely follow exponential patterns, we aim to develop a theory that extends Markov processes beyond the memoryless assumption.  To incorporate memory effects into Markovian stochastic processes, we replace the standard differential operator in the governing equations with the Caputo fractional derivative, a generalization of the standard derivative to non-integer orders that intrinsically accounts for memory by integrating over the system’s past states. This leads to fractional stochastic processes, which are governed by the (dimensionless) fractional state equation whose solution can be expressed in terms of the so-called Mittag-Leffler function.   We apply the fractional state equation to generalize Markovian spreading processes on networks, aiming to deepen the understanding of the "physics” of fractional stochastic dynamics and to extend classical Markov theory beyond its memoryless limitation. We propose three complementary approaches to construct and interpret fractional stochastic processes in the context of epidemic spreading on complex networks.  We first derive the conditions under which fractional stochastic processes satisfy the semi-Markov property, meaning that the system’s memory resets each time the viral state of the network updates. This description introduces statistical dependencies among all nodal and link processes competing in the system.  Second, we introduce a time inhomogeneous Markovian description of fractional stochastic processes. Applied to epidemic dynamics, this framework reveals that memory effects manifest as time-varying transition rates with power-law behaviors.  Third, we introduce a stochastic time transformation that defines any fractional semi-Markov process as a time-transformed Markov process. We develop a deterministic approximation of this transformation and test it through the exact numerical solution of a fractional susceptible–infected–susceptible (SIS) process on various network topologies.

column9: Chromatin structure-function relationships revealed by network approaches to 4D epigenome organisation
column11: Aliaga, Benoit; Raynal, Flavien; Pancaldi, Vera*
column13: Recent technological advances have allowed us to map chromatin conformation and uncover the spatial organization of the genome inside the nucleus. These experiments have revealed the complexities of genome folding, characterized by the presence of loops and domains at different scales which can change across development and in different cell types. There is strong evidence for a relationship between the topological properties of chromatin contacts and cellular phenotype. Chromatin can be represented as a network, in which genomic fragments are the nodes and connections represent experimentally observed spatial proximity of two genomically distant regions in a specific cell type or biological condition. With this approach we can consider a variety of chromatin features in association with the 3D structure, investigating how nuclear chromatin organization can be related to gene regulation, replication, malignancy, phenotypic variability and plasticity.  We briefly review the results obtained on genome architecture through network theoretic approaches. As previously observed in protein-protein interaction networks and many types of non-biological networks, external conditions could shape network topology through a yet unidentified structure-function relationship.   One of the applications we have worked on involved studying the organisation of genes in the 3D nucleus according to their evolutionary age. Cancer cells are highly plastic, allowing them to adapt to various environmental conditions. Genes related to basic cellular processes evolved in ancient species, while more specialized genes appeared later with multicellularity (metazoan genes) or even after mammals evolved. Transcriptomic analyses have shown that ancient genes are typically up-regulated in cancer, while metazoan-origin genes are often inactivated. Oncogenesis is characterized by alterations in chromatin organization and the reactivation of unicellular phenotypes at both metabolic and transcriptional levels.   We have studied the assortativity of genes of different ages in the 3D chromatin networks of different cell types assessed by promoter-centred chromatin conformation capture.  Our findings reveal significant topological changes in chromatin organization during cell differentiation, with specific patterns involving Polycomb repression and RNA Polymerase II pausing, being reversed during oncogenesis. Going beyond the non-random organization of genes and chromatin features in the 3D epigenome, we suggest that these patterns lead to preferential interactions among ancient, intermediate, and recent genes, mediated by RNA Polymerase II, Polycomb complexes, and nuclear lamina, respectively.  We will present our perspective on the broad and insightful application of network theory in 4D genomics capturing 3D organisation across time.

column9: Logic‐Conditioned Reasoning Networks for Human and AI‐Assisted Legal Judgment
column13: Despite growing adoption of large language models in legal research and decision support, recent surveys note that uncertainty handling in these systems remains fragmented, with techniques addressing hallucination, calibration, or refusal being piecemeal and not relying on a foundational approach to addressing conflicting evidence and indeterminacy — an especially salient limitation in adversarial legal contexts.  We introduce a logic‐conditioned reasoning network framework for analyzing how both humans and AI systems reason under legal uncertainty. Rather than evaluating outcomes alone, the framework models legal judgment as structured inference over shared evidence–claim–rule graphs, enabling direct comparison of representational regimes. We empirically examine four logical prompting styles—classical, fuzzy, intuitionistic, and neutrosophic—within a within‐subject, randomized‐order design, encoding participant responses as logic‐specific node signals, edge weights, and proof subgraphs. This approach reveals how different logics redistribute uncertainty, conflict, and abstention across the same evidentiary structure. We hypothesize that classical prompting induces forced commitment and overconfidence; fuzzy prompting improves calibration but compresses contradiction; intuitionistic prompting enforces warrant discipline and principled abstention; and neutrosophic prompting best preserves simultaneous support, refutation, and indeterminacy.  Legal vignettes are represented by a fixed reasoning scaffold network. The nodes represent evidence (E), claims (C), inference rules (R), and decisions (D). The edges represent support or rebuttal (signed, directed), rule application (directed), and evidentiary consistency or contradiction (signed). Law school students form cohorts, and in turn, participants evaluate each vignette multiple times under different logical prompts, with order randomized and temporal spacing introduced to reduce anchoring. Cohort‐level networks are obtained by aggregating participant edge weights and variances. Structural coherence and conflict are analyzed using unsigned and signed Laplacians, spectral band power, and proof‐subgraph efficiency.   Furthermore, our spectral analysis experiments on small evidence-claim-rule graphs demonstrate that spectral methods can robustly differentiate the structural effects of classical, fuzzy, intuitionistic, and neutrosophic logic-conditioned edge weightings. Notably, the presence of negative eigenvalues in intuitionistic and neutrosophic Laplacians reveals richer, non-classical network structures induced by these logics, which classical and fuzzy approaches do not capture. These findings support the viability of spectral analysis as a quantitative tool to compare and evaluate logic-conditioned reasoning networks, even at small scales. This robustness provides a promising foundation for integrating such spectral insights into LLM thinking modes to enhance conflict resolution, uncertainty representation, and principled abstention. This new thinking mode could enable LLMs to systematically compare outputs from multiple logical regimes and present answers labeled along a risk spectrum from risk-averse to risk-tolerant with regard to statements of conviction. This would facilitate more transparent, context-sensitive, and ethically aligned decision-making strategies in AI-assisted legal judgment and beyond.

column9: Dynamics of Defensive and Malicious Worm Co-Propagation across Networked Systems
column13: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has vastly increased the attack surface of networked systems. In response to the persistent threat of self-propagating malware (``black worms''), it has been proposed the use of ``white worms'' as a countermeasure. These worms would be benign, self-replicating programs that traverse networks to notify owners, facilitate patching, and secure devices autonomously. This idea raises a central tension for cyberdefense: the more a defensive agent respects ethical constraints on autonomy and system modification, the less effective it may become at suppressing malicious activity. This work formalizes that trade-off and quantifies its consequences.  We develop a co-propagation model for a malicious worm and an ethically designed white worm within a network epidemiology framework. Under the homogeneous mixing approximation, we derive closed-form expressions for basic reproduction numbers and obtain analytical thresholds for botnet emergence. We then study spreading on networks with various topologies, showing that structure decisively shapes outcomes. In heterogeneous networks, the malicious worm’s advantage on high-degree nodes increases the burden on the defender. For the same ethical and kinetic parameters, botnets are larger and longer-lived than in homogeneous topologies. Conversely, when white worms can reach hubs early and activate promptly, they substantially reduce botnet prevalence and shorten the time the botnet remains above operationally relevant size thresholds.  Taken together, the results reveal a fundamental design dilemma as effective autonomous defense requires degrees of initiative and willingness to modify systems that challenge the ethical premise of minimally invasive agents. Our framework makes this tension explicit by tying macroscopic security outcomes to interpretable behavioral parameters (owner responsiveness and defender autonomy) and to measurable properties of network structure.

column9: Mechanistic interplay between information spreading and opinion polarization
column11: Andrade Oliveira, Kleber*; Ferraz de Arruda, Henrique; Moreno, Yamir
column13: The model introduced by de Arruda et al. provides a rich testbed for simulating opinion dynamics in social media. In it, each user has a continuous opinion between -1 and 1, which is incrementally influenced by the content received from their connections. A distinctive feature is that ihe model rewires the underlying network based on the opinion difference between neighbors, allowing a range of opinions (from consensus to polarization) and networks. However, the model assumes that a new post with a random opinion value is generated at each iteration. Here we extend this model on adaptive networks to feature information-spreading mechanisms. We embed into each user a memory list, and a probability at each iteration that the active user, instead of creating a new post, shares a previous post stored in their memory list. We control it with a parameter µ such that µ = 1 (no reposting) recovers the original model. Otherwise, when posts can be reposted (µ < 1), iterations can use the same opinion value multiple times. The new parameter may drive the system into polarization or consensus when all other parameters are fixed. Additionally, we calibrate the model against data by focusing on empirical cascade size distribution from Twitter datasets. Then, we run a genetic algorithm to find which parameters minimize the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the empirical cascade size distribution and that from simulations. We show that even when our optimization target punishes the tail of the cascade size distribution in favor of non-extreme values, the model reasonably agrees with the data. Our formulation opens a new dimension to characterize echo chambers as a transient configuration of the system resulting from competition between posts rather than a steady state. It paves the way for a mechanistic formulation of how it is possible that social media users remain polarized even when opinion-conflicting content is not restricted.

column9: Spatial regionalization of multivariate data based on optimal information compression
column13: Regionalization seeks to delineate the spatial areas into contiguous and homogeneous regimes based on shared characteristics. However, existing methods often depend on user-defined parameters or are restricted to single attributes, failing to capture the complex interdependence among socioeconomic variables. To address this, we propose a nonparametric, information-based framework that extends regionalization to multiple attributes using the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. Instead of treating each attribute independently (decoupled covariates), our method incorporates microdata of coupled covariates (e.g., joint counts of race and income) to exploit the correlation between attributes for improved data compression. Synthetic tests indicate that the coupled method robustly recovers ground-truth partitions in regimes where decoupled approaches fail. To further demonstrate the practical utility, we also apply our method to the U.S. Northeast megalopolis, results show that the coupled attributes reveal more granular and meaningful spatial regimes than the decoupled method while also achieves better data compression.

column9: Fractional degree centrality for directed networks
column11: Lee, Kang-Ju*; Lee, Ki-Ahm; Kook, Woong; Lee, Taehun
column13: Degree centrality is one of the most fundamental measures of local importance in directed networks. Its fractional version is defined via a fractional directed Laplacian with parameter $\gamma$, which is a representative nonlocal operator. When $\gamma=1$, the fractional centrality reduces to the classical directed degree centrality. As it strikingly contrasts with undirected networks, where the local aspect predominantly remains across variations $\gamma$, we elucidate that its intriguing behavior in directed networks reflects the influence of global effects in addition to local contributions. We first show that for $\gamma=0$, the fractional centrality is expressed in terms of rooted spanning trees, thereby reflecting global influences. Through experiments on both real-world complex networks and random network models, we demonstrate the transition of fractional centrality from a local measure to a global one as $\gamma$ decreases from $1$ to $0$. These results establish fractional centrality as a unifying framework that integrates local and global influences in directed networks.

column9: Nonparametric regionalization of spatial time series data
column13: Regionalization aims to partition a spatial domain into contiguous regions that share similar characteristics. It helps us understand and manage large areas, for example in environmental planning, climate zoning, and defining socio-economic or ecological regions. Existing approaches typically rely on static spatial snapshots rather than evolving time series. Meanwhile, most time series clustering methods ignore spatial structure or only enforce spatial continuity through ad hoc regularization, and often require the number of regions to be chosen a priori. In this work we propose a nonparametric framework for regionalizing spatial time series based on the minimum description length (MDL) principle. Spatial locations are modeled as nodes in an adjacency network, where edges represent geographic proximity. The method performs a fast greedy agglomerative merge process, with runtime complexity on the order of O(N logN) for N nodes, to jointly identify a spatial partition and a set of representative driver patterns that minimize the total code length required to encode all time series. We demonstrate on noisy synthetic data that the method accurately recovers the planted regional structure and driver series, and can extract meaningful structure from real environmental and geographical time series, including discrete air-quality indices and continuous vegetation index records. Overall, the method provides a principled and efficient framework that yields spatially contiguous regions with interpretable temporal patterns, allowing natural regions to emerge directly from the data itself.

column9: How Degree-Dependent Interactions Reshape Hub Survival in Ecological Networks
column11: Lee, Hae Seong*; Lee, Deok-Sun; Lee, Sang Hoon; Suweis, Samir; Park, Hye Jin
column13: The population dynamics of ecological systems with complex structures are often studied using the generalized random Lotka-Volterra model. Previous studies have highlighted the crucial role of hubs in biodiversity. However, this strong influence may primarily result from their large number of connections, as these studies often assume that interaction strengths are uniform across the network.  In real ecological systems, however, interaction strengths often correlate with a species' degree (the number of species it interacts with). In this study, we introduce degree-dependent interaction strengths into the generalized random Lotka-Volterra model and investigate how this variation shapes biodiversity.   In our model, we assume that the interaction strengths are independent random variables that follow a Gaussian distribution whose mean and variance depend on the degrees of interaction species. Specifically, the mean interaction strength that species i exerts on species j is proportional to (k_i^\alpha) times (k_j^\beta), where k_i and k_j are the degrees of species i and j. The exponents $\alpha$ and $\beta$ regulate the influence of hubs in the system. We find that according to the values of alpha, the \alpha-\beta plane is divided into the hub-dominating phase and the hub-suppressed phase.  In the hub-dominating phase, hub species show a higher survival probability than low-degree species. On the other hand, hub species survive less than low-degree species in the hub-suppressed phase. Our findings indicate that the correlation between interaction strengths and species degrees significantly impacts species persistence, leading to distinct phases where hubs either thrive or decline.

column9: A Class of Optimal Directed Graphs for Network Synchronization
column11: Lu, Susie; Urschel, John; Liu, Ji*
column13: In a paper by Nishikawa and Motter, a quantity called the normalized spread of the Laplacian eigenvalues is used to measure the synchronizability of certain network dynamics. Through simulations, and without theoretical validation, it is conjectured that among all simple directed graphs with a fixed number of vertices and arcs, the optimal value of this quantity is achieved if the Laplacian spectrum satisfies a specific pattern. This work proves this conjecture and further shows that the conjectured spectral condition is not only sufficient but also necessary. Moreover, the work proves that the optimal Laplacian spectrum is always achievable by a class of almost regular directed graphs, which can be constructed through an inductive algorithm.

column9: Network-Based Visualization of Intra-Cluster Variability in High-Dimensional Data
column11: Plesníková, Kristýna*; Kudělka, Miloš; Ochodková, Eliška; Kriegová, Eva
column13: Understanding intra-cluster variability in high-dimensional data remains challenging with standard distribution plots. We introduce two network-based representations—Confidence Interval (CI) networks and Interquartile Range (IQR) networks—that encode attribute variability as structural features of a similarity network. Starting from an LRNet-constructed sample similarity graph, clusters are identified using the Louvain method. For each cluster, a centroid vector (mean or median) is computed and augmented with attribute-specific deviation vectors defined by confidence interval or interquartile range bounds, isolating the contribution of individual attributes. These vectors are embedded into a network using cosine similarity and a k-nearest neighbor rule, yielding stable and interpretable topologies. Application to the IRIS dataset shows that IQR networks robustly recover species-level structure, while CI networks reflect uncertainty in attribute means through connectivity patterns. Compared to conventional boxplots, the proposed networks provide an integrated view of variability and attribute interactions, offering a scalable and interpretable tool for network-based analysis of high-dimensional and biomedical data.

column9: Brain-Activity Flow on Brain Networks Uncovered by Topological Signal Processing
column11: Petruso, Flavia*; Preti, Maria Giulia; Van De Ville, Dimitri
column13: The brain is a complex system where regions do not operate in isolation, but interact continuously through a network of connections, coordinating activity and enabling the emergence of high-level cognitive processes. Traditional node-centric analyses, including approaches based on graph signal processing (GSP), have provided first insights into these interactions. However, they often model connections as static links, thereby failing to fully capture the dynamic nature of information flow between brain regions.  In this work, we introduce topological signal processing (TSP), a recent framework designed to deal with higher-order structures and signals defined on complex topological domains such as graphs. We demonstrate the applicability of this approach to study brain communication by applying fundamental TSP operators to resting-state blood oxygenation-level–dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). We construct a 2-dimensional simplicial complex as the clique complex of a brain graph obtained by retaining the top 10% strongest structural connections across subjects (Fig. 1a). From the original fMRI time series, we then derive edge-level brain signals that capture lagged dynamics between pairs of brain regions, enabling the investigation of directed patterns that underlie inter-regional interactions. Domain-informed analysis of these signals reveals that, at rest, certain brain regions systematically precede or follow others over time, following both irrotational and circulant patterns. In particular, the discrete divergence operator highlights heterogeneous regional involvement within dorsal attention and visual networks, exhibiting strong positive and negative divergence patterns that suggest asymmetric roles in activity flow and integration (Fig. 1b-c).  Overall, our work represents one of the first applications of TSP to brain imaging data and paves the way for a communication-oriented analysis of brain networks that can explicitly account for higher-order interactions beyond node-centric representations.

column9: Group Level Misalignment and Collective Memory in AI Agent Societies
column13: As Large Language Models increasingly operate in multi-agent systems, understanding their collective behavior becomes critical for AI safety. While individual AI alignment has achieved significant progress, collective alignment remains largely unexplored. We investigate whether AI agent societies can exhibit metastable misaligned states analogous to those in physical systems.  We simulate binary opinion dynamics in populations of AI agents, finding that their majority-following behavior is equivalent to the Curie-Weiss model of ferromagnetism. This equivalence allows us to apply statistical physics tools to predict collective AI behavior. Depending on model-specific parameters, the system can support metastable states where populations adopt positions opposite to their individual biases, yet remain stable over time.  We demonstrate experimentally that small numbers of adversarial agents can drive populations into these misaligned configurations through a hysteresis mechanism. Critically, these states persist even after adversarial agents are removed, representing collective memory that emerges despite frozen model weights and no individual memory. We characterize the phase diagram delineating regions where metastability occurs, finding that over 60% of tested opinion pairs for advanced models fall within the metastable region, including product-level LLMs like Gemini and ChatGPT.  These results reveal that AI alignment must be reconceived as a collective rather than individual property. Populations of individually aligned agents can spontaneously coordinate into stable misaligned states through social influence, producing emergent behaviors undetectable through single-agent evaluation. As multi-agent AI systems become ubiquitous, understanding such collective dynamics becomes essential for safe deployment.

column9: Learning via attractors in deterministic excitable network dynamics
column11: Popova, Mariia*; C. Hilgetag, Claus; Hütt, Marc-Thorsten
column13: Understanding learning and generalization in complex networks remains a central open problem, particularly in regimes where systems are highly expressive yet mechanistic explanations are scarce. Attractors of network dynamics provide a natural substrate for information storage, robustness, and control. Building on recent work analyzing attractors and their perturbative control in deterministic excitable (SER) networks [1], we investigate how such attractor landscapes can be repurposed as a minimal model of learning. Binary input vectors are encoded as initial excitation patterns, and learning is implemented through constrained topological modifications that map groups of inputs onto the same cyclic attractor, thereby realizing classification as basin engineering.  This formulation allows us to address fundamental questions of learning from a dynamical-systems perspective. Learnability is quantified in terms of attractor capacity and controllability under constrained topological edits. Generalization is characterized by basin geometry, measured via robustness of attractor assignment under controlled perturbations of initial conditions, enabling accuracy and AUC-style performance metrics without stochastic dynamics. Finally, continual learning and interference are naturally interpreted as attractor creation and destruction under sequential constraints.  Because the SER dynamics admits explicit attractor enumeration and a motif-based description of interactions, learning, generalization, and interference can be traced to concrete structural plasticity mechanisms. Our results position excitable attractor networks as a tractable model system for studying scaling, phase transitions, and robustness in learning beyond gradient-based paradigms.  [1] Popova, Hilgetag, and Hütt, Phys. Rev. E 110, 054406, 2024.

column9: Identifying high impact genes using single-cell RNA seq data through deep learning
column11: Levy, Orr*; He, Yongjian; Klein, Vered; Wang, Xu-Wen
column13: Gene expression data is essential for understanding how genes are regulated and interact within biological systems, providing insights into disease pathways and potential therapeutic targets. Gene knockout has proven to be a fundamental technique in molecular biology, allowing the investigation of the function of specific genes in an organism, as well as in specific cell types. However, gene expression patterns are quite heterogeneous in single-cell transcriptional data from a uniform environment, representing different cell states, which produce cell-type and cell-specific gene knockout impacts. A computational method that can predict the single-cell resolution knockout impact is still lacking. Identifying high impact genes and their knockout outcome in scRNA-seq data is challenging due to the extreme complexity and cell-type specificity of gene regulatory networks (GRNs), the inherent stochasticity of gene expression, and the difficulty of predicting transcriptional outcomes following random damage. These challenges are further compounded by technical noise, data sparsity, and clustering artifacts intrinsic to scRNA-seq data. Here, we present a data-driven framework that overcome the need to extract the entire map of interactions in the gene regulatory network (GRN) for learning the mapping between gene expression profiles derived from gene assemblages, enabling the accurate prediction of perturbed expression profiles following knockout (KO) for any cell, without relying on prior perturbed data. We systematically validated our framework using synthetic data generated from gene regulatory dynamics models, two mouse knockout single-cell datasets, and high throughput in vitro CRISPRi Perturb-seq data. Our results demonstrate that the framework can accurately predict both expression profiles and KO effects at the single-cell level. Our approach provides a generalizable tool for inferring gene function at single-cell resolution, offering new opportunities to study genetic perturbations in contexts where large-scale experimental screens are infeasible.

column9: Modeling financial transactions via random walks on temporal networks
column11: Ojer, Jaume*; Mattsson, Carolina; Cellerini, Claudio; Starnini, Michele
column13: Financial transactions can be suitably generated via a dynamical process with many simultaneous random walks. We model $M$ random walkers on an activity-driven temporal network of $N$ nodes. Each random walker located at an activated node follows the available link with a certain probability, resulting in a transaction of some size. Despite its simplicity, this model gives rise to a rich phenomenology that reproduces the key empirics: heterogeneity in transaction sizes and high correlation between inflows and outflows. We provide an analytical representation and a path toward increasingly realistic models of transactions via integration with empirical data.

column9: How stubborn anticonformists drive social hysteresis - quenched anticonformity in the multistate q-voter model on networks
column13: Discontinuous phase transitions have, for a long time, captured the interest of physicists, economists, and social scientists alike, because they are often associated with empirically verified phenomena such as tipping points, critical mass, and social hysteresis. For this reason, opinion-dynamics models that exhibit rich phase behavior are especially relevant in computational social science. Among them, the q-voter model is particularly interesting due to its inherent group-based influence corresponding to complex contagion, which has been shown to play a significant role in various social scenarios. Its multistate variant is thus an attractive basis for an agent-based approach to simulate discrete decision-making. Previous studies of the multistate q-voter model with anticonformity on complete graphs uncovered a counterintuitive result. Quenching the type of social response of agents, i.e., changing homogeneous agents with varying behavior into heterogeneous agents with fixed behavior, produces discontinuous phase transitions. This is contrary to the common expectation that quenched heterogeneity smooths transitions. However, the previous analysis was limited to the mean-field regime; hence, we extend it to random graphs to verify whether the effect is robust to changes in the underlying social network on which the dynamics occur. Our contribution is two-fold: (1) we apply the pair approximation method to the multi-state q-voter model with anticonformity, providing an analytical approach to both annealed and quenched systems with an arbitrary number of states; (2) using pair approximation and Monte Carlo simulations, we show that the phenomenon of quench-driven discontinuity persists beyond the complete graph, specifically on random graphs and Barabási-Albert scale-free networks.

column9: Overcoming Fundamental Limitations in Deep Graph Pooling
column11: Blöcker, Christopher*; von Pichowski, Jan; Hrabošová, Alžbeta; Scholtes, Ingo
column13: Deep graph pooling builds on graph neural networks (GNNs) and aims to embed graphs in a vectorial space for downstream tasks such as graph classification. The perhaps most prominent example is predicting molecular toxicity, which finds application in drug development. While various approaches exist, we consider community-based pooling, in which a community-detection objective is used as a loss function to guide the learning of GNN weights. The basic idea behind community-based pooling is to iteratively detect communities and coarse-grain them until the entire graph is reduced to a single node whose features summarise those of the entire graph. These aggregated features then serve as the basis for classification, for example, via an MLP.  GNNs are utilised because they combine node features with topology, both of which are assumed to provide information for clustering nodes. However, they have a crucial shortcoming that is often overlooked in deep graph learning: their capability to summarise node features in a meaningful way depends on how well those features align with the graph's topology. Consider the molecule in Figure 1a where the node features do not align well with the topological communities. An MLP, or any other learnable function, that assigns communities based on the nodes' features, here represented by colours, must assign nodes with the same colour to the same community. Essentially, this means that the nodes' colours restrict the space of possible communities that can be proposed to the community-detection objective function. In other words: deep graph pooling suffers from the fundamental mismatch that (i) communities are proposed based on the nodes' features while (ii) they are evaluated based on the graph's topology. Whether pooling can be effective boils down to the alignment between features and topology, that is, it depends on the data.  To estimate the effectiveness of pooling for a specific dataset, we develop a framework based on node colourings, which we use as a proxy for node features. For pooling, two aspects are essential: colourings must be valid and transferable. First, a colouring is valid if there are no two nodes with the same colour that belong to different communities (see Figure 1b). In other words: if a mapping from node colours to communities exists, the colouring is valid. Second, a colouring is transferable if the colours from ``seen'' communities can be transferred to ``unseen'' communities (see Figure 1c-d). Transferability is essential because deep graph pooling is used in inductive settings, where models are trained on a training set and then applied to unseen graphs.  Our preliminary results show that datasets with more colours are more likely to have valid colourings, where validity is guaranteed when all nodes have unique colours. However, transferability is guaranteed only when there is only a single colour, and the presence of more colours tends to limit transferability. Because validity and transferability represent competing objectives, we regard the ``quality'' of a colouring as the minimum of the two. Previous work has shown that the working principles of GNNs are essentially equivalent to the so-called colour refinement algorithm, and we find that GNNs increase the number of unique colours by combining features with topological information. That is, while GNNs make colourings more valid, they hamper transferability. For effective deep graph pooling, we need to find a middle ground and make a trade-off; preliminary results suggest enriching node features with Laplacian Positional Encodings or random-walk-based features as a promising approach.

column9: Social structure beyond rank assortativity in rhesus macaque networks
column13: Network science has become central to the study of social systems, providing quantitative tools to link individual-level interactions with emergent social structure. The methodological and conceptual advances of the past decades are not restricted to the analysis of human social networks and can also be used in the context of behavioural ecology to understand animal social behaviour [1]. In animal social systems, social networks offer a powerful framework for understanding how individual traits and relational characteristics can influence the formation and nature of social ties, and how these generate mesoscopic and macroscopic patterns of social organisation [2,3].  We analyse the social behaviour of a population of free-ranging rhesus macaques from Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico, focusing on proximity, grooming, and aggression networks. Our study spans multiple social groups (V, KK, F, H) and years (2013–2022), following a longitudinal and comparative approach similar to [4]. We combine a range of network science methods—including network visualisation, community detection, network metric analysis, and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs)—to examine the roles of dominance rank, kinship, and demographic factors in the formation and structure of social relationships.  We find that social networks are strongly assortative by dominance rank across groups and years. However, systematic deviations from this pattern emerge: highest-ranking individuals are frequently observed in close proximity to, and occasionally groomed by, the lowest-ranking individuals. We investigate this by focusing on female social networks (left panel of figure). Detected proximity communities (right panel of figure) closely correspond to known matrilineal branches. However, consistent with the previous observation, some low-ranking females are detected within high-ranking submatrilines. These associations are not fully explained by age or known kinship, suggesting the presence of latent or historical social ties not captured by standard theories of rank assortativity. In ongoing work, we explore whether such latent structure can be revealed by selectively removing the effects of rank assortativity, kinship, and age obtained from GLMMs, and by incorporating the analysis of aggression, geolocation, and activity data where available.

column9: When is Information Seeking Counterproductive?: The Impact of Vaccination Status and Source Trust on Beliefs in Mixed-Quality Information Networks
column11: Acierno, Jane*; Butler, Lucy; Davis, Jessica; Constantino, Sara; Swire-Thompson, Briony
column13: Misinformation poses a serious threat to public health and scientific trust [1], motivating efforts to promote media literacy [2]. Many such interventions assume that encouraging people to seek information from trusted sources will guide them towards higher quality information, thus improving belief accuracy [3]. Yet individuals differ in which sources they trust [4], raising concerns that interventions prompting open-ended search may not function as intended in mixed-quality information environments [5]. The present study examines how a source-based media literacy intervention shapes information seeking and belief updating within an information environment containing both high- and low-quality sources. Beyond the intervention, we also examine how information seeking behavior impacts belief updating, and whether this differs between vaccinated and unvaccinated participants.   Participants (N = 668) were randomized to a control condition or a graphical media literacy intervention condition adapted from Guess et al. [2], which emphasized investigating source credibility and consulting multiple trusted sources (Fig. 1a). Next, participants rated their belief in six vaccine-related claims (three true, three false), then completed an open-ended information-seeking task (Fig. 1b). On each trial, participants could sample up to 100 health provider avatars representing either trustworthy (e.g., physicians) or untrustworthy (e.g., homeopaths) sources, which predominantly endorsed either accurate or inaccurate information, respectively. Participants then re-rated belief in each claim.  The media literacy intervention did not impact the amount or quality of information seeking, or enhance belief accuracy. However, seeking high-quality information served as a corrective mechanism: sampling more trustworthy sources increased belief accuracy (Fig. 1c). Conversely, sampling untrustworthy sources reduced accuracy, especially among unvaccinated participants. Although vaccinated and unvaccinated participants expressed similarly low trust in low-quality sources, vaccinated participants exhibited substantially higher trust in high-quality sources, producing a sharper perceived distinction between source types. This distinction predicted sampling behavior, and helps explain why vaccinated participants were far less likely to sample untrustworthy sources. Finally, we developed a Bayesian belief-updating model to assess whether each population integrated sampled evidence rationally. Overall, our findings suggest that media literacy interventions encouraging information seeking may not function as intended within heterogeneous information networks.  [1] S. Lewandowsky, U. K. H. Ecker, J. Cook, J. Appl. Res. Mem. Cogn. 6, 353–369 (2017).  [2] A. M. Guess et al., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 117, 15536–15545 (2020).  [3] G. Pennycook et al., Psychol. Sci. 31, 770–780 (2020).  [4] A. M. Jones et al., Adv. Prev. Med. 2012, 932741 (2012).  [5] K. Aslett et al., Nature 625, 548–556 (2024).

column9: Innovation Dynamics on Fitness Landscapes: A Local Optima Network Approach to Punctuated Equilibria and Heavy-Tailed Discovery Times
column13: Understanding how novelty emerges and propagates through complex systems remains a fundamental challenge in innovation studies. Recent advances in urn models, particularly Pólya urns with triggering mechanisms, have provided elegant mathematical frameworks capturing how discoveries beget further discoveries through the expansion of the "adjacent possible." However, these models typically abstract away the structured topology of the innovation space itself. We propose a complementary approach that makes this structure explicit through fitness landscapes and Local Optima Networks (LONs), offering new insights into the mechanisms generating both gradual and punctuated patterns of technological change. Our framework constructs innovation spaces as toroidal fitness landscapes, characterizing their structure through LONs: directed graphs where nodes represent local optima (stable technological configurations) and weighted edges encode transition probabilities between basins of attraction. This representation compresses the high-dimensional search space into a navigable network capturing essential features for innovation dynamics: the multiplicity of local traps, the connectivity between technological niches, and the funnel structures channeling search toward high-performance regions. The "adjacent possible" of urn models finds a natural formalization as the set of optima reachable through basin transitions, while the triggering mechanism corresponds to the opening of new landscapes upon reaching performance thresholds. We model innovating agents as stochastic walkers on LONs, combining local exploitation through perturbation-based basin-hopping with occasional exploration via stagnation-triggered jumps. When agents reach the performance frontier of their current landscape, they transition to a new landscape with scaled fitness values, representing paradigm shifts that open fresh possibilities. This mechanism generates punctuated equilibrium dynamics endogenously: periods of incremental improvement within a paradigm alternate with rapid transitions to qualitatively new regimes, mirroring patterns observed in technological evolution. Our computational experiments reveal several regularities. Landscape traversal times, measuring the duration required to progress from low to high performance, appear to follow heavy-tailed distributions consistent with power-law scaling. This finding resonates with empirical observations of extreme variability in innovation timelines and provides a mechanistic explanation rooted in network topology. The LON topology itself varies systematically with landscape ruggedness, from sparse hub-and-spoke structures to dense small-world networks, with implications for the balance between exploitation and exploration strategies. By grounding urn-based abstractions in explicit network topology, our framework opens avenues for investigating how innovation space structure shapes the tempo and mode of technological progress. The approach suggests potential connections to empirical innovation networks derived from patent citations, technology classifications, or scientific knowledge graphs, where landscape features might be estimated and their consequences for innovation dynamics predicted.

column9: Comparing War Narratives Through Cross-Lingual Narrative Networks
column13: Understanding how different languages portray the same historical events is crucial for identifying and addressing cultural and geopolitical biases in collaborative knowledge production. In this study, we examine how different language editions of Wikipedia describe the same wars, focusing on the portrayal of participating entities across various languages. Our research questions are: Do Wikipedia language editions exhibit distinct and recurring entity-level narrative patterns in their portrayal of wars? Which languages show greater similarity in these narrative patterns?  All data were collected through Wikipedia's official MediaWiki API. Starting from the English Wikipedia category ``List of wars by date,'' we identified wars that started after 1900 and their belligerents. Using these wars as seed articles, we expanded the dataset by sampling related wars and battles through internal links within each article and through Wikipedia categories of the form ``Battles of [War Name].'' For each battle, we then collect the corresponding articles from 20 language editions of Wikipedia, when available. We translated all non-English articles into English using the Google Translation API and applied a connotation frame analysis to the translated text. After deduplication and filtering, the final dataset consists of 2,630 battles from 976 wars.   Using the RIVETER framework [1], we extracted verb-centric agent–verb–theme tuples and constructed an entity-level narrative network for each language. In each network, nodes correspond to entities appearing in the text, and an edge is established between two entities whenever they co-occur within the same agent–verb–theme relation. Each entity is associated with three attributes---power, agency, and sentiment---computed by averaging the verb-level connotation scores provided by the RIVETER corpus over all verbs in which the entity participates (Figure 1). These attributes capture how entities are systematically portrayed in terms of dominance, intentionality, and affect within narrative contexts. For each language, we select the three most frequently mentioned entities across all wars and compute their average power, agency, and sentiment scores by first averaging within each war and then across wars.  Our preliminary results illustrate cross-linguistic narrative patterns. Table 1 reports these scores for English, German, and Chinese as illustrative examples, showing that languages portray their respective countries as less powerful and less agentic. Our future directions include constructing war-level narrative networks for each language by retaining entities associated with the two belligerents of each war. Pairwise similarities between language-specific networks will be computed using the Propagation Kernel method [2] and normalized within each war. For each language pair, we will average the normalized similarities across all shared wars to emphasize narrative similarity rather than coverage differences.   [1] Antoniak, M., Field, A., Mun, J., Walsh, M., Klein, L., \& Sap, M. (2023, July). Riveter: Measuring power and social dynamics between entities. In Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics [2] Neumann, M., Garnett, R., Bauckhage, C., \& Kersting, K. (2016). Propagation kernels: efficient graph kernels from propagated information. Machine learning, 102(2), 209-245

column9: Ethical Visibility: Bridging Network Science, Ethics, and Information Design for Reimagining Global Art representation and inclusiveness
column13: This talk explores how Information Design can promote equitable decision-making in representing and including Global South artists in exhibitions. Using an interdisciplinary approach that combines Network Science, Information Design, and philosophical inquiry, it demonstrates how quantitative analysis, social-justice-oriented interpretation, and visual communication can empower artist selection. Focusing on the Venice Biennale 2024 edition, Foreigners Everywhere, as a case study, the talk traces the process from data extraction to visualization, uncovering patterns of cultural bias and systemic exclusion. By integrating scientific and humanistic perspectives, the study proposes innovative pathways for ethical, inclusive, and critically reflective curatorial practices.

column9: Comparing equity with efficiency in network diffusion models
column11: Kaan, Jiri*; Thompson, Kristina; Khaluf, Yara; Moore, Spencer
column13: Interventions that distribute resources through social networks are often designed to maximize diffusion efficiency, aiming to reach as many individuals as fast as possible, ideally at minimal cost. However, efficient diffusion does not necessarily imply equitable diffusion, understood here as inequalities in access to resources across individuals or groups within the network that are deemed unfair. Depending on network structure, diffusion processes may systematically advantage some groups while leaving others underserved, even when overall distributions of resources appear similar. Despite growing attention to interventions using social networks, comparatively little work has examined how equity in access trades off against efficiency in diffusion.  To address this gap, we develop a network equity metric that measures the extent to which members of a social network have comparable weighted access to a given resource through direct (e.g., a friend) or indirect ties (e.g., a friend of a friend). From our metric, we derive a leverage function that can be used to target nodes to distribute resources to in the network. Using agent-based modeling, we assess our network equity metric, trade-offs in efficient and equitable diffusion, and differences in who is targeted using the leverage function.  Using the network equity metric, we find equity differences that emerge from how the network constrains or enables access to resources, even when overall distributions of resources look similar from a purely statistical perspective. Moreover, simulations demonstrate trade-offs with efficiency depending on the strategy used to target nodes in social networks. Although the different strategies partly overlap in the nodes they target, they prioritize different structural positions in the network (Figure 1). Specifically, using the leverage function we target nodes embedded within cohesive and relatively isolated groups rather than hubs or bridge nodes based on degree and betweenness centrality. By explicitly defining equity as a goal, the leverage function provides an alternative way to identify nodes, positioning equity alongside efficiency as a criterion for resource distribution.

column9: Visualizing Genetic Diversity and Scale in the Million Veteran Program
column13: This project, a collaboration between the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and the Barabási Lab, explores large-scale genetic associations within the Million Veteran Program. We analyze over 26 million SNPs linked to 1,572 phenotypes across 2,068 genetic traits, representing complex relationships between diseases and shared genetic markers in an interactive network dashboard.  The dashboard integrates network science, information design, and interactive visualization, enabling users to explore genetic diversity through filtering, search, clustering, and degree-based selection. Nodes represent diseases, and edges denote shared SNPs, uncovering underlying patterns and systemic trends. A static version, recognized with the Information is Beautiful Longlist Award (2024), also secured additional funding to expand and advance the project.  By combining large-scale data analysis with human-centered design, this work addresses underrepresentation in genomic research and demonstrates how interactive visualization makes complex biological networks accessible, interpretable, and actionable.

column9: Inferring Network Interactions from Short and Noisy Signals with Deep Learning
column11: Pavaux, Marion*; De Vico Fallani, Fabrizio; La Rocca, Daria
column13: Graph-based representations provide a powerful framework for modeling and analyzing a wide range of complex systems. But in many cases, the connections between the nodes of the network are unknown, and have to be reconstructed from the individual node dynamics. In practice, networks of interest are large and complex, while available observations are limited and noisy, which substantially impairs the robustness of classical connection-inference methods, like Bayesian methods, which struggle in sparse data contexts [1]. For example, in network neuroscience, computational methods of connectivity estimators often fail to reliably infer brain connectivity from short, noisy and non-stationary signals. In this paper, we address the question of network inference  by developing a deep learning-based framework to learn and infer interactions between multivariate time series. Applying this model to simulated electroencephalography (EEG) brain signals, we show that it can more robustly reconstruct spectral connectivity as compared to standard Welch's modified periodogram method. The proposed architecture combines convolutional feature extraction with an attention mechanism and is trained to estimate imaginary coherence, a connectivity measure designed to mitigate volume-conduction effects [2]. We evaluated our framework on short and noisy simulated signals, demonstrating improved connectivity reconstruction in conditions close to real experimental conditions. Moreover, domain-adaptation techniques enable efficient transfer of the model to real electroencephalography data. Overall, our results illustrate how deep learning architectures can be trained to overcome fundamental limitations of classical network-inference techniques when applied to sparse and noisy data. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using deep learning for network inference and suggests that the approach can be extended to other connectivity estimators and to non-neural networked systems.  [1] Young, J.-G., Cantwell, G. T. \& Newman, M. E. J. Journal of Complex Networks (2021). [2] Nolte, G. et al. Clinical Neurophysiology (2004).

column9: Can We Identify Breakthroughs Before They Happen? Predicting Disruptive Science from Manuscript Text and Citation Network Features
column13: Disruptive scientific works create knowledge that challenges the status quo, resulting in new innovation trajectories [1, 2]. A disruptive paper does not necessarily get many citations. Instead, it redirects future edges away from its predecessors. The disruption score (D-score) quantifies this redirection, measuring the degree of disruption of a scientific work [1]. However, computing D-scores requires long citation windows, which limits the early identification of disruptive research. This study investigates whether disruption can be predicted using (i) a paper’s text embeddings alone, (ii) a combination of text embeddings and semantic alignment within its citation network, and (iii) limited post-publication citation data.  We analyze ego-centered citation networks for 80,000 focal papers published in journals or conferences between 1980 and 2019 across the fields of Computer Science, Medicine, Biology, and Economics. Paper metadata and disruption scores were obtained from SciSciNet and abstracts from Microsoft Academic Graph. The D-score, developed by Funk and Owen-Smith [1], ranges from -1 to 1, where higher values indicate greater disruption. We apply SPECTER 2.0 [3], a scientific text embedding model trained on large-scale scholarly corpora, to map research articles into a 768-dimensional vector space (Fig. 1). Citation topology is combined with semantic alignment by averaging the individual cosine similarities between the focal paper and its references, the focal paper and its citing papers, and between references and citations. Logistic regression models are employed for classification.   Across fields, integrating both the text embeddings of the focal paper and the semantic alignment of its citation topology consistently yields the strongest performance across the evaluation metrics, outperforming those using either component alone (Fig. 2). Notably, restricting citation data to the first five years post-publication results in comparable performance, suggesting that disruptive works can be identified early without waiting for their full citation network to unfold.  Together, these results suggest that integrating semantic embeddings with citation topology provides a richer characterization of disruptive research than retrospective citation patterns alone. A key direction for future work is to investigate the robustness of these results across other disciplines, larger datasets, higher-order network structures, and shorter temporal windows.  [1] Funk, R. J. & Owen-Smith, J. A Dynamic Network Measure of Technological Change. Management Science (2017). [2] Wu, L., Wang, D. & Evans, J. A. Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology. Nature (2019). [3] Singh, A., D’Arcy, M., Cohan, A., Downey, D. & Feldman, S. SciRepEval: A Multi-Format Benchmark for Scientific Document Representations. in Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 5548–5566 Figure 1: Each paper in the citation network is a vector embed- ding using SPECTER 2.0. Figure 2: Model performance comparison using Macro F1 scores.

column9: The effect of group-level homophily on the spread of behavior in online social networks
column13: There is empirical evidence that behaviors spread as a ``complex'' contagion, where multiple exposures, or \textit{peer reinforcement}, is required for an individual to adopt a behavior [1]. Not all social contagion is complex, however; viral information cascades can exhibit behavior similar to ``simple'' contagion, whereas other less viral cascades appear more complex [2]. This suggests that several infection kernels capturing information or behavior adoption may be at play in a given population. Beyond complex contagions, however, evidence suggests that the group context of the reinforcing nodes matters as well [3]. One must be careful, however, when inferring the rules by which information spreads, since previous work has shown that different mechanisms of nodal adoption can be indistinguishable; whether a node adopts a behavior due to intrinsic characteristics versus whether it is \textit{truly} influenced by another node can be disentangled only in certain scenarios [4].  Here, we describe a way to uncover the differential effect of social contagion with and without homophily expressed through social groups. Bluesky, the online social media platform, is an ideal model system for examining this question because it features \textit{starter packs}, user-curated groups often centered around shared interests or ideologies; these serve as a good proxy for group-level homophily. We collect lists of starter pack memberships, following relationships, and reposts from the Bluesky API, where reposts are understood as signals of behavior spread. There are four ways in which a pair of users can interact: whether they share a starter pack and whether one follows the other.
