We model the spread of behavior as a neighborhood-based Susceptible-Infected contagion process, where each user's adoption probability is a mixture of kernels corresponding to each of the four scenarios. Using a Bayesian inferential framework [5], each kernel is nonparametrically estimated from the observed repost cascades. The differences in kernels and their relative mixing within each individual quantifies the effect of group-level homophily on the spread of behavior.

column9: Topological Higher-Order Features for Brain Network State Classification
column11: Skhiri, Wafa*; De Vico Fallani, Fabrizio
column13: Characterizing functional brain networks is crucial to model and analyze brain states in basic and clinical applications. Most current approaches rely on pairwise functional connectivity or linear spectral features, which capture only a fraction of the complexity of brain dynamics [1]. Neuroscience evidence increasingly suggests that neural computation involves higher- order interactions (HOI)-dependencies arising from the simultaneous coordination of multiple neural populations rather than isolated pairwise connections [2]. These HOI have been shown to reveal organizational features that remain hidden in classical graph-based analyses of brain networks and may therefore provide a richer substrate for brain state decoding. In this work, we investigate whether HOI-inspired network structure can improve the characterization of EEG activity during a typical brain-computer interface task based on motor imagery (MI). Instead of focusing on power modulation, we estimate instantaneous phase differences between EEG channels and treat these as a multivariate dynamical interaction pattern. Using these phase-based similarity networks, we construct a higher-order topological representation of neural interactions through spectral graph embedding followed by a topological data analysis (TDA) pipeline (Fig. 1a). We evaluate whether these topological features reliably distinguish MI tasks from resting states across several EEG recording sessions. Preliminary results indicate that simplicial-complex–based analysis applied to phase-interaction structure capture discriminative information that complement standard functional connectivity metrics (Fig. 1b,c). This suggests that topological characterizations—inspired by the notion of HOI as simultaneous multi-node coordination—may capture aspects of neural organization that are behaviorally relevant and potentially useful for many applications in cognitive and clinical neuroscience. [1] De Vico Fallani F, Richiardi J, Chavez M, Achard S. Graph analysis of functional brain networks. Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci. 2014;369:20130521. [2] Santoro A, Battiston F, Lucas M, Petri G, Amico E. Higher-order connectomics of human brain function. Nat Commun. 2024;15:10244 .

column9: Beyond Partisan Echo Chambers: Age and Gender Segregation in  Information Ecosystem
column13: A central concern for democratic deliberation is whether citizens share a common informational foundation or instead sort into separate information environments. The echo chamber thesis argues that online platforms can intensify this sorting by segregating publics into ideologically homogeneous groups [1, 2]. Yet empirical investigations have focused primarily on partisan segregation [3, 4], overlooking other demographic dimensions that may also structure information consumption.  We analyze URL-sharing behavior among 1.6 million Twitter users matched to U.S. voter files via unique name-location combinations, providing validated demographic attributes (age, gender, party affiliation) rather than inferred characteristics. Our dataset comprises 43 million unique URLs shared between January 2017 and December 2022, enabling longitudinal analysis at both the domain level (information sources) and the URL level (specific stories). Using the multigroup Theil H index [5], a decomposable measure of segregation, we quantify segregation along partisan, age, and gender dimensions and establish statistical significance through permutation tests that randomly shuffle demographic labels while preserving the observed sharing structure.  Three findings emerge. First, URL-level segregation (H ≈ 0.32–0.40) substantially exceeds domain-level segregation (H ≈ 0.10–0.17), indicating that demographic groups rely on similar sources but select systematically different content within them, a pattern that domain-level analyses miss. Second, age-based segregation rivals or exceeds partisan segregation throughout the observation period, reaching H ≈ 0.39 by late 2022, consistent with emerging work on demographic homophily online [6]. Third, we identify a structural break in January 2021, after which age and gender segregation increase sharply while partisan segregation plateaus, suggesting a shift from a primarily partisan-organized information ecosystem to one segregated along multiple demographic dimensions.

column9: Unifying Information-Theoretic and Pair-Counting Community Similarity
column13: Comparing community structures is fundamental to evaluating unsupervised methods in network science, yet existing similarity measures often yield inconsistent or even contradictory assessments[1].  Community similarity measures are typically divided into two broad families: pair-counting and information-theoretic, depending on whether agreement is quantified through element pairs or through aggregate information over community contingency tables.  While prior work has noted empirical relationships between these families and proposed normalization or chance-correction schemes, their underlying analytical connection remains incomplete[2].  Here, we introduce a unifying framework that links pair-counting and information-theoretic community similarity measures through two complementary perspectives. First, we show that both families can be written as weighted expansions of observed versus expected co-occurrences: pair-counting measures arise as low-order approximations, whereas information-theoretic measures correspond to higher-order, frequency-weighted expansions of community residuals (Fig 1C,D).  Second, we generalize pair-counting to $k$-tuples and demonstrate that information-theoretic measures can be interpreted as systematically accumulating higher-order co-assignment structure beyond the pairwise level (Fig 1A,B).  We illustrate these connections analytically for the Rand index and Mutual Information, and show how other commonly used measures in each family emerge as natural extensions of this framework.   Our key insight is that reported agreement between community detection algorithms can be fundamentally scale-biased.  In networks with heterogeneous community sizes, high similarity scores may indicate consensus on a few large communities while concealing substantial and systematic disagreement in mesoscale and peripheral organization.  Our framework clarifies when and why pair-counting and information-theoretic measures diverge, links their behavior directly to weighting and approximation order, and establishes a principled foundation for evaluating and designing community similarity measures that faithfully reflect network structure across scales.

column9: Disruption and Adaptation of Social Connectedness at Third Places after Disasters
column13: Disaster induced population dynamics trigger changes in socio-spatial patterns in affected communities leading to fragmentation and weakening of existing social ties, that have been considered an important factor for resilience in various studies. However, the dynamics and transformations of social networks resulting from disaster-induced displacement remain largely unexplored in the literature. To bridge this gap, using large scale mobile phone GPS data, we measure how the level of connectivity of social networks (measured through co-location in third places) changes, in communities affected by the 2021 Marshall Fires in Colorado. By comparing network metrics such as the clustering coefficient and mean degree between pre- and post-disaster social networks, we find that post-disaster social networks significantly lose connectivity. To investigate the mechanisms of why social networks lose connectively after disasters, we build several counterfactual network models.  First, we find that randomly removing individuals (nodes) with rates proportional to the actual displacement leads to underestimation in network connectivity. This suggests that some form of behavioral adaptation leads to preservation of connectivity in the social networks. Second, we find that using heterogeneous reduction rates in visitation patterns to points-of-interest (POIs) based on three factors: 1) distance from home to POIs, 2) distance between the fire and POIs, and 3) POI category, enables the replication of the post-disaster network characteristics. This suggests that POI visitation behavior significantly determines the dynamics of social networks after disasters.

column9: Temporal Multiplex Networks of Rebel Cooperation and the Emergence of Wartime Governance in Syria
column13: How do evolving patterns of cooperation and rivalry among armed organizations shape the institutions that govern civilians during war? This study advances a network science account of wartime governance by treating local institutions as outcomes of temporal relational structure rather than products of actor attributes alone. I model Syrian rebel organizations as nodes in a temporal multi-actor network in which layers capture alliances and defections, violent interaction, and ties to governance institutions. The central claim is that governance capacity and inclusiveness are constrained by network topology, particularly coalition density, dominance, brokerage, and the persistence of meso-scale blocs. In this view, institutional consolidation is expected when relational control becomes centralized and cross faction ties become selective or unstable, whereas more inclusive arrangements require durable boundary spanning cooperation that can sustain coordination costs.  Empirically, I construct time indexed network snapshots using alliance and defection data (Gade, Hafez, and Gabbay 2019), conflict event data (Sundberg and Melander 2013), and measures of rebel governance institutions (Albert 2022). I combine descriptive network measures with model based inference. Descriptively, I track density and  centralization by ideological attributes, and community structure persistence across war stages. For inference, I estimate additive and multiplicative effects models to recover latent dimensions of cooperation and ERGMs to test structural dependencies including triadic closure  and degree based dominance.  The dynamics motivating the framework are illustrated in Figure 1, which visualizes the evolution of HTS’ cooperation network from 2012 to 2017. The panels show rapid densification and coalition embedding in 2013 and 2014, followed by sharp contraction and thinning after 2014, with cooperation reorganizing around fewer partners and reduced redundancy.   A within country comparative component links these network trajectories to governance outcomes for HTS in northwest Syria, ISIS in Raqqa, and the PYD in northeast Syria, each representing distinct configurations of dominance, coalition structure, and cross group connectivity. The contribution is twofold. Substantively, the study explains persistent fragmentation in local governance as a path dependent consequence of wartime relational structure. Methodologically, it demonstrates how temporal multiplex and signed network modeling can connect micro level tie dynamics to meso scale coalition structure and macro level institutional governance.

column9: Characterizing agglomeration economies by blockmodeling spatial proximity graphs
column11: Wu, Jianrui*; He, Baiyue; Kirkley, Alec
column13: Agglomeration economies are a spatial phenomenon in which industries of the same type concentrate for the advantage it provides for sharing labor, resources, infrastructure, and knowledge. Urban amenities such as restaurants, shops, and services often exhibit pronounced spatial clustering to reap these benefits of agglomeration. A good deal of existing research in urban planning and geography has focused on agglomeration economies, with various measures developed to characterize the the extent to which industries cluster [1]. However, these existing measures either require the tuning of manual input parameters or expensive computational simulations for determining statistical significance of a given observed level of spatial clustering. This reduces their effectiveness for understanding how spatial agglomeration tendency varies across industries and spatial scales, both of which are critical for future city planning [2]. Furthermore, it is important for measures of spatial agglomeration to account for both homophily \emph{and} heterophily on a consistent scale.   Here we propose principled, computationally efficient, fully nonparametric measures of spatial homophily and heterophily using Bayesian stochastic blockmodeling. Given $N$ geo-located points (e.g. amenities, points of interest) with categorical labels, we construct a proximity graph $\bm{A}(\epsilon)$ connecting all point pairs within distance $\epsilon$ and characterize the level of homophily among these amenities using the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. Specifically, we compare three competing models for $\bm{A}(\epsilon)$ using their corresponding description lengths $-\log P(\bm{A}|\text{model})$: a \emph{neutral} Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi model; a \emph{homophilic} block model in which the edge probability $\rho_{\text{in}}$ among identical amenity types exceeds the cross-type probability $\rho_{\text{out}}$; and a \emph{heterophilic} block model with the opposite constraint. For fair comparison, the latter two models also encode the categorical labels $\bm{b}$ under a non-informative prior jointly with the graph. These three models can be compared scalably with careful parallelization and analytical marginalization over the blockmodel priors.  Applying this framework to an open source Foursquare amenity dataset spanning 779 cities worldwide, we discovered \emph{consistent spatial scales} of urban organization: homophilic clustering peaks at a walkable neighborhood scale, while heterophilic mixing peaks at district-level scales. These patterns are common across city sizes and geographic regions. Our results reveal a shared hierarchical urban organization in which similar amenities agglomerate locally, while diverse amenities mix at larger scales to form functionally integrated areas. The Bayesian framework provides a principled, parameter-free approach for detecting these patterns, and offers new tools for urban science and planning.

column9: Cover and Hitting Times of Random Walks on Hyperbolic Random Graphs
column11: Kiwi, Marcos; Schepers, Markus*; Sylvester, John
column13: Hyperbolic random graphs (HRGs) constitute a geometric model for complex networks that captures heavy-tailed degree distributions, strong clustering, and logarithmic distances. These properties suggest efficient navigation, yet their implications for exploration dynamics remain poorly understood. In this work, we study simple random walks on the giant component of HRGs in the regime where the degree distribution follows a power law with exponent in $(2,3)$. We characterize several fundamental time scales governing exploration. With high probability, and up to constant factors, the average hitting time is linear in the number of vertices $n$, the maximum hitting time scales as $n \log n$, and the cover time scales as $n \log^2 n$.   These results reveal a clear separation between navigation and exploration: despite ultra-small distances, uniform coverage is asymptotically slower than in expander-like networks, incurring an additional logarithmic factor beyond the general lower bound. Our analysis relies on effective resistance estimates obtained via carefully constructed flows adapted to a tiling of the hyperbolic plane. Numerical simulations support the predicted scaling behavior for moderate system sizes. Ongoing work investigates how (coalescing) branching random walks alter exploration efficiency in hyperbolic networks.  [1] Kiwi, M., Schepers, M., \& Sylvester, J. (2024). Cover and hitting times of hyperbolic random graphs. Random Structures \& Algorithms, 65(4), 915-978.

column9: Characterizing the scholarly influence of three canonical community detection algorithms through citation networks
column13: Girvan-Newman, label propagation, and Louvain are three canonical community detection algorithms. In order to understand their influence to the broader scientific community, we studied the 2-hop neighborhood of the citation networks of the three papers reporting those algorithms using a snapshot of the COCI, the OpenCitations Index of Crossref open DOI-to-DOI references. We discovered different temporal transitive closure behaviors in the 2-hop neighborhood. We defined three types of citations: 1st-gen citations (1-hop neighbors) are those cites a focal paper; 2nd-gen citations (2-hop neighbors) are those cites a paper that cites a focal paper; transitive closure (TC) citations are those that are both 1st-gen and 2nd-gen, meaning they cite the focal paper and cite (at least) one paper that cites the focal paper. We constructed two types of time series: P1 and P2. P1(x) is the proportion of the number of TC citations over the number of 1st-gen citations, both limited to those published in year x. P2(x) is the proportion of the number of TC citations over the number of 2nd-gen citations, both limited to those published in year x. While the P2(x) traces are similar, the P1(x) trace of Blondel et al., 2008, which reported the Louvain algorithm, is markedly different from the other two. Blondel et al., 2008 has a higher proportion of 1st-gen citations that do not cite any other citations of it. A possible explanation is that Louvain has stronger trans-disciplinary influences than Girvan-Newman and label propagation, which causes more papers citing Blondel et al., 2008 do not cite any other citations of it. Further investigation is underway.

column9: Finding Patient Zero at Scale: How Training Data Size Impacts Detection Performance
column13: Identifying the source of an epidemic (the "patient zero") is crucial for containing outbreaks. Several source detection methods use simulated outbreaks as training data. Unlike deterministic methods, these approaches face a trade-off between performance and the cost of large training datasets, raising the question of how many simulations are sufficient in practice. Yet, little is known about their scaling behavior or optimal training set size.  Formally, given a static or temporal contact network, a starting time $t_0$, and a snapshot of node states at $t_{end} > t_0$, the goal is to identify the epidemic source. We use a susceptible–infectious (SI) model without recovery. For training, we simulate n outbreaks per node. Parameters are set so that the average outbreak infects roughly 50% of nodes. Ground-truth snapshots for evaluation are generated with the same SI model and parameters.  We compare three simulation-based methods with the leading deterministic approach, the Individual Based Approximation (IBA) [1]. (i) Monte Carlo Mean Field (MCMF) is a Monte Carlo approach that uses a mean-field assumption [2], while IBA is based on deterministic update equations with the same mean-field assumption. (ii) The Soft Margin Estimator (SME) is inspired by Approximate Bayesian Computing with the key parameter a>0 [3]. Smaller values of a place more relative weight on simulation outcomes that match the observed snapshot more closely. Under the SI model, SME converges theoretically to optimal detection performance as $n\to\infty$ and $a\to 0$, effectively approaching direct Monte Carlo. (iii) A standard Graph Neural Network (GNN) using graph convolutional layers [4] which, in case of a temporal network, is trained on the static network projection.  Figure 1 shows the first empirically demonstrated upper performance bound for the source detection problem, attained by SME on two small networks with progressively decreasing values of a (panels a-b). However, the number of simulations per node required to reach this performance plateau grows exponentially with network size, making it intractable for empirical networks (panels c-e). In contrast, MCMF and IBA perform reasonably well with little or no training data, respectively, but remain sub-optimal. Most strikingly, GNNs achieve near-optimal performance while also scaling rapidly.

column9: Graph-aware proper scoring rules for node selection tasks
column11: Hilfiker, Lorenz*; Brack, Nathan; Sterchi, Martin
column13: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph with $N=|V|$ nodes. A \emph{node selection task} on $G$ consists of inferring a single node $i\in V$. This subsumes important graph learning problems such as epidemic source detection, influence maximisation, or fault detection. Any edge selection task can also be recast as a node selection task on the line graph. Many approaches to such problems are probabilistic (e.g., Monte Carlo methods or graph neural networks), which means they estimate $i$ by providing a probability distribution $\vec{p}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^N$, $\|\vec{p}\|_1=1$, over $V$. Standard evaluation metrics in this setting such as top-$K$ error rate or the rank of $i$ are unsatisfactory for at least two reasons: (a)~these metrics do not take into account the graph structure when assessing how closely a prediction matches the observed true node, and (b)~they do not penalise unjustified overconfidence appropriately.  We address this gap by introducing two graph-aware scores for node selection tasks: firstly, the \emph{resistance score} $S(\vec{p},i)=-\frac{N}{2}(\vec{p}-\vec{e}_i)^\top\Omega(\vec{p}-\vec{e}_i)$ where $\vec{e}_i$ is the $i$-th unit vector and $\Omega$ is the matrix of resistance distances between all pairs of nodes~[1]; secondly, the \emph{diffusion score} $S_\tau(\vec{p}, i)=\frac{1}{4}(\vec{p}-\vec{e}_i)^\top e^{-\frac{\tau}{2}(L-\mathbb{I})}(\vec{p}-\vec{e}_i)$ with scaling parameter $\tau\in(0,\infty)$ where $L$ denotes the Laplacian of $G$. We show that these scores are \emph{proper scoring rules} [2] in the statistical sense, i.e., they are optimised when $\vec{p}$ coincides with the true distribution of $i$, discouraging unjustified overconfidence. On the complete graph both scores reduce to the well-known multi-class Brier score for $N$ independent classes. The resistance score admits an intuitive interpretation in terms of the recently introduced variance of Devriendt et al. [1] and reduces on the path graph $P_N$ to the standard ranked probability score for ordinal data [3]. The diffusion score, meanwhile, behaves like the Brier score at different scales: it coincides with the Brier score for $\tau\to 0$, while for $\tau\to\infty$ it only assesses whether $\vec{p}$ is concentrated on the correct global cluster. In this sense, it connects to recent work on Laplacian coarse-graining [4].  Figure~\ref{fig:fig1} illustrates the improved discriminative ability of our scores in a toy example. Further simulation experiments for source detection on empirical networks demonstrate that our scores successfully distinguish between models that traditional metrics fail to separate. Moreover, we demonstrate that both scores can be efficiently approximated even for very large networks using techniques based on Krylov subspaces and Laplacian solvers as explored in [5]. Their use as loss functions in graph neural networks is left for future work.

column9: Homophily and Classroom Composition in Adolescent Friendship Networks: Evidence from the Czech Republic
column11: Cartier van Dissel, Mauritz*; Lintner, Tomáš; Martin-Gutierrez, Samuel; Karimi, Fariba
column13: As adolescents spend a substantial portion of their daily lives in schools, peer relationships formed in classrooms play a central role in shaping their social, emotional, and academic development. Classroom friendships influence well-being, school engagement, and achievement, and they also provide early foundations for later-life weak ties with long-term social and economic relevance [3,4]. One of the most robust organizing principles of these networks is homophily—the tendency to form ties with similar others—particularly along dimensions such as gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status (SES).  Despite its centrality, empirical evidence on how classroom composition moderates homophily remains inconsistent. Contact theory predicts that increased diversity promotes intergroup ties and weakens homophilic tendencies, whereas conflict theory suggests that larger or more salient minority presence intensifies within-group bonding and intergroup separation [1,2]. Existing studies provide support for both perspectives, pointing to a need for integrative network-based approaches capable of disentangling individual-level tendencies from contextual effects. We address this gap using a large-scale, multi-dataset analysis of friendship networks among 4,697 students nested in 228 lower-secondary classrooms in the Czech Republic, from six independent studies, including a nationally representative sample. Focusing on gender, ethnicity, and SES, we apply an attractiveness–mixing model [5] to estimate group-specific homophily while accounting for individual differences in tie attractiveness. Results from the studies are synthesized using Bayesian meta-analysis and meta-regression, allowing us to assess robustness across datasets and to evaluate classroom composition as a systematic moderator of homophilic tendencies.  Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity in homophily across social dimensions. Gender homophily is largely symmetric for boys and girls, while ethnic homophily is stronger among majority (Czech) students than among ethnic minorities. High-SES students exhibit pronounced homophilic tendencies, whereas low-SES students do not. Classroom composition plays a decisive role: a higher proportion of girls amplifies girl–girl homophily and attenuates boy–boy homophily, while a higher proportion of ethnic minority students increases ethnic homophily for both majority and minority students. These results reconcile elements of contact and conflict theories and demonstrate how meso-level network environments condition micro-level tie formation in adolescent social networks.

column9: Pairwise and higher-order triads in neuronal activity networks
column11: Civilini, Andrea*; Latora, Vito; De Vico Fallani, Fabrizio
column13: In this study, we investigate the nature of the interactions between neurons in the visual system.  To this end, we considered neuronal spiking activity from the Neuropixels Visual Coding dataset (n=32 mice) of the Allen Brain Institute. We focus on primary visual area (VISp) and secondary visual areas, also referred to as "higher-order" because they receive direct input from VISp, exchange information among themselves, and send outputs to multimodal and motor-related regions.  First, we extract functional higher-order networks from multivariate time series of neuronal spiking activity.  Here, we employ a novel symbolic Bayesian approach that identifies higher-order relations in multivariate time series by mapping the original signals into symbolic sequences. Using this method, we extract 2- and 3-motifs, represented as 2- and 3-hyperedges in the functional hypergraph. Then, we compute the fraction of higher-order triads (3-motifs, i.e., closed triangles) relative to pairwise triads (3-cliques, i.e., open triangles). Specifically, the three neurons may all belong to the same area 'A', to two different areas 'A' and 'B', or to three distinct areas 'A', 'B', and 'C'.  Results show that neurons in the secondary areas of the visual system tend to exhibit a relatively larger fraction of higher-order triads compared to neurons in the primary visual area.  However, when looking at interactions between primary and secondary areas, we found that higher-order triads are significantly more represented when they involve two neurons in the same area, whether primary or secondary. These findings support a potential role of common-input schemes in the origin of higher-order interactions in the brain.

column9: The relevance of higher-order ties
column13: Higher-order networks effectively represent complex systems with group interactions. Existing methods usually overlook the relative contribution of group interactions (hyperedges) of different sizes to the overall network structure. Yet, this has many important applications, especially when the network has meaningful node labels. In this work, we propose a methodology to precisely measure the contribution of different orders to topological network properties. First, we propose the order contribution measure, which quantifies the contribution of hyperedges of different orders to the link weights (local scale), number of triangles (mesoscale) and size of the largest connected component (global scale) of the pairwise weighted network. Second, we propose the measure of order relevance, which gives insights in how hyperedges of different orders contribute to the considered network property. Most interestingly, it enables an assessment of whether this contribution is synergistic or redundant with respect to that of hyperedges of other orders. Third, to account for labels, we propose a metric of label group balance to assess how hyperedges of different orders connect label-induced groups of nodes. We applied these metrics to a large-scale board interlock network and scientific collaboration network, in which node labels correspond to geographical location of the nodes. Experiments including a comparison with randomized null models reveal how from the global level perspective, we observe synergistic contributions of orders in the board interlock network, whereas in the collaboration network orders contribute more redundantly. The findings shed new light on social scientific debates on the role of busy directors in global business networks and the connective effects of large author teams in scientific collaboration networks.

column9: Hierarchical structures in public procurement markets
column11: Pinheiro, Flávio L. *;  Sturm, Niclas Frederic; Candia, Cristian; Damásio, Bruno
column13: This study explores the structure of firm networks in Portugal’s public procurement market (2009–2022). Co-bidding networks for three legislative periods reveal a modular, hierarchical market with firms clustering by activity, region, or government entity. Increasing modularity suggests growing segmentation, while exponential degree distributions indicate connections based on shared operational scopes. Regression analysis shows that higher centrality (degree, betweenness, eigenvector) is associated with increased earnings per bid. Dominant firms within communities suppress competition, amplifying winning rate inequalities and reflecting broader European trends of declining competition. Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) face significant entry barriers, particularly outside core communities. The findings emphasize the need for targeted policies to strengthen SME competitiveness and promote equitable market access. The study advocates for interventions addressing structural inequalities to create a more inclusive, competitive public procurement environment, ensuring fair opportunities for all market participants.

column9: Emergence of giant component in percolated artificial neural networks
column11: Pontlevy, Adrien*; De Vico Fallani, Fabrizio
column13: Despite the fact that major recent artificial intelligence breakthroughs rely on the introduction of new architectures [1], from a theoretical perspective, the structure-function relationship of such networks remains largely unexplored. In this work, we explore how sparsity affects functional robustness, particularly in the context of pruning techniques designed to reduce parameter count. Recent studies have demonstrated that training deep learning models can induce heavy-tailed degree distributions [2, 3], which are known to significantly influence network dynamics. These distributions are revealed by diverse pruning strategies. We explore the implications of such an observation through the framework of percolation theory applied to the MNIST dataset (Fig. 1a). Our results show that the formation of a giant connected component systematically precedes the recovery of network performance. Specifically, percolating edges in descending order of weight accelerates the emergence of a giant component compared to random Bernoulli percolation. This phenomenon correlates with an early recovery of network performance (Fig. 1b,c). Notably, by adapting the theoretical percolation threshold for random networks, we derived an accurate analytical prediction of the percolation threshold in layered networks. We show that in networks composed of successive same-sized layers, the threshold stays independent of the number of layers in the limit of large width compared to the number of layers. Thus, the threshold only depends on the width of the network and is given by ρ = 1/2n where n is the number of nodes of each layer (Fig. 1c, top panel). Our findings suggest that learning inherently promotes sparse and robust structures, offering insights into the implicit architectural biases of trained networks.

column9: Structural reducibility of hypergraphs
column11: Kirkley, Alec*; Felippe, Helcio; Battiston, Federico
column13: Higher-order interactions provide a nuanced understanding of the relational structure of complex systems beyond traditional pairwise interactions. However, higher-order network analyses also incur more cumbersome interpretations and greater computational demands than their pairwise counterparts. Here we present an information-theoretic framework for determining the extent to which a hypergraph representation of a networked system is structurally redundant, and for identifying its most critical higher orders of interaction that allow us to remove these redundancies while preserving essential higher-order structure.

column9: Investigating the Effects of EEG Volume Conduction on Higher Order Interactions
column13: Volume conduction refers to the spread of electrical fields through the conductive tissues of the head, whereby each scalp electrode records a linear mixture of activity from multiple underlying neural sources, preventing sensor-level EEG signals from directly reflecting localized generators [1]. While functional brain interactions are typically assessed using pairwise measures, such approaches cannot capture higher-order interactions (HOIs) that arise when the joint behaviour of multiple regions cannot be reduced to pairwise contributions. The O-information rate (OIR) enables the spectral characterization of collective brain interactions, distinguishing synergistic effects (OIR< 0) emerging only at the group level from redundant interactions (OIR> 0) explained by subgroups of regions [2]. Although the impact of volume conduction on bivariate connectivity measures is well known, its effect on HOIs remains largely unexplored. This work aims at investigating whether and to what extent HOI analyses performed at the EEG sensor level allow a meaningful interpretation of synergistic or redundant interactions in terms of the underlying interacting neural sources. Given M cortical sources as realizations of a stochastic process, Xt = [X1,t, . . . , XM,t], and L scalp sensors as realizations of Yt = [Y1,t, . . . , YL,t], source dynamics are modelled via a strictly causal vector autoregressive (VAR) process Xt =∑p k=1 AkXn−k + Un, where p is the model order, Ak is the M × M matrix of coefficients and Un are white and uncorrelated innovation processes. The mapping from source space to sensor space can be expressed as follows: Yt = LXt, where L is an L × M matrix representing the extent to which the sources are mixed [1]. Here, we investigate the effect of volume conduction on HOIs in two configurations of M = L = 3 interacting cortical sources, namely a common-child and a common-driver structure, by setting the diagonal elements of L to unity and the off-diagonal elements to α. Figure 1 shows that mixing induces instantaneous couplings that alter the OIR, introducing spurious spectral components and progressively shifting the interaction balance toward redundancy as α increases. Our findings suggest that stronger mixing drives the network toward redundancy-dominated time-domain interactions and introduces spurious redundant or synergistic spectral components.

column9: Targeted County-Level Interventions Achieve Epidemic Control Without Statewide Lockdowns
column11: Das, Haridas; Hu, Tao; Santillana, Mauricio; Martins Stolerman, Lucas*
column13: When a new pathogen emerges, public health authorities must act rapidly to mitigate its spread while minimizing socioeconomic disruption. Despite extensive debate on localized epidemic control, no model-based study has systematically evaluated county-level interventions for statewide epidemic suppression in the United States. We present a metapopulation model that integrates county-level mobility data to identify epidemic hotspots and assess targeted intervention strategies for pandemic preparedness. We identify epidemic hotspots as counties that generate disproportionately large statewide epidemics when serving as outbreak origins. These hotspots align with population-dense and highly connected locations but provide sharper spatial contrast than traditional centrality metrics. Targeted interventions reducing the basic reproduction number (R0) only at hotspots achieve substantial epidemic control—reducing statewide epidemics by 60–90% in four representative states (Oklahoma, New York, Florida, and California)—without requiring broad lockdown measures. Hybrid strategies combining moderate reductions in R0 (10–30%) with partial mobility restrictions (30–80%) from hotspot counties, while preserving activity elsewhere, achieve control equivalent to full suppression at hotspots. This framework demonstrates that strategic, location-specific interventions can replace blanket pandemic responses. It provides state and county decision-makers with a quantitative tool for prospective pandemic planning, enabling rapid hotspot identification and intervention design grounded in empirical mobility networks.

column9: Integrating comparative protein biology with network medicine to elucidate the therapeutic role of plant chemicals for cardiovascular disease
column13: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death globally. Epidemiological studies demonstrate that plant-based diets provide cardioprotective benefits, yet our inability to predict precise molecular mechanisms limit precise dietary interventions. While network medicine offers a powerful framework for predicting how compounds modulate disease, the poor protein target characterization of plant chemicals creates severe data sparsity that prevents the systematic analysis of potential cardiovascular effects. We developed a computational framework that addresses this critical data limitation by integrating comparative protein biology with network medicine. This approach leverages the shared evolutionary origin and the co-evolutionary history of plants and humans, offering insight into how plant chemicals are recognized in human processes despite not being endogenously produced. Evolutionary conserved proteins and their associated functions between humans and plants account for 17{\%} of the human genome, allowing us to use the substantial body of plant biochemistry research to expand phytochemical-protein interaction data in humans. We identify a conserved homology module of 5,077 orthologous proteins within the human protein-protein interactome, creating a statistically significant largest connected component for use in network medicine analysis. For ten commonly consumed plants, we identify their plant chemicals and their human protein targets. We find that their targets are enriched within the homology module, indicating their importance to the modulation of the plant-human homology module. Additionally, the homology module is enriched with genes from cardiovascular disease modules. While the homology module contains many genes essential to eukaryotic life whose alternations typically associate with pathophenotypically severe Mendelian disorders or death rather than chronic, complex diseases, these orthologous proteins also include less connected proteins that contribute to CVD pathophysiology. By integrating plant-human homology with network medicine we create a systematic framework for predicting how plant chemicals affect cardiovascular health.

column9: Higher-order information-theoretic organization of motor modularity in health and stroke
column11: Deshpande, Raj*; Huber, Maximilian; Yarossi, Matthew; Petri, Giovanni
column13: Motor coordination subserving even simple activities of daily living requires navigating a high-dimensional space of muscle activations through nonlinear and task-dependent transformations. Despite this apparent complexity, the human motor system achieves robust, flexible, and transferable behavior across a wide range of tasks and contexts.  A leading theoretical explanation for this efficiency is the existence of muscle modules: low-dimensional coordination patterns that constrain and organize muscle activity (d'Avella, A., & Bizzi, E.; 2005). Traditionally, muscle modules have been extracted using linear dimensionality-reduction techniques, which provide compact representations but are limited in their ability to characterize multivariate and higher-order dependencies among muscles.  Here, we adopt a higher-order network perspective to investigate muscle coordination, leveraging information-theoretic tools that explicitly disentangle redundancy and synergy in multivariate interactions.  We analyze publicly available data comprising electromyography (EMG) recordings from 12 upper-limb muscles during 30 distinct motor tasks, performed by 23 healthy controls and 21 individuals with mild stroke (Wrist/Hand Fugl-Meyer: 14-20) (Averta, et al., 2021).  For each participant, we computed the O-information, a multivariate measure quantifying the balance between redundant and synergistic interactions across muscle subsets (Rosas et al.,2019). From the top-k multiplets, we constructed participant-specific hypergraphs capturing dominant redundancy- and synergy-based interactions (Figure 1A). Interpreting redundancy as reflecting stable muscle modules and synergy as a marker of inter-module coordination, we observed marked reorganization in stroke participants. At the group level, stroke patients exhibited increased redundancy alongside significantly reduced synergistic interactions (Figure 1B), consistent with more rigid or stereotyped motor control.  Crucially, at the participant level, this imbalance was highly heterogeneous (Figure 1C), revealing substantial inter-individual variability in higher-order coordination patterns following stroke—variability that may inform individualized rehabilitation strategies. Together, these results demonstrate that higher-order information-theoretic networks provide a principled framework for characterizing motor coordination beyond pairwise interactions, revealing clinically relevant alterations in the balance between stability and flexibility of muscle control after stroke.

column9: Breakdown and recovery dynamics of gene regulatory networks
column11: Aranha, Fellipe*; Levy, Orr; Sanhedrai, Hillel; Havlin, Shlomo; Medzhitov, Ruslan
column13: Recent single-cell experiments on Escherichia coli revealed that both breakdown and recovery exhibit long-tailed lag-time power-law distributions, with the complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) displaying a power-law decay with an exponent close to -2, associated with persister cells. This behavior occurs across various stress conditions, including starvation and antibiotic exposure, suggesting the existence of a universal underlying mechanism.  Assuming that living cells are complex dynamical systems whose survival under stress emerges from collective interactions within gene regulatory networks (GRNs), we combine experimental data, network theory, and dynamical models to study breakdown and recovery time based on GRNs. Essentially, gene regulatory dynamics arise from intrinsic decay, nonlinear regulatory interactions, and basal activity. We modeled breakdown and recovery as the weakening and restoration of regulatory interactions in a random network and the E. coli regulatory network.  Numerical simulations reveal a discontinuous transition between functional (gene expression) and non-functional (no gene expression) network states, leading to hysteresis between breakdown and recovery trajectories. Remarkably, the critical transition points can be predicted using the Gao–Barzel–Barabási universal resilience framework, which reduces the high-dimensional GRN dynamics to an effective one-dimensional control equation.  Our results show that the complementary cumulative distributions of breakdown and recovery lag times emerge from network-level dynamics exhibiting power-law tails with exponents close to -2, in quantitative agreement with single-cell experiments. These results suggest that persistence, aging, and memory effects arise from network-level dynamics rather than molecular fine-tuning, which is analogous to interdependent networks. Together, these findings provide a unifying network-based explanation for stress responses in cells, bridging experimental microbiology and statistical physics.

column9: Using Environmental Features to Improve Models of Urban Pedestrian Movement
column11: Johnson, Andrew*; Thakur, Gautam; Smyth, T.M.
column13: Predicting pedestrian movement remains difficult, and many approaches treat it primarily as a consequence of internal navigation rules. Yet movement is also shaped by the built environment [1]. Street segments differ in the destinations, services, and physical conditions they offer, and these differences can concentrate or disperse pedestrians over space. Here, we will treat an urban grid as a network of street segments, where pedestrian population at each segment acts as an observable signal of these forces. Focusing on Philadelphia (USA), Mexico City (Mexico), and Taipei (Taiwan), we ask which segment-level urban features best predict where pedestrians accumulate at a fixed time, and then use those learned relationships to parameterize and evaluate alternative agent-based movement models.  Our outcome feature for the built-environment analysis is the average street-segment pedestrian population from 12:00 pm to 3:00 pm local time on summertime weekends, defined as the number of unique devices present on each segment using aggregated, fine-grained mobility observations from Veraset. We will align these segment-level outcomes with built-environment and environmental covariates derived from Veraset built-feature data and Google Earth Engine.  Using a supervised regression workflow, we will predict segment-level pedestrian population from built-environment features and evaluate out-of-sample performance on randomly held-out segments. We will then use SHAP-based explanations to quantify positive and negative feature contributions to predicted segment population. We will translate these contributions into a segment 'preference' score that captures attraction and avoidance signals and use this score to weight the street network. This yields a diffusion network in which segment weights increase for segments predicted to concentrate pedestrians and decrease for segments predicted to repel presence.  Finally, we will compare two agent-based movement models. Model 1 uses standard shortest-path routing on an unweighted street network. Model 2 implements feature-weighted shortest-path routing, in which the cost of traversing a segment combines distance with its learned preference weight.  We will assess how well the feature-weighted model captures human deviations from shortest paths by comparing, for each origin–destination pair, the ratio of path length to metric shortest-path length for simulated and observed trajectories; the pure shortest-path model provides a baseline with ratio 1.0 for all pairs [2]. Second, we will use a likelihood-based comparison: for each observed human path, we will simulate many trajectories under each model on the same origin–destination pair, estimate the probability of reproducing that path, and aggregate log-likelihoods across paths. Following Bongiorno et al., we will bin paths by origin–destination separation, tune feature-weighted model parameters within each bin via leave-one-out cross-validation, and compute the fraction of paths in each bin for which the feature-weighted model attains higher pointwise likelihood than the baseline shortest-path model [2].

column9: Impact of top venues on creative careers in science and art
column11: Liu, Yixuan*; Dorantes-Gilardi, Rodrigo; Han, Larry; László Barabási, Albert
column13: Career opportunities and recognition in creative fields are enhanced by access to top venues, such as publication in elite journals for scientists or invitations to exclusive biennials for artists. Yet, little is known about the magnitude of these effects or how selective access to venues reinforces discrimination based on gender, career stage, and nationality. We reconstruct the careers of over 3.4 million physicists and 1 million visual artists using annual performance data from Dimensions and Artfacts.net. Our results reveal a statistically significant venue-mediated effect associated with top venues in both science and art.

column9: DomiCoarse: dominance-based coarsening that preserves structure and dynamics in complex networks
column11: Engsig, Marcus*; Tejedor, Alejandro; Fernandez, Marco; Moreno, Yamir
column13: The rapid growth of empirical network data has pushed many classical analysis and simulation techniques beyond computational feasibility, motivating the development of network coarsening methods that reduce system size while preserving essential structure and dynamics. Existing approaches typically rely on similarity-based aggregation, spectral embeddings, or community detection, often at the cost of interpretability, scalability, or dynamical fidelity. Here, we introduce a dominance-based coarsening framework in which nodes are hierarchically absorbed according to their structural influence (dominance), producing a reduced network that preserves both local and global connectivity patterns. Coarsening is performed through a new absorption mechanism whereby dominant nodes fractionally incorporate subdominant neighbors and inherit their interactions through a principled rewiring scheme, ensuring degree preservation and conservation of key structural and dynamical properties (see Fig 1a). Focusing on spreading dynamics (SIR), we show that the coarse-grained representation faithfully reproduces the temporal evolution observed on the original network, despite a substantial reduction in network size. In particular, the coarsened network captures both the timing and amplitude of the spreading process, indicating that the reduction does not distort the dominant dynamical pathways (Fig 1b).   Beyond synthetic benchmarks, the dominance-based approach preserves key structural and spectral properties across a wide range of networks, enabling efficient simulations and multiscale analysis of large complex systems. By explicitly encoding hierarchical dominance rather than similarity, this new framework offers an interpretable and scalable alternative to existing coarsening techniques, opening new possibilities for the analysis of network dynamics at previously inaccessible scales.

column9: The geometry of persuasion: Social judgement theory in a belief embedding space
column11: Lee, Byunghwee*; An, Jisun; Kwak, Haewoon; Ahn, Yong-Yeol
column13: How much can we be persuaded by an argument? Social Judgment Theory (SJT) predicts an inverted-U relationship between belief discrepancy and persuasion magnitude, whereby messages that are neither too similar to nor too distant from a receiver’s position can persuade the most. Yet empirical validation has largely been restricted to small-scale, tightly controlled surveys on specific issues. Here, we present systematic behavioral evidence for this prediction in a natural setting by integrating real-world debate behavior with a computational framework for measuring meaningful distance between beliefs and positions–belief embeddings. The embedding space functions as a continuous analogue of a belief network, where beliefs are connected by co-occurrences and embedding is trained by the empirical trajectories of users on this network. Using a large language model (LLM) fine-tuned on belief trajectories from 40,280 users across 59,986 debates on Debate.org, we map beliefs and individuals into a high-dimensional space where geometric distances encode the likelihood that a user holding one belief will hold another.  We find that the relative discrepancy d_rel, reflecting the user's relative proximity to two opposing beliefs, robustly predicts both initial belief choices and post-debate belief changes. These changes take the form of persuasion (movement toward the farther belief, Fig.1b) and reversion (movement toward the closer belief, Fig.1c). Aggregating thousands of belief-change events, we observe a clear inverted-U pattern: although the probability of persuasion decreases with d_rel, the overall magnitude peaks at intermediate d_rel (Fig.1d,f), consistent with SJT. In contrast, the probability of reversion remains nearly constant, resulting in a magnitude that increases linearly with d_rel (Fig.1e,g). At the topic level, categories with moderate relative discrepancy exhibit larger magnitudes of persuasion, offering an explanation for why beliefs about “Entertainment”, “Arts”, shift more readily than those about “Religion” or “Philosophy”.  These structured geometric patterns do not arise in pretrained base LLMs, which produce distance-insensitive predictions. This contrast demonstrates that the observed persuasion geometry is not an artifact of LLMs but emerges only when embeddings encode meaningful semantic and contextual relationships among beliefs. Together, our findings reveal how the geometry of latent belief space provides a quantitative framework for understanding belief change, offering a scalable approach to studying persuasion in natural environments and a foundation for modeling belief dynamics.

column9: Origins of the Fittest: Clonal interference in the World Aviation Network
column13: Clonal interference, the competition between strains carrying different beneficial mutations, plays a crucial role in shaping evolutionary outcomes in asexual populations.  Since the spread of new mutations is critical for CI, it is strongly influenced by the structure of the population. In particular, linear or planar structures restrict spread to slow, wave-like patterns, hindering adaptation, whereas long-range connections can rapidly distribute new strains, decreasing clonal competition. We investigate how this phenomenon unfolds in the the World Aviation Network (WAN), which shapes the population structure of microorganisms that use humans as hosts, including pathogens.   Our novel analytical framework models the succession of adaptive mutations as a Markov Renewal Process. This process is built by leveraging epidemic modeling methods that have been very successful in predicting pathogen spread on the WAN, here used to model mutation spread.  Or approach reveals how the interplay between mutation rate and network topology gives rise to evolutionary regimes: At low mutation rates, strains originating from globally central nodes have higher fixation probabilities, while at higher mutation rates, meso-scale and local properties become more important (see Panel A).  Applied to the WAN, affluent, western regions are most likely origins of high-fitness lineages in the low-rate regime, shifting to more populous nations in Asia at high rates (see Panel B).  Because of the logarithmic scaling of arrival time with traveler flux, reducing travel in low-travel, long-range links has usually a stronger impact on spreading behavior (per traveler). In the CI regime however, low-traffic nodes become particularly unlikely origins of new strains.   The framework provides valuable insights how spatial structure shapes evolutionary outcome, with particular relevance for control strategies aiming to slow down the spread of high-fitness strains.

column9: Resonance in Social Media: Novelty, Network Position, and Diffusion in Online Mobilization
column13: Research on framing alignment in social movements and protest mobilization has long emphasized the importance of constructing interpretations of the social world that resonate with broader audiences by appealing to shared interests, values, and beliefs [1]. However, despite extensive work on framing processes, less is known about the mechanisms through which particular messages achieve resonance [2], especially from a network perspective. Importantly, resonance has increasingly been understood as an emergent property of social interaction rather than a fixed attribute of messages, yet prior studies—while highlighting the role of emotional content, linguistic variation, and semantic novelty [2]—have rarely accounted for the relational structures through which these interactions unfold. To address this gap, we examine how semantic novelty and network position jointly shape message diffusion during large-scale protest mobilization.  We investigate these dynamics using Twitter data from the 2019 Chilean estallido social, a wave of sustained, large-scale protest characterized by decentralized organization and the coexistence of multiple competing frames. This context provides a particularly good case for studying resonance as an emergent phenomenon, since no single actor or narrative dominated attention and message uptake depended on how frames circulated through the communication network. Using a dataset of 1,800,000 retweets from the #ChileDesperto, we construct a temporal interaction network of Twitter users, measuring message resonance as retweet counts, semantic novelty using a word embedding–based approach [3], and network position as authors’ cumulative in-degree prior to each tweet.  Our preliminary results suggest that, while the analysis replicates previous findings of a curvilinear relationship between semantic novelty and diffusion, this relationship is systematically moderated by network position. As novelty increases, the relative advantage of centrality diminishes, allowing highly novel messages from peripheral actors to achieve levels of diffusion comparable to those of more central users. Together, these findings contribute to theoretical understandings of resonance in the framing literature and suggest plausible mechanisms through which peripheral actors may emerge as “crowdsourced elites”[4] in social media networks.  [1] Snow et al. (1986). Frame Alignment Processes, Micromobilization, and Movement Participation. American Sociological Review, 51(4), 464–481. [2] McDonnell et al. (2017). A Theory of Resonance. Sociological Theory, 35(1), 1–14. [3] Shi and Evans (2020). Science and technology advance through surprise. ArXiv:1910.09370. [4] Papacharissi and de Fatima Oliveira (2012). Affective new and networked publics: The rhythms of news storytelling on #Egypt. Journal of Communication, 62, 266–282.

column9: Multi-Scale Network Structure Amplifies Measles Transmission Risk in the U.S.: Dimensionality Reduction Reveals Four Independent Axes of Spatial Heterogeneity
column13: Spatial networks of disease transmission exhibit scale-dependent properties emerging from the interplay between administrative boundaries, geographic connectivity, and population mixing patterns, yet the optimal spatial scale for quantifying outbreak risk remains poorly characterized. We construct multi-layer spatial networks of measles transmission across the U.S. using school (n≈50,000), district (n≈13,000), and county (n≈3,000) nodes connected via gravity-model kernels calibrated to R_0=15. Integrating state-by-state MMR vaccination coverage from 2015–2024, we compute effective reproduction numbers, R_v as dominant eigenvalues of connectivity-weighted next-generation matrices at each scale. District-level networks consistently exhibit the highest R_v—a robust non-monotonic pattern (district > school > county) arising from optimal network topology at intermediate spatial aggregation. This amplification reflects three mechanisms: (1) enrollment-weighted aggregation emphasizes large under-vaccinated schools within districts, (2) moderate connectivity density balances local clustering with broader reach, and (3) administrative boundary misalignment enables cross-boundary spillover, school district boundaries frequently overlap multiple counties, creating connectivity pathways where students interact across county lines through shared district facilities, transportation networks, and activities, thereby enhancing disease transmission potential beyond what county-level aggregation captures. School-level networks show fragmented high-risk clusters; county-level aggregation over-smooths this heterogeneity despite similar mean susceptibility.  To disentangle transmission risk drivers beyond mean coverage, which correlates with all measured indices, we apply non-metric multidimensional scaling to five state-level metrics: mean coverage, median coverage, R_v, Gini index, and Geary's C (spatial autocorrelation). Four significant dimensions emerge: Dimension 1 captures correlated coverage-R_v; Dimension 2 isolates spatial heterogeneity (Geary's C) independent of mean coverage, separating high-clustering states (Minnesota) from uniform states (Virginia, Connecticut) at comparable average coverage; Dimension 3 reflects distributional skewness (median independent of mean), identifying vulnerable lower-tail populations; Dimension 4 captures R_vvariance orthogonal to coverage, demonstrating network connectivity effects beyond susceptibility alone. Temporal analysis shows divergent trajectories: Minnesota exhibits increasing prevalence of susceptible aged from 5 to 17 years with geographic expansion, while California shows decreasing prevalence with spatial contraction, corresponding to movement through MDS feature space. This framework establishes districts as the critical spatial scale where topology and susceptibility synergistically amplify outbreak risk, while four-dimensional characterization identifies actionable intervention typologies for heterogeneous vaccination landscapes.

column9: Who gets seen? Nationality bias in international art exhibitions
column13: The global art world, despite its purported embrace of diversity and internationalism [1], frequently exhibits a discernible nationality bias. This phenomenon refers to the disproportionate inclusion, recognition, and visibility of artists and art originating from certain nations, predominantly Western ones, over those from other regions [2,3,4]. Existing research is predominantly qualitative or measures nationality bias using raw proportions unadjusted for population baselines, creating a need for large-scale computational analysis that systematically accounts for underlying artist distributions.    We use publicly available datasets from [5] to examine patterns of nationality bias in global art exhibitions. Our sample consists of 22,338 artists from 177 nationalities who exhibited at least 10 times since 1985 in venues spanning 93 exhibiting countries. We first compare, for each country, the observed entropy of artist-nationality distributions across its exhibitions to a null model derived from Monte Carlo simulations in which artists are drawn from the global pool with equal probability at matched sample sizes. The divergence between the empirical entropy (blue line) and the random sampling from the global artist population (grey line) indicates systematic under-representation of nationality diversity in the global exhibition system (Fig. 1A). The inverted U-shaped trajectory of the empirical entropy shows that nations with the highest exhibition frequencies exhibit diminishing marginal returns to diversity despite their greater capacity. This naturally raises a question:  To what extent does the over-/under-representation relationship between venue countries and artists' nationalities explain the systematic under-representation of nationality diversity?  To address this question, we quantify the over-/under-representation of each artist's nationality within each venue country using standardized residuals from multinomial tests. This enables us to characterize the distribution of statistically significant home bias (Fig. 1D) and construct a network of over-representation patterns between countries (Fig. 1E).  Through Monte Carlo simulations, we identify that home country preference emerges as the dominant bias mechanism (Pearson's r = 0.909, p-value<0.01), and community-based cultural affinities represent a secondary but significant influence that reinforces clustering beyond domestic favoritism (Pearson's r = 0.796, p-value<0.01) (Fig. 1B). Together, dual bias control yields a near-perfect fit, accounting for roughly 94% of the variance in nationality diversity (Fig. 1C).    These findings suggest that policies aimed at increasing nationality diversity are likely to be constrained unless they address the preference-based mechanisms embedded in institutional selection processes and transnational cultural networks.

column9: From batch correction to covariate modeling in coexpression networks
column13: Gene coexpression networks are widely used to model interrelationships between gene pairs in various biological contexts [1]. Because gene transcriptional activity can be measured under various conditions, technical factors can introduce unwanted variation in gene expression, which can spread through downstream analyses such as the inference of correlation networks. A standard approach for controlling these effects is to correct for batch [2], for example due to sequencing platforms and locations before computing correlations, akin to a partial correlation. However, this procedure does not correct for non-linear effects such batch effects introducing changes in correlations between genes, which is crucial for building robust correlation networks.  In this presentation, we will discuss our recent work quantifying the magnitude and persistence of batch effects in correlation networks (Figure 1) even after batch correction with standard procedures such as LIMMA and discuss a method we developed called Coexpression Batch Reduction Adjustment (COBRA) that effectively addresses high-order batch effects by estimating association scores for each condition separately, for example, effects due to case/control as opposed to those induced by batch/location. We have applied our approach to build gene regulatory networks in thyroid cancer using The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and have shown that the batch corrected networks estimated by COBRA reflect more meaningful biology for thyroid physiology than networks without batch correction. We have recently expanded our method to account for general covariate modeling in coexpression networks, which required a new formulation that results in positive semi-definite decomposition of covariate matrices, thereby expanding scope and interpretability of components decomposing coexpression matrices for each covariate.  As coexpression networks continue to be used for comparisons between biological conditions either as a stand alone approach [1] or as input for machine learning methods [3], it is crucial to address unwanted variation induced by batch effects and isolate intervention effects to better estimate accurate effect sizes in health, disease, and due to treatment.

column9: Self-consistent analysis of the Higher-Order Kuramoto Model
column13: The Kuramoto model on networks with higher-order interactions has recently been shown to exhibit bistability, explosive transitions, and rich dynamical behavior. However, most existing analytical approaches rely on all-to-all coupling or mean-field descriptions of network structure. While these methods accurately predict typical dynamics in the thermodynamic limit, they perform poorly for finite networks, specific network realizations, or particular oscillator frequency configurations. To address these limitations, we develop a self-consistent analytical framework for the Kuramoto model with higher-order interactions defined on hypergraphs. We introduce generalized local order parameters that capture the collective influence of both dyadic and triadic phase interactions and employ two complementary approximation schemes to obtain closed-form expressions for these local order parameters, which can be used to determine the global order parameter and the onset of synchronization.  The first approximation, the Time-Averaged Theory (TAT), averages oscillator phases over time at equilibrium without averaging over oscillator frequencies, therefore capturing the effect of correlations between oscillator frequencies and network structure. The second approach, the Frequency Distribution Approximation (FDA), averages over both phase and frequency distributions. Using the FDA formalism, we perform a perturbative analysis near the critical point, yielding explicit expressions for the synchronization threshold in arbitrary finite-size networks and identifying a critical point that separates regimes with and without bistability. Analytical results show that triadic interactions significantly modify the bifurcation structure, introducing bistable regimes and hysteretic transitions. Numerical simulations on networks with homogeneous (uniform) and heterogeneous (power-law) degree distributions support the theoretical predictions and highlight differences in the applicability of the two approximation schemes. Overall, this framework provides a unified perspective on multi-body synchronization and emphasizes the role of higher-order network topology in controlling collective dynamics.

column9: Unveiling the Spatial Structure of Primary Care Networks: A Network-Based Digital Twin of the Austrian Healthcare System
column13: Healthcare systems operate as adaptive spatial networks in which patients continuously reorganize care pathways while providers enter and exit the system. Yet most policy analyses remain static and capacity-based, limiting insight into system-level resilience. We present a network-based digital twin of the Austrian primary care system, implemented as a stochastic agent- based model grounded in nationwide administrative claims data covering millions of patient–doctor interactions across all municipalities. The framework integrates a bipartite patient–doctor network, a derived patient-sharing network among providers, and explicit geographic embedding to capture spatial frictions and competitive structure. Patient behavior is modeled through a utility-based agent decision framework, where care choices depend on distance, provider availability, and local competition. Without imposing route-level targets or aggregate flow constraints, patient reallocations arise endogenously as an emergent outcome of decentralized decision-making. The digital twin enables simulation of realistic system shocks, such as physician retirements and regional workforce imbalances, and tracks the resulting reconfiguration of patient flows. Applied to Austria, the model reveals pronounced urban–rural asymmetries. Despite its stochastic micro-level formulation, the model generate the dominant mesoscopic spatial structure of observed patient flow networks. Our model shows that national healthcare systems can be represented as adaptive spatial networks, and how data- driven digital twins can support anticipatory, network-based health system analysis. This framework supports scenario- based exploration of healthcare system resilience under demographic and workforce change.

column9: Behavior-driven dynamics of urban mobility networks improve epidemic forecasting
column11: Yao, Qing; Ashcroft-Jones, Sarah; Yang, Wan; Ruggeri, Kai; Pei, Sen*
column13: Urban mobility networks mediate infectious disease transmission by dynamically reshaping contact patterns across space and time. However, most epidemic models treat mobility networks as static or externally prescribed, overlooking how individual decision-making and local epidemic conditions reconfigure network structure. Here, we examine how behavioral heterogeneity drives the evolution of urban mobility networks and how explicitly forecasting these networks improves neighborhood-level epidemic predictions.  Using New York City as a case study, we integrate survey-derived behavioral measures with high-resolution mobility data to characterize adaptive changes in inter-neighborhood mobility networks during the COVID-19 pandemic. Mobility networks are represented as weighted, directed origin–destination matrices constructed from aggregated, anonymized mobile device visits to points of interest (POIs). Behavioral attributes—including temporal discounting, loss aversion, and a newly constructed agency score—are measured through a series of financial and daily activity-based choice tasks for 816 individuals across 16 ZIP-code areas. These traits exhibit clear spatial clustering and are systematically associated with changes in mobility network structure, including edge weights and persistence across activity layers [1].  To model the temporal evolution of mobility networks, we develop a Graph Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory (GNN–LSTM) framework that predicts weekly, activity-specific mobility matrices among 42 neighborhoods. The model integrates historical network states, local COVID-19 incidence, behavioral attributes, and socioeconomic covariates, enabling forecasting of mobility networks under changing epidemic conditions. The predicted mobility networks are then embedded within a networked SEIRV model to simulate disease transmission dynamics [2]. Retrospective analyses show that explicitly forecasting mobility networks—rather than relying on static or lagged flows—significantly improves short-term (1–4 week) epidemic forecasts, particularly during periods of rapid behavioral adaptation.  Together, these findings demonstrate that mobility networks are not passive or static structures, but adaptive systems shaped by behavioral responses and epidemic pressure. Incorporating behavior-driven mobility network dynamics provides a principled pathway for improving epidemic forecasting and offers a general framework for studying coevolving networks in human–disease systems.  [1] Yao, Qing, et al. "Person, place, or preference? Combining subjective and objective decision agency with choice preferences predicts behavior during major shifts in human mobility." medRxiv (2025): 2025-09. [2] Zhang, Renquan, et al. "Behavior-driven forecasts of neighborhood-level COVID-19 spread in New York City." PLOS Computational Biology 21.4 (2025): e1012979.

column9: Networked inequities in regional climate impacts research production
column11: Burattini Freire, Isabela*; Madruga de Brito, Mariana; Nunes Carvalho, Taís Maria
column13: Low-income countries remain significantly underrepresented in global climate research production, largely due to limitations in scientific funding and institutional capacity[1]. This imbalance has been shown to undermine the legitimacy and credibility of international climate agreements[2]. Key questions remain about how regional climate impacts research production has evolved over time, and how its geographic focus is distributed. In this study, we examine global inequalities in climate impacts research production using a network approach, with particular emphasis on the divide between the Global North and South. We quantify structural inequalities in collaboration patterns by measuring homophily in co-authorship networks using adjusted assortativity, which corrects for imbalances in group sizes between low-income (minority group) and middle- and high-income countries (majority group). These networks are constructed from a dataset of more than 100,000 open- and closed-access climate impacts-related scientific publications sourced from OpenAlex, whose relevance is identified through a machine-learning pipeline. Preliminary results indicate that the propensity for low-income countries to engage in international research collaborations has increased, as evidenced by a decline in assortativity over time (Fig. 1a). However, disparities in research productivity persist: assortativity measured in publication-weighted networks remains stable, suggesting that increased connectivity has not yet translated into more equitable research output (Fig 1b). We further investigate the geographic focus of climate impacts research, distinguishing between studies conducted within specific world regions, targeting particular regions, or in collaboration with researchers from those regions. Through this analysis, we assess whether international collaborations function as bridges that enhance research capacity in the Global South or, instead, reinforce North-centric dominance in climate impacts research production. By making disparities visible and measurable, this work provides empirical foundations for more equitable and just climate impacts research collaborations, and more coherent international policy frameworks.
