Change 7, pp. 21–27, 2017, doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate3163. [2]	Collyer, F.M., “Global patterns in the publishing of academic knowledge: Global North, global South”. Curr. Sociol. 66, pp. 56–73, 2018, doi: https://doi.org/10.1177/0011392116680020.

column9: Detection of Anomalous Delays in Real-time New York City Subway Data
column11: Ginige, Nipuna; LaRock, Timothy*; Hackl, Jürgen
column13: The New York City subway, operated by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), is one of the largest and well-used subway systems in the world, with around 472 stations, 22 train lines, and daily ridership of more than 3 million people [1]. As with any major transit system, delays on the subway are inevitable. Despite recent investments, as of 2024 the Office of the New York State Comptroller reported that about 18\% of trains did not reach their destination on time, with the majority of delays caused by infrastructure failures, planned maintenance work, and delays from police actions/medical responses [2]. The subway also has to contend with flooding from major rain events, which are anticipated to increase in frequency and severity due to climate change. When stations and lines are disrupted, MTA operators must make critical decisions about how to minimize system-wide impact and guarantee the safety of riders. These decisions must be made by human operators, who combine their experience and knowledge of the subway system with insights from computer-aided data analysis to make decisions.  Our goal in this work is to use public subway schedule and real-time data to build a network-informed anomaly detection model for delays that not only identifies whether trains are on time, but also predicts the potential overall severity of a delay, accounting for cascade effects that individual local delays may have through the larger network. As a first step, here we show preliminary results on the pattern of delays on a typical Friday (October 26th, 2025) in the subway. We retrieve subway schedules and historical arrival and departure data from the public MTA Developer API [3]. In Figure 1 we show the subway network excluding the Staten Island Railway, which is not connected to the rest of the system by rail. Nodes are stations and colors represent the average arrival delay in minutes across all trains arriving at that station on October 26th, where darker colors indicate larger average delay. The stations with the largest average delays on this day were distributed throughout the system, with some near the extremes (Broad Channel on the Rockaway line) and others near the heart of the system (145th St in Harlem serving the A, B, C, and D lines).  The middle plot shows a histogram of per-station delays, which follows a roughly normal distribution, with most stations having average delays of about 2 minutes, but a few having average delays of over 4 minutes. Since many stations in the subway serve multiple lines, in the right-hand plot we show the distribution of mean delay per station within each line, sorted along the vertical axis by the maximum average delay, shown by the right whisker. From this plot we can see that stations serving the F train had the widest distribution, with at least one station seeing a mean delay of more than 15 minutes and another seeing trains leave early on average, possibly due to previous delays. In contrast, the C train (8th Avenue Local) showed the closest to ideal behavior, with both mean and maximum station delays close to 0.  As next steps, we plan to expand this analysis by characterizing delay patterns and correlations across different operational, temporal, and spatial resolutions. Then, we will develop models for anomalous delay detection that go beyond the difference between scheduled and real arrival times at individual stations to predict the potential for severe disruption across the network. We will connect ideas from the dynamics of cascading failures, path-based higher-order network science, and transportation engineering to develop efficient and effective predictive models that can be leveraged to assist in decision making for subway operators and riders alike. Accessed December 18, 2025. https://api.mta.info/#/

column9: Epidemic surveillance and control on mobility-driven metapopulation networks
column13: Understanding how network structure shapes epidemic dynamics is critical for surveillance and intervention in spatially structured populations. Human mobility generates heterogeneous, directed contact networks that strongly influence outbreak timing, spatial spread, and the effectiveness of control strategies. Here, we present a general network-based framework that integrates fine-scale mobility networks with epidemic dynamics to support early outbreak detection and targeted intervention. We construct directed, weighted mobility networks at the Zip Code Tabulation Area (ZCTA) level using large-scale visitation and commuting data, where nodes represent communities and edge weights encode movement intensity. Focusing on pre-season mobility networks, we quantify how network structure—captured through centrality and connectivity measures—relates to epidemic outcomes such as outbreak onset, peak timing, and cumulative burden. These network features are embedded into a stochastic metapopulation SEIRS model, allowing transmission parameters and intervention processes to vary across nodes and time. Applying the framework to multi-year data on influenza, COVID-19, and RSV in Texas, we find that ZCTAs occupying central positions in mobility networks consistently experience earlier outbreak onset and higher disease burden. Incorporating network-informed risk metrics improves lead time for outbreak detection and enables the evaluation of surveillance placement and vaccine allocation strategies on the network. While Texas serves as a detailed case study, the framework is designed to be scalable and transferable across regions and pathogens. Overall, our results demonstrate how combining mobility-driven network structure with epidemic dynamics provides a unified, generalizable approach to surveillance and control on spatial contact networks. This work highlights the role of pre-season network organization in shaping epidemic trajectories and offers a generalizable methodology for network-based public health interventions.

column9: Modeling Sleep Dynamics in the Wild: State Networks from Large-Scale Wearable Data
column13: The widespread adoption of consumer wearables enables large-scale, longitudinal observation of sleep–wake behaviour outside laboratory settings, yielding heterogeneous and irregularly sampled time series across individuals. We leverage data from the German Corona Data Donation Project (Corona-Datenspende-App), comprising resting heart rate, physical activity (step count), and sleep duration time series from over 120,000 voluntary participants in uncontrolled, real-world settings. [1] From wearable-derived sleep–wake trajectories, we construct nightly summaries capturing sleep timing, fragmentation, and wake burden across multi-day windows, and identify a small number of stable sleep phenotypes using manifold learning (UMAP) and density-based clustering (DBSCAN) (Fig. 1). While these phenotypes provide a compact description of sleep organization, their relevance lies not only in static structure but in how individuals transition between them over time. [2,3] To study the temporal organization of sleep phenotypes under irregular sampling, we model phenotype sequences using continuous-time Markov and continuous-time hidden Markov frameworks that explicitly account for variable observation intervals common in longitudinal wearable data. [4] We treat cluster-derived phenotypes as interpretable observed states, yielding a low-dimensional transition network with edges parametrized by transition rates and implied lag-specific transition probabilities. In parallel, we explore Bayesian non-parametric state inference, learning the effective number of persistent states directly from data.This approach provides a principled route to validate and refine the low-dimensional observed phenotypes. [5] Because sleep phenotype changes are not spontaneous but driven by physiology and behaviour, we extend transition modeling with covariates: resting heart rate and physical activity are used to explain variation in transition probabilities between phenotypes. Finally, to investigate the broader interplay between sleep phenotypes and physiological markers, we employ time-varying dynamic Bayesian networks to infer temporal dependency structures from readily available wearablederived covariates. This approach enables the construction of a network, which could be used to test for time-varying physiological alterations associated with clinical labels, such as persistent post-infection symptoms (e.g., long COVID).

column9: Designing interlayer coupling in multilayer networks of the human musculoskeletal system
column13: The musculoskeletal system is characterized by the coexistence of diverse and complex interactions among heterogeneous entities. It involves multiple types of connections, and this heterogeneity highlights the limitations of existing network representations, such as bipartite and hypergraph models. Multilayer networks provide a natural way to address this limitation by incorporating interlayer dependencies. However, how to design interlayer couplings that preserve structurally meaningful differences between layers remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigated several multilayer models with different interlayer coupling schemes and assessed their applicability to musculoskeletal systems. We compared full replica coupling, targeted partial coupling in which only bone replicas form interlayer links, and single-layer aggregation. Using a supra-matrix formulation, we analyzed the spectral properties of these models constructed from human musculoskeletal data and found that, unlike full coupling, partial coupling led to a non-trivial maximization of spectral entropy at intermediate interlayer coupling strengths. This behavior reflects a regime in which contributions from distinct structural modes are maximally differentiated, indicating a balanced interplay among heterogeneous components that would otherwise be concealed by full coupling or aggregation.

column9: Bridging Silos: Visualizing Intra-University Collaboration Networks
column11: Liu, Zhuoqi*; 	Murray, Dakota; Lungeanu, Alina
column13: Universities invest heavily in interdisciplinary research initiatives, such as cluster hiring and cross-department research centers. However, administrators often lack effective tools to target and evaluate these investments, and silos remain entrenched [1]. We address this gap by developing a visualization tool for analysis of intra-university collaboration.  We construct internal collaboration networks by identifying faculty in the bibliometric database OpenAlex and extracting co-authorship relationships. So far, we have examined three institutions, including The Rockefeller University (Fig. 1a), Harvard Medical School (Fig. 1b), and Northeastern University. Specifically for Northeastern University, we manually curated a dataset of faculty and research units and built temporal network snapshots (Fig. 1c). Instead of focusing on cross-national or cross-university networks of collaboration, our approach reveals the mesoscale structure of collaboration inside institutions. The community clusters we identify align with departmental boundaries and confirm the presence of disciplinary silos.  Our framework attempts to address a dual-audience design challenge: serving both administrators needing strategic insights and researchers seeking collaborators. The interactive prototype (Fig. 1d) implements Shneiderman's mantra [2] through force-directed layouts with filtering by unit, time, and collaboration strength, allowing comparison between departments and research centers.  Preliminary findings reveal considerable variation in network topology. Rockefeller's laboratory-centric model produces tightly clustered communities, while Harvard Medical School's consolidated departments show more integrated structures with numerous bridging ties. Temporal snapshots from Northeastern University show how these patterns evolve (Fig. 1c), with inter-unit views (Fig. 1e) revealing collaboration boundaries across organizational units. Individual researchers also differ: some collaborate within their department, while others serve as cross-disciplinary bridges (Fig. 1f). These bridging positions do not appear on organizational charts but are key to knowledge flow and show untapped opportunities.  This work shows a reproducible methodology applicable to any university. It supports current interdisciplinary efforts by making silos visible and uncovering hidden opportunities for collaboration.

column9: Markovian ε-SIR on the complete graph
column13: We investigate the continuous-time Markovian SIR epidemic with self-infection on the complete graph. We introduce a labelling of the state space based on Cantor’s zig-zag enumeration and show that, under this ordering, the infinitesimal generator of the process is an upper triangular matrix with a bidiagonal block structure. This structure allows us to derive an exact analytical solution for the time evolution of the state probabilities. However, given the complexity of the explicit solution, we derive an asymptotic expansion valid in the large-system limit, thus allowing a clearer understanding of the model’s limiting behavior as the system size becomes arbitrarily large. We then compare the exact dynamics of the Markovian SIR on the complete graph with the classical Kermack McKendrick (KM) approximation and also derive an analytical criterion to evaluate the accuracy of the approximation. Our analysis indicates that the KM model overestimates the number of infected individuals, in agreement with mean-field approximations. The discrepancy between Markovian SIR and KM is particularly significant near the epidemic threshold, consistent with theoretical predictions.

column9: Mobility Constraints and Social Choices Drive Age Segregation
column13: Urban segregation increasingly reflects patterns of everyday social encounters rather than residential separation alone. From a network science perspective, segregation can be understood as an emergent property of repeated interactions embedded in mobility networks, where individuals are linked through co-presence in shared activity spaces. While age segregation is widely observed across cities, the mechanisms shaping these interaction patterns remain poorly understood.  Using large-scale individual-level mobility data from 100 major U.S. metropolitan areas, we quantify age segregation through two complementary exposure-based measures that capture different network dimensions of social mixing: an entropy-based index measuring individual-level diversity of encounters, and a correlation-based index capturing population-level age homophily. Across cities, we find a systematic divergence between these two dimensions: larger metropolitan areas provide more diverse individual exposure opportunities, yet exhibit stronger age-based sorting at the population level.  Importantly, by constructing matched pairs of individuals with statistically indistinguishable mobility profiles, we show that age differences in segregation persist even after controlling for physical mobility constraints, indicating the presence of non-spatial drivers.   Building on these empirical findings, we propose a parsimonious mobility choice model in which individuals balance physical distance costs and social distance preferences when selecting locations. The model introduces two interpretable parameters: $\alpha$, capturing sensitivity to physical distance, and $\beta$, capturing sensitivity to social distance. Model estimation reveals a shared decision structure across age groups, but with systematic variation in parameter regimes. Older adults exhibit higher sensitivity to physical distance and weaker aversion to social difference, while younger individuals display lower physical constraints but stronger active social selection. Together, these results demonstrate how mobility networks and social preferences jointly shape urban segregation.

column9: Network-induced control of sustained oscillations in SIRS epidemics
column11: Ropert, Samuel*; Perez-Acle, Tomas; Brockmann, Dirk
column13: Sustained oscillations in SIRS epidemic models are well understood in well-mixed populations when infectious and immune periods deviate from exponential waiting times. In contrast, the role of contact network structure in generating or suppressing such oscillations has received little attention. Existing work on small-world networks reports oscillations but does not relate them to effective transition-time distributions. This work investigates how network topology shapes oscillatory SIRS dynamics by simulating a stochastic SIRS process on self-similar modular hierarchical (SSMH) networks. These networks interpolate between random-like graphs and strongly modular, hierarchical structures while preserving system size and mean degree. A single structural parameter controls edge placement across hierarchical levels, reshaping effective distances between communities. Simulation results show that random-like networks support robust, coherent oscillations in global prevalence, whereas increasing hierarchical modularity desynchronizes outbreaks across communities and gradually destroys the global limit cycle, leading to damped or irregular fluctuations. These findings support an interpretation of epidemic oscillations as a synchronization phenomenon of individual SIRS cycles, where network topology promotes or inhibits global coherence by reshaping the time-to-infection distribution through changes in effective distances.

column9: Fast inference for maximum entropy configuration models
column13: Random graph models serve as null models to identify structural regularities in real-world networks. The Chung-Lu model is widely used but systematically overconnects hubs, creating spurious rich-club structures and inflated triangle counts. Maximum entropy models avoid these biases by generating maximally random networks subject to degree constraints, but their high computational complexity has limited adoption. We present FastMaxEnt, a method that accelerates parameter estimation for maximum entropy network models by 10 to 100 times relative to the popular NEMtropy algorithm. Rather than analytically computing gradients over all O(N^2) potential edges, FastMaxEnt estimates gradients by sampling a small number of networks from the current parameter estimate, reducing complexity to linear in the number of edges. Despite this approximation, the method achieves reliable parameter inference comparable to exact analytical approaches. We further improve performance through parametric interpolation, i.e., computing exact gradients for representative nodes and interpolating for others, along with a mean-field initialization heuristic that accelerates convergence. FastMaxEnt enables practical maximum entropy inference for large networks previously intractable with existing methods.

column9: Entropy-based targeted attacks on networks: Disrupting Watts-Strogatz and power grid networks
column13: One way to assess the importance of a node in a network is to observe what happens to the size of largest connected component ($LCC$) after that node is removed. If we keep removing nodes we obtain a disconnected network [1]. For each node $i$ we have $N -1$ other nodes reachable, we pick the paths that minimizes this quantity: $K_{ij} =  min(\prod_{h=i}^{j-1} k_{h})$ where $j$ is the target node and $k_h$ is the degree of the node $h \in \mathcal{P}(i,j) $ among those paths we pick the shortest path. We can define the normalized generalize Shannon entropy ($NGSE$) as: \begin{equation} S_{i}^N = \sum_{h \neq i}^{N} \frac{\log_2 (Q_{i}{K}_{ih})}{{Q_{i}K}_{ih}} \label{SN} \end{equation} Where $ Q_i= \sum_{h \neq  i}^{N} \frac{1} {K_{ih}}$ is the normalization factor, for $Q =1$ we have the un-normalized version.  This quantity has been used to perform targeted attacks on Watts-Strogatz ($WS$) networks [1] along with classical network centralities such as Degree, Betweenness, Closeness, Eigenvector centrality and as a benchmark, we performed random node removal. The more significant a node category, the smaller the fraction of nodes ($f_r$) is required to reduce $LCC$ to the chosen thresholds of $10\%$ and $5\%$ . We have generated $100$ $WS$ networks with $N =400$ $k=8$ and $p=0.04$ and report the averages $LCC$ in function of $f_r$ for each attack strategy. As we can see on the left plot $NGSE$ identifies key nodes early, reaching the $10\%$ of the $LCC$ after removing the $54.4\%$ of nodes, then for the $5\%$ threshold the best strategy is the Betweenness. Aa a real-world case study, we have analyzed the Great Britain power-grid network ($GBPN$) [2] the network is composed by the high voltage nodes and the connections among them are the links. We considered only the giant connected component of the network, ignoring isolated nodes. We ignored other features of the grid and the network has been transformed in a undirected unweighted version. Since the network is uniquely defined, only the random strategy has been reiterated $100$ times. The connected grid is composed by $494$ nodes and $598$ links. As shown in the plot on the right side: Degree, Betweenness and $NGSE$ are pretty good in disrupting the network, however $NGSE$ reached the $10\%$  threshold after removing only the $17.4\%$ of the nodes. It has been shown that $NGSE$ could be used to assess the list of the most ”important” nodes in $WS$ networks and can be used to perform targeted attacks that outperform in the early phases the well established network centralities. This attack strategy has been applied to a real world case of the $GBPN$, this quantity can be used to assess network weak points that with other methods would not be considered, this can help to mitigate the risks protecting nodes that are not considered important from the standpoint of other classical network centralities.

column9: Exploiting Graph Structure for Author Verification
column13: Text-based author verification has various applications, from detecting sock-puppets on platforms like Wikipedia [1] to detecting text generated by large language models (LLMs) [2]. However, the performance of text-based machine learning models trained on source verification tasks may be affected by topic bias in the text, where different authors within the same topic are confused as the same author, and frequency bias (i.e., label imbalance), where there is a skewed distribution in number of authored works [3].   We propose a graph-based method for improving performance of author verification models trained using text embeddings. We construct a graph from authorship verification tests of document pairs, with their verification scores serving as weights on edges between documents. Our method strengthens edges between graph communities and removes edges where there are weak connections between the subgraphs. Afterwards, each isolated subgraph in the resulting graph should correspond to an author identity.  Our method exploits graph structure to mitigate effects of topic bias and label imbalance; it boosts AUC scores from 0.9 to 0.96 and needs 8x fewer training examples than current verification models to achieve comparable results. Our work also bridges the gap between author verification and author identification by mapping author identities to subgraph structures. We demonstrate that this can improve mutual-information scores by 36\% over baseline models in one instance.  [1] Solorio, Thamar, Ragib Hasan, and Mainul Mizan.” Sockpuppet Detection in Wikipedia: A Corpus of Real-World Deceptive Writing for Linking Identities.” Proceedings of the Ninth International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation. 2014. [2] Bevendorff, Janek, et al. ”The Two Paradigms of LLM Detection: Authorship Attribution vs Authorship Verification.” Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL. 2025. [3] Nguyen, Trang, et al. ”Improving long-text authorship verification via model selection and data tuning.” Proceedings of the 7th Joint SIGHUM Workshop on Computational Linguistics for Cultural Heritage, Social Sciences, Humanities and Literature. 2023.

column9: Change of the worldwide air transportation network: A weighted network approach
column11: Klamser, Pascal*; Zachariae , Adrian; Brockmann, Dirk
column13: How a disease distributes during a pandemic is strongly linked to the mobility  pattern, which is on the international level well approximated by the worldwide air transportation network (WAN). Its extreme importance for pandemics is highlighted by (i) the effective distance derived from it, which correlates with the arrival time of the disease, and (ii) by the import risk method, which assumes a mechanistic distribution of passengers on the WAN to infer the importation risk of a disease to specific countries. During the COVID-19 pandemic an extreme reduction in mobility was observed in almost all countries, also reflected in the international mobility by a reduction of the WAN down to only about 10%. This extreme change in mobility was observed as well on smaller, national scales, as for example in Germany, where it was shown that long range connections got reduced the most, resulting in an increase in clustering and shortest path length. Do we observe similar changes in mobility on a larger scale? How does the network structure changes and how does the change depend on the choice of distance or edge weight measure? We take a weighted network analysis approach combined with epidemic simulations to answer these question and find among others that (i) clustering decreases with an increase in shortest path length, (ii) mid-range flight got reduced less compared to other ranges,  (iv) a strong heterogeneity in delay of arrival time due to network adaption and (v) the high robustness in shortest path measures based on effective distance.

column9: When Fluid Dynamics Meets Epidemics: A Navier–Stokes–Inspired SIR Flow on Networks
column11: Zhang, Zonghan*; Benbrahim, Marouane; Rashme, Tamanna; Mu, Lin; Chen, Zhiqian
column13: Fluid dynamics and epidemic spreading describe seemingly different phenomena, yet both govern how quantities move, accumulate, and dissipate over structured domains. In fluid systems, momentum, pressure, and viscosity determine how mass is transported through space; in epidemics, infection propagates through contact networks under heterogeneous transmission, recovery, and intervention effects. While fluid dynamics explicitly models transport through conservation laws and flow equations, epidemic spreading is often described using compartmental models such as SIR, which emphasize local reaction dynamics at nodes. As a result, transport-related effects in epidemics, such as directional propagation, spatial smoothing, and inertia in spreading dynamics, are typically treated implicitly rather than modeled directly.  Motivated by this analogy, we introduce a Navier-Stokes-inspired SIR (NS-SIR) formulation that recasts epidemic spreading as a physical flow evolving on a network. Building on the classical SIR framework, we define the \textit{infection velocity} $u_i(t)$ as the rate of change of infection at node $i$ and model its evolution using graph-based differential operators. As illustrated in \textbf{Fig.~1(Middle)}, the dynamics combine pressure-driven transport, viscous diffusion over network structure, external forcing that captures interventions or behavioral adaptation, and recovery-induced damping. Infection pressure is determined by a graph Poisson equation, which provides a closure condition that enforces conservation of epidemic flow across the network. Together, these components yield a network analogue of the Navier-Stokes equations while preserving epidemiological interpretability.  The NS--SIR formulation naturally supports \textbf{data-driven operator discovery}. By decomposing epidemic evolution into explicit graph operators, including gradient, diffusion, pressure-velocity coupling, and nonlinear reaction, the model aligns well with symbolic regression and neuro-symbolic learning approaches. These tools can recover dominant transport pathways, estimate latent advection fields, infer effective viscosity, or identify additional coupling terms from simulated or empirical time series. This perspective enables researchers to assess when classical SIR dynamics provide an adequate approximation and when transport-dominated behavior requires a more expressive physical formulation. Under the assumptions of network homogeneity and flow conservation, the NS-SIR model reduces smoothly to the classical SIR ODEs, demonstrating that the proposed model generalizes standard epidemiological dynamics while capturing spatial, structural, and dynamical heterogeneity.

column9: Approximate Triangular Maximally Filtered Graph
column13: Information Filtering Networks (IFNs), particularly the Triangulated Maximally Filtered Graph (TMFG) [3, 2], offer a solution by generating planar, modular, and sparse graphs (with 3N − 6 edges) that capture topological features such as cliques—often expressions of local shared dynamics [1]. However, the traditional TMFG requires the pre-computation and storage of a dense correlation matrix (N^2 coefficients). This memory and runtime complexity renders the method unscalable for datasets for medium to big data. We present a novel approach that leverages the TMFG graph construction principles while strictly controlling memory and runtime complexity to mitigate combinatorial explosion. We introduce three key innovations by pre-computing a k- nearest neighbors (KNN) graph as our initialization, implementing a memory management strategy to search and estimate missing graph edges only as needed, and finally we restrict further the search space of triangular faces by implementing “forgetting” heuristics. We evaluate our method on synthetic Gaussian mixtures, and our results demonstrate that we are able to preserve the desirable topological features of the original TMFG while achieving drastic reductions in runtime.

column9: Centrality as a form of higher-order cumulative advantage
column11: Gangadhar, Akshay*; Fujita, Yoshiaki; Kojaku, Sadamori
column13: Competition for attention is a defining feature of many social systems, where early success often amplifies future success through processes collectively described as cumulative advantage (CA) or the Matthew effect. In scientific citation networks, CA is often quantified through direct measures of attention, such as the number of citations a paper receives. However, attention can also spread beyond the node itself, e.g., a paper that is cited by an influential study often gains more visibility, and scientists gain popularity by collaborating with renowned scientists. While such higher-order CAs have been observed, it remains unclear to what extent they are common and contribute to the visibility of works in science. Here, we conduct a systematic study to identify higher-order CAs and their impact on the long-term citation trajectories of scientific publications. We utilize publication data from the American Physical Society (APS) spanning 1883-2019 focusing on papers between 1970- 2002 for the analysis. First-order CA was confirmed by plotting cumulative citations at year t against new citations received in subsequent years. Following this, we first test if higher-order CA exists by replacing cumulative citations with network centrality as a predictor of citation success. We divide the citation network into training and evaluation sets based on focal year t. The training set contains papers and their references published up to and including year t+5, while the evaluation set contains citations accrued afterward. This five-year “training” gap ensures that papers published in year t have sufficient time to form distinct local neighborhoods in the citation network, allowing centrality measures to assign differentiated scores. Centrality values computed on the training network for focal papers are then compared against citations accrued in the evaluation period, and success is measured by whether a paper ranks among the top 10% most cited papers in subsequent five-year windows. We control for first-order effects by comparing papers with similar citation counts at the end of the training period – a condition under which citations alone cannot predict future success better than chance. If network centrality can distinguish which papers go on to receive more citations among such comparable peers, this provides evidence of higher-order CA. We focus on PageRank (PR), which captures the essence of higher-order CA – a paper is important if it is surrounded (cited) by other influential papers – and second-order PageRank (PR2), a biased PR that assigns additional weight to nodes forming triangles. Both PR and PR2 outperform random selection, with precision increasing for higher citation strata (Figure). These results demonstrate that higher-order CA is observable even in off-the-shelf centrality measures not explicitly designed to capture this effect. With this, our focus shifts from detection to understanding: what structural features do these measures encode, and what do they reveal about citation practices in science? Here, interpretability and explainability are central. Ongoing work examines why PR and PR2 perform particularly well by analyzing the local structural patterns and reinforcement mechanisms they capture. We hope to report on these results and more at NetSci 2026.

column9: The complex evolution of chess openings
column13: Chess is a board game that demands deep positional understanding from the very first move of the opening to the end of the game. The initial moves, by both White and Black, contain information at the individual level about each player's strengths, knowledge of the adversary, and personal preferences, as well as broader insights into the state of the art of the game itself.  The evolution of chess can be traced back to the fifteenth century, with major transformations linked to the formal establishment of rules—such as Ruy López’s treatise—, the beginning of organized tournaments in London, the formation of FIDE—Fédération Internationale des Échecs or International Chess Federation, and the establishment of the Chess Olympiads.  Several tournaments have been reserved for high-level players, with selection processes ranging from direct invitations, such as the Hastings call, to eliminatory systems like the Chess Olympiads and the World Championship Candidates Tournament. Participants in these events bring well-established strategies and techniques, and innovations that emerge from the global practice of chess.  In this study, we analyze the development of chess openings over the course of a century, using the complete dataset of matches played in the Olympiads from 1924 to 2024. We combine two theoretical and methodological approaches: on one hand, we represent matches and tournaments using graphs; on the other, we apply entropy measures and complexity indices to explore and trace the organizational processes underlying the evolution of the game.  Graphs are constructed by adding directed dyads corresponding to the first move of each match, with nodes representing Black’s responses to White’s moves using Descriptive Notation (e.g., Pawn to King 4 as PK4), recorded in a 20×20 matrix.  We compute the following measures of complexity: Shannon entropy, Tsallis entropy, the Shiner-Davison-Landsberg complexity index, and the López-Ruiz-Mancini complexity index—based on both degree and strength of the nodes. These are analyzed across three match outcomes: White wins, Black wins and draws. In- and out-degree and strength are associated with the player's perspective (White or Black), while outcomes are treated as subsystems to estimate Tsallis entropy.  Our results show that chess has evolved towards increasing diversity, due to broader explorations and preferences for rare strategies, reflecting both innovation and adaptation to evolving winning patterns: While Shannon entropy captures the growing dispersion of opening choices and shifts in player´s preferences, and complexity indices highlight rising interdependence between moves, assuming superadditivity Tsallis entropy parameter ( $q$), ranges from $1.1$ to $3.0$, signals a transition toward correlated structures.  [1] Matanović, A. (Ed.). (1979). Encyclopedia of Chess Openings, Volume E. Chess Informant. [2] Tsallis, C. (2009). Introduction to Nonextensive Statistical Mechanics: Approaching a Complex World. Springer, New York.

column9: Network Topology Determines When Small AI Models Collectively Outperform a Single Larger Model
column11: Xu, Yilun*; Rocher, Luc; Dong, Xiaowen
column13: Large language models (LLMs) with a greater number of parameters are generally believed to exhibit better performance in task-solving situations compared to smaller models. It is hypothesized that the scaled-up number of parameters of larger LLMs allows stronger memorization and reasoning capabilities, which make emergent abilities more prevail in these models [3]. Inspired by the potential emergent capabilities in smaller models [3] and higher computational and infrastructure demands of larger LLMs [2], this work studies how smaller models can be more effectively leveraged to solve complex problems, with larger LLM performance as a reference point and accounting for cost-effectiveness trade-offs.  We consider LLM-driven multi-agent systems (MASs) in task solving centering on network topology. Motivated by results from the complex systems literature [1], we investigate if and what certain topological structures can enable an MAS composed of smaller LLMs to achieve performance comparable to larger models across different tasks. We fix the number of agents (ten) and only vary the collaboration networks where agents are connected and have chances to interact with network neighbors. Initially, each agent works on an assigned task independently. In each subsequent simulation round, agents read their neighbors’ responses and update their own responses. After a preset number of rounds, a final answer is produced using 1) majority voting and 2) a ranker LLM who reviews all agents’ most-updated answers and generates a response as the collective final output. We utilize three benchmarks to measure MAS performances on tasks at difficult, intermediate and easy levels respectively, where difficulty level is determined by the overall and potentially outstanding performances of different LLMs. Six collaboration networks are assessed (Figure 1). Figure 2 presents the MASs’ performance under various collaboration networks on tested subset of tasks. The impact of network structure (bars) is evaluated through comparisons with: 1) the average performance of agents’ initial independent work (olive lines), 2) and the ranker’s response after agents’ collaboration (blue lines), and 3) the larger LLM (red lines).  As expected, agent collaboration in a MAS (six bars in each facet) improved performance compared to agents’ initial individual work (olive lines). Facet 1 in Figure 2 shows the existing minimal performance gap between super and small models on easier tasks, as smaller models can sometimes even surpass larger ones on the test subset. The ranker (blue lines) consistently outperforms the larger LLM (red lines) on both easy and hard tasks. However, the scores are achieved on the intermediate tasks shown in Figure 2 when partial credit is not allowed. Otherwise, the same phenomenon also applies, indicating improved (though still imperfect) reasoning. Besides, collaboration impact fueled across networks varies particularly in harder tasks. Notably, random networks (BA, ER, and WS) produce no-less performance gains than the rest on all finished tasks. These preliminary findings suggest that small-model MASs have the potential to match or sometimes even outperform larger models with well-designed topological structures. The robustness of such observed performance gains will be further validated in future experiments across twenty-two network instances and four classes of LLMs from different providers (Alibaba Cloud/Qwen, Meta/Llama, Mistral AI/Mistral and OpenAI/GPT).

column9: From Structure-Coupled to Structure-Decoupled: A Unified ICA Framework for Dynamic Brain State Mapping
column11: Fouladivanda, Mahshid*; Iraji, Armin; Calhoun, Vince
column13: Dynamic functional connectivity reflects time-varying neural interactions constrained by white-matter architecture, yet conventional fMRI analyses largely ignore this coupling, limiting interpretability [1]. We propose a Structural–Dynamic Constrained ICA framework to jointly identify structure-coupled and structure-decoupled brain states in schizophrenia.  Resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI from the FBIRN phase III cohort [2] (274 quality-controlled subjects) were preprocessed through the SPM12 and FSL using the pipelines in [3]. Data were parcellated into 53 intrinsic connectivity networks from the NeuroMark_fMRI_1.0 atlas. Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) was computed using a 30-TR sliding window, and structural connectivity (SC) was defined via streamline counts between network pairs. ICA of concatenated SC matrices identified six stable structural bases. A unified multi-objective ICA model [4] jointly maximized functional independence and alignment with these bases to estimate six structure-coupled dynamic states. Structure-decoupled states were obtained by regressing out coupled components using a GLM, followed by ICA of residual functional connectivity. Group effects were assessed using FDR-corrected GLMs. Structure-coupled states aligned significantly with structural bases (r = 0.48–0.61), explaining ~30% of dynamic variance. Structure-decoupled states showed negligible structural correlation but captured substantial residual functional variability. Schizophrenia-related dysconnectivity differed across domains, with distributed alterations in coupled states and more localized default-mode and cognitive-control disruptions in decoupled states. This framework disentangles structure-constrained and intrinsic functional dynamics, improving biological interpretability and sensitivity to schizophrenia-related dysconnectivity.

column9: Two Geometric Mechanisms of Eigenvector Localization in Networks
column13: Eigenvector localization plays a central role in signal confinement, functional specialization, and fragility in complex networks[1]. In this work, we identify and rigorously characterize two distinct mechanisms by which \emph{graph geometry alone}—independent of randomness—induces localization of eigenvectors of graph Laplacians.  Localization of Laplacian eigenvectors has been widely observed across disciplines. Classical results in mathematical physics established Anderson localization[2], where randomness in a potential produces exponentially localized states. More recently, it has become clear that \emph{deterministic geometric features}—such as bottlenecks, defects, weak interconnections, or hierarchical structure—can produce similarly localized modes [3]. Despite extensive empirical and numerical evidence, a unified explanation of how geometry induces localization, and how it determines decay rates, remains incomplete.  We study graph Laplacians that admit a decomposition \[ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_0 + E, \] where $\mathcal{L}_0$ captures the global backbone of the network and $E$ encodes localized or structured heterogeneities. We identify two qualitatively different geometrical localization mechanisms:  \medskip \noindent\textbf{(i) Strong local confinement.} When $E$ is supported on a small subset of nodes and creates a strong local perturbation (e.g., a defect, boundary condition, or bottleneck), the localized eigenvectors of $\cL$ decay exponentially away from the support of $E$. The decay rate is governed by how efficiently signals propagate through the underlying network backbone, as quantified by resolvent decay of $\mathcal{L}_0$.  \medskip \noindent\textbf{(ii) Spectral incoherence with large-support perturbations.} When $E$ acts on a macroscopic fraction of the network and its eigenvectors are nearly orthogonal to those of $\mathcal{L}_0$ —for example, settings where all eigenvectors of $\cL_0$ are delocalized and those of $E$ are localized — the localized eigenvectors of $\mathcal{L}$ closely follow the structure of $E$. In this regime, spatial decay is controlled by spectral gaps of $E$ rather than by global network geometry.  \medskip Together, these mechanisms explain why geometrically induced localization can exhibit either polynomial or exponential decay, depending on network structure and perturbation type. Our results provide a unified framework for understanding how local structural features shape global spectral behavior in large deterministic networks, with implications for network dynamics, robustness, and control.

column9: Unified Framework for Comparing Evolutionary Models for Complex Network
column13: Since the groundbreaking discovery of small-world and scale-free models in the late 1990s, the research community has actively pursued the development of network generation models. The primary objective of these models is to mimic the evolution of complex networks emerging in a variety of real-world domains. The study of network models assists the research community in several ways. It enables the generation of networks that exhibit characteristics similar to real-world networks, but at larger scales and with desired structural properties, thereby helping researchers understand the evolution and dynamics underlying the formation of many real-world networks.  Recently, a number of models have been proposed to capture both distinctive and common characteristics of networks, such as small-world and scale-free properties, hierarchical structure, presence of communities, assortative mixing, and homophily. These models also facilitate the generation of synthetic networks with varying structural properties, which can be used in simulation studies of different dynamic processes, such as epidemic spreading and influence mining.  Since these models have been proposed by scholars from different domains - including sociology, mathematics, physics, and computer science - questions arise regarding the similarities and differences among them. Various classifications have been proposed by different scholars. For example, Goldenberg et al. distinguished between static and dynamic network models in their work [1], whereas Toivonen et al. classified models into Network Evolution Models (NEM) and Nodal Attribute Models [2]. However, at present, there is no established mechanism to systematically compare the similarities or differences between two network models. Such a mechanism could help answer questions such as how similar or different two models are when they generate networks with comparable characteristics, or what specific steps are introduced in a model to produce certain network attributes.  After analyzing several network models available in the literature, we conclude that we can generalize the process of synthetic network generation into six steps: Initialization, Induction, Selection, Engagement, Dispatch and Exit. We are not considering models like p1 and p∗ or ERGM models as they do not explicitly describe network evolution processes [2]. This gives us a unified framework for comparing different network models to achieve a deeper understanding of their underlying mechanisms. The framework provides a means for the research community to examine models at a granular level and to answer questions about the precise ways in which one model differs from or resembles another, rather than relying on broad categorical classifications. We believe that such a framework can enhance the understanding of models proposed by scholars across different domains and can also assist emerging researchers in comprehending the operational details of existing network models. A comparison of around 25 models proposed in the last two decades has been conducted using this framework and will be presented and discussed during the presentation.

column9: Interdisciplinarity and Emerging Trends in Scientific Careers via Hybrid Structural--Semantic Author Embeddings
column11: Lupi, Federico; Pretolesi, Daniele; Vian, Andrea; Barla, Annalisa*
column13: Science of Science investigates how research systems evolve by combining large-scale data, network analysis, and computational modeling [1]. A persistent limitation in current evaluation practices is that research impact is often treated as a near-monotonic function of scientific production (e.g., counts and citations), implicitly assuming stable notions of relevance across fields. In addition, notions of relevance vary substantially across disciplinary communities, and standard indicators only partially capture contributions that are interdisciplinary by construction, even as such crossdomain efforts become increasingly common and necessary as science progresses and research problems demand deeper integration across fields. This motivates the search for new impact descriptors that account for how scientists move across topics, communities, and methods throughout their careers and how they contribute to emerging themes at disciplinary boundaries. Crucially, such career shifts and adjustments are not exceptional but pervasive: lateral moves, gradual repositioning, and “branching” trajectories are a core mechanism through which scientific careers unfold. Systematically failing to represent and measure these translations and branching processes—i.e., the dynamics of the very actors who literally advance science—substantially weakens our ability to analyze the scientific corpus, potentially undermining both the usefulness and the scope of Science of Science precisely when it is most needed: when the problems science faces increasingly demand interdisciplinarity, collaboration, lateral shifts, and the formation of new thematic lines. Building on recent work that uses AI and network science to illustrate research evolution in interdisciplinary contexts [2], we propose a framework that links collaboration structure with semantic trajectories to describe career-level thematic transitions. We construct longitudinal co-authorship graphs with weighted edges proportional to joint publications, and derive author topic fingerprints through a semantic pipeline derived from structured topic extraction from titles and abstracts, followed by LLM-assigned concise labels for the resulting topics. For each author, we compute a hybrid representation that combines topological embeddings with transformer-based topic embeddings (semantic proximity). We focus on a single reference community and characterize its evolution by estimating yearly topic-dedication profiles, marking emergent themes and distinguishing newly appearing versus already established topical patterns. We then use these community-level emerging trends as an interpretive filter to illustrate how an individual author evolves within (and relative to) the community’s shifting thematic landscape. From these signals we derive interpretable indicators of interdisciplinarity and career dynamics—including cross-topic breadth, dedication entropy, emergent-topic rate, community persistence, and structural–semantic alignment—enabling comparisons across researchers, groups, and fields and supporting richer impact narratives that complement production-centric metrics (see Figure 1).
