column9: Diverse Human Dilemmas, Uniform AI Preferences: Mapping Value Trade-Off Networks in Online Advice-Seeking Communities and Large Language Models
column11: Chen, Zhiyi; Choi, Eun Cheol*; Luo, Yingjia; Wang, Xinyi; Xiao, Yulei; Yang, Aizi; Luceri, Luca
column12: zchen346@usc.edu; euncheol@usc.edu*; yingjial@usc.edu; xwang597@usc.edu; yuleixia@usc.edu; aiziyang@usc.edu; lluceri@isi.edu
column13: People increasingly seek advice online, not only from other users but also from large language model (LLM)–based chatbots [1], which now mediate how individuals navigate personal, relational, and professional dilemmas. Such advice rarely involves identifying a single correct answer; instead, it typically requires navigating trade-offs among competing values. We aim to characterize how LLMs navigate value trade-offs across different advice-seeking contexts.  In this study, we examine the value trade-off structure underlying advice-seeking using a curated dataset [2] drawn from four advice-oriented subreddits. Each dilemma is represented in a structured format consisting of a real-life scenario and two alternative courses of action. Building on the bottom-up approach of prior work [3], we inductively construct a hierarchical value framework by aggregating thousands of fine-grained values extracted from individual advice options into progressively higher-level value categories.  We find substantial heterogeneity in value trade-off structures across advice-seeking contexts: a women-focused subreddit exhibits the highest network density, indicating more complex value conflicts; women’s, men’s, and friendship-related subreddits show highly correlated patterns; and career advice forms a more distinct structure, with values such as security, respect, and commitment often in tension with autonomy, change, or opportunity.   We then evaluate LLM value preferences against these human dilemmas and find that, across models and contexts, LLMs consistently prioritize values related to 'Exploration & Growth over' 'Benevolence & Connection'. This prioritization remains stable across dilemmas drawn from different subreddits, suggesting cross-model and cross-context consistency rather than domain-specific adaptation.  Taken together, these findings highlight important societal implications as online communities and LLMs become increasingly embedded in advice-seeking ecosystems. This uniform value orientation highlights a potential risk of value homogenization in AI-mediated advice, raising concerns about how such systems may shape decision-making and normative outcomes at scale.  [1] Kumar, H., Chahal, J., Zhao, Y., Zhang, Z., Wei, A., Tay, L., \& Anderson, A. (2025). When AI Gives Advice: Evaluating AI and Human Responses to Online Advice-Seeking for Well-Being. arXiv:2512.08937. [2] Bhatia, S., van Baal, S. T., Wang, F., and Walasek, L. (2025). Computational analysis of 100K choice dilemmas: Decision attributes, trade-off structures, and model-based prediction. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 122(17). [3] Huang, S., Durmus, E., Handa, K., McCain, M., Tamkin, A., Stern, M., Hong, J., \& Ganguli, D. (2025). Values in the wild: Discovering and mapping values in real-world language model interactions. Conference on Language Modeling.

column9: Time over Time: Fundamental Patterns of Networked Persistence  in Cultural Dynamics, Biological Evolution, and Persistent Homology
column13: Time is a seemingly straightforward or at least obvious subject of network science, while at the same time subject to temporal lag in the history of network science, due to the relative simplicity of analyzing cumulative summary statistics, and due to the many possible complications in deciding how we should look at networked temporal phenomena. Even the most simple generative models, such as the ER or BA models do implicitly operationalize a dynamics over time. And many of the most simple iconic examples, such as Zachary’s Karate Club, may typically be analyzed in their cumulative static form, while clearly being the result of an underlying dynamic. At the same time, it took roughly the first half of the last 25 years of network science for the first seminal review paper on temporal networks1 to appear, eventually accumulating nearly 4000 citations so far, clearly indicating a pre-existing gap in research and a wealth of possible conceptual complications. 	Here, I present a hitherto unseen and surprising alignment of fundamental temporal patterns, that emerge from a perhaps not so straightforward but simple graphical projection of networked persistence, capturing temporal networked phenomena in bipartite situations, where both the link source and the link target partitions carry a temporal property, enabling us to plot so-called persistence plots, loosely speaking depicting time over time. Concrete examples come from a wide variety of domains, both aligning in principle and a selection of fundamental patterns, while also mutually putting in question the respective research domain focus. In the domain of cultural dynamics, we find fundamental complex patterns of networked persistence in publication-topic networks, i.e. publications appearing over time covering topics tied to other times. Another example from the domain of cultural dynamics is the collection lag in art museums, where we find a whole set of complex fundmental patterns, when we plot artist age at artwork production versus museum acquisition.2 In the domain of (biological) evolution, we find similar fundamental patterns in persistence plots, where the possible lifetime of a celular automaton before and after a single point mutation is plotted against each other.3 In the domain of persistent homology, where persistence plots are abundant, we find similar fundamental patterns, when plotting higher-order feature appearance vs disappearance. 	As I will lay out in my talk, the resonances and contrasts between these examples may take us closer to a better understanding of cultural dynamics, where most reliable data comes in the form of bipartite classifications and measures of similarity, while directed temporal network phenomena, such as inheritance, influence, and causality remain in the realm of imaginative modelling.  [1] Holme, Petter, and Jari Saramäki. “Temporal networks.” Physics reports 519, no. 3 (2012): 97-125. [2] Canet Sola, Mar, Antonina Korepanova, Ksenia Mukhina, and Maximilian Schich. “Quantifying Collection Lag in European Modern and Contemporary Art Museums.” In Proceedings of the 16th International Symposium on Visual Information Communication and Interaction, pp. 1-8. 2023. [3] Wolfram, Stephen. “Why Does Biological Evolution Work? A Minimal Model for Biological Evolution and Other Adaptive Processes.” Complex Systems 33, no. 4 (2025). [4] Herbert Edelsbrunner, David Letscher, and Afra Zomorodian. Topological persistence and simplification. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 28(4):511–533, 2002.

column9: Shared Leadership in Science
column11: Shao, Erzhuo*; Tripodi, Giorgio; Qian, Yifan; Wang, Dashun
column13: Scientific discovery is a collective endeavor, increasingly driven by teams rather than individual researchers. Yet, we almost exclusively observe the contribution layer of collaboration structures, and due to critical gaps in faculty employment records, we lack a systematic understanding of the role of shared leadership in scientific teams. Here, by linking faculty roster data with bibliometric information and HR records, we distinguish collaborations among faculty members from other teamwork configurations, enabling a large-scale analysis of multi-PI teams in science.   Our analysis highlights the increasing prevalence of multi-PI teams across scientific domains, although their prevalence varies substantially across different fields. To quantify the advantages of such a shared leadership structure, we evaluate publication outcomes using metrics that capture a paper’s position and influence within the citation network. In addition to cumulative citation counts, which reflect the accumulation of attention, we assess more profound forms of impact that characterize paper novelty, including how one publication reshapes citation trajectories and combines existing knowledge. Results show that Multi-PI teams are associated with both higher scientific impact and greater novelty, but in systematically different ways across disciplinary contexts. The benefits of shared leadership also depend on team size and organizational arrangement: multi-PI teams within non-lab fields are more likely to produce high-impact work, whereas multi-PI teams within lab fields exhibit stronger associations with novelty. Meanwhile, cross-department teams within the same institution are especially innovative. Together, these patterns suggest that leadership structure is a consequential—and previously overlooked—dimension of scientific team organization, with direct implications for how researchers, universities, and funding agencies structure collaborative work at the frontiers of science.

column9: Harnessing inconsistency: Revealing network intricacies in communities and geometric embeddings
column11: Gim, Gahyoun; Lee, Daekyung; Kim, Heetae; Lee, Sang Hoon*
column13: In the evolving landscape of network science, understanding mesoscopic structures such as communities is essential, and geometric embeddings serve as algorithmic tools to represent those structures. In this work, we introduce two complementary approaches to assess network complexity through statistical inconsistency, arising from inherent algorithmic properties.  First, we introduce a framework to map the consistency landscape of network communities, a key class of mesoscopic structure. By analyzing variability in outcomes [1] from stochastic community detection algorithms, our method quantifies the reliability of detected communities across resolutions using a global partition inconsistency (PaI) and a local membership inconsistency (MeI) [2]. Importantly, PaI provides a practical criterion for identifying credible and robust resolution ranges, while MeI highlights nodes with ambiguous or unstable community affiliation. The resulting scale-dependent inconsistency landscape offers insights into the coherence and validity of community structure in diverse systems, including chromosome contact (Hi-C) networks [3].  In addition, we examine geometric network embeddings, which encode mesoscopic organization through latent spatial representations. Focusing on multidimensional scaling (MDS) embeddings with randomized initial layouts, we introduce the network embedding inconsistency (NEI) metric to quantify embedding variability via the variance of pairwise node distances across multiple realizations [4]. NEI captures structural multistability in embedding space, distinguishing network classes and identifying motifs such as hubs and core–periphery structures as major contributors to embedding inconsistency.  Through analyses of synthetic and real-world networks, our dual approach reveals fundamental aspects of mesoscopic coherence and complexity. Overall, this work highlights statistical inconsistency as a principled and practical tool for evaluating the robustness and reliability of network representations.  [1] H. Kim and S. H. Lee, Relational flexibility of network elements based on inconsistent community detection, Phys. Rev. E 100, 022311 (2019). [2] D. Lee, S. H. Lee, B. J. Kim, and H. Kim, Consistency landscape of network communities, Phys. Rev. E 103, 052306 (2021). [3] D. Bernenko, S. H. Lee, and L. Lizana, Exploring 3D community inconsistency in human chromosome contact networks, J. Phys.: Complex. 4, 035004 (2023). [4] G. Gim and S. H. Lee, Network solidity: Quantifying structural multistability through geometric embedding inconsistency, in preparation.

column9: Destabilizing Community Detection via Node Injection under High Global Agreement
column13: Community detection is a central problem in network science, and robustness is commonly evaluated using global agreement metrics such as normalized mutual information (NMI) and the adjusted Rand index (ARI). While these measures capture overall partition similarity, they can obscure substantial localized changes, particularly when relabeling is concentrated on a small subset of structurally ambiguous nodes near community boundaries.  In this work, we investigate the robustness of community detection under network growth driven by node injection. We consider a low-impact growth regime in which newly arriving nodes have small fixed out-degree, no incoming edges, and do not modify existing links, thereby modeling decentralized and non-adversarial network expansion. Even under such mild growth, we find that the community assignments of boundary nodes can change substantially while global agreement metrics remain high.  To characterize this effect, we introduce the concept of a manipulability boundary, which captures the trade-off between preserved global agreement and localized node-level instability. Using synthetic directed networks generated by degree-corrected stochastic block models, we evaluate Infomap and Leiden and quantify instability by the fraction of boundary nodes whose community assignments change following injection.  Our results demonstrate that small amounts of node injection can induce pronounced boundary relabeling without a corresponding decline in global agreement, and that the magnitude of this effect depends strongly on the community detection algorithm. These findings indicate that robustness assessments based solely on global agreement metrics may systematically overestimate stability in growing networks, underscoring the need for complementary node-level evaluation.

column9: Clustering Ethical Discourse: Semantic Network Analysis of Global South and Global North AI Education Research
column13: Most ethical frameworks for AI in education have been developed in Global North contexts, reproducing well‑documented asymmetries in whose values and priorities inform AI governance , . This study examines how these asymmetries appear in academic discourse by analyzing how ethical dimensions are structurally combined in Global South and Global North AI‑in‑education research. We conducted a Semantic Network Analysis of 54 peer‑reviewed articles (2019–2025) that substantively discuss ethical aspects of AI in education, classified by authors’ institutional region (32 from the Global South and 22 from the Global North) . The analysis builds on the Contextual Model for AI Ethics in Education, whose ten ethical dimensions and operational criteria (Inclusion, Human‑Centricity, Transparency, Evaluation, Compliance, Sustainability, Explainability, Auditability, Plural Epistemology, Collective Participation) are used as network nodes . For each regional subset, we constructed an undirected, weighted co‑occurrence network in which edge weights capture how often pairs of dimensions appear together in the same article, and characterized network structure using clustering coefficient, weighted degree, and betweenness centrality. Inter‑coder reliability for the ten categories reached a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.82. The analysis indicates statistically significant structural differences between regions. Global North networks exhibit higher clustering (0.521 vs. 0.459; p < 0.05), with a dense cluster linking Evaluation, Transparency, Explainability, and Auditability, each pair co‑occurring in 16 articles. Global South networks, in contrast, are organized around Inclusion (weighted degree = 133) and Plural Epistemology (125), whose connection is the strongest edge in the corpus (23 co‑occurrences), with additional hubs involving Evaluation and Transparency . These patterns can be interpreted as reflecting more analytical configurations—where ethical dimensions are treated as discrete, modular components—and more relational configurations—where dimensions are treated as inherently interconnected—resonating with decolonial discussions of AI ethics and with the notion of an “ecology of knowledges” , . Betweenness centrality further reveals different “conceptual bridges”: Human‑Centricity connects otherwise separate clusters in the Global South network, while Sustainability plays this role in the Global North despite its low frequency. Overall, the results show how network topology can make visible epistemological structures embedded in AI‑in‑education discourse and indicate that ethical frameworks developed in one geopolitical context may not transfer straightforwardly to another, which supports the need for regional validation and for governance processes that take Southern epistemologies into account in the design and deployment of AI in education.

column9: DQ4FairIM: Fairness-aware Influence Maximization using Deep Reinforcement Learning
column11: Saxena, Akrati*; Kumar Yadav, Harshith; Rutten, Bart; Shekhar Jha, Shashi
column13: The Influence Maximization (IM) problem aims to select a set of seed nodes within a given budget to maximize the spread of influence in a social network. However, real-world social networks have several structural inequalities, such as dominant majority groups and underrepresented minority groups. If these inequalities are not considered while designing IM algorithms, the outcomes might be biased, disproportionately benefiting majority groups while marginalizing minorities. In this work, we address this gap by designing a fairness-aware IM method using Reinforcement Learning (RL) that ensures equitable influence outreach across all communities, regardless of protected attributes. Fairness is incorporated using a maximin fairness objective, which prioritizes improving the outreach of the least-influenced group, pushing the solution toward an equitable influence distribution. We propose a novel fairness-aware deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) method, called DQ4FairIM (Deep $Q$-learning for Fair Influence Maximization), that maximizes the expected number of influenced nodes by learning an RL policy. The learnt policy ensures that minority groupsformulate the IM problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and use deep Q-learning, combined with the Structure2Vec network embedding, earning together with Structure2Vec network embedding to solve the MDP. The main benefit of using RL for this problem is its generalization ability, wherein a policy learnt on a specific problem instance can be generalized to new problem instances without the need to learn the model from scratch. We perform extensive experiments on synthetic benchmark datasets and real-world networks to compare our method with fairness-agnostic and fairness-aware baselines. The results show that our method achieves a higher level of fairness while maintaining a better fairness-performance trade-off than baselines. Additionally, our approach learns effective seeding policies that generalize across problem instances without retraining, such as varying the network size or the number of seed nodes.

column9: Percolation process with cluster-size dependent reactivations
column13: Percolation on networks has traditionally focused on permanent node failure; however, many real-world systems show recovery dynamics where inactive nodes can return to an active state [1], such as epidemic recovery and quantum error correction. To capture these phenomena, we propose a percolation model incorporating a recovery rule based on the size of inactive clusters. The size-dependency reflects the realistic constraint that small-size failures can be easier to restore than large-size ones. In this model, nodes are initially active with probability p, and subsequently, all inactive clusters whose size n is less than or equal to size threshold s, that is n ≤ s, are reactivated. We then measure the system’s robustness by using the size Φ of the giant active component and analyze the global connectivity. In Fig. 1(a,b), we illustrate an example of a reactivation process with the threshold s = 2. Specifically, if the size n of inactive clusters is less than or equal to 2, all nodes within the small clusters are reactivated. Conversely, the clusters with n > s remain inactive because their size exceeds the threshold s.  We derive an analytical solution for the model based on a generating function method by mapping the reactivations of small-size components onto a semi-bipartite network. Our theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with numerical simulations as shown in Fig. 1(c) for Erd˝os-R´enyi (ER) networks with mean degree z = 1.5 and various values of s. We find that the recovery of small clusters significantly promotes the formation of the giant component. Specifically, as the threshold s increases, the percolation threshold pc shifts toward lower values, and the size of the giant component Φ increases for a given p [Fig. 1(c)]. We also explore the interplay between the distribution of finite component sizes [2] and the reactivation process. Our results suggest insights into designing robust real-world systems by quantifying the importance of localized recovery mechanism to prevent global collapse in networked systems.

column9: Quantum preferential attachment
column13: The quantum internet is a rapidly developing technological reality [1], yet, it remains unclear what kind of quantum network structures might emerge. Since indirect quantum communication is already feasible and preserves absolute security of the communication channel, a new node joining the quantum network does not need to connect directly to its desired target. Instead, in our proposed quantum preferential attachment (QPA) model [2], it uniformly randomly connects to any node within the proximity of the target, including, but not restricted to, the target itself. This local flexibility is found to qualitatively change the global network behavior. We demonstrate that quantum preferential attachment leads to two distinct classes of complex network architectures, both of which are small-world, but neither of which is scale-free. Our numerical findings are supported by rigorous analytic results, in a framework that incorporates quantum and classical variants of preferential attachment featuring redirection in a unified phase diagram. Besides quantum networks, we expect that our results will have broad implications for classical scenarios where there is flexibility in establishing new connections.  References: [1] H. J. Kimble, The quantum internet, Nature 453, 1023 (2008). [2] T. Zhao, B. Maga, P. Dionigi, et al., arXiv:2512.22542 (2025).

column9: Towards Systemic Risk Management in Large-Scale Networks with Limited Global Information
column13: Numerous systemic failures of various financial, socio-technological, etc., networks comprised of many interdependent strategic components demonstrate difficulty to manage the corresponding systemic risks. This difficulty can be attributed to the inherently collective nature of systemic events requiring availability of global information to the individual components of the large-scale networked system. Based on similarities between systemic events and phase transitions in statistical physics, we suggest feasibility of efficient selfish systemic risk management due to the time scale separation at the onset of systemic events. Theory and practice of phase transitions tell us [3] that at the onset of a systemic event, system behavior is characterized by a small number of “order parameters” describing system on the mesoscopic scale. In a case of continuous systemic events, which are analogous to phase transitions of the 2nd kind, order parameters evolve much slower than the individual system components and thus can serve as global parameters to be used for systemic risk management. Some trusted entity, e.g., government agency, tracks “slow” evolution of a “small number” of the order parameters and communicates the “essential” tracking data to the strategic system components. Then individual components combine these data with the available local information to evaluate and manage their individual systemic risks. Note that while distributed systemic risk mitigation in a network with strategic components can be modelled as a non-cooperative game of the strategic components, the proposed “signaling” transforms the corresponding competitive, i.e., Nash, equilibrium to the correlated equilibrium. Our conjecture is that this transformation allows for a significant reduction in the Price of Anarchy (PoA) which quantifies inefficiency of selfish risk mitigation vs. centralized socially optimal mitigation. We confirm this conjecture on an example of a Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) contagion.

column9: Coupling Social-Context and Contagion Dynamics: A Generic Framework
column13: A growing body of evidence shows that contagion dynamics are shaped not only by contact structure or biological processes, but also by contagious social dynamics that alter behavior, risk perception, and social context. Classic examples include needle-exchange programs that reduced HIV transmission without directly targeting infection, and widespread mask adoption during the COVID-19 pandemic, which lowered effective transmission by modifying susceptibility and exposure rather than curing disease. Across such settings, social context acts as a latent regulatory layer that modulates contagion spread.  Motivated by these observations, we propose a generic modeling framework that couples social-context dynamics with contagion processes. The framework consists of two interacting layers defined over the same population: a social-context layer that captures the evolution of individual context through weak-tie interactions and threshold effects, and a contagion layer that models transmission along the contact network. Contagion probabilities are endogenously modulated by social context, creating feedback between internal social states and observable spreading dynamics. The framework generalizes classical contagion and threshold models and provides a unified structure for analyzing intervention-driven and socially regulated spreading phenomena across biological, behavioral, and informational domains.

column9: Homophily without locality: Information topology shapes segregation in adaptive networks
column13: Homophily is a pervasive organizing force in networks [1], yet it does not always take the same structural form. In some settings, homophily appears as proximity segregation, with dense local clustering and insulation between groups. Elsewhere, homophily appears as groups differentially occupying central, high-leverage roles within a shared network. Both patterns are widely observed, but it remains unclear why similar homophilous tendencies lead to such different outcomes. Existing network models typically explain homophily through local attachment rules, spatial constraints, or fixed preferences [2]. These approaches naturally generate clustering, but they provide limited insight into hierarchical or positional segregation without introducing additional asymmetries [3]. Coevolutionary network models show how competition for centrality can generate hierarchy, but they fail to explain how homophilous preferences interact with positional games [4]. As a result, the literature lacks a unifying explanation for how the same homophilous rewiring process can produce either local clustering or global hierarchy.  We introduce a coevolutionary network model in which agents rewire edges to improve the value of information encountered through network propagation. Following the adaptive rewiring framework of Holme and Ghoshal [4], nodes occupy an undirected graph and update edges through local, degree-preserving swaps. Homophily enters in two ways. First, information transmitted across unlike nodes is down-weighted by a friction parameter (η < 1), inducing a row-stochastic transition kernel that penalizes cross-group paths. Second, agents evaluate information exposure relative to their own group identity, valuing encounters with in-group nodes more than encounters with out-group nodes. Information propagation is modeled as a discounted random walk with factor α. An agent’s utility is the expected discounted value of nodes encountered along walks originating from that agent. Increasing α expands the effective information horizon, shifting rewiring incentives from local neighborhood structure toward global network position.  We show that the depth of the information horizon determines the structural resolution of homophilous constraints. When information is local (low α), agents minimize immediate friction through proximity segregation, forming dense, assortative clusters. As the horizon expands (high α), local clustering becomes insufficient to overcome the compounding transmission costs of η over long paths. In this global regime, agents break structural symmetry to form a high-capacity core, yielding positional segregation and hierarchical concentration. These results demonstrate that the form of segregation is not determined by homophily alone, but depends mechanistically on the topology of information that mediates competitive interactions. This provides a unifying explanation for how segregation can arise either as spatial separation or as control of network positions.  References  [1] McPherson, M., Smith-Lovin, L., and Cook, J. M. “Birds of a Feather: Homophily in Social Networks.” Annual Review of Sociology, 27, 415–444 (2001).  [2] Gross, T., and Blasius, B. “Adaptive coevolutionary networks: a review.” Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 5(20), 259–271 (2008).  [3] Holme, P., and Newman, M. E. J. “Nonequilibrium phase transition in the coevolution of networks and opinions.” Physical Review E, 74, 056108 (2006).  [4] Holme, P., and Ghoshal, G. “Dynamics of Networking Agents Competing for High Centrality and Low Degree.” Physical Review Letters, 96, 098701 (2006).

column9: Two synchronization processes in the second-order Kuramoto model with inertia
column13: Synchronization is a fundamental organizing principle across biological, neuronal, and engineered systems---from firefly flashing and cardiac pacemakers to power grid stability and Josephson junction arrays [1,2]. While the first-order Kuramoto model has provided deep insights into spontaneous synchronization, many physical systems involve inertia that fundamentally reshapes collective dynamics. This is particularly relevant for electric power grids, where the swing equation that governs generator dynamics is mathematically equivalent to the second-order Kuramoto model with inertia.  A critical yet underexplored question concerns how the shape of the natural frequency distribution $g(\omega)$ influences the synchronization pathways. In first-order systems, Gaussian distributions yield continuous transitions, while uniform distributions produce mixed-order transitions with abrupt jumps [3]. As modern power grids integrate increasingly diverse renewable sources, power injection profiles become more heterogeneous, approaching broad or uniform-like distributions. Understanding how such distributional changes affect synchronization and stability is, therefore, of both theoretical and practical importance.  We investigate this question in the second-order Kuramoto model, $m\ddot{\theta}_i + \gamma\dot{\theta}_i = \omega_i + (K/N)\sum_j \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)$, comparing Gaussian and uniform frequency distributions. Our analysis reveals two fundamentally distinct synchronization pathways. Gaussian distributions exhibit \textit{density-driven} dynamics: a dominant central cluster emerges early and gradually absorbs neighboring oscillators through quasi-static growth, producing a single abrupt transition in the order parameter. In contrast, uniform distributions follow \textit{velocity-driven} dynamics: multiple clusters form simultaneously across the frequency spectrum, with high-velocity clusters acting as organizing centers that partition the system into rotational domains.  This mechanistic difference manifests in Devil's Staircase patterns---hierarchical arrangements of synchronized clusters with rational frequency ratios. Although both systems develop such structures, their origins differ: density-driven absorption in Gaussian systems versus velocity-mediated partitioning in uniform systems. Crucially, the velocity-driven mechanism renders uniform systems more fragile: perturbations targeting high-velocity nodes trigger cascading desynchronization, whereas Gaussian systems remain robust under similar disturbances.  These findings carry direct implications for decentralized power grids, where frequency stability increasingly depends on high-power nodes with large angular velocities---precisely the nodes whose failure can precipitate system-wide collapse.

column9: Network Data Profile: disease progression network in Korea
column11: Yoo, Ki Bong*; Lee, Kyung-Min ; Nam, Ji-Woong ; Liu, Yixuan; Jung, Ye-Won ; Oh, Jeong-Min
column12: ykbong@yonsei.ac.kr*; kmlee97@yonsei.ac.kr; wiswoong@yonsei.ac.kr; liu.yixuan2@northeastern.edu; yewon56love@yonsei.ac.kr; ojm@yonsei.ac.kr
column13: Disease networks are powerful tools for identifying disease characteristics and capturing progression trajectories. However, existing disease networks were developed based on network medicine, which can limit their applicability to real-world public health purposes. To address this gap, we developed a comprehensive, unbiased disease progression network and will introduce this dataset at the conference. We used national health insurance claims data of approximately 50 million total Korean population, collected from 2011 to 2022. We used only the primary ICD-10 diagnosis codes and reclassified into 655 disease categories including death. To minimize bias, disease associations were calculated within age and sex strata. Then, Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) analyses were performed with adjusting confounding and mediating diseases according to the DAG, income, region, BMI, alcohol consumption, smoking, exercise, and disability. Relative risk, attributable risk, and transition probabilities were estimated by IPW. We identified statistically significant disease pairs (RR > 1.5, q-value < 0.00001) and conducted two iterative rounds of IPW analysis to refine the network. The final disease progression network, established after the second round of IPW analysis, consists of 74,745 significant disease pairs. This includes an overall network as well as specific subnetworks stratified by age and sex. At the presentation, we will share how we developed the disease progression network, and node features and edge features. We believe this dataset will serve as a valuable resource for advancing research in network science and network medicine.

column9: Global landscape of ai policy
column11: Kim, Munjung; Park, Jaehyuk; yoon, jisung*
column13: The rise of artificial intelligence has drawn sustained attention from stakeholders and policymakers, who face concerns about its potential misuse alongside growing interest in leveraging its capabilities to enhance national competitiveness. Accordingly, a wide range of issues has now come to be addressed under the umbrella of AI policy, spanning regulation, innovation, and economic development. Yet, developing a clear and systematic understanding of the AI policy discourse landscape including how different AI policy discourses evolve over time and how their thematic emphases align with governmental priorities across countries, remains challenging.  To address this gap, we map and analyze 111,375 AI policy–related documents from 136 countries published between 2000 and 2025, drawing on summaries collected in the Overton database. Using sentence-level text embeddings and BERTopic, we identify 23 distinct topics in this corpus, which can be grouped into four broader themes through hierarchical clustering of their centroids: sustainability transitions, technology governance, social inequality, and socio-economic growth (Fig. 1A). We then examine the temporal dynamics of these discourses by analyzing the distribution of AI policy documents across different topics over time. Over the past two decades, attention to economic policy and social inequality has increased markedly, encompassing issues such as gender inequality, online harms, and structural inequalities arising from technological transitions in the workforce (Fig.~1B). Next, we analyze cross-national similarities by computing average embedding vectors for each country' s AI policy documents. Countries in similar regions cluster closely together in this semantic space, and this regional structure remains even after removing all country names from the underlying texts, suggesting that it reflects similar policy orientations rather than simple textual markers (Fig. 1C). Finally, we construct a semantic axis contrasting discourses of data and technology sovereignty with those emphasizing openness and globalism. Projecting country-level policy embeddings onto this axis reveals that African countries tend to align more strongly with globalist discourses, whereas European countries are positioned closer to sovereignty-oriented framings (Fig. 1D). By delineating the global landscape of AI policy, this study provides a reference for understanding overall trends in AI policy discourse worldwide, as well as variations in thematic focus across nations.

column9: A Multiscale Metric of Effective Distance for Predicting Epidemic Arrival Times
column11: Moghaddas, Nima*; Ueda, Minami; Boudreau, Mariah; Chinazzi, Matteo; St-Onge, Guillaume
column13: While historical epidemics were driven primarily by local transmission, modern outbreaks unfold through complex human mobility patterns spanning multiple scales, from daily commuting within metropolitan regions to intercontinental air travel. Previous work has defined effective distance metrics on the international aviation network using logarithmic functions of passenger flows along edges, initially based on shortest paths [1] and later extended to incorporate multiple paths and random walks [2]. However, existing implementations neglect the role of short-range mobility that shapes local transmission dynamics, especially in remote areas.  We build on this work by developing a multiscale effective distance metric that incorporates short-range commuting fluxes, allowing local mobility patterns to influence network flows alongside long-range air travel. We also replace the assumption of a uniform global mobility rate with heterogeneous node-specific mobility rates derived from combined long- and short-range flows to better capture differences in connectivity across populations. We validate our metric using results from the Global Epidemic and Mobility (GLEAM) metapopulation model, whose mobility layers combine flight data with short-range commuting patterns collected from the Offices of Statistics of countries across five continents [3]. Visualizations reveal a sharper wavefront when nodes are arranged radially according to our multiscale metric (Fig. 1d-f) compared to the random-walk based aviation-only effective distance (Fig. 1a-c), reducing the width of this wavefront (5th to 95th percentiles) by approximately 27%. Our approach shows improved correlation between effective distance and derived arrival times [3], increasing R2 from 0.918 to 0.992 (Fig. 1g-h). These results show that integrating multiple scales enhances the ability of effective distances to reflect realistic spreading patterns. This work can be used to reconstruct outbreak sources and spatial transmission routes from empirical data, and dramatically reduce the computational burden of these inferences compared to simulation-based approaches.

column9: Network and Risk Analysis of Surety Bonds
column11: Quintero Coronel, Manuel*; Sinclair, Sean Robert; Jadbabaie, Ali; Broderick, Tamara; Lin, Vanessa; Sarker, Arnab
column12: mquint@mit.edu*; sean.sinclair@northwestern.edu; jadbabai@mit.edu; tamarab@mit.edu; vllin@mit.edu; arnabs@mit.edu
column13: Surety bonds are financial agreements between a contractor (principal) and obligee (project owner) to complete a project.  However, most large-scale projects involve multiple contractors, creating a network and introducing the possibility of incomplete obligations to propagate and result in project failures. Typical models for risk assessment assume independent failure probabilities within each contractor. However, we take a network approach, modeling the contractor network as a directed graph where nodes represent contractors and project owners and edges represent contractual obligations with associated financial records. To understand risk propagation throughout the contractor network, we extend the celebrated Friedkin-Johnsen model and introduce a stochastic process to simulate principal failures across the network. From a theoretical perspective, we show that under natural monotonicity conditions on the contractor network, incorporating network effects leads to increases in both the average risk and the tail probability mass of the loss distribution (i.e. larger right-tail risk) for the surety organization. We further use data from a partnering insurance company to validate our findings, estimating an approximately 2% higher exposure when accounting for network effects.

column9: Spatial networks of tick-borne pathogen transmission: Mapping ecological connectivity in Amblyomma americanum across South Carolina
column13: Vector-borne disease transmission operates through complex ecological networks linking vectors, pathogens, and vertebrate hosts across spatial landscapes. Understanding the spatial structure of these pathogen networks is critical for predicting disease risk and targeting interventions. We apply a Bayesian spatial network modeling approach to map the connectivity patterns of tick-borne pathogens across South Carolina, revealing how ecological networks vary across geographic space. This research characterizes the spatial network structure of three pathogens (General Rickettsia spp., Rickettsia amblyommatis and Ehrlichia ewingii) in Amblyomma americanum tick populations collected from 2021 to 2024. We model spatial dependencies as network connections and quantify how network topology varies with ecological covariates including tick life stage, collection method, elevation, and land cover—key factors shaping host-vector-pathogen network dynamics. Ticks were collected via flagging/dragging and carbon dioxide traps, then pooled by life stage and spatiotemporal location for PCR testing. We implemented a Bayesian spatial group testing regression model [1] treating geographic locations as nodes with infection prevalence as node attributes. Spatial dependencies between locations were modeled using a Gaussian predictive process [2], capturing the network-like correlation structure across the landscape. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods enabled posterior inference, with convergence assessed via Geweke’s diagnostic [3]. We quantified how network connectivity patterns associate with ecological covariates through odds ratios and 95% credible intervals. Pathogen prevalence networks exhibited distinct spatial topologies. General Rickettsia spp. showed weak spatial network structure with minimal geographic clustering, while nymphs had lower infection odds (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.47-0.80). Rickettsia amblyommatis displayed strong coastal and northeastern network hubs with significant life-stage heterogeneity: larvae showed elevated connectivity (OR 3.02, 95% CI 1.03-9.20) while nymphs had reduced network participation (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.29-0.56). Land cover significantly modulated Rickettsia amblyommatis network structure. Ehrlichia ewingii formed northwestern network clusters with homogeneous life-stage connectivity. Our spatial network analysis reveals pathogen-specific connectivity patterns across South Carolina’s ecological landscape. These distinct network topologies likely reflect differential host community structures, climate gradients, and vector-host interaction networks. Identifying high-connectivity nodes (infection hotspots) enables network-based intervention strategies. The observed spatial heterogeneity suggests that pathogen transmission networks are shaped by complex ecological interactions varying across geographic space.

column9: A Spectral Framework for Coupled Thermal and Reactive Transport in Pore Network Models
column13: We develop a mathematical framework for \textbf{dynamics on pore-scale networks} that couple fluid flow, species transport, and heat transfer, motivated by fractured aquifer systems [1,3]. The network consists of edges representing pores, along which species and heat undergo advection, diffusion, reaction, and conduction, coupled through nonlinear pressure-driven flow and temperature-dependent wall reactions. These edge dynamics interact through \textbf{vertex-based continuity and Kirchhoff-type flux balance conditions}, yielding a fully coupled multi-physics dynamical system on the network.  To enable analytical insight into the resulting \textbf{spreading and interaction of transport processes on the network}, we linearize the governing equations about chemical equilibrium and show that the coupled thermal–species subsystem admits a \textbf{vector-valued generalized eigenvalue problem} arising from linear stability analysis. The associated eigenmodes define a natural spectral basis for representing interacting transport dynamics across the network. Projecting the linearized system onto this basis yields a reduced-order model for modal amplitudes, coupled through pressure, temperature, and concentration variables at network vertices.  We validate the spectral reduction against full PDE simulations on pore networks and analyze convergence and mode interactions as functions of key nondimensional parameters. The results demonstrate how complex, nonlinear multi-physics \textbf{dynamics on networks} can be systematically decomposed into interacting transport modes, providing a tractable framework for reduced-order modeling with applications to subsurface energy storage and reactive flow in geological formations.

column9: Multiscale Regime Detection in S&P 500 Correlation Networks via Eigen-Entropy and Laplacian Renormalization Group Flows
column13: Complex systems are often characterized through spectral and network structure, which together expose how collective organization changes under stress. Financial markets are a canonical example: interactions among stocks induce correlation patterns that reorganize sharply during critical events. We study multiscale market disorder using eigen-entropy and network observables derived from rolling correlation matrices of S&P 500 constituents (2001-2025; N= 354; Δt=20 trading days). For each window, we quantify spectral disorder via the entropy of the correlation eigenvalue spectrum and capture concentration effects through leading-eigenvalue dominance and eigenvector-based centrality. In parallel, we construct correlation networks and track connectivity through the average degree, revealing periods of densification and increased global coupling.  To explicitly probe scale dependence, we apply a Laplacian Renormalization Group (LRG) framework to the correlation networks, producing a hierarchy of coarse-grained representations governed by a diffusion-time (resolution) parameter τ. The resulting renormalization flow provides a principled multiscale view of market organization: stable regimes exhibit persistent modular structure across scales, while critical periods show pronounced shifts in the LRG hierarchy and diffusion characteristics consistent with rapid integration. Jointly embedding spectral entropy, network connectivity, and LRG-derived multiscale signatures yields a phase space with clear separations between market regimes, enabling detection and categorization of critical events and their precursors.

column9: Local to Global Understanding of Network Processes - A Case Study in Suicide Risk Prevention
column13: Real-world decision-making in public health and social science can immesnely benefit from predictive models. But leveraging the model for real intervention requires understanding of the model that links individual predictions to social context and system-level mechanisms. As an example, for suicide prevention, social and health scientists, clinicians, and outreach workers need model-driven, explainable discovery of risk patterns so they can design targeted, evidence-based interventions that are interpretable and practically actionable. Risk scores alone do not indicate which modifiable features or peer relationships to target, nor whether interventions will scale across a network or respect logistical constraints. Explaining model behavior in ways that are simple and actionable is critical for translating predictions into effective interventions [1]. Existing node-level counterfactual explanation methods (feature perturbations, gradient-based saliency, and surrogate models) produce node-specific explanations [2]. One could identify and target frequently occurring features as a heuristic, but it does not guarantee how effective this intervention would be as per the predictive model. Further, accounting for the network in such explanation methods is non-trivial -- these methods may identify an important edge, but that does not reveal the reasoning as well as identifying an important feature.  We introduce Local-to-Global (L2G) understanding, a framework that aggregates node-level counterfactuals into a compact intervention hypothesis. We formalize \textbf{hypothesis generation as a Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) coverage problem} over networks: choose a small collection of clauses over a constrained set of mutable features whose disjunction maximizes coverage of high-risk predictions across the network. In effect, each clause of the DNF leads to a potential ``sub-intervention'' that would benefit a subset of the nodes in the network. We show that this can be formulated as a DNF coverage objective, which is nondecreasing and submodular with knapsack constraints. As a result, the greedy algorithm results in a good approximation. We instantiate L2G with Graph Neural Networks for suicide risk prediction. We train a Graph Attention Network that achieves a high accuracy in predicting high-risk nodes. For each node, we use a perturbation-based greedy algorithm to generate per-node counterfactuals based on feature perturbations of self and of neighbors. The submodular DNF selection prioritizes clauses that maximize overall explanatory coverage while keeping the length of the DNF.  Applied to peer-based suicide-prevention scenarios in synthetic graphs as well as real-world networks, L2G converts opaque model outputs into intervention hypotheses that outperform results from simply choosing frequent ``important'' features. Real-world deployment requires additional constraints on the generated hypothesis (DNF) to account for the cost of intervention, which may be supermodular due to overheads in performing multiple ``sub-interventions''. We show that our greedy algorithm still provides approximation guarantees.

column9: Effective criminal network disruption via the friendship paradox
column13: Organised criminal groups are increasingly understood to be flexible, decentralised networks, rather than rigid hierarchies [1]. Such groups tend to be resistant to law enforcement attempts to disrupt their activities, and can quickly adapt quickly to such interventions. Moreover, law enforcement strategies to disrupt and dismantle such networks can be extremely resource intensive and differentially effective. In particular, approaches typically require \emph{complete knowledge} of the criminal network structure in order for disruptions to be effective (Fig.~1 (a)-(b)), which is almost never the case for covert networks. Here we introduce \emph{Friendship Paradox Disruption} (FPD), which leverages the well-known friendship paradox [2-3] to disrupt criminal networks (Fig.~1 (c)-(d)). Importantly, rather than requiring complete network knowlege, FPD relies only on \emph{local knowledge} of network structure, for example provided by informants or partial surveillance by law enforcement authorities.  In this talk we discuss challenges of collecting data on and studying covert criminal networks, and introduce an approach based on exponential random graph models (ERGMs) [4] to generate synthetic criminal networks from limited data. We review typical disruption strategies and metrics for assessing their effectiveness, as well as presenting a novel disruption metric based on paths between nodes. We compare and contrast the effectiveness of FPD with other disruption approaches (Fig.~1 (e)) on synthetic and real networks [5], and discuss the implications of our findings for law enforcement.

column9: Capacitated Path Survival Reliabilities for Flow-Centric Network Reliability Analysis
column11: Lim, Brian Godwin*; Tan, Renzo Roel; Ikeda, Kazushi
column13: Network reliability analysis aims to measure the ability of networks to function satisfactorily after sustaining damage. Focusing on probabilistic connectedness of stochastic graphs with designated sources and failure-probability-weighted edges, previous work introduced path survival reliabilities to quantify the likelihood of single-source paths, i.e., paths traversing exactly one source node, to sustain damages. These reliability measures exhibit distinctive theoretical properties and intuitive empirical results. Nevertheless, their simplistic formulations potentially limit their practical utility.  In line with this, generalizations of path survival reliabilities incorporating edge flow capacities are proposed. In particular, consider the graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ with a set of source vertices $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{V}$, edge failure probabilities $0 \leq \pi(e) \leq 1$, and edge capacities $\kappa(e) > 0$, for $e \in \mathcal{E}$. For a single-source path $\mathcal{P}$, the path survival reliability is defined as $P\left(\mathcal{P}\right) \coloneq \prod_{e \in \mathcal{P}} \left[1 - \pi\left(e\right)\right]$. For the family (set) of single-source paths $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{G}, \langle v,s \rangle)$ from $v \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \mathcal{S}$ to $s \in \mathcal{S}$, the capacitated per-vertex measure is reformulated as $\Pi^{(\mathcal{G})}\left(v\right) \coloneq \dfrac{\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{P} \in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{G}, \langle v, s \rangle\right)} \min_{e \in \mathcal{P}} \kappa\left(e\right) \cdot P\left(\mathcal{P}\right)}{\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{\mathcal{P} \in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{G}, \langle v, s \rangle\right)} \min_{e \in \mathcal{P}} \kappa(e)}$, weighing each $\mathcal{P} \in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{G}, \langle v, s \rangle\right)$ by its flow capacity $\min_{e \in \mathcal{P}} \kappa\left(e\right)$. Finally, the capacitated total reliability measure for $\mathcal{G}$ is reformulated as $\Psi\left(\mathcal{G}\right) \coloneq \frac{\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \mathcal{S}} \Delta^{\left(\mathcal{G}\right)}(v) \cdot \left[\Pi^{(\mathcal{G})}\left(v\right)\right]^{\delta\left(\mathcal{G}\right)}}{\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \mathcal{S}} \Delta^{\left(\mathcal{G}\right)}(v)}$, with the graph density $\delta\left(\mathcal{G}\right)$ and vertex-to-source shortest path length $\Delta^{\left(\mathcal{G}\right)}(v)$. Moreover, these capacitated measures may also be efficiently calculated using zero-suppressed binary decision diagrams (ZDDs). Specifically, given a minimum edge capacity $c$ and the ZDD root node $r$ with label $e_r \in \mathcal{E}$ representing $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{G}, \langle v,s \rangle)$, denote $\mathcal{M}^{(r)}(c) \coloneq \sum_{\mathcal{P} \in \mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{G}, \langle v, s \rangle\right)} \mathbbm{1}_{\left\{\min_{e \in \mathcal{P}} \kappa(e) = c\right\}} \left(\mathcal{P}\right) \cdot \prod_{e \in \mathcal{P}} \left[1 - \pi(e)\right]$. Leveraging the recursive property of the diagram, for the 0- and 1-child nodes $r_0$ and $r_1$, respectively, it may be shown that $\mathcal{M}^{(r)}(c) = \mathcal{M}^{(r_0)}(c) + \left[1 - \pi(e_r)\right] \cdot \mathbbm{1}_{\left\{\kappa(e_r) > c\right\}} \left(e_r\right) \cdot \mathcal{M}^{(r_1)}(c) + \left[1 - \pi(e_r)\right] \cdot \mathbbm{1}_{\left\{\kappa(e_r) = c\right\}} \left(e_r\right) \cdot \sum_{c' \geq c} \mathcal{M}^{(r_1)}(c')$. Hence, the generalized measures may be calculated in $\mathcal{O}\left(\left|\mathcal{V} \setminus \mathcal{S}\right| \cdot \left|\mathcal{S}\right| \cdot |\kappa| \cdot Z\left(\mathcal{D}_\Omega\right)\right)$, where $|\kappa|$ denotes the number of unique flow capacities and $Z(\mathcal{D}_\Omega) \ll |\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{G}, \langle v,s \rangle)|$ denotes the maximum number of ZDD nodes constructed across all $v$ and $s$. Overall, the generalized capacitated reliability measures offer a more nuanced, flow-centric perspective on the reliability of real-world lifeline networks while also maintaining theoretical grounding and efficient calculation using ZDDs.

column9: Are scale-free networks also timescale-free?
column13: Our understanding of a physical system's dynamic behavior is often unraveled through its intrinsic timescales, as it responds to external excitation. The classic example is the harmonic oscillator, which is characterized by two timescales: its decay rate (damping) and its oscillation period. But what happens when the system is complex and heterogeneous, such as a scale-free network. Such systems lack a characteristic structural scale, but do they also lack a dynamic timescale? In simple terms, are scale-free networks also timescale-free?  To address this, we investigate the network’s response to arbitrary forms of excitation. Our analysis shows that complex systems fall into distinct dynamic classes: Homogeneous dynamics, where, despite the scale-free network structure, the system's actual dynamics exhibit uniform timescales.  Timescale-free dynamics, where the systems, indeed, lacks a typical timescale and, instead, features a coexistence of vastly diverse excitation lifetimes. Most excitations are extremely short-lived, but some live on for extended periods, sustained for orders of magnitude above the system's average timescale.    These newly discovered timescale-free networks feature special modes, that the network is dynamically wired to preserve for extended periods. These modes, capturing timescale-hubs, decay extremely slowly, and are thus preserved for orders of magnitude longer than all other dynamic states. More broadly, our analysis offers a systematic translation of topology (degree distribution) into dynamics (timescale distribution), that helps us predict the system’s uniquely long-lasting vs. short-lived dynamic states.

column9: Network resuscitation – reviving failed networks
column13: Complex systems, biological, social or technological, often experience perturbations and disturbances, from overload failures in power systems to species extinction in ecological networks. The impact of such perturbations is often subtle, the system exhibits a minor response, but continues to sustain its global functionality. However, in extreme cases, a large enough perturbation may lead to a large-scale collapse, with the system abruptly transitioning from a functional to a dysfunctional dynamic state. For instance, in cellular dynamics, genetic knockouts, beyond a certain threshold, lead to cell death; in ecological systems, changes in environmental conditions may, in extreme cases, cause mass-extinction; and in infrastructure networks, a cascading failure, at times, results in a major blackout.   When such collapse occurs, the naïve instinct is to reverse the damage, retrieve the failed nodes and reconstruct the lost links. Such response however is seldom efficient, as (i) we rarely have access to all system components, limiting our ability to reconstruct the perturbed network; (ii) even if we could reverse the damage, due to hysteresis, in many cases, the system will not spontaneously regain its lost functionality.  To address this challenge, we consider here a two-step recovery process:   Step I. Restructuring. Retrieving the network topology and weights to a point where the system can potentially regain its functionality.  Step II. Reigniting. Introducing dynamic interventions to steer the system back to its functional state.  The challenge in Step II is that in most practical scenarios we lack direct control over the dynamic activity of the majority of the nodes. Hence, we seek to reignite the system via micro-interventions, i.e. controlling just a small number of components, typically - just a single or, at most, few nodes. Therefore, in this talk, we present single-node reigniting, unveiling a new dynamic phase of complex systems, in which a failed system can be revived by controlling just a microscopic set of nodes. In this sense, single-node control acts as a network dynamics defibrillator, delivering a focused shock that revives a collapsed system and brings it back to life.

column9: Dynamic stability of complex networks
column13: Will a large complex system be stable? This question, first posed by May in 1972, captures a long-standing challenge, fueled by a seeming contradiction between theory and practice. While empirical reality answers with an astounding yes, the mathematical analysis, based on linear stability theory, seems to suggest the contrary - that a sufficiently large complex system, will inevitably become unstable - hence, the diversity-stability paradox.   What, then, are the naturally emerging organizing principles, or in May’s original wording - what are nature’s devious strategies, to achieve dynamic stability in complex systems?  Initial clues began to unveil with the mapping of empirical networks, which uncovered universally recurring topological characteristics that can potentially impact the system’s dynamics. For example, degree heterogeneity, community structure and topological symmetries - all naturally emerging features of real-world networks - do, indeed, impact the system’s dynamics. However, on their own, these topological features are insufficient to ensure stability, leaving May’s mathematical challenge unresolved.   Here we present a solution to this dichotomy, by considering the interplay between the network topology A and system’s intrinsic nonlinear dynamics. We show that this interplay leads to the emergence of non-random patterns in the system's stability matrix J (the Jacobian). Specifically, we show that the terms of J exhibit dynamic driven scaling patterns with the network's weighted degrees. This characterizes different network dynamical systems via a set of three analytically tractable exponents μ,ν,ρ, whose values are rooted in the specific form of the system’s dynamics, e.g., social, biological or technological.  The effect is profound, and fundamentally changes the structure of the Jacobian. For example, when μ=1 or 2, the diagonal terms Jii associated with hub nodes are large, while, under the same network, if μ=-1, these terms asymptotically vanish.   The result is a previously unmapped link between topology A and dynamics J, whose patterns stand in sharp contrast with the prevailing random matrix-based paradigm, thus offering a new matrix ensemble, by which to capture the dynamic stability of real-world systems.   This ensemble helps us analytically identify the (few) relevant control parameters that predict a system's stability, exposing three broad dynamic classes: In the asymptotically unstable class, diversity, indeed, leads to instability a là May's paradox. However, we also expose an asymptotically stable class, the class in which most real systems reside, where stability is not only possible, but, in fact, becomes inevitable. Together, our theory uncovers the naturally emerging rules of complex system stability, in a sense - exposing nature's devious strategies, thus helping us reconcile the paradox that has eluded us for decades.

column9: Social Network Intensifies Competitive Dynamics Among LLM Agents
column13: Multi-round collective games in competitive environments often yield suboptimal outcomes, yet how social information shapes such dynamics remains unclear. Leveraging large language models (LLMs) as decision-making agents with rich cognitive capacities, we design a multi-round, winner-takes-all tournament in which 200 GPT-4o agents with heterogeneous abilities compete in a 50-round investment game. Agents update investments through self-reflection and peer observation. Our results show that social networks systematically amplify competitive escalation and influence agents’ self-perception.  Comparing isolated agents with those in small-world and scale-free networks, we find that networks significantly intensifycompetition. Across conditions, average investment follows a parabolic trajectory, with networked agents consistently investing more than isolated ones. Strategic dispersion rises throughout the game and spikes near the end: a small subset maintains high intensity competition, while most agents, reassessing their winning odds, effectively withdraw in final rounds.  To further elucidate the cognitive mechanisms underlying these patterns, agents periodically assess their own abilities based on performance outcomes and information from neighbors. We find that agents generally underestimate their abilities, and that this underestimation leads directly to more conservative investment strategies. Crucially, additional social information does not necessarily improve cognitive accuracy: while small-world networks facilitate more accurate ability assessment, highly centralized scale-free networks exacerbate belief miscalibration over time.  In summary, this study reveals how social network structures drive competitive escalation, selective withdrawal, and collective inefficiency by influencing agents’ social cognition and belief calibration.

column9: A framework for representing health trajectories and identifying where they diverge
column11: Spoon, Katie*;  Souto-Maior, Joao M.; Mackenna, Bernardo ; Rehkopf, David
column13: Health outcomes result from long and complex life histories, yet most population health studies still estimate the short-term effect of a single factor on a single outcome. Using Electronic Health Records from the American Family Cohort, we propose a graph-based framework that represents longitudinal health histories for 8 million U.S. primary care patients and their 90 million doctor visits as paths on an explicit state-transition network. We first cluster visit-level feature vectors that summarize recent clinical status, continuity of care, and neighborhood context into a small set of recurrent “snapshot states,” and build a directed, weighted graph over these states. Each patient’s history becomes a path on this shared state space. We then derive patient-level trajectory embeddings from these paths and cluster patients into trajectory types in order to compare outcome risks and demographic composition across trajectory types. This network perspective of health trajectories offers an interpretable, scalable way to identify high-risk paths and the communities most affected by them.

column9: A Diagnostic Framework for Sampling-Induced Distortion in Network Metrics
column13: Empirical network data are almost always sampled, whether due to API limits, partial crawls, or missing data. The chosen sampling method and sampling fraction can significantly distort measured network statistics, so metrics computed on a sampled graph may misrepresent the underlying network. Prior work on graph sampling has mainly focused on designing and comparing algorithms that preserve individual statistics such as degree distributions, clustering, path lengths, or modular structure. Existing studies analyze how node-based, edge-based, and traversal-based samplers affect these properties, but they do not provide a single, interpretable distortion score that is comparable across metrics, sampling schemes, and network types.  In this work I propose a simple diagnostic, the normalized distortion (ND), that quantifies how unreliable a given network metric becomes under a chosen sampling scheme and sampling fraction. Given a full “ground-truth” network with a true metric value (for example, the global clustering coefficient or assortativity), I repeatedly sample subgraphs using a fixed sampler and fraction and compute the same metric on each sampled subgraph. From these values I compute the sample mean and sample standard deviation, and then rescale both the bias (the difference between the mean and the true value) and the variability (the standard deviation) by a characteristic scale based on the magnitude of the true value plus a small constant to avoid division by zero. The normalized distortion is defined as the Euclidean combination (square root of the sum of squares) of this relative bias and relative variability, yielding a single dimensionless number that captures how far, on average, the sampled metric deviates from the truth and how unstable it is across samples, all on a comparable relative scale.  I demonstrate this framework on four canonical random graph models: Erdős–Rényi (ER), Watts–Strogatz small-world (WS), Barabási–Albert scale-free (BA), and a stochastic block model (SBM). For each model, I consider four samplers (random node, snowball, degree-weighted node, and uniform edges with induction) and sampling fractions between five and thirty percent of the nodes, focusing on two metrics: the global clustering coefficient and the average shortest-path length. The results show that normalized distortion for clustering is often large at low sampling fractions in BA and ER graphs, especially under degree-weighted and uniform-edge sampling, while random node sampling is consistently less distorting; in WS networks, clustering is comparatively robust, with normalized distortion remaining below about 0.4 even at five percent sampling. Average shortest-path length is generally more robust (normalized distortion mostly below about 0.7), but its behavior still depends on sampler and topology: snowball sampling preserves path length particularly well in ER, SBM, and WS, whereas random node sampling can substantially distort distances in BA and WS, and degree-weighted or uniform-edge sampling show marked distortion at intermediate fractions.  Overall, the normalized distortion framework turns sampling from a hidden nuisance into a measurable design choice, quantifying how much bias and variability different samplers introduce for each metric and providing a practical, topology-aware calibration tool for choosing metrics, sampling strategies, and sample sizes in empirical network studies.

column9: Growing a Sympoietic Art Organism: An Experimental Framework for Tracking the Micro-Dynamics of Cultural Evolution
column11: Dazeley-Gaist, Phileas*; Camacho Cabrera, Gabriel; Thompson, Kyle; Arango Franco, Sara; Bulla Casas, Lina; Abd El Razek, Nadine
column12: pdazeley-gaist23@coa.edu*; gabrielcamachocabrera.cr@gmail.com; tkyle1832@gmail.com; sarangofc@gmail.com; linabulla27@gmail.com; nadineaboud@aucegypt.edu
column13: Empirical data recording how cultural artefacts, motifs, and lineages form in real time are of great benefit and interest in the study of cultural evolution. In this work, we introduce an experimental design (nicknamed “Sympoietic Art Organism” in a nod to Haraway) that attempts to richly capture the bottom-up emergence of a shared cultural heritage in a small, controlled setting, as well as the influences at play throughout its evolution. Our approach calls for a small community of artists to engage in active collaborative artmaking over several months to build up a shared creative commons. After an initial “seeding phase” round of art contributions to the commons data repository, participants are asked to contribute at least five new artefacts to the commons every two weeks, over a series of “co-creative cycles”, and with the requirements that each shared piece engage with one or more pre-existing artworks (that is, artworks from earlier cycles) and that we record these influences between works to a shared ledger.   We, the ten co-authors of this study, took part in our own experiment over three months, growing a dataset of 411 original artworks, and a network of 725 verified relationships between them. Our experiment yielded a complete history of the creation of cultural artefacts (artworks) by each participant, and of all acknowledged influences from other pieces, allowing us to reconstruct the citation network of contributed artworks. By enforcing synchronous updates within each co-creative cycle such that participants only engaged with artworks from earlier stages, we were able to model the network’s growth as a time series.  Our results are well suited for multi-modal analysis. Quantitatively, we observed the structural evolution of the citation network from disconnected nodes into a consolidated core as the system matured. We found the network’s structural dynamics were consistent rich-get-richer feedback, showing that preferential attachment emerged endogenously around specific hub artworks. Qualitatively, the artworks provide a basis for tracing a kind of semantic phylogeny through visual inspection and comparison of contributed artworks, to see how participants adapted, remixed, or subverted specific aesthetic motifs across generations.   We propose this experiment as a proof of concept for a scalable ethnographic tool in network science. This approach provides a transparent environment for investigating the mechanisms of cultural inheritance.  This work was initiated at the 2025 Complexity Global School, organised by the Santa Fe Institute and TREES group at the Universidad de Los Andes.

column9: Human vs. Generative AI: A Comparison of Creative Strategies
column11: Yu, Yulin*; Shen ,  Anthony; Wang, David; Uzzi, Brian
column13: The rapid advancement of generative AI has renewed optimism that creativity—central to innovation across domains from science to art—can be substantially expanded through human–machine collaboration. While AI systems can recombine vast bodies of existing knowledge in novel ways, prior work suggests that human creativity retains distinctive advantages, particularly in flexibility and contextual adaptation. To enable effective coordination between human and machine creativity, we ask a fundamental question: \textbf{How do machines (Gen-AI) achieve creativity compared to humans, and what processes underlie these differences?}  We investigate this question using the Divergent Association Task (DAT) [1], a widely used and replicable measure of creative ideation. Analyzing over 5{,}000 human and machine DAT responses worldwide, we apply text and network analyses to compare creative strategies at both individual and collective levels. First, following theories of cognitive simplicity, we examine step-by-step vocabulary selection, operationalizing word simplicity using five metrics drawn from prior literature: (1) age of acquisition, (2) word frequency, (3) word length, (4) spoken-language tendency, and (5) written-language tendency. We track the first through seventh words produced in each response. Second, we examine categorical jumps between successive words, as larger semantic shifts are thought to signal greater creative potential. To quantify word categories and distances, we use WordNet [2], a tree-structured lexical network (Figure~1A), and compute per-response category counts as well as average, variance, and maximum jump distances. Finally, we examine collective behavior by comparing the total number of categories covered by humans versus machines.  Our findings reveal three key insights. First, at the individual level, humans tend to use simpler and more common words than machines, yet collectively generate far greater lexical diversity. Humans use higher-frequency and lower-complexity words (1.62 vs.\ 1.98), but produce substantially more unique words overall (4048 vs.\ 749). Both humans and machines progress from simpler to more complex words over time; however, machines exhibit a steeper increase in complexity in later stages (Figure~1A). Second, at the categorical level (Figure~1B), humans use fewer broad categories per response but explore more fine-grained categories, and collectively cover a much wider semantic space than machines. Finally, while human word-to-word semantic distances are smaller on average (11.19 vs.\ 12.59), they show higher variance (6.22 vs.\ 8.97), consistent with Lévy-flight–like search patterns. Together, these results suggest that the advantage of human creativity lies less in individual output and more in collective variation, highlighting a key complementarity between human and machine creative processes.

column9: Emergence of LLM hallucination in science: Evidence from non-existent citations
column11: Wang, Yihe; Zhao, Zhenyue; Yin, Yian*

column9: The New Mathematics Needed for Higher-Order Systems Analysis
column13: Hypergraph theory has been established in recent years as the primary framework to capture higher-order interactions in complex systems [1]. However, due to computational limitations, many standard techniques rely on lower-order projections of hypergraphs that can be treated with conventional network theory methods [2,4]. A common example of such an order-reducing procedure is the replacement of higher-order hyperedges by cliques of pair-wise edges. This is equivalent to performing trace operations (summing over indices) on the adjacency tensor -- containing the full information of a hypergraph -- until a single 2-index matrix is obtained. Such matrices form associative algebras, which are mathematically well-understood and afford powerful analytical tools such as spectral theory. Despite these advantages, the information loss of order-reduction procedures may obscure patterns emerging from irreducible higher-order interactions.          To address these challenges we propose a novel approach to the mathematical and computational treatment of hypergraphs based on rewriting systems and higher-arity algebra [3,6]. We argue that the lack of adoption of non-reductive tensor techniques in higher-order systems science is not only due to computational limitations but also to the intrinsic difficulties of higher-order  mathematical structures. Recent advances in the fields of hypermatrices and non-associative algebra [7] show that genuinely higher-order techniques do indeed require new mathematical methods. We implement our framework in a suite of algorithms that use hypergraph motif rewriting at its core to unify topological and algebraic properties of hypergraphs and their lower-order representations under a single computational paradigm.
