column9: Genotype networks drive oscillating endemicity and epidemic trajectories in viral evolution
column11: Lamata Otín, Santiago*; Rotita Ion, Octavian C. ; Arenas, Alex; Soriano Paños, David; Gómez Gardeñes, Jesús
column13: Rapidly evolving viruses use antigenic drift as a key mechanism to evade host immunity and persist in real populations. While traditional models of antigenic drift and epidemic spread rely on low-dimensional antigenic spaces, genomic surveillance data reveal that viral evolution produces complex antigenic genotype networks with hierarchical modular structures. In this study, we present an eco-evolutionary framework in which viral evolution and population immunity dynamics are shaped by the structure of antigenic genotype networks. Using synthetic networks, we demonstrate that network topology alone can drive transitions between stable endemic states and recurrent seasonal epidemics. Furthermore, our results show how the integration of the genotype network of the H3N2 influenza in our model allows for estimating the emergence times of various haplotypes resulting from its evolution. Our findings underscore the critical role of the topology of genotype networks in shaping epidemic behavior and, besides, provide a robust framework for integrating real-world genomic data into predictive epidemic models.

column9: Construction of Hidden Metric Space with Community Structure
column13: Recent research has demonstrated that many empirical networks possess a hidden metric space (HMS)—a metric space that underlies and shapes the observable network topology. Distances within the HMS generally reflect the similarity between nodes, making it particularly well-suited for network routing via the greedy routing strategy (GRS). When the HMS of a given network is known, the GRS can establish routes between any pair of nodes without relying on global information, a key advantage over alternative routing methods. Various approaches have been proposed for constructing the HMS, yielding different metric spaces such as planar, hyperbolic, and high-dimensional spaces. However, no principled method exists for selecting the appropriate metric space, and embedding a network into an unsuitable metric space can substantially degrade the GRS routing performance.  This work introduces a hierarchical approach for computing the HMS of a given network. Unlike traditional methods that embed networks into a single metric space, our approach relies on the network's community structure to construct a hierarchical HMS, thereby avoiding the performance limitations imposed by a predetermined metric space. Fig. 1(a) illustrates the application of our algorithm to a US population model network, where the result is a two-layer HMS. We demonstrate that this approach can be applied to an arbitrary network regardless of its physical embedding, as shown in Fig. 1(b). Compared to existing embedding algorithms, the hierarchical HMS approach consistently achieves superior routing performance while significantly reducing computational time, particularly for large-scale networks. Moreover, for certain networks, routing performance with the hierarchical HMS surpasses that achieved using real-space coordinates, suggesting that the constructed HMS captures network structure more effectively than physical embedding.

column9: Increasing digital media visibility and tourism messaging promote US National Park system integration
column11: Petersen, Alexander*; Arroyave, Felber; Shackelton, Stephen; Jenkins, Jeffrey
column13: The National Park Service (NPS) faces a paradoxical dual mandate – to preserve invaluable environmental and cultural resources for future generations, and to ensure their public accessibility for recreational enjoyment. Yet with >124 million visitors in 2019, the US national parks (NPs) are at risk of being ‘loved to death’, a challenge faced by protected areas the world over. This growing demand for ecosystem services calls for new strategies to enhance public appreciation and commitment to protecting natural capital. Against this backdrop, we analyzed the structure and dynamics of the NP system through a public-facing lens constructed from >426,000 digital media articles mentioning at least one park by its official name. Our analysis reveals that from 2010-2019, NP media visibility grew by over 3,900%, outpacing 29% growth in visitation and a 15% decline in federal budget support for NPs. We find that this disproportionate media growth is driven by tourism-oriented articles referencing multiple NPs, which has become the principal driver of NP system integration in the public sphere. Consequently, ecotourism marketing has displaced public attention from critical issues such associated with environmental, wildfire and wildlife management. With many NPs operating at or near capacity, tourism-driven integration of the NP system may intensify fundamental tensions within the NPS dual mandate, as rising demand for ecosystem services collides with limited federal resources and growing environmental risks.

column9: Investment Flows in Venture Capital
column13: The distribution of private investment across sectors has attracted sustained scholarly attention, in part because sectoral allocation is a primary determinant of aggregate financial returns and long-run growth. Yet, despite extensive empirical work, there is still no consensus on how such distributions emerge, nor on how profitable investment windows shift over time from one industry to another. A key reason is that industries are typically treated as discrete, well-defined silos, implicitly assuming stable boundaries and limited cross-sectoral spillovers. This representation obscures the underlying technological, functional, and informational continuities that shape capital reallocation and innovation dynamics.  To address this limitation, we adopt a bottom-up approach to sector formation. Rather than imposing ex-ante industry classifications, we construct sectors endogenously by clustering firms along three complementary dimensions: similarity in tasks and production activities, following recent advances in task-based representations of firms (Acemoglu, 2024); similarity in products and capabilities, grounded in the economic complexity framework (Tacchella et al., 2012, 2018); and textual similarity in firm descriptions, capturing latent technological and strategic proximity (Gordon & Phillips, 2009). Integrating these dimensions, we embed firms in a high-dimensional network space in which distance reflects economic and technological relatedness rather than administrative classification.  Within this network, private investment flows can be interpreted as a diffusion process operating over an irregular, evolving structure. Using three decades of U.S. private investment data, we show that the spatial propagation of investment is not well described by smooth reallocation or sector-by-sector rotation. Instead, it exhibits scaling properties and clustering patterns consistent with fractal geometry, closely resembling growth dynamics in disordered media. In particular, investment expansion follows dynamics analogous to correlated percolation, whereby capital propagates through locally dense clusters of related firms and technologies, occasionally triggering rapid phase transitions when previously disconnected regions of the network become accessible.  This perspective reframes sectoral investment dynamics as an emergent phenomenon arising from micro-level firm relatedness, rather than as a sequence of independent sectoral cycles. Profitable investment windows do not simply “move” across predefined industries; they percolate through a continuously reconfiguring economic space shaped by task overlap, product complementarities, and shared narratives. As a result, sectoral boundaries appear porous, endogenous, and time-varying, offering a unifying framework to explain both the persistence of investment clusters and the sudden reorientation of capital toward new technological domains.

column9: Information exchange processes leads to ultra-small world networks
column13: A substantial body of evidence indicates that real-world networks exhibit the small-world property, meaning that the maximal distance between any two nodes grows logarithmically rather than linearly with network size. In 2023, we proposed a game-theoretic approach based on a weighted analogue of betweenness centrality as a utility function, improving upon existing models at that time - most notably the Watts–Strogatz model. Our framework provided an explanation for why, in real social networks, this principle can be stated even more strongly: most social networks are organized such that no individual is more than six connections away from any other, an empirical regularity known as the six degrees of separation.  The proposed game-theoretic approach showed that the “six degrees of separation” property naturally arises as an equilibrium outcome in networks where individuals balance their aspiration to improve their centrality,captured by the standard notion of betweenness centrality, against the costs of forming and maintaining connections. However, two important aspects remained unaddressed: first, the motivation for forming directed connections beyond pure intermediation roles (which are clearly relevant in real-world settings), and second, the absence of an explicit payoff formulation.  In the present work, we adopt a different perspective. Each agent is now modeled as both a sender and a receiver of information. During information transmission, agents prefer to use shortest paths, as information becomes progressively distorted with each transmission step, akin to the “telephone game.” A node derives utility when a sufficiently large amount of high-quality, minimally distorted information passes through it—both as a destination and as an intermediary.  The proposed framework not only reproduces the tendency toward ultra-small-world structures (with only technical modifications relative to our original model), but also naturally accommodates the utility of directed links and allows for agent heterogeneity. Moreover, it provides a promising foundation for analyzing the emerging agentic web: a paradigm of the Internet that, according to current forecasts, may replace the classical web architecture by 2030th.

column9: Untangling Memory and Influence in Complex Systems: Separable Markov Models for Sequence Generation
column13: When we aim to predict sequences of interactions, movements, or events in complex networked systems, it is often necessary to account for temporal memory and structural correlations in the underlying dynamics. Traditional higher-order Markov models are commonly used to capture such dependencies, but they suffer from an exponentially growing parameter space and limited interpretability, particularly in data-sparse settings.  In this talk, we discuss the separable Markov model, a subset of higher-order Markov models in which transitions are generated by mixing contributions from past states through a stochastic memory kernel. Similar models have been described by [1, 2]. This model assumes a linearised, conditionally independent relationship between transitions and the history of the process, providing a principled trade-off between expressivity and parsimony, with parameter complexity growing linearly in the memory length.  In comparison to full higher-order Markov models, this assumption substantially reduces the number of parameters required, making the model a promising alternative when long-range memory is present but data or computational resources are limited. We describe the formal relationship between separable and full higher-order Markov models and identify settings where the separability assumption leads to limited information loss relative to gains in statistical efficiency.  Using simulated dynamics, we illustrate how the memory kernel controls long-range association structure and autocorrelation patterns in generated sequences. We further outline an expectation–maximisation framework for fitting the model and discuss practical issues of identifiability and model selection.   We conclude with an exploration of the performance on a selection of datasets, demonstrating how the separable Markov model is a practical and interpretable tool for modelling memory-driven dynamics on networks.

column9: Borda Aggregation Dynamics of Preference Orderings on Networks
column13: We introduce and analyze a discrete-time network process in which each node holds a (weak) preference ordering over a finite set of alternatives and updates by local \emph{Borda aggregation}. At each step, a node forms a weighted average (row-stochastic random-walk normalization) of its neighbors' Borda score vectors and projects the aggregated score back to a weak order. Updates are \emph{bounded}: in each round, a node advances by at most one step along a shortest path in the fixed graph of preference orderings, following the direction prescribed by its neighbors’ Borda-aggregated preferences. Our emphasis is dynamical: we develop sufficient conditions, stated directly in terms of graph topology, weights, and the bounded step rule, for (i) \emph{self-sustained oscillations} in the absence of persistent sources, and (ii) \emph{forced oscillations} under contrarian persistent camps. We also record robustness (structural stability) away from score-tie hyperplanes and contrast synchronous (Variant~S) and asynchronous (Variant~A) updating.

column9: Impact of one-way constraints on random walk dynamics: a case study on urban street networks
column13: Understanding the relation between network structure and dynamical processes is of utmost importance in many fields and in recent studies, there has been growing interest in analyzing the effect of partial edge damage on random walk dynamics to better understand network functionality. In this work, we consider the effect of full damage to edges (i.e., edge removal) on the movement of a random walker and present a general framework for studying the response of random walk dynamics to one-way constraints on networks. We then apply the proposed framework to examine the impact of one-way streets on random walk dynamics in 55 urban street networks around the world.

column9: The fragile nature of rewarded cooperation in social networks: a mixed game model.
column13: Issues around sustainable development frequently spills down to the tension between self-interest and altruism or in other terms the willingness to take cooperative action at the cost of individual payoffs. This paper investigates some aspects of sustainable cooperation through an extended Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) game, which is extended along four dimensions.  First, the model distinguishes between individualist and conformist attitudes [1]. Indivdualist players follow the standard PD game, while conformists play a coordination game and align their strategy with that of the majority of their social connections. Unlike existing models, this mixed game setup assigns different payoff functions to conformists. Second, adjusted replicator dynamics [2] is applied, where attitudes evolve based on their relative payoffs, recognizing that social attitudes change more slowly than strategy choices. Third, equilibrium outcomes are analyzed within complex social network structures [3]. Fourth, the effect of monetary incentives for cooperation is examined in interaction with attitude dynamics and network structure [4].  Equilibrium results show that cooperation only persists if both cooperation and conformism are in the majority at the game outset, otherwise individualism and defection prevail. If this condition holds, then a stable yet heterogeneous equilibrium can emerge where conformists cooperate and individualists defect.   Rewarding promotes a shift toward cooperation, but its effectiveness depends on the composition of the population. If all players are conformists, the reward will be ineffective as the decision rule of conformists only indirectly depend on the reward. The reward encourages individualism, potentially altering the direction of attitude dynamics. While the reward is active, individualism spreads, even if individualists cooperate. In a complete network, this often leads to complete cooperation, but once the reward is withdrawn, the system collapses into full defection. These patterns persist in incomplete networks. The reward boosts cooperation but also promotes individualism, causing cooperation to drop below pre-reward levels once. Network structure plays a crucial role in shaping these dynamics. Sparse social networks help sustain cooperation, but degree asymmetry has an even stronger impact on equilibrium outcomes. Equilibrium cooperation is more likely to persist and the effect of the reward is greater in scale free networks compared to symmetric (Erdős-Rényi type) random or complete networks. Moreover, the dispersion across independent simulation runs is smaller and outcomes are typically closer to full cooperation, reflecting the role of highly connected nodes that bridge local neighborhoods. Scale free network structures also lead to sharper declines in cooperation once the reward is withdrawn. These results are driven by the stronger influence of degree asymmetry on the spread of individualism.  [1] Pena, J., Volken, H., Pestelacci, E., Tomassini, M. DOI:10.1016/j.physrep.2007.04.004.  [4] Jimenez, R., Lugo, H., Cuesta, J.A., Sanchez, A. (2008): Emergence and resilience of cooperation in the spatial prisoner’s dilemma via a reward mechanism. Journal of Theoretical Biology 250, 475–483. DOI:10.1016/j.jtbi.2007.10.010.

column9: Adaptive Cannistraci Hebb Network Automata Modelling of Complex Networks for Path based Link Prediction
column11: Zhao, Jialin; Muscoloni, Alessandro; Michieli, Umberto; Zhang, Yingtao; Cannistraci, Carlo*
column13: Many complex networks have partially observed or evolving connectivity, making link prediction a fundamental task. Topological link prediction infers missing links using only network topology, with applications in social, biological, and technological systems. T he Cannistraci Hebb (CH) theory provides a topological formulation of Hebbian learning, grounded on two pillars: (1) the minimization of external links within local communities, and (2) the path based definition of local communities that capture homophilic (similarity driven) interactions via paths of length 2 and synergetic (diversity driven) interactions via paths of length 3. Building on this, we introduce the Cannistraci Hebb Adaptive (CHA) network automata, an adaptive learning machine that automatically selects the optimal CH rule and path length to model each network. CHA unifies theoretical interpretability and data driven adaptivity, bridging physics inspired network science and machine intelligence. Across 1,269 networks from 14 domains, CHA consistently surpasses state of the art methods including Structural Perturbation Method (SPM) SPM), Stochastic Block Models SBM )), graph embedding methods, and message passing graph neural networks while revealing the mechanistic principles governing link formation. Our code is available at https://github.com/biomedical cybernetics/Cannistraci_Hebb_network_automata

column9: Hypergraphs And Hoops: Uncovering NBA Player Interactions Through APM
column13: In team sports, standard ranking metrics do not consider how smaller groups of players interact. Individual performance measures rarely reflect the synergy or friction among pairs or trios, while full-lineup assessments can’t pinpoint the exact contributions of these lower-order combinations. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel adjusted plus-minus (APM) framework that simultaneously evaluates individuals, smaller groups, and entire lineups. Underlying our approach is a link between APM and the hypergraph representation of a team, which captures these overlapping interactions. In this talk, we’ll demonstrate how this perspective applies to NBA data from 2012–2022 and highlight the insights gained from viewing a team as a network.

column9: A graph generation algorithm for network meta-analysis
column13: Network meta-analysis (NMA) is a statistical method to synthesize evidence from multiple clinical trials that compare treatment options for the same condition. The method derives its name from a graphical representation of the data where nodes are treatments, and edges represent comparisons between treatments in trials [1]. Because of the higher-order structures introduced by trials that compare more than two treatments, these networks are more accurately described by bipartite graphs [2]. Here, trials define a second type of node, and edges connect trial nodes to the treatment nodes they compare.   NMA is widely used in healthcare decision-making and is an active area of methods development. Model validation, methods comparisons, and investigation of model behaviour require comprehensive simulation studies. However, simulating NMA datasets typically involves manually specifying the network structure, which becomes increasingly difficult for large datasets. Simulated datasets have therefore been limited to small networks (<= 10 treatments) with a limited range of geometries, and trials that involve only two treatments. As a result, simulation studies of NMA often fail to represent the full range of network structures encountered in practice. To overcome these challenges, we develop an algorithm to automatically generate NMA networks with realistic properties.  To inform our algorithm, we investigate the typical structural properties of an ensemble of 300 NMA networks drawn from analyses published in 2023. We begin with a bipartite version of the configuration model [3] which samples the degrees of the treatment nodes (the number of trials involving that treatment) and degrees of the trial nodes (the number of treatments compared in that trial) from the observed degree distributions of the ensemble. As shown in Fig. 1, this algorithm generates ensembles of random graphs whose degree distributions closely resemble those of the real world NMAs, both in their bipartite and unipartite representations. To more accurately reproduce the high proportion of star networks observed in the real world ensemble, we adapt the algorithm by sampling the degrees from a mixture model informed by the different distributions associated with star and non-star networks.   To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm designed to generate realistic NMA networks. This will facilitate efficient and flexible simulation studies of NMA methods. It also provides a starting point for generating more complex datasets that are becoming increasingly common in this area.

column9: Changes in social interactions following digital exposure notifications: a case-control study among mobile phone contact tracing application users
column11: Citron, Daniel*; Loh, Po-Shen; Yee, Shannon; Bershteyn, Anna
column13: Background: In the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, many digital contact tracing smartphone applications were developed for the purpose of reducing transmission by encouraging exposed individuals to voluntarily quarantine after exposure1. While in theory such tools have great potential in reducing COVID-19 transmission2, the privacy protocols of many apps prevented longitudinal linkage of users’ contact network data, making it difficult to observe whether users reduced social contact following digital exposure notification. We used anonymous data from a digital exposure notification app, NOVID3, which used privacy measures which retained longitudinal interaction data, to evaluate changes in the users’ time in proximity to other users after digital exposure notification. Methods: We analyzed de-identified user data collected by NOVID, a digital contact tracing app. Our contact network dataset was collected from NOVID users affiliated with the Georgia Tech community from January-March 20214, before vaccines were widely available and social distancing was the primary recommendation for preventing COVID-19 spread. The app recorded each user’s contacts with others over time, instances of self-reporting positive COVID-19 diagnosis, and digital exposure notifications received. We conducted pre-post analysis of contact time with other users before and after self-reporting a positive COVID-19 diagnosis, and before and after receiving exposure notification by the app. We compared each self-reporting and notified user against a matched control group of users with similar baseline contact rates during the same period. Results: Users who reported a positive case to the app reduced their total contact time with others by 29% (p = .002) in the 7-day period following the time of the report compared to the 7-day period before the time of the report. This was markedly different from the behavior of the matched control group, which did not appear to alter their contact time with others in the same way. By contract, we observed no statistically significant difference in contact time before vs. after exposure notification. The 7-day cumulative contact time of users who received exposure notifications did not differ significantly compared to matched controls who did not receive an exposure notification. Conclusion: The lack of detectable user response to digital exposure notifications suggests that app users did not or were unable to take meaningful measures to reduce their social contacts with others. Our study provides one of the first direct evaluations of the effectiveness of digital exposure notifications during the pre-vaccination period of the pandemic, with the intention of informing the assumptions around social distancing behavior in models of infectious disease as well as improving the design and implementation of future digital contact tracing apps.

column9: How Overlapping Input Structures Amplify Systemic Risk in Global Supply Chains?
column11: Gyimesi, András*; Braun, Erik; Longauer, Dóra; Sebestyén, Tamás
column13: Disrupting global supply chains (GSCs), recent global events drew attention to their fragility and the systemic risks they pose to the global economy. This paper examines the underlying structural characteristics of GSC networks that exacerbate their vulnerability. Using a general equilibrium model with production networks, similar to [1, 2], we develop an indicator called Structural Vulnerability (SV) based on input-side structural factors, such as supplier concentration and overlapping input linkages. The example in Figure 1 shows that if the input sources of the S1 sector become more concentrated towards itself (Model C) or become correlated with another sector (S3 in Model D), then SV is amplified. We also measure each sector's contribution to vulnerability (denoted by SVC), which shows that S1 has a larger SVC in Model D than in Model B, despite having an identical input structure.  Empirical analysis shows that increased economic specialization and interconnectedness have led to a significant rise in systemic risks between 1995 and 2019, especially up until 2012. This is evident in Figure 2, where the SVC of almost all countries and sectors increased between the two dates. We identify that the manufacturing sectors of developing countries were the main contributors to the growing vulnerability. The input structures of developing countries and manufacturing sectors changed in a way that their SVC values got inflated, as shown in Figure 2. The results suggest that the reason behind this increased vulnerability is the increasing homogeneity across sectors’ input sourcing structures, rather than by more concentration within individual sectors. This finding calls for coordination of supply chain and risk management decisions, as micro-level decisions can build up systemic risk by homogenizing input sourcing structures across GSC networks.

column9: Energetic constraints predict the diversity of feasible ecological networks
column11: Long, Chengyi*; Saavedra, Serguei; Angulo, Marco; Ogbunugafor, C. Brandon; Sole, Ricard
column13: Ever since Boltzmann, life has often been framed as a struggle for free energy—a perspective that highlights the centrality of energy flows in biological networks. Dissipative living systems, such as ecological networks, rely on external energy supply and internal energy exchange. However, it remains unclear whether specific levels of external energy supply enhance the feasibility and observability of such open systems—an insight that could clarify the energetic conditions conducive to life’s persistence and organization. Here, we use an energy-based formalism to quantify the feasibility of ecological networks as a function of energy supply and exchange. We identify three key findings: (1) The probability that a network is feasible with minimal biomass increases monotonically and saturates with higher external energy supply. (2) The probability of a network achieving feasibility with steady-state biomass follows a unimodal relationship with external energy supply—indicating a highest-feasibility zone. (3) Networks with longer chains of internal energy exchange tend to exhibit lower feasibility, regardless of external energy availability. We showcase our theoretical predictions using human gut microbial communities, showing that their frequency of observability also exhibits a unimodal relationship with caloric intake. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that more energy supply is always beneficial. Instead, they reveal that internal energetic constraints may play a dominant role in shaping the diversity of complex ecological networks.

column9: Bridge Criticality in a Spatial Road Network
column13: Transportation network vulnerability has become increasingly important given the critical role infrastructure plays in national mobility and economic resilience and remains an important problem to understand how these systems can withstand and recover from failures and disruptions. While extensive research has examined the robustness of road networks through various frameworks, the critical role bridges play in road networks and the risks posed by bridge infrastructure to transportation network connectivity is understudied. As structural bottlenecks in highway systems, bridge failures can disproportionately impact network connectivity, making their assessment vital for transportation planning and risk management. Here, using National Bridge Inventory data from the Long Term Bridge Performance project of the Federal Highway Administration of the US, we study the National Highway System and develop a percolation analysis framework to study the impact of removal of bridges on the network. Different removal scenarios are compared, and we describe a combined risk score accounting for increases in distance from detours caused by removal of bridges, which can be used to identify critical bridges based on their position in their network as well as features of their infrastructure such as condition and age. Accounting for bridge feature conditions and daily traffic volume highlights the bridges that are critical in disconnecting the network and delays in travel time caused by their disruption can be identified. The figure shows the case for a single county in the state of Iowa, where a small subset of bridges removed lead to non-trivial delays and disconnection of the network. This framework when extended to the entire system can be used to provide actionable insights for infrastructure resilience and planning in the event of disruptions caused by systemic failures or natural disasters.

column9: A network of cycles from random minimum cycle bases for material networks
column13: Many material networks are well-described by their cycles. Graphene, carbon nanotubes, and diamond are periodic tilings of hexagonal carbon rings in the plane, on a cylinder, and in 3D space, respectively. The formalism of this is complex. One application we are particularly intereseted in is predicting molecular structures and giant (macroscale) molecules formed in hydrocarbon pyrolysis under extreme temperatures and pressures. We model the ensemble of carbon skeletons as a random graph [1,2]. Our most recent “disjoint loop model” [1] yielded excellent predictions for giant molecules with H/C ratios ≥ 2.5, as in butane (C4H10). In carbon-rich systems the accuracy of our disjoint loop model’s prediction of the size of the largest molecule deteriorates as carbon rings form clusters, thereby violating the “disjoint loop” assumption. This led us to building theory and designing algorithms for extracting cycles to characterize large, complex graphs, as in Fig. 1(a) [6]. We propose a method to sample the minimum cycle bases of a graph uniformly at random. From this, we define a dual graph, a network whose nodes represent cycles in the random minimum cycle basis, and whose edges represent their intersection paths, Fig. 1(d).  The set of simple cycles cannot be used because it grows exponentially with graph size. Instead, the conventional approach is to treat the set of cycles as a vector space, where addition is the symmetric difference, and scalars are 0 and 1. Then, cycles can be sampled from a minimum cycle basis (MCB), a basis of the cycle space that minimizes the sum of lengths. Unfortunately, an MCB of a graph is not unique. Because of this, several authors extend MCBs to a unique set of cycles, e.g., Vismara [3] defines the relevant cycles as the union of all the MCBs of a graph. The size of the relevant cycles, however, may still grow exponentially with graph size.  Because of the size limitations of the relevant cycles – and other extensions of MCBs – Gleiss et al. [4] and Kolodzik et al. [5] construct equivalence relations for the relevant cycles. These partition the relevant cycles into a smaller number of equivalence classes. We modify this approach and define polyhedron-interchangeability (pi) and short loop-interchangeability (sli) classes. pi and sli classes identify 3D structures and nested rings, respectively. See Fig. 1(b). We sample the MCBs of a graph uniformly at random from the pi and sli classes using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach. We post-process this MCB so that pairs of cycles intersect over a single path as in Fig. 1(c). The final MCB permits a notion of dual graph as shown in Fig. 1(d).  We sampled MCBs and visualized loop clusters from a large collection of molecular dynamics simulations of hydrocarbon pyrolysis of large systems. We observed a phase transition in the loop cluster size distribution and a counterintuitive statistics of the largest molecule size.

column9: Phase Transitions in Heider Balance with Heterogeneous Social Temperatures
column13:
Heider’s balance theory provides a fundamental framework for understanding polarization and alliance formation in social networks through triadic interactions [1]. Most existing stochastic formulations assume a homogeneous social temperature, implicitly treating all interpersonal relations as equally volatile [2]. Empirical social systems, however, are highly heterogeneous: social ties differ widely in stability, susceptibility to change, and exposure to noise [3].  We introduce a generalized Heider balance model in which each link is assigned its own social temperature to capture heterogeneity of fluctuations. By mapping the dynamics onto a higher-order Ising-type system with heterogeneous effective couplings, we derive a distribution-dependent mean-field theory that governs the average opinion $x$:  egin{equation}     x=\int_0^{+\infty}	anh\left( eta x^2ight)ho( eta)d eta, \end{equation} where $ eta$ is the heterogeneous inverse temperature and $ho$ is the distribution for $ eta$. The self consistence equation shows that collective behavior depends not only on the average inverse temperature but on the entire distribution of heterogeneity.  From the self consistence equation, we establish universal bounds controlled by the third order momentum $\gamma^3$ for the critical transition between polarized and non-polarized states, $C_* \leq \mu_{m C} <  rac{5}{4}\left( rac{4}{3}\gamma^3ight)^{ rac{1}{5}}$, and prove that the homogeneous limit provides a universal lower bound $C_* \approx 1.716$ for the critical average inverse temperature $\mu_{m C}$. Crucially, we theoretically show that light-tailed and heavy-tailed distributions lead to qualitatively distinct phase diagrams as Fig. 1 shows: while increasing heterogeneity such as standard deviation $\sigma$ destabilizes polarization in light-tailed cases, heavy-tailed distributions can sustain polarized states even under arbitrarily large fluctuations.     igskip {\small

column9: A Network Perspective of the Stock Market Using Mutual Information and Transfer Entropy
column13: Financial markets exhibit complex, evolving interdependencies that intensify during periods of systemic stress. Traditional network analyses of equity markets rely primarily on linear dependence measures such as Pearson correlation, which fail to capture nonlinear co-movement and directional information flow. We extend the correlation-based market network framework of Tse et al. (2010) by incorporating two information-theoretic measures—mutual information (MI) and transfer entropy (TE)—to obtain a more complete characterization of market structure and information transmission.  Using daily adjusted closing prices for approximately 1,000 U.S. equities from 2017–2021, we construct stock networks for pre- and post-COVID periods. Pearson correlation networks provide a linear benchmark, while normalized MI networks capture nonlinear dependencies without parametric assumptions. To examine directionality, we estimate TE among highly connected stocks, enabling analysis of asymmetric predictive information flow at both firm and sector levels. Network structure is evaluated through degree distributions, path-length statistics, hub dominance, and sector aggregation.  Across all specifications, U.S. equity markets exhibit scale-free structure dominated by a small number of influential nodes. MI reveals additional nonlinear cross-sector connections absent in correlation-based networks but does not alter the identity of dominant hubs. The Financial sector consistently emerges as the primary structural anchor of the market. TE analysis further shows that financial stocks act as dominant sources of predictive information flow, with this asymmetry intensifying following the COVID-19 market disruption.  These results demonstrate that combining MI and TE with correlation-based networks provides deeper insight into both the structure and dynamics of systemic risk. While correlation captures co-movement, MI uncovers hidden nonlinear dependencies, and TE highlights asymmetric predictive relationships that become more pronounced during periods of market stress.

column9: Towards understanding evolution of science through language model series
column13: We present AnnualBERT, a series of language models aimed specifically to track the temporal evolution of scientific text and facilitate the representation of scientific knowledge over time. AnnualBERT adopts whole-word tokenization and is composed of a base RoBERTa model pretrained from scratch on the full-text of arXiv papers published until 2008 and a collection of progressively trained models on arXiv papers at an annual basis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AnnualBERT models by showing that they not only have comparable performance in standard scientific NLP tasks but also achieve state-of-the-art performance on domain-specific NLP tasks like predicting subject category and interdisciplinarity of papers. Furthermore, AnnualBERT outperforms other existing scientific language models in link prediction tasks in the arXiv citation network (Figs.~\ref{fig}A--E).  Finally, leveraging whole-word tokenization and the probabilistic feature of RoBERTa models to predict the masked token given its context, we analyze the dynamics of research by examining how the probability of each word change over time, as assessed by different models. For example, consider the sentence shown in Fig.~\ref{fig}F about edge representation in image models, we mask ``ResNet'' and ask each of the AnnualBERT models to output the most likely tokens and their associated probabilities (Fig.~\ref{fig}F). For comparisons, we also test with the one-time trained model $\overline{\mathcal{M}}$ (a single RoBERTa model pretrained on the entire arXiv full-text corpus; Fig.~\ref{fig}G) and SciBERT (Fig.~\ref{fig}H). For SciBERT, as it uses subword tokenization, meaningful ideas like ``ResNet'', ``AlexNet'', and ``GoogLeNet'' are all broken into subwords like ``alex'' and ``google''. Consequently, SciBERT is not able to make the correct guess, leaving ``cnn'' as the most likely token and ``sub-ideas'' like ``alex'' and ``google'' small probabilities. By contrast, $\overline{\mathcal{M}}$ adopts whole-word tokenization, and most of the top choices are image models. Yet, the probability of ``ResNet'' (0.45) does not overwhelmingly dominate that of ``AlexNet'' (0.18), indicating that the latter one is still a viable choice. Finally, annually trained AnnualBERT models $\mathcal{M}_t$ consider further the temporal dimension and reveal the dynamics of the competition between AlexNet and ResNet. AnnualBERT can be used to encode scientific documents to enable downstream inquiries in science of science and innovation where the temporal dimension is particularly relevant. The series of the models is available at https://huggingface.co/jd445/AnnualBERTs.

column9: Topological Structure versus Spatial Constraints in Disaster Mobility Networks
column13: Human mobility networks are shaped by both topological connectivity and spatial embedding, yet most networkbased analyses emphasize topological structure while overlooking spatial constraints, a limitation that becomes especially consequential during natural disasters. This study examines how topological and spatial constraints jointly–and diﬀerentially–govern mobility network organization under extreme disruption, using Hurricane Ian as a natural experiment. We construct daily directed mobility networks for Lee County, Florida, from anonymized GPS data spanning periods before, during, and after landfall, and apply a series of controlled network randomization experiments to disentangle the roles of topological connectivity and spatial embedding. Three complementary null models are implemented that preserve (i) topological constraints only, (ii) spatial constraints only, and (iii) both topological and spatial constraints simultaneously, and observed networks are evaluated against these baselines using macro-scale metrics and substructural motif compositions. Results reveal a pronounced regime shift during the disaster: under normal conditions, mobility patterns reﬂect the joint inﬂuence of topology and spatial embedding, whereas during landfall, spatially constrained null models reproduce observed network structures more accurately than topology-preserving models, indicating that geographic proximity becomes the dominant organizing principle of mobility. Motif analysis further shows a contraction toward short-distance, locally clustered structures, highlighting heightened spatial dependence under disruption. Together, these ﬁndings demonstrate that spatial constraints can temporarily override topological organization in disaster contexts and underscore the importance of explicitly incorporating spatial embedding into network analyses of mobility resilience.

column9: Emergence of Covid-19 Variants via Dominance in a Multi-Variant Epidemic Model
column11: Ivry, Aviel; Cohen, Reuven; Patron, Amikam*
column13: We investigate the emergence and spreading of dominant Covid-19 variants – Alpha, Beta, Delta and Omicron – throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, based on a network multi-mutation epidemic spreading model that we developed. We characterize properties of a pathogen’s mutation that lead it to reach dominance over other mutations that spread simultaneously with it. Based on this model we explain the following pandemic related facts: (i) Three pandemic waves refer to three variants that reached dominance over other coexisting variants during three periods : Alpha wave in 2020, Delta wave in 2021, and the Omicron wave in 2022 - mid-2023. We explain the successive replacements of Alpha by Delta and Delta by Omicron. (ii) The importance and severity ascribed to the Beta variant. In our epidemic spreading model, a pathogen can mutate continuously during the epidemic spreading. We consider pathogens whose mutating parameter is the mortality mean-time and study the evolution of this parameter over the spreading process.  Based on this, we compute the probability of an individual (node) carrying a pathogen variant to infect other individuals (nodes), depending on the mutating parameter of the specific variant. We show that less aggressive mutations with a higher mortality meantime have a higher probability of infecting their neighbors and a larger proportion relative to other mutations. Using Epidemiological metrics of the Covid-19 variants, we calculated the parameters of our model for these variants. Based on this, we deduce that the replacements of Alpha by Delta and Delta by Omicron throughout the pandemic, were not due to the emergence of a variant with a much higher infection probability, but rather to the emergence of a variant with a shorter infection mean time and a low mortality probability. We also show that the sufficiently high infection probability of the Beta variant combined with it relatively high mortality probability, makes it a significant variant.

column9: Urban Multilayer Network Framework from the Space-Society Perspective: Modeling, Characterizing and Understanding on the Dynamics of Urban Space
column13: Applying network-based methods to urban issues is increasingly important, yet most studies still separate visible physical networks like road networks from invisible social networks. Research that treats the built environment as a container of human activities and uses complex network analysis methods to reveal characteristics and laws of urban spatial structures remains limited.     We propose a modeling strategy that integrates urban physical space with social associations patterns by representing resident activity-related buildings as nodes and social communication as edges (ties). Spatial functional differences among buildings are further used to construct attribute-specific layers, forming a spatial multilayer network of urban area.     Preliminarily and empirically, we have finished the analysis on the central urban area of metropolitan Shanghai. We built a single-layer residential space network for 6731 gated communities, using community centroids as nodes and opportunities of inter-community social interaction in public space as edges (ties). On the basis of network measurement, like robustness and degree distribution, the identified “network community” has been proved to be in line with the geographical sense of “regional identity”. Furthermore, the multi-layer network of urban space is an extension of the single attribute network. Because the urban residents’ activities—such as working, trading (including consuming) and leisure—occur in specific buildings, architectural complexes or blocks, the spatial scope of different activities can be defined accurately. Meanwhile, residents move among these functional urban spaces with varying modes, frequencies, and purposes. These spatial and behavioral definitions with the connotation of planning theory are very suitable for all the basic conditions of constructing multi-layer network of space. And, residents’ movements define intra-layer ties and cross-layer couplings, satisfying the theoretical conditions for constructing a multilayer spatial network analogous to a diverse ecological system.     This spatial multilayer network offers a promising analytical paradigm for capturing urban complexity, encompassing major physical spaces and generalized social linkages. With richer functional details and behavioral data, this integrated spatial–social network approach may yield deeper insights and support predictions of urban evolution.     In sum, applying complex network analysis to the spatial–social structure of cities provides new methods and perspectives for urban research and contributes to theoretical development in network science.  Keywords: Multilayer Network of Urban Space; Physical Space; Social Interaction; Dynamic Mechanism; Spatial Pattern Research Paradigm

column9: Measuring Scientific Novelty as Network Rewiring
column13: Scientific novelty is central to innovation but remains difficult to operationalize at scale. Existing measures based on citations or textual similarity often overlook the structural dimension of novelty, namely how new ideas bridge previously unconnected regions of the knowledge landscape. We introduce a network-based framework that formalizes scientific novelty as structural brokerage in semantic similarity networks. Building on Burt’s concept of structural holes, we construct semantic networks in which nodes represent manuscripts and edges reflect semantic proximity derived from large language model embeddings and topic similarity. We apply this framework to a large corpus of funded and unfunded grant applications from the Novo Nordisk Foundation and compute network features capturing local clustering, centrality, community structure, and neighborhood success. Using these features, a logistic regression model predicts grant success with an ROC–AUC of 0.74. Rejected grants tend to be embedded in densely clustered semantic neighborhoods, whereas successful grants more often occupy brokerage positions connecting weakly linked regions of the network, consistent with a structural interpretation of scientific novelty. In ongoing work, we will systematically compare our network-based novelty measure against established novelty indicators, including combinatorial novelty [1] and disruption-based metrics [3]. This comparison will allow us to assess when and why structural brokerage captures dimensions of innovation not observable through citation or content-based measures alone. From a network science perspective, this work contributes to the study of innovation dynamics and knowledge recom- bination by modeling scientific novelty through temporal semantic networks. By grounding novelty in network topology rather than textual similarity or citation history, we link micro-level semantic relationships to macro-level structural evolu- tion. The framework is general and readily extendable to other domains with semantic representations, including patents and software repositories. Overall, this study reframes scientific novelty as a network-structural phenomenon and provides a scalable, interpretable approach for analyzing how new ideas emerge and gain recognition within complex knowledge systems.

column9: Reconstructing Historical Social Networks as Complex Systems: Analyzing Diaries from the Reform War (1858-1860) in Mexico
column11: Motilla, Jose Antonio*; Espitia , Diego ; Ugalde , Edgardo; Galán-Vásquez, Edgardo
column13: Social systems are inherently complex, shaped by dynamic interactions, power structures, and historical contingencies. Understanding how these networks evolve over time is crucial for reconstructing past societies and identifying underlying structural patterns. This study applies network science, text mining, and Natural Language Processing (NLP) [1] to reconstruct historical social networks from personal diaries written during the Reform War (1858-1860) in Mexico, one of the most violent conflicts in mexican history. In previous research [2, 3], we reconstructed networks from Juan de Vildosola’s Diary and developed growth models that capture the social network as seen from the observer’s perspective, as a subgraph of a larger system exhibiting a Barabási-Albert structure, thus revealing key actors and ideological affiliations. Expanding this approach, we analyze four additional diaries from the same period, written by individuals with diverse political perspectives, as well as texts from traditional, non-academic historical sources. Using NLP and named entity recognition (NER), we extract and normalize historical figures, using them as building blocks to construct interaction networks. We hypothesize that these reconstructed networks allow us to examine structural similarities and resilience in wartime societies. This comparative analysis provides new insights into how official historical narratives may oversimplify the complexity of past societies during civil wars. Our findings contribute to modeling social systems as evolving networks, offering an interdisciplinary perspective that addresses key challenges in historical data analysis, such as fragmentation, ambiguity, and bias in primary sources. Furthermore, we demonstrate how computational approaches and exceptional historical documents can serve as valuable methodologies for complex systems research, particularly in the study of civil conflicts and long-term social dynamics. column9: Multiplicity without Switching in Evolving Correlation Networks: A Coupling–Localization Atlas of Market Organization (US vs EU)
column13: Complex networks are often summarized by a single number, implicitly treating organization as one-dimensional. We report “multiplicity without switching” in financial correlation networks: at comparable overall coupling, the market’s dominant mode supports multiple, distinct organizations, while stress mainly shifts where observations sit in coupling space rather than causing frequent within-band state flips.  Using daily sector returns (2006–present) and rolling correlation matrices (90-day windows), we build a coupling–localization atlas and test for bimodality within a fixed-coverage, rank-matched coupling band. Both U.S. and European sector networks show strong bimodality, confirmed by a nonparametric multimodality test with overlap-aware block bootstrap. A declustered high-coupling stress gate reveals occupancy migration in event windows: coupling rises, localization falls, and inflow into the highest-coupling bin increases sharply, while within-band switching remains rare. Results persist under coarser sampling strides and under shrinkage-based correlation estimation.

column9: How Digitalization is Reshaping Sustainable Workplace and Urban Growth: The Role of Human Capital
column13: Digitalization is transforming the relationship between people and place, reshaping how firms use office space and how cities attract and retain talent.  This study examines how remote work adoption and the rise of digitally-intensive occupations interact with human capital and workforce mobility to shape firms’ decisions to occupy sustainable office space.   Sustainability practices –initially adopted for environmental and cost-saving reasons– have become a strategic tool for attracting and retaining high-quality human capital. A growing body of evidence shows that high workplace quality, particularly with respect to environmental standards, not only enhances workers’ cognitive performance but also improves firms’ ability to attract and retain a highly skilled workforce.  These developments suggest that sustainability in the built environment is no longer peripheral to firm strategy, but closely intertwined with labour-market dynamics.  Concurrently, the ongoing shift in the workforce toward digitally-intensive and AI-complementary jobs is reshaping the types of work environments workers expect and require, raising critical questions about the interaction between technological change in the labor market and sustainability transitions of their workplace. Specifically, how does the relationship between digitalization —expressed through the rise of remote work and the expansion of digitally skilled jobs— and sustainability vary across urban contexts, potentially exacerbating spatial disparities? How does it reshape corporate decisions regarding investments in human capital assets and their workplace?   We conceptualize these processes as unfolding within an urban system where workers move across firms, office buildings, and cities, thereby forming a city–office network. We construct a unique, large-scale, multi-layered dataset linking over  3.5 million LinkedIn professional profiles with more than 2,500 commercial real estate records, associated with 83 leading firms from the 2025 Fortune 500 list. These firms span a diverse set of industries—including transportation, retail, technology, finance, healthcare, and manufacturing—with offices located across 140 U.S. cities over the period 2018–2024.  We pursue two complementary lines of analysis. First, we reconstruct the career trajectories of more than 3.5 million workers, tracking their movements across office locations, firms, and cities. Using a Markov chain formalism on the city–office network, we model career mobility as a stochastic process and estimate workers’ long-run likelihood of accessing sustainable office spaces relative to non-sustainable ones. This approach allows us to assess disparities in access to high-quality workplaces. We show that workers with higher education, greater experience, and digitally skilled occupations are substantially more likely to reach and remain in sustainable offices over their career paths, reinforcing existing inequalities in access to high-quality workplaces. In the U.S., sustainable office space is highly concentrated in a small number of major cities, with 80% of sustainable office space located in the top 12 U.S. cities.  Second, we examine how workforce composition shapes firms’ adoption of sustainable office space using Poisson pseudo–maximum likelihood estimation. We show that firms employing more digital-skilled and sustainability-oriented workers allocate a significantly larger share of their office portfolio to sustainable buildings, even after accounting for education, firm size, profitability, and industry affiliation. This association is further strengthened among firms with formal science-based climate commitments, indicating that bottom-up workforce characteristics and top-down organizational strategies act as complementary drivers of sustainable space adoption. Remote work further moderates this relationship: sustainability-oriented workers exert the greatest influence on sustainable space usage when firms operate with moderate levels of remote work, suggesting that hybrid work amplifies the value of high-quality office environments.   Our results highlight how digitalization and workforce composition jointly drive sustainable workplace investment and contribute to emerging disparities in sustainable urban growth.

column9: Friendship, Popularity, and Smoking Among College Students: A Social Network Analysis
column13: Smoking behavior is not solely an individual health decision but a socially embedded phenomenon shaped by interpersonal relationships, peer influence, and the structure of social networks. Friendship networks, in particular, provide a critical context in which smoking initiation, maintenance, and cessation occur. This study investigates how social ties, peer influence, and network-based measures of popularity are associated with smoking behavior among the students of a medical college in Turkey, using a social network analysis framework. By moving beyond individual-level predictors and incorporating relational and structural dimensions, this research aims to deepen understanding of how smoking diffuses through social systems and how network position moderates behavioral risk.  Using friendship network data collected from a defined population, the study constructs sociocentric networks in which nodes represent individuals and edges represent friendship ties. Smoking behavior is measured as a behavioral outcome variable, while social network metrics capture individuals’ embeddedness within the network. Key predictors include network centrality measures (e.g., degree, eigenvector, and betweenness centrality), indicators of popularity and social visibility, exposure to smoking peers, and structural features such as clustering and homophily. Individual-level covariates such as demographic characteristics are incorporated to isolate network effects from compositional factors.  Analytically, the study employs a combination of descriptive network analysis and statistical modeling techniques to assess the relationship between social network properties and smoking behavior. The analysis examines whether individuals with higher popularity or more central network positions are more or less likely to smoke, and whether smoking behavior is associated with increased exposure to smoking peers. Special attention is given to disentangling peer influence effects from selection processes, acknowledging that smokers may preferentially form friendships with other smokers while also influencing non-smoking peers over time.  The findings demonstrate that smoking behavior is unevenly distributed across the social network and that individuals occupying central or popular positions may play a disproportionate role in shaping normative behaviors. Popularity may function both as a protective factor and a risk factor, depending on whether dominant norms within the network favor or discourage smoking. Additionally, peripheral individuals may exhibit distinct vulnerability patterns due to limited social support or greater susceptibility to peer pressure within small friendship clusters.  From a public health perspective, the study highlights the importance of incorporating social network structures into smoking prevention and intervention strategies. Traditional interventions that target individuals in isolation may overlook the relational pathways through which smoking behaviors spread. Network-informed approaches—such as targeting influential individuals or modifying peer norms within tightly connected groups—may offer more effective strategies for reducing smoking prevalence. By identifying key network positions associated with elevated smoking risk, this research provides actionable insights for designing socially informed health interventions.  The study also contributes methodologically by demonstrating the value of social network analysis in behavioral health research. By integrating network metrics with behavioral outcomes, the research illustrates how relational data can uncover patterns that remain hidden in individual-level analyses. This approach underscores the broader relevance of network science for understanding health-related behaviors that are inherently social in nature.  In conclusion, this research advances the understanding of smoking behavior by situating it within the structure of friendship networks. It emphasizes that social ties and popularity are not merely contextual variables but central mechanisms through which health behaviors emerge and persist. The findings underscore the need for network-aware theories and interventions that recognize the social embeddedness of health behaviors, offering a more nuanced and effective framework for addressing smoking and other health-risk behaviors in social populations.

column9: Uncovering Transcriptional Deregulation as a Driver of Aging Through Deep Learning
column13: Aging is often attributed to the slow buildup of stochastic cellular damage, but much of that damage falls in regulatory DNA rather than protein-coding exons. This points to a simple possibility: aging may be driven less by broken proteins and more by gradually “frayed” gene regulatory networks (GRNs). In such networks, even modest disruptions to key motifs and circuits can ripple through transcriptional dynamics, eventually showing up as widespread transcriptional deregulation (TD). From this perspective, TD is not just a long list of differentially expressed genes; it is a system-level, multi-scale loss of control over gene expression programs that can destabilize cellular states and erode function. Despite the appeal of this view, we still lack practical computational tools that quantify TD from a network standpoint at single-cell and single-gene resolution. That gap leaves basic questions unanswered: which genetic or epigenetic insults most strongly induce TD, which circuits and genes are most fragile, what TD looks like as a coherent, multi-scale network phenotype, and how diverse deregulated states across cells accumulate into tissue-level dysfunction. Most single-cell analyses emphasize differential expression, increased variability, or pathway signatures, but they rarely model the mechanism we care about how stochastic damage to GRN architecture propagates into TD. Here we introduce a deep learning framework that makes TD measurable directly from single-cell transcriptomes and reports interpretable readouts across four linked scales: cell-cohort organization, pathway-level programs, gene-level vulnerability, and cell-level deregulation states. By connecting these levels within one model, our approach offers a quantitative bridge between accumulated regulatory damage and the emergent transcriptional breakdown observed in aging.

column9: Using Causal Loop Diagrams to model public-private relations in the Harbour of Rotterdam
column13: Public–private security cooperation (PPS) is central to countering cocaine trafficking in major European ports, yet its effectiveness depends on complex and adaptive interactions between public authorities and private actors. In the Port of Rotterdam, cooperation outcomes are shaped by feedback mechanisms involving trust, information sharing, funding stability, regulatory consistency, and stakeholder engagement [1]. This study proposes a structured and replicable methodology for modeling these dynamics using causal loop diagrams (CLDs) as an intermediate network representation linking qualitative knowledge to computational models [2,3]. An initial CLD is generated using the Causalix programme, which extracts causal relationships and variable definitions from scientific and grey literature. This automatically derived structure is systematically documented, aligned with a targeted literature review on port security, trafficking risk environments, and collaborative governance, and subsequently refined through expert elicitation. Semi-structured interviews and workshops are used to validate, revise, and augment the model. The resulting expert-validated CLD identifies key reinforcing and balancing feedback loops governing PPS sustainability, including trust–information-sharing reinforcement, funding–engagement stabilization, and regulatory inconsistency–trust erosion. The validated CLD serves as the conceptual backbone for computational translation within the FREIDA framework [3], enabling future development of a system-dynamics or agent-based model representing interactions between public and private actors. By formalizing public–private cooperation as a network of causal dependencies, this work provides both conceptual clarity and a foundation for analyzing the resilience and sustainability of port security governance.

column9: Reconstructing and Modelling Cocaine Trafficking Dynamics in Rotterdam and Antwerp Using MNAR Bayesian Multiple Imputation
column13: This study develops an econometric framework to analyze cocaine trafficking through the ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp by integrating multi-source indicators of supply, demand, enforcement, and market outcomes across Europe. The analysis uses a harmonized dataset of 38 annual observations (2010–2024) and 282 variables, including production proxies, port-level seizures, wastewater-based consumption estimates, purity, prices, treatment demand, and drug-related mortality. Analysis is hindered by substantial structured missingness, affecting approximately 69% of numeric entries and reflecting systematic reporting biases across countries and surveillance domains [1,2]. Missing values are reconstructed using a Bayesian Missing-Not-At-Random (MNAR) multiple imputation framework with scenario-based δ-shift parameters (δ = −0.5, 0, +0.5). Posterior inference is conducted using the No-U-Turn Sampler, generating fifteen completed datasets that pass numerical and substantive diagnostics. Using the reconstructed data, simultaneous equation and time-series models examine relationships among production, trade flows, seizures, consumption, price formation, and criminal profit margins. Estimates are pooled using Rubin’s rules to incorporate imputation uncertainty. Results indicate that production volume is the dominant driver of retail prices, while seizures, purity, and wastewater-based consumption affect market dynamics indirectly. Comparative analysis shows converging trafficking patterns but distinct enforcement and consumption signatures in Rotterdam and Antwerp, consistent with their roles as complementary hubs in the European cocaine distribution network [3]. By treating indicators as interdependent components of a socio-economic network, this study demonstrates that Bayesian MNAR reconstruction enables robust inference despite severe data limitations.

Over the past few decades, network theory has emerged as a powerful framework for modelling and analysing a wide range of real-world systems, including social, biological, economic, transportation, and World Wide Web networks [1, 2]. The analysis of such systems, which consist of many interacting constituents, provides crucial insights into the nature of interconnectivity and the underlying mechanisms that govern system-level behaviour.  In this work, we focus on random mixed graphs (RMGs) [3], which are characterised by the coexistence of directed and undirected edges. A convenient representation of an RMG is provided by its adjacency matrix, whose entries take values 0 (no connection), 1 (undirected edge), and  ±$i$ (directed edge), assigned with different edge probabilities. We first define the random mixed graph in terms of the probabilities of undirected and directed edges. By varying these probabilities, one can continuously tune the relative contributions of directed and undirected interactions. We investigate how these changes influence the spectral properties of the corresponding adjacency matrices.  For an RMG with purely undirected connections, the adjacency matrix is real symmetric, and its spectral statistics are well described by the universal predictions of the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) of random matrix theory (RMT) [4]. In contrast, for a fully directed RMG, the adjacency matrix becomes Hermitian, and the spectral statistics follow those of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE). Consequently, by varying the edge probabilities, the system exhibits a continuous crossover from the GOE to the GUE statistics [5].  We analyse this crossover using both short-range spectral statistics, including the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution (NNSD) and the spacing ratio distribution, with intermediate interpolation function as well as long-range correlations, quantified by the spectral rigidity or $\Delta_3(L)$  statistics [6]. Furthermore, we employ the Kullback–Leibler divergence (KLD) as a quantitative measure to compare the spectral statistics of RMG adjacency matrices with the corresponding GOE and GUE predictions, thereby providing a systematic characterisation of the crossover behaviour. In addition to spectral statistics, we measure the multifractal dimensions of the eigenvectors to quantify the crossover behaviour between GOE and GUE regimes [7].     igskip {\small
