column9: Collective dynamics of health (mis)information contagion during the COVID-19 pandemic
column13: The spread of health misinformation through social media has become a major public health challenge. Despite broad consensus among health professionals, researchers, and policymakers on the need to curb misleading health messages, there is still limited evidence on how misinformation contagion unfolds across different social environments and how it shapes health decision-making [1]. This study aims to characterize the dynamics of the COVID-19 infodemic and to assess how specific mechanisms, actors, and network structures influence the diffusion and reduction of health misinformation. We adopt a mixed-methods approach that integrates survey data [2], social media mining, and agent-based modelling (ABM) to analyse both empirical patterns and simulated scenarios of misinformation spread.  Analysis of a large Twitter dataset collected during the early months of the pandemic reveals a strong politicization of health issues and deep ideological divisions around vaccination and preventive behaviours, with social bots acting as key amplifiers of misleading content and contributors to polarization, particularly among far-right and low-SES groups [2]. Complementing this, ABM experiments show that the effectiveness of misinformation reduction strategies varies substantially across scenarios and network types. High-learning interventions consistently produce the greatest reductions in misinformation, especially within scale-free and random networks, whereas regular and small-world structures exhibit more resistance to change. Moreover, the models indicate that “hesitant” agents benefit less from corrective mechanisms than “informed” agents, particularly in tightly clustered networks, reflecting the persistence and resilience of misinformation pockets.   These findings highlight that misinformation dynamics depend not only on sources and content but also on the structural and behavioural properties of the networks through which information circulates. Understanding these interactions is essential for developing targeted public health strategies capable of mitigating misinformation and strengthening informed decision-making.

column9: Suspense and surprise in the book of technology
column11: Kwon, Oh-Hyun*; Ha, Seungwoong; Yoon, Jisung; Varshney, Lav R.; Jung, Woo-Sung; Youn, Hyejin
column12: ohhyun@postech.ac.kr*; seungwoong.ha@santafe.edu; jsyoon@kdischool.ac.kr; varshney@illinois.edu; wsjung@postech.ac.kr; h.youn@snu.ac.kr
column13: Innovation can be understood as a combinatorial process in which inventors recombine existing ideas within a technological network. Similar to narrative construction, technological innovation generates suspense by following expectations and surprise by violating expectations. We formalize these concepts by comparing predicted and realized combinations of technological ideas. We estimate the likelihood that two technology codes will be recombined in the following year using two cognitive models of innovative search. The popularity model, based on the frequency of technology codes, captures combinations driven by visibility. The context model, derived from word2vec embeddings, captures semantic similarity and whether a combination “makes sense” technologically. When a realized recombination receives a high predicted score (above 0.75), it is classified as suspense; when the score is low (below 0.25), it is classified as surprise.We find that inventors mainly rely on suspenseful recombinations that meet common expectations in both models. In contrast, exceptional inventors such as Nikola Tesla more frequently pursue popularity-based surprises that deviate from prevailing trends. Although Tesla’s work was not successful in its own time, such breakthrough innovations have become the most impactful in later periods. In contemporary innovation, the most successful outcomes arise from combinations that are novel yet make sense: popularity–surprise and context–suspense pairs show the highest probabilities of citation impact and market value. While popularity–surprise strategies are riskier, they offer greater potential success, whereas popularity–suspense strategies provide more reliable outcomes. Overall, this framework of suspense and surprise captures the reflexive relationship between inventive expectations and realized outcomes in the technological network, offering a novel approach to understanding strategic choice and impact in technological innovation.

column9: Mixture models uncover polycentric urban structure from mobility networks
column13: The modern city is often characterized by a tension between centralizing forces and decentralizing forces. Human mobility patterns offer a powerful lens to understand a city’s dynamic structure, often revealing complexities hidden in static maps of population or land use. Tracking where and when people travel – their daily moves across the city – yields a map of functional urban connectivity, effectively the "revealed preference" of residents using and experiencing the city. Here we exploit GPS mobility data for urban residents in cities across Germany, France and the United Kingdom to develop a method for understanding how cities balance the forces of centralization and decentralization. In doing so, we find regularities in how people distribute activities in space with implications social mixing, productivity, and sustainability. We analyze GPS traces for 50 million residents across 226 functional urban areas in France, Germany, and the United Kingdom. We use home- and stop-detection to define each trip of length d, the distance between home and stop. Each pooled home hexagon (H3 level 9) is assigned a vector of trip distances. Because these length distributions are comprised of trips generated from different processes, which include leisure activities and commutes, we employ finite mixture models to separate shorter-range routine mobility from longer-range travel within a single, interpretable framework.  For each home hexagon we model the empirical distribution of trip lengths with a Gamma mixture representing proximal, medial, and distal mobility scales. Mixture parameters are obtained by maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization and the components are ordered by increasing mean distance. The resulting means represent the typical trip distance within each component, or scale, while the weights quantify the share of all trips undertaken in that scale for the neighborhood in question. To understand how these values vary with respect to urban spatial structure, we estimate an urban nucleus for each city by taking the centroid of the busiest location by GPS pings and computing each neighborhood's distance to that centroid.   Fitting mixture models to ~20,000 neighborhoods across cities in Europe, we see a number of important regularities. The distal mean grows with distance to the nucleus: peripheral households pay a systematic distance premium. The proximal distances do not systematically vary by distance to the nucleus, and they are invariant to city size, suggesting that local activity operates at a similar scale no matter than neighborhood; medial distances scale but less so than distal. We show the slope of the best fit line for each city, with brigher colors corresponding to larger cities; we find stratification where larger cities have both lower slopes and lower intercepts: smaller cities are more dependent on their urban centers while larger cities fragment into subcenters. An advantage of this method is that it lets us assign individual trips to components and examine the composition of them. We divide each neighbourhood into socio-economic quantiles to show that 50% and 30% of intergroup interaction across cities comes from distal and medial components, respectively, with implications for social contact given remote work trends; if centralized work declines, intergroup exposure may decrease. Cities face an efficiency–mixing trade‑off, and strengthening medial hubs raises medial weights and flattens medial means, reducing peripheral burdens while preserving access to the core. An ``efficient polycentric'' configuration therefore retains a strong, accessible nucleus while distributing everyday amenities to the medial scale.

column9: How robust are node metrics? Implications for partially observed networks
column13: Node metrics are fundamental quantitative measures used in network science to characterize the roles and structural properties of nodes in complex networks. Over the years, an extraordinary number of such metrics have been proposed, drawing on ideas from graph theory, information theory, game theory, voting theory, physics, biology, geometry and other disciplines. The most comprehensive encyclopedia of node metrics to date is presented in [1] and a publicly available online resource (https://centralityzoo.github.io/) that documents more than 400 measures and reflects the diversity of perspectives on how node roles can be quantified in complex networks.   Despite their widespread use, node metrics are typically applied under the implicit assumption that network data are complete and accurate. In practice, however, most real-world networks are only partially observed or contain inaccuracies due to measurement costs, sampling biases, temporal limitations of the data collection process or data privacy constraints. Under such conditions, small errors such as missing or spurious links can substantially alter the values and rankings produced by certain node metrics, potentially leading to misleading interpretations of node roles in empirical networks.  In this talk, we investigate the robustness of a broad collection of node metrics from the CentralityZoo [1] when applied to empirical networks subject to incomplete or incorrect data. Using empirical networks of varying sizes and domains from the Index of Complex Networks (ICON) [2], we simulate the most common effects of incomplete or inaccurate data by adding or removing links and analyze how these perturbations affect node metrics and the resulting rankings of nodes. Our methodology is illustrated in Figure 1a: for each empirical network, we apply multiple perturbation strategies (adding or removing links according to different rules) and compare the rankings of nodes in the perturbed networks to those in the original network to quantify the sensitivity of each node metric. Figure 1b provides an illustrative example, averaged across 110 empirical networks [3], showing how the rankings of selected node metrics (here, centrality measures) change when k% of links, relative to the total number of links in the network, are added using a preferential-attachment strategy based on node degree. The sensitivity of each node metric is quantified using the Kendall rank correlation coefficient, showing that shortest-path-based metrics tend to exhibit the largest changes under this type of structural perturbation. Figure 1c shows the average correlation matrix of these node metrics across the original networks, illustrating that some metrics, especially those with the highest sensitivity to perturbations, are strongly correlated with each other.  Our results reveal substantial variability in how node metrics respond to network perturbations. Some metrics remain stable across networks and perturbations, while others can undergo substantial changes in node rankings even under small structural modifications. These findings underscore that the choice of node metric is not trivial: selecting appropriate metrics without accounting for network incompleteness can lead to misleading conclusions about node importance. Understanding the robustness of different metrics is therefore essential for reliable analysis of partially observed networks.   [1] Shvydun, S. (2025). Zoo of Centralities: Encyclopedia of Node Metrics in Complex Networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.05122. [2] Clauset, A., Tucker, E. \& Sainz, M. The Colorado Index of Complex Networks. 2016. Available: https://icon.colorado.edu/ [3] Shvydun, S. (2025). Centrality in complex networks under incomplete data. PLOS Complex Systems, 2(5), e0000042.

column9: Emergence and Evolution of Semantic Complexity in Urban Digital Twins
column13: Contemporary urban dynamics are increasingly driven by pervasive digitalization, producing complex interdependencies between online platforms and offline behaviors. To adequately capture and analyze these intertwined processes, such dynamics need to be framed comprehensively through Urban Digital Twins (UDTs), which provide an integrated representation of both digital (e.g.: smart water city traffic solution) and physical urban systems (e.g.: transportation network)[1]. The complexity brought by UDTs raises the need for an systemic approach to trace its emergence and evolution across the evolving spectrum through science of science perspective[2]. While bibliometric indicators and science mapping techniques trace the emergence and evolution of concepts, they often rely on fragmented workflows across multiple tools and custom scripts. This limitation often arises when tracking conceptual development over time. Conceptual evolution is highly sensitive to choices in query formulation, database selection, filtering, and modeling, even minor differences in search strategies, pre-processing, or network construction can yield divergent narratives. Without an integrated workflow, distinguishing robust patterns from analytical artifacts is difficult. This study makes a twofold contribution. First, it develops an integrated pipeline linking literature retrieval (OpenAlex API), pre-processing, network construction and embeddings (Word2Vec), analytical metrics (centrality, edge scaling, community detection, temporal expansion), and interactive visualization (Dash), providing a fully transparent workflow. Second, a front-end interface allows end-to-end investigation of any topic’s conceptual emergence and evolution. These contributions underscore the importance of transparency and reproducibility in bibliometric reviews, illustrated here with literature on ‘Urban Digital Twins’ in titles or abstracts without date restrictions (Figure 1).  The network can be specified as a co-occurrence network where for every unordered pair (k1, k2) of distinct keywords that appear together in a publication, a co-occurrence count is increased by one. Jaccard similarity of keyword sets between years is stored as a graph-level attribute and provides a simple indicator of how much the set of active keywords changes from year to year where in year t and t − 1, with keyword sets Kt and Kt−1 and denoted as J(Kt,Kt−1) = |Kt∩Kt−1| |Kt∪Kt−1| . Furthermore, concept-method relations are modeled with a bipartite network from the same dataset. In this representation, one set of nodes corresponds to keywords interpreted as concepts and the other set corresponds to keywords interpreted as methods or technologies. An edge between a concept and a method indicates that they co-occur in at least one publication. To construct this network, the pipeline first classifies keywords into three categories: concept, method, or other. Each unique keyword from the corpus is presented to five open-source language models (Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma 2, Phi-3, and Qwen 2.5). Each model is prompted to return exactly one of the three labels, framed in the context of Urban Digital Twins research to reduce ambiguity. In the end, this study provides a coherent understanding of the conceptual development of Urban Digital Twins and offers a generic, transparent, and reproducible bibliometric method and tool, supplemented by a front-end interactive interface that enables spatiotemporal exploration of the conceptual network.

column9: A local eigenvector centrality
column13: Eigenvector centrality is a long-established network measure that assesses node centrality in terms of global reach. It is defined by the first, principal, eigenvector of a network’s adjacency matrix that is associated with the largest eigenvalue. This measurement of a node's ability to send and receive information across the whole network is primarily of interest when influence is dominated by a single central hub or when high global connectivity reduces the relevance of local structures. However, it is often the case for real-world networks – ranging from social and biological to technological systems – that modular, local, structures can drive global activities and function.  We introduce local eigenvector centrality to consider the most topologically relevant scales for detecting centrality. This measure reflects the influence of prominent community structures within the global network by referencing large eigengaps, i.e. large differences between adjacent non-negative eigenvalues, to select eigenvectors that are combined via the Euclidean norm. For example, if i=4 corresponded with a prominent eigengap, then the eigenvectors associated with the four largest eigenvalues would be combined with additional considerations and adjustments for complex conjugates.  In networks with clearly defined community structures, local eigenvector centrality is validated by and enhances the insights from eigenvector centrality calculated for each community in isolation. A primary school contact network [2] is analysed in Figure 1, where the eigengaps expose high global connectivity, as well as responding to the five year groups and ten classes. By comparing local eigenvector centrality (Local) for the eigengap at i=10 with eigenvector centrality calculated for each class independently (Class) in Figure 1b, a close match  is observed between the centrality distributions. The discrepancies between the Local and Class eigenvector measures highlights a lack of node conformity to their defined community structures, e.g. nodes with more connections outside of their defined community than within it. In networks without clearly defined communities, local eigenvector centrality is shown to identify both locally prominent and globally connected hubs including for city road networks [1], satellite constellations [3] and cell networks within veins [4]. Localisation effects can restrict the applicability of eigenvector-based measures in large networks. To mitigate against these effects, a nonlinear rescaling strategy is also proposed that references PageRank's centrality assessment.  [1] R. Clark, et al. A local eigenvector centrality. arXiv, 2025. [2] J. Stehle, et al. High-resolution measurements of face-to-face contact patterns in a primary school. PLOS ONE, 2011. [3] A. Bouis, et al. Insights on structure and influence from the adjacency and Laplacian eigenspectra of intersecting ring networks. arXiv, 2025. [4] M. Lee, et al. Endothelial Cell Organization Drives Distinct Agonist‐Specific Ca2+ Dynamics in Arteries and Veins. Acta Physiologica, 2025.

column9: Mapping the Portuguese Business-to-Business Production Network: Structure, Dynamics, and Sectoral Heterogeneity
column13: This paper analyzes Portugal's business-to-business production network using for the first time administrative transaction data from 2016–2024. Drawing on over 45 million firm-to-firm relationships among approximately 770.000 firms, the study documents structural asymmetries and sectoral differences that illuminate the foundations of production networks and their implications for shock propagation and aggregate output volatility in Portugal.  The analysis reveals a highly concentrated network: the top 1% of firms by connectivity account for 79% of all firm-to-firm links, while the top 10% capture 96% of observed relationships and 87% of aggregate B2B sales. The network exhibits a pronounced supplier-customer asymmetry that varies systematically by sector, reflecting how production technology and market structure jointly shape network structure.  Several network metrics are strongly heavy-tailed (approximately power-law in the upper tail), with important implications for aggregate fluctuations. Shocks to large firms may not average out, potentially generating macroeconomic volatility through granular mechanisms. The distribution of customer relationships shows a fatter tail than that of supplier relationships, a pattern consistent with stronger downstream concentration and potentially more intense propagation of demand-side shocks than supply-side shocks.  The analysis also reveals strong regularities: measures of systemic importance scale with firm size, firms face trade-offs between customer counts and sales per customer, and production chain position measures capture distinct and complementary dimensions of value chain structure.  Temporal analysis demonstrates network resilience: despite a 12–13% contraction in network activity during the 2020 pandemic, the network recovered rapidly by 2024. These findings advance understanding of production network formation, sectoral vulnerabilities to supply chain disruptions, and the potential for firm-level shocks to generate aggregate volatility through network amplification.

column9: Subsumption Rules in Higher-Order Contagion
column13: Conventional models of higher-order contagion, such as those defined on simplicial complexes, typically assume that higher-order interactions act as additive reinforcements to pairwise spreading. This synergy is widely recognized as the primary driver of discontinuous phase transitions and multi-stability. In this work, we challenge this additive paradigm by introducing a "subsumption rule": when a higher-order structure (e.g., a $2$-simplex) is activated, its constituent lower-order components (edges) are effectively covered and cease to function as independent transmission channels.  By the mean-field approach, we derive that the effective transmission rate in our model follows a binomial inversion. This analytical framework reveals that higher-order structures can counterintuitively act as inhibitors of spreading under certain conditions. By assuming a power-law scaling of the form $\beta_m = \beta_1 \cdot m^\alpha$, we show that our model recovers the classic network spreading behavior if and only of $\alpha=1$. Crucially, we identify a "Structural Braking" regime in the sub-linear case ($\alpha < 1$), where the subsumption of lower-order links outweighs the higher-order promotion, leading to a suppression of the steady-state prevalence.  Focusing on $2$-simplices, we systematically map the transition landscape across different scaling regimes: For $\alpha < 1$ (Regime I, suppression): Increasing simplicial density $k_{\Delta}$ leads to a consistent decrease in the steady-state prevalence $\rho^*$, confirming the suppression effect. For $\alpha > 1$ but relatively small (Regime II, weak promotion), the higher-order reinforcement is insufficient to trigger bi-stability. The system remains constrained by the topological saturation limit ($k_{\Delta} \leq k_1/2$), exhibiting a continuous phase transition. At sufficiently large $\alpha$ (Regime III, strong promotion), the model recovers the subcritical transcritical bifurcations and prominent hysteresis loops characteristic of explosive contagion, aligning with classical results but now understood as a competition between subsumption and scaling.  Our results provide a unified perspective on how local interaction rules—beyond mere topology—dictate the global phase transitions of complex systems. By bridging the gap between additive synergy and resource-constrained spreading, this work offers a theoretical foundation for more realistic modeling of information and disease diffusion.

column9: Islands of synchronized order in a world of networked chaos
column13: Synchronization is one of the most striking examples of emergent collective behavior in complex systems. From the firing of neurons to the operation of power grids, coordinated dynamics can arise spontaneously from simple local interactions. While the phenomenon of complete synchronization (where all nodes in a network evolve identically) has been thoroughly studied using the Master Stability Function formalism, many real-world systems display richer and more structured patterns of coordination. In these cases, the network self-organizes into clusters of nodes that synchronize internally but not with each other, a state known as cluster synchronization.  Here, I will present recent theoretical and computational developments in understanding how these cluster states emerge in networks of coupled chaotic oscillators. I will show how the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian reveal the building blocks of synchronization, introducing the concept of localized spectral blocks as a key mathematical tool to detect and predict cluster formation. These insights naturally lead to the graph-theoretic notion of equitability, which we can generalize to include dynamical information.  Finally, I will discuss extensions of these ideas to multilayer and higher-order (hypergraph) networks, where interactions go beyond simple pairwise couplings. These generalizations uncover new mechanisms for coordination and provide a unified perspective on synchronization phenomena across networked systems, while explaining the ubiquitous lack of cluster synchronization in these network models.

column9: Resilience of China’s Domestic Inter-Firm Transaction Network via Bow-Tie Architecture and LLM-Optimized OSINT
column13: China’s domestic inter-firm transaction network—often described as the backbone of the world’s factory—has attracted growing strategic attention, yet remains highly opaque. This interest has intensified following the December 2025 revelations surrounding China’s semiconductor self-sufficiency initiatives and the rapid rise of domestic firms such as BYD in the electric vehicle sector. Conventional analyses of China’s domestic supply chain networks, however, are severely constrained by information asymmetry: in government-disclosed corporate filings, approximately 83\% of transaction partners are anonymized [1]. As a result, strategic inter-firm transaction networks are largely invisible in official records, creating a “black box” that prevents systemic resilience assessment. In this study, we focus explicitly on China’s domestic inter-firm transaction network, representing supplier–customer relationships among firms operating within China, rather than international trade flows.  To overcome the opacity of official disclosures, we develop a proprietary OSINT pipeline to aggregate fragmented evidence of inter-firm transaction relationships scattered across the web. We target 4,331 listed Chinese firms and 20,000 large Chinese enterprises with operating income exceeding \$130M. Even when focal firms do not disclose their transaction partners, we reconstruct domestic inter-firm links by triangulating partial disclosures from counterpart firms’ investor relations materials and reports from major media outlets. Using the Google Search API, we retrieve the top five sources per firm and process the resulting unstructured text using Qwen 3 with DSPy-optimized prompting [2]. Data reliability is further supported through randomized consistency checks using an LLM-as-a-Judge framework based on Gemini 3 Pro as an auxiliary validation tool.  The reconstructed domestic inter-firm transaction network provides an unprecedented view of China’s internal supply chain structure, capturing 26$\times$ more unique firms and 55$\times$ more transaction relationships than official disclosure-based datasets. Crucially, as shown in Figure 1(a), the resulting network restores plausible global topology: whereas official records exhibit an artificial truncation in degree beyond ten partners due to disclosure limits, fragmenting the network and undermining inference, the OSINT-derived network reproduces power-law-like degree patterns commonly observed in real-world inter-firm transaction networks [3]. Bow-tie decomposition reveals a giant strongly connected core (SCC) comprising 68,775 firms (56.2\%), accompanied by an upstream IN component comprising 11.2\% of firms and a downstream OUT component comprising 15.6\%.  Simulated targeted attacks further expose structural vulnerabilities concentrated in high-degree hubs, as shown in Figure 1(b). Degree-based hub attacks most effectively degrade global connectivity, yielding a robustness index of $R = 0.0267$, which is slightly lower (i.e., more destructive) than SCC-targeted attacks ($R = 0.0268$), while random failures are substantially less damaging ($R = 0.2496$). These findings indicate that the resilience of China’s domestic supply chain is governed not by the scale of individual firms, but by its structural dependence on a small set of central hub nodes within the domestic inter-firm transaction network.

column9: Computational Framework for Sustainable Transport Planning on Street Networks
column11: Zorina, Yana; Kontsevik, Georgii*; Mityagin, Sergey; Tupikina, Liubov
column13: Current street classification plans remain largely car-centric, failing to reflect the diverse morphology and function of urban streets; recent advancements in the classification of street patterns on a global scale [1], comprehensive analytical analysis of street classification [2], transportation type popularity per street subgraph classes [3, 4], such as regular grid, loops & lollipops, spars etc., network comparison methods and agent-based approaches on transport network generation and optimization [5] provide strong evidence for the necessity of such proposed computational frameworks.  We propose a computational framework that applies graph-based machine learning to street networks for sustainable urban transport planning. Structural complexity of street networks subgraphs is introduced to the task of route generation for public transport modelling. Since the urban fabric itself is not constant,  the approach also suggests modeling of network rewiring for class transition for subgraphs. The suggested framework then can be directly linked with the applications such as  flexible planning or design of the sustainable, e.g.non-car-centric transportation systems.

column9: Diversification and Convergence in Research Outputs by US Universities
column11: Qian, Yifan*; Gao, Jian; Yin, Yian; Schiffer, Peter; Wang, Dashun
column13: Research universities in the United States (US) significantly influence the global research landscape and drive economic and security agendas at regional, national, and international levels. Broadly speaking, the US research university ecosystem includes three types of universities: public land-grant (PLG) universities, public non-land-grant (PNLG) universities, and private (PVT) universities. These three different types of institutions give the American academic research ecosystem a unique structure that has been widely recognized not only for its range of diverse institutions but also for its critical role in sustaining the US’s leadership in global research. The extent to which these institutions maintain distinct identities and pursue disparate research portfolios, however, has not been explored in detail. We present a large-scale longitudinal network analysis of research portfolios across 146 US R1 universities from 1996 to 2020, using 7.1 million publications  (Fig. 1a). Each university’s research profile is represented by its relative emphasis across scientific subfields, enabling systematic comparison across institutions and types. We find that all three types have increasingly diversified their portfolios, expanding the range of topics in which they publish. However, research portfolios across institutional types have become progressively more similar over the past 25 years. This pattern extends beyond publications to downstream societal impact. By linking university papers to patents and to policy documents via citation networks, we observe the same trends. We further examine the role of federal funding in shaping these dynamics. We find that this convergence is most sharply reflected in publications associated with federal funding, reflecting the strong partnership between universities and the federal government (Figs. 1b-c); such an association highlights the need for careful balancing within federal funding strategies to augment the system’s overall resilience and capacity to address a broad range of challenges. These findings raise important questions for policymakers and academic leaders about how best to sustain and enhance the diversity, adaptability, and societal relevance of the US academic research enterprise.

column9: Simplicial Complex Emergence on Directed Hypergraphs
column13: We study when co-evolving (or adaptive) higher-order networks defined on directed hypergraphs admit a simplicial description. Binary and triadic couplings are modelled by time-dependent weight tensors. Using representation theory of the symmetric group $S_k$, we decompose these tensors into fully symmetric, fully antisymmetric, and mixed isotypic components, and track their Frobenius norms to define three asymptotic regimes and a quantitative notion of convergence. In the symmetric (resp. antisymmetric) limit, we certify emergence and stability of simplicial complexes via a local boundary test and interior drift conditions that enforce downward-closure; in the mixed limit, we show that the minimal faithful object is a semi-simplicial set. We illustrate the theory with simulations that track the isotypic Frobenius norms and the higher-order structure. Practically, our work provides rigorous conditions under which homological tools are justified for adaptive higher-order systems.

column9: Assessing the risk in statistically reconstructed firm-level critical raw material supply networks
column11: Baum, Sophia*; Heß, Maximilian; Klimek, Peter
column13: Critical raw materials (CRMs) are essential for producing goods for everyday life and modern technologies. They are therefore of strategic importance to the EU economy but are also associated with a high risk of supply disruption. For example, over 80% of the global tungsten supply is mined in China and is primarily used to produce extremely hard and durable alloys for high-performance industrial tools, as well as in catalysts, pigments, lighting, and electronic applications. Dependencies on raw materials are often assessed only at the level of mined or minimally processed forms. Vulnerabilities that emerge further downstream are more challenging to identify and require a comprehensive, detailed representation of industrial value chains, which has so far proved difficult to achieve. The assessment is typically performed at the country level, only taking trade into account, not at the firm level, and therefore does not account for domestic production or company ownership. This study introduces (a) a novel approach to map value chain networks for critical raw materials (CRMs), combining AI-based generation, trade data, and statistical validation, and (b) a statistical reconstruction of the underlying firm network. The resulting networks can be used to evaluate and quantify concentration effects and vulnerabilities for individual regions and the global value chains in which they are embedded.  To automatically construct a value chain originating from a raw material at the sixth-digit level of the Harmonized System (HS), we use a two-step process. First, we identify a broad set of products related to the extracted or minimally processed material using a previously proposed production network [2]. These product pairs serve as provisional inputs to an LLM, which generates granular production paths from input to output using HS-like product descriptions. The embeddings of these descriptions are then matched to real HS descriptions using cosine similarity. Second, we post-process the preliminary network using four hyperparameters: an embedding threshold, a frequency threshold (how often a link is generated in step 1), an evaluation threshold (LLM-based pairwise validation), and a trade significance threshold (the correlation between input imports and output exports under a permutation test). The hyperparameters are calibrated using a manually researched phosphorus rock network. For the core components, basic phosphorus compounds, phosphates, and phosphatic fertilizers, accounting for about 90% of global phosphate rock use, we recover 100% of actual nodes and links with no false positives. To map the underlying firm network, we identify companies from the ORBIS database involved in the extraction, processing, or manufacturing of the focus critical raw material or products derived from it. This is done by first filtering ORBIS firm descriptions for keywords related to the critical raw material and its broad applications. To assign a firm to specific HS code, we first map the HS-based value chain network to its NACE4 equivalent. To evaluate whether a firm produces a certain HS code, the firm must be assigned to the mapped NACE4 sector or one of the first-order neighbors on the NACE4-based value chain network. This relaxes the strict requirement of an exact NACE4 sector match, as such assignments are often imprecise. We then task an LLM to evaluate whether a specific firm is involved in the production of a given product. If the evaluation is positive, we consider the firm a producer of that product. Thus, for each product in the HS-based value chain network, we obtain a list of producing firms. We then connect the firms using a gravity model of trade, incorporating the underlying input-output structure and trade data [3] as constraints. Figure 1 shows one example of such a network for tungsten, including companies that extract and process tungsten or manufacture intermediate products part of the tungsten value chain. Companies are scored using network centrality, concentration indices, and governance indicators.  We discuss how estimates of risk based on firm properties and production structure differ from those based on country-level trade and production data alone. Our findings suggest that analyses based solely on country-level data obscure such relationships between companies, leading to distorted risk estimates. This is particularly the case when companies carry out multiple processing steps within the same country.   In summary, we present a method for statistically reconstructing firm-level supply networks based on a mapping of a 6-digit HS code value chain network, providing finer granularity than the country-level. This represents an important step toward understanding global value chains in much greater detail and assessing risk within the supply network, as comprehensive knowledge of these networks can help identify dependencies and evaluate resilience. column9: Product-level value chains from firm data: mapping trophic levels into economic growth
column11: Fessina, Massimiliano; Tacchella, Andrea ; Zaccaria, Andrea*
column13: Global value chains shape everything from the price of coffee to the roll-out of clean technology, yet policy still relies on sector-level input–output maps that gloss over the differences among the single products. Our study reconstructs a detailed product-level value chain by identifying statistically significant input-output relationships between products derived from firm-level trade data. The result is a network of about 5000 products, which provides a tool for analyzing the structure and function of global value chains at an unprecedented level of detail. Leveraging concepts from ecological network theory, we assign a trophic level to each product, providing a topology-based measure of its production stage and allowing us to assess the overall hierarchical structure of the network through the trophic coherence. This enables the computation of the average trophic level of imports and exports for firms and countries, which provides information about industrial specialization patterns and economic growth. We show that the trophic structure of value chains is only detectable at a fine product resolution, and that firms tend to operate with a positive trophic jump - i.e., they export more downstream products than they import. At the country level, we observe a strong negative correlation between export diversification and the average trophic level of imports: more diversified economies import more upstream products, while countries with low diversification are constrained to import downstream goods — a pattern we define trophic barrier. This relationship reflects differences in industrial specialization, with manufacturing-intensive countries like China and Italy importing more basic inputs than service-oriented economies like the US and France. Similarly, we find that trophic jump correlates positively with diversification, indicating that more advanced countries add greater value by transforming basic inputs into complex outputs. Crucially, these trophic metrics are not just descriptive: we demonstrate that both the average trophic level of a country’s imports and its trophic jump are strong predictors of future economic growth. Our detailed, totally data-driven input-output network of products provides a practical reference for trade strategists, development planners, and researchers navigating supply-chain reconfiguration and geopolitical fragmentation.

column9: Distance Dependent Bayesian Community Detection
column11: Beaudry, Isabelle*; Mendoza, Marcelo; Bro, Naim
column13: Community detection in networks seeks to identify to which cluster the nodes belong. Various traditional methods consider only the connections among the members of the population to make this classification. The rationale behind those methods is that highly connected nodes are more likely to belong to the same cluster than poorly connected ones. Although structure-based community detection algorithms may perform well under some circumstances, these methods ignore information included in many real-world networks, such as the characteristics of their members. For instance, nodal attributes may represent a person's characteristics, such as age, gender, and interests. The node attributes may affect the formation of clusters in a population. This phenomenon is well documented in the social science literature and is known as network homophily. Consequently, models leveraging link density and attribute homogeneity may help improve community detection. The main contribution of this work is to propose a community detection method that guarantees a lower link density across clusters than within clusters for any community pairs and also considers the similarity of the nodes with respect to their attributes. The inference is then performed under a Bayesian nonparametric framework. We assess the performance of the method through an extensive simulation study. Furthermore, we compare our results in real data with state-of-the-art community detection methodology for network data.

column9: Investigating the Capital Flows of DeFi Yield Aggregators
column11: Kitzler, Stefan*; Zarinehbaf Asadi, Kasra; Kremer, Svetlana; Haslhofer, Bernhard
column13: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) provides financial services for cryptoassets (digital currencies). DeFi and cryptoassets are based on smart contracts, program code that contains financial logic, and operate on distributed ledger technology, such as the Ethereum blockchain [1]. Yield aggregators are a specific form of DeFi service that pools user deposits and strategically invests across multiple DeFi platforms to optimize returns [3, 2]. The operation of yield aggregators within multi-layered financial services and asset interactions introduces significant complexity, making it challenging to understand underlying capital flows, dependencies, and risk exposures. Despite growing capital under management, systematic research on their operational mechanisms and network interactions remains limited. We investigate how yield aggregators generate profits by analyzing two major platforms, Yearn Finance and Cian Yield Layer, through their interactions with other financial services over one year (May 2024–May 2025). The Ethereum blockchain, built on distributed ledger technology, provides transparency for all DeFi transactions. We decompose operations into two cycles: (1) user deposits/withdrawals, and (2) strategic capital allocation across platforms. We collect a dataset of 5,850 cryptoasset transfers for Yearn (involves user investments of $15.7M in USDC, a US dollar-pegged asset) and 1,718 for Cian ($54M in stETH, a staked ETH asset) from the Ethereum blockchain. Using network analysis, we construct temporal cryptoasset transfer networks where nodes represent addresses and directed edges represent asset movements. Figure 1 shows Yearn’s aggregated deposit flows to five lending platforms (Compound, Aave, Sky, Morpho, Spark); note that rebalancing operations create double-counting. Throughout our analysis, we reveal fundamentally distinct strategies in complexity, diversification, and risk exposure. Yearn Finance implements a diversified, multi-service strategy, dynamically allocating capital across established lending platforms (Aave, Compound, Sky, Morpho), achieving 5.41% APY. In contrast, Cian employs sophisticated, leveraged operations through a multi-layered architecture involving several services and asset exchanges, resulting in 4.22% APY. Our findings demonstrate that strategic complexity does not guarantee superior performance, with simpler diversification outperforming sophisticated leverage during our observation period. This work highlights the importance of network science in unraveling modern capital flows and service interconnections in DeFi.

column9: Interactive Visualization of Urban Segregation Networks: Bridging Physical and Virtual Social Spaces
column13: Urban segregation fractures social spaces and constrains information flows, promoting polarization rather than homogenization of behaviors. While U.S. metropolitan areas have experienced declining racial stratification since 1990, income-based segregation persists and increasingly manifests in online spaces. We present an interactive visualization platform that maps the network structure of social segregation in major American cities, revealing how physical and virtual segregation reinforce each other across scales.

column9: From Case Counts to Contact Networks: Inferring Epidemic Coupling in Space and Time
Beyond Euclidean Distance-Based Clustering: A Network Approach to Unsupervised Classification
column13: Unsupervised classification is a fundamental tool for organizing complex datasets into groups of similar elements, enabling the identification of shared characteristics and underlying processes, while averaging out individual data point variability. Traditional unsupervised learning approaches, such as k-means and hierarchical clustering, typically operate in a vector space and rely on Euclidean distance to compute class centroids and relationships among the data. This setup is often poorly suited to empirical data, where features are correlated, information is redundant, and meaningful relationships may not be adequately captured by Euclidean metrics. Although dimensionality reduction is commonly employed to address feature correlations, Euclidean distances remain susceptible to degradation in moderately to high-dimensional spaces and may fail to encode non-linear or directional dependencies.  We introduce a network-based workflow for unsupervised classification that replaces vector-space representations with similarity networks. Pairwise relationships between data points, computed using arbitrary similarity or dependency measures (e.g., cosine similarity or mutual information), are encoded as weighted edges in a fully connected graph. This formulation decouples clustering from Euclidean geometry and enables the use of metrics tailored to the structure of the data and the scientific question of interest. To reveal the underlying informative network topology, we extract a statistically significant network backbone using the disparity filter. Community detection is then applied to the backbone network to identify classes of data points. By simultaneously constructing a network of data points and a network of features, the proposed framework enables the direct interpretability of clusters in terms of their dominant characteristics.  We demonstrate the approach on the Geospatial Attributes of Gages for Evaluating Streamflow (GAGES) dataset, comprising 9,067 watersheds in the continental United States described by over 300 environmental variables. The resulting watershed communities show strong spatial coherence and distinct signatures associated with natural and anthropogenic drivers, and correspond to markedly different hydrological behaviors. We show that tuning the workflow parameters controls edge density and community resolution, enabling investigation at different granularities. In addition, network-specific measures, such as degree centrality, can be used to select representative elements within each class, useful to prioritize instruments deployment. Due to its metric flexibility and reliance on network topology, the proposed method is domain-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of high-dimensional datasets.

column9: Disparity-in-Differences: Extracting Hierarchical Backbones of Weighted Directed Networks
column13: Empirical networks often consist of heterogeneous and asymmetrical relations. Existing network backbone extraction methods have successfully identified significant relations based on heterogeneity but are not designed to incorporate asymmetry that may encode hierarchical structures. To fill the gap, motivated by the concept of power-dependence relations [1], this paper proposes a new method named "disparity-in-differences" that measures a statistical significance of asymmetric dependence, which is defined as the difference of normalized edge weights between two nodes. The term "disparity" is adopted from the disparity filter [2], a widely used network backbone extraction method.   According to the concept of power-dependence relations [1], the dependence of i on j is equal to the power of j over i. In this framework, power imbalance between i and j can be represented as the difference in dependencies. For two nodes i and j, the normalized weight of an edge i -> j is considered as the extent that i depends on j and vice versa. The difference between the normalized weights of i -> j and j -> i would thus serve as a proxy for a hierarchical relation. To calculate its statistical significance, the proposed method samples values from a null model that assumes edge weights are uniformly distributed over neighbors as used in the disparity filter [2]. A sampled value for a node i (x_{ij}) follows a Beta distribution, Beta(1,k_{i}-1), where k_{i} is the number of out-neighbors of i. If the difference between two associated normalized weights is significantly higher or lower than x_{ij} - x_{ji} values, the proposed method assigns an unweighted edge i -> j or j -> i to indicate j or i is at a higher position in a hierarchy, respectively (Figure 1).   For evaluation, the proposed method is applied to a journal citation network, a U.S. airport network, the Enron email network, and a world trade network. Compared to existing network backbone extraction methods, it better captures hierarchical relations that align with journal quality ratings, airport hub categories by size, levels of management, and a core-periphery structure of countries, respectively. Backbones extracted by the disparity-in-differences method will provide insights into not only known hierarchies but also emerging, fading, or missing hierarchical relations.  [1] Emerson, R. M. (1962). Power-dependence relations. American Sociological Review, 27(1), 31-41.  [2] Serrano, M. Á., Boguná, M., & Vespignani, A. (2009). Extracting the multiscale backbone of complex weighted networks. Proceedings of the national academy of sciences, 106(16), 6483-6488.

column9: Compressibility of Neuronal Activity Across Dynamical Regimes
column13: Complex networks often exhibit rich collective dynamics that depend sensitively on patterns of interactions between nodes. In neuronal systems, these interactions can lead to distinct dynamical regimes—subcritical, critical, and supercritical— each characterized by different patterns of propagation, correlation, and information flow [1,2]. A central hypothesis in this field is that healthy brain activity operates near a critical point [1], enabling efficient communication and flexible computation. This motivates the central question in this work: to what extent is the apparent variability in brain activity driven by a relatively small set of informative correlations, and how does this depend on the underlying neural dynamics? In this work, we study neuronal systems through the lens of information compressibility [3], a measure that quantifies how much uncertainty in collective dynamics can be reduced by a subset of pairwise interactions. This measure is grounded in the minimax entropy principle [4], which seeks the least-biased probabilistic model consistent with a chosen set of constraints. Specifically, neural activity is modeled using a multivariate Gaussian maximum-entropy distribution constrained by selected pairwise covariances. As correlations are added, the model’s entropy decreases, indicating that more structure is being captured. The greedy minimax-entropy algorithm determines, at each step, which correlation, when included, results in the most substantial reduction in global entropy. This process creates an optimal compression curve that measures how effectively network interactions account for collective variability. We replicate the greedy minimax-entropy compression framework introduced in [3] and extend it to synthetic neuronal activity generated using networks of Izhikevich neurons [5]. Our initial results focus on activity simulated on random networks (Erd˝os-R´enyi graphs, p = 0.2) consisting of N neurons with excitatory (80%) and inhibitory (20%) populations [6]. Different dynamical regimes were produced by tuning the effective branching ratio or, equivalently, adjusting the balance of excitation and inhibition. Fig. 1 shows a schematic of the analysis pipeline. Fig. 1A shows an example of simulated neural time series generated in a near-critical regime (branching ratio, σ = 0.9), while Fig. 1B shows its corresponding correlation matrix. Fig. 1C shows the resulting greedy minimax-entropy compression curves across several branching ratios, showing systematic differences in compressibility based on the branching ratio of the dynamics. Fig. 1D summarizes these results by plotting the area above the compression curves in 1C as a function of branching ratio. We find that strongly subcritical dynamics are easy to compress because the activity is highly redundant and quickly dies out. In contrast, supercritical dynamics are harder to compress, as bursting and unstable activity produce noisy correlation patterns. Near-critical regimes fall between these extremes: their activity can be compressed efficiently but not trivially, indicating a balance between structure and variability. Together, these results show that information compressibility provides a clear, system-level indicator of the underlying neural dynamical regime.   1] Beggs & Plenz (2003). Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits. Journal of Neuroscience, 23(35), 11167-11177. [2] Shew, Yang, Yu, Roy, & Plenz (2011). Physical Review E, 111(5). [5] Izhikevich (2003). Simple model of spiking neurons. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 14(6), 1569-1572. [6] Braitenberg & Sch¨uz (2013). column9: Effects of screen time and activities on mental health in children
column13: Children and adolescents are engaging with digital technologies at increasingly younger ages, and recent years have seen a  rapid expansion of interactive tools such as AI chatbots and wellness applications. A growing body of literature links screen time and digital media use to mental health outcomes in youth, including depressive symptoms, sleep disruption, and suicidal ideation, suggesting a complex interplay between individual differences, contextual factors, and environmental  characteristics [1,2]. To investigate divergent associations between screen use (e.g., social media, video games, TV,  phone), physical activities, and mental health during childhood and early adolescence, we used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, a large (N ≈ 12, 000) longitudinal (t = 4) dataset. We conducted an exploratory analysis at baseline (year 0), selecting participants with ≥ 80% valid responses across screen time, activity, mental health, and social measures (n = 3, 713). Heterogeneity in screen time and activity profiles was examined by  computing subject × subject similarity matrices and applying the Louvain algorithm for modularity maximization [3]. We  retained clusters with at least 10% of the subjects, resulting in six clusters covering 91% of the selected participants. Clusters were characterized by screen time and activity patterns, and their associations with mental health outcomes. In Figure 1 we can observe preliminary analysis with different clusters presenting distinct screen usage patterns. For example, in Figure 1B, Cluster 2 expresses higher screen activity reported both by the children and their parents and  correspondent higher scores in most problematic mental health outcomes. Further analysis is being developed. Future  work will also explore this approach longitudinally, investigating how patterns of screen use and categorized activities  relate to mental health trajectories and brain organization, with a focus on developing analytical frameworks that can capture the complex, bidirectional relationships between digital media use and youth mental health.

column9: Complexity, Risk and Resilience in Policy Sub-Systems
column13: In this paper we assess systemic resilience [1] by considering risk complexity and risk predictability in a simulation of a policy making sub-system. The aim is to determine whether a range of different risks have a differential impact on the production of consensus or the conditions that lead them to degenerate to polarisation and conflict. We account for different types of power for political agents, such as influence, authority, relational and information advantage. We further acknowledge complexity in that policy domains are interdependent and that external shocks can alter system properties (i.e. affect the terms of reference for the interaction between actors). We also account for policy issue salience among political agents; the different phases of the policy process, which determine the level of their engagement; and the level of agitation contingent to proximity to a decision/vote. We employ data from well documented cases of longitudinal policy making [2] and use t1 as baseline of networks of policy making comparing to t2 with Agent Based Model simulations which provide an opportunity to test for different network and complexity effects. The synthetic data simulate deliberations during a specific stage of the agenda setting and consultation stage in the policy process. The aim is to test for the impact of a range of political risks, including system polarization, sensitivity to conflict during negotiations, system disintegration, and variance from ex ante preferences of policy actors (i.e. risk in the predictability of outcomes ex ante). The model employed is a hybrid network model, combined with an agent-based model. Modeling includes variables for issue salience, clustering level, network properties (reciprocity, transitivity, etc), tie maintenance costs, and agent power among others. Extreme events are also modeled such as external shocks, while agents impact one another via a DeGroot and a bounded-confidence Friedkin-Johnsen influence process. Also modeled is the presence of exceptional agents, such as political entrepreneurs and leaders. Initial results indicate resilient political systems are affected by risks from policy shifts, and shocks from policy debates when they degenerate to echo-chamber exchanges [3]. Resilience also appears to have a negative relationship to entropy risks. Furthermore, the presence of political entrepreneurs significantly affects the probability of achieving policy consensus and reduces policy variance. This study confirms the sensitivity of political outcomes to the interaction between policy system resilience, risk level and risk type.

column9: Layer interdependence in the multiplex international system
column13: The international system is a paradigmatic example of a multiplex network, and is increasingly analyzed as such. States interact with one another through multiple relational network layers ranging across the diplomatic, economic, and military realms. The proliferation of relational data in international relations research has enabled even more detailed models to represent the system as a high-dimensional multiplex network, but it has also raised new challenges: which layers are the most structurally informative?  I create a multiplex network constructed from eleven layers representing different types of international relationships. Each layer is represented as a binary unipartite network, and the full multiplex network is encoded as a four-dimensional adjacency tensor, with each annual observation within being a three-dimensional adjacency tensor. I apply a nonnegative Tucker decomposition (NNTuck) technique to systematically analyze the dependence structure among layers in the international system, uncovering layer communities. Firstly, I find that the international multiplex network exhibits layer dependent properties. Secondly, I find that the network of bilateral arms trade is the most informative of all interstate networks, followed by alliances. In contrast, international trade exhibits little overlap with any other networks. This means that understanding the structure of the arms trade network may be exceptionally informative in terms of understanding the larger structure of the international system and its collective structural processes.

column9: Comparative study of networks of writers in different historical periods obtained by Wikipedia-mining
column11: Cwilich, Gabriel*; Agapitos, Paschalis; Spivak, Yonatan; Schwartz, Gustavo A.
column13: From the English version of Wikipedia, we extracted the pages corresponding to persons in the literary world, and we created six networks organized by birth date, from 1700 to 1999. The weighted links among them are not the standard hyperlinks but their more subtle relatedness which is  obtained calculating the Google distance[1,2] (GD)  between the pages of the most relevant authors in each period (as measured by the in-degree  of their Wikipedia pages); the relatedness is the negative exponential of their GD.  Many of the characteristics of these networks  (their size, average connectivity, size and order of the largest core) follow clear temporal patterns, presenting an exponential growth across time (with an exception for the last historical period which represents a "work in progress"), and that trend is consistent with the trends of Wikipedia as a whole;  in spite of that, the strengths of the weighted links remain almost identical  across the different historical periods, presenting in all cases a clear bimodal distribution of weak and strong links; the relative weight of weak links increases in time as the relations between writers diversify.   We implemented a spectral analysis of the different networks, using the eigenvalue distribution of the normalized Laplacian; while the average eigvenvalue remains constant in time, their  distribution narrows; but remarkable, the algebraic connectivity of all the networks remains constant in spite of the size of the networks changing by more than an order of magnitude (from 50 to 1100) and the increasing value of their (Shannon) spectral entropy[3].  Since the networks described above  are dense, we used some procedures of sparsification (triangular inequality backbone extraction, standard thresholding and disparity filtering, keeping equal levels of connectivity across networks) in order to further or analysis, and the different discussed lead to similar results.   The identity of the writers belonging to the highest cores provides insights on their  connections, not gleaned  apriori from the structure of Wikipedia itself. In some cases it reveals connections linked to national origin or language, in others to the thematic content of their writing, or some unexpected connections between two different national groups.  We studied the process of disintegration of each  network upon successive removal of nodes in decreasing order of their degree or closeness or edges in decreasing order of their betweenness, monitoring  the evolution of the largest components.  The removal of nodes based on closeness uncovered an interesting hierarchical structure, since across all networks and connectivity levels, at certain points the removal  of a node results in the splitting of the network in two pieces of similar size, revealing the existence of  communities, and sub-communities within them (see Figure 1) which had no links connecting them in the original network (and not  visible in the overall structure of the network). Normally these communities split along national or linguistic lines; their study might provide valuable insights to complement what a more "microscopic”, discipline specific,  approach can provide. Biamonte., Phys Rev X, 6 ,040062 (2016)

column9: The King Is Dead, Long Live the King. Conflict in Centralized Networks
column13: Star-like networks are commonly interpreted as structures that concentrate coordination, consensus, or leadership around a preponderant node. In this view, centralization is assumed to reflect dominance, stability, or effective control by a single political or social actor (Sueur et al., 2012). This paper advances a different thesis: star networks systematically concentrate conflict rather than consensus. To examine this claim, the study analyzes an empirical network derived from a Mexican government commission in charge of the construction of a large-scale infrastructure project between 1972 and 1973. The network comprises more than 70 actors and over 2,000 edges, and is observed at two historical moments: one characterized by high centralization and another by reduced centralization. Relational conflict is operationalized using weighted degree centrality, which captures repeated interactions rather than single events and allows centrality to be assessed not only in terms of interaction volume but also in relation to the qualitative balance of ties. The results show, first, that weighted degree centrality is not monolithic, as commonly assumed in the approach of Opsahl et al. (2010). Central actors tend to accumulate ties that combine contradictory edge attributes, such as cooperation and disagreement, within the same dyadic relationships. Second, higher levels of network centralization are associated with a greater proportion of weighted ties in which disagreement outweighs cooperation. Conversely, when centralization decreases, conflict becomes less concentrated and relational tension diminishes. These findings suggest that conflict concentration is a structural property of star-like networks. Rather than signaling consensus or cohesion, high centralization amplifies resistance through repeated and ambivalent interactions focused on central nodes. More broadly, this perspective helps explain, from a network science standpoint, the structural fragility of highly centralized political regimes, including dictatorships, in which the concentration of power is systematically accompanied by elevated levels of conflict and opposition.

column9: Network-based prediction of economic growth
column13: Recent research, primarily focusing on the characteristics of individual industries rather than on the complexity of the evolving economy in which they are embedded, seems insufficient to investigate growth. The network-based approach to industrial growth brings a new perspective to the table. Network metrics that consider the industry’s influence on the national economy can also encompass the structure and functioning of the production network and provide a relevant approach to industrial growth alongside current measures based on trade volumes. This is the first study to use only these network measures and the production network framework alone to prove that the position of a sector in the production cycle considerably impacts its economic growth. Research questions include to what extent we can determine the growth of an industry purely from its place in the production cycle and what production network characteristics lead to one sector’s development and the other’s decline. We find that almost a third of the industry’s growth is explained by its location in the production network topology alone. This significant amount cannot be overseen, thus suggesting that the network approach to national economic trade has the potential for beneficial applications in national policy and development.

column9: Unanimous Mimetic Equilibrium: Scapegoating as an Extreme Case of Structural Balance in Signed Networks
column13: Structural balance theory explains how local triadic tensions in signed networks can be resolved globally: in its classic form, a balanced network admits a partition into two groups with predominantly positive ties within groups and negative ties between groups [Heider, 1946, Cartwright and Harary, 1956], while generalized balance allows more than two mutually antagonistic factions. Here we propose that scapegoating can be formalized as a limit case of balance: a Unanimous Mimetic Equilibrium (UME) in which one node (or a small set) becomes the unique out-group while the rest of the network synchronizes into a comparatively cohesive in-group. This reframes the “all-against-one” pattern as a structurally legible outcome of signed-network dynamics under mimetic pressure [Girard, 1982]. We operationalize UME in two complementary ways. First, in a parsimonious agent-based model (ABM) on a small-world topology [?], agents accumulate tension, opportunistically generate leaders, and converge on a victim through an accusation rite that relieves collective pressure and reconfigures ties. Second, in empirical data from four Brazilian “cancellation” episodes on X/Twitter, time-windowed interaction graphs near the peak consistently become star-shaped, with the victim at the center (high in-degree). To measure convergence toward UME, we use a compact signature set: attention inequality (Gini/HHI), target-centered in-degree centralization (hub–victim inversion) [Freeman, 1979], stance-based assortativity and modularity shifts, and distance-to-victim /post-rite avoidance as a topological “scar.” Across model and data, these metrics trace a coherent trajectory: pre-peak concentration and centralization rise, community boundaries are crossed at the climax, and post-rite re-linking leaves measurable residue. The UME framing yields a network-science vocabulary for a Girardian mechanism and suggests early-warning indicators for reputational crises and online harassment [Paes da Silva et al., 2025].

column9: All contacts are not equal: Spatiotemporal constraints shape network structure and transmission dynamics
column11: Taube, Juliana*; Tiu, Andrew; Bansal, Shweta
column13: Contact network structure is widely studied because of its influential role in infectious disease transmission. Since the POLYMOD study [1], routine contact surveys have consistently used similar distance (e.g., 2 meters) and duration (e.g., 5 minutes) constraints to define close contacts relevant to respiratory transmission. This standardization facilitates comparison between studies but critically overlooks the unique transmission profiles of respiratory viruses [2]. We hypothesize that pathogens may be limited to different contact network structures based on their spatiotemporal transmission constraints and thus demonstrate distinct transmission dynamics. Using a dataset with fine-scale interaction data, we investigate how changes in contact definition impact contact network structure and respiratory disease dynamics.   To characterize how network structure varies with different contact distance and duration thresholds, we use app-based GPS location data from anonymized and opted-in mobile devices aggregated to protect individual privacy. We focus our analysis on locations relevant to public health (e.g., restaurants, grocery stores), transmission constraints that are realistic for respiratory pathogens (e.g., influenza, measles, coronaviruses), and network features known to predict epidemic outcomes (e.g., mean degree, degree heterogeneity, transitivity).  After adjusting for network sampling biases [3], we find that contact network structure is sensitive to contact definition (Figure 1). Pathogens capable of transmission over large distances or through brief exposures have access to denser and more heterogeneously connected contact networks, whereas pathogens requiring close proximity or longer interactions are restricted to sparser networks with lower degree heterogeneity. Through network disease modeling, we show that this structural variation leads to distinct transmission dynamics, which can inform the inference of transmission modes for emerging pathogens from epidemiological data. These findings shed light on the evolutionary pressures faced by different respiratory pathogens and help characterize which pathogens are more likely to exhibit superspreading. Transmissibility and transmission of respiratory viruses. Nat Rev Microbiol. 2021 Aug;19(8):528–45. [3] Kolaczyk ED. Statistical Analysis of Network Data: Methods and Models. New York, NY: Springer; 2009.

column9: Arriving Young, Leaving Old(er): Age-structured International Migration on Subnational Scale in Austria
column13: Modelling migration is complicated, as people move for many reasons. Some leave their country for the first time, others return to places they once called home, or move on to new destinations. However, most models focus only on who arrives, missing the full picture of how migrant populations evolve. We introduce a model for diaspora flows that estimates both arrivals and exits using daily migration flow rates, disaggregated by age and nationality. Drawing on high-resolution administrative data from Austria covering over 1.8 million foreign nationals, the model allocates these movements across more than 2,000 municipalities based on the size of local diaspora communities. We find that exits are not exceptions but a consistent and predictable feature across all groups. Migration rejuvenates Austria's population, as both arriving and departing migrants are younger than the average resident. This effect has distinct age-geography patterns: younger migrants are drawn to cities, while older migrants are more evenly distributed in the country. By capturing both arrivals and exits simultaneously, our approach provides a more comprehensive and interpretable picture of migration dynamics, how populations change over time, and how they are influenced by space, age, and national origins.

column9: Network science techniques applied to soft matter simulations
column13: Soft matter provides a concrete instance of networks leading to complex physical properties. In this poster, we demonstrate the use of network science tools to study transitions in connectivity and mechanics of soft matter systems. These tools provide tangible evidence for the physical mechanisms that underlie material properties in two systems of interest: percolation robustness in ion exchange membranes, and graph coarsening in granular systems.  For material systems, the transition between a state of percolation to a state of disjointedness can have important ramifications on their properties. To computationally track a percolation process, we propose the use of k-stub decomposition (KSD) [1], which excludes particles with degree less than k from the network. In physical networks, increasing k has the effect of peeling back layers from the surface; hence, increasing k can remove weakly connected surface dendrites and bottlenecks. For example, in our study [2], anion exchange membranes undergo a sharp increase in ionic conductivity at specific relative humidities, presumably due to percolation of ion channels comprising water molecules. KSD analysis of molecular simulations reveals that this transition takes place when channels are robust at the k = 3 level, revealing that 3 water molecules are needed in the channel at a minimum to enable a vehicular transport of ions.   The second system we have studied deals with dense granular suspensions: under the right conditions, these systems undergo shear thickening due to frictional constraints between the particles. As these systems flow, the frictional force chain network (FFCN) evolves as frictional contacts are formed and broken. The properties of FFCN are dependent on the kind of constraints (frictional constants, rolling/sliding frictions, etc.) and conditions (density, shear rate). In this study [3], we used graph coarsening to identify independent force chains, hubs, and terminals. The force chain length distribution and the connectivity of the FFCN provide useful insight into the trends in rheology of these systems.   Beyond these two examples, we are currently applying these techniques to other soft matter systems, including complex polymeric mesophases, metamaterials, and nanoparticle self-assembly. Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment, 2021 (1), 013212. [2] Wang, Z., Sun, G., Lewis, N. H., Mandal, M., Sharma, A., Kim, M., ... & de Pablo, J. J. (2025). Water-mediated ion transport in an anion exchange membrane. Nature Communications, 16 (1), 1099. [3] Sharma, S., Sharma, A., & Singh, A. (2025).
