column9: A Metapopulation Network Framework for Evaluating Travel-Based Intervention Strategies for Global Outbreak Control
column11: Bay, Clara*; Davis, Jessica; Chinazzi, Matteo; Vespignani, Alessandro
column13: Early intervention at the source of an outbreak is widely recognized as the most effective way to curb spread in the initial phase. Travel restrictions and border-control measures are a common example: they are frequently among the first internationally deployed actions, despite mixed evidence on their effectiveness. In practice, however, policy responses are often reactive, introduced only after epidemiological thresholds are crossed. Here, we explicitly evaluate timing as the key policy lever by comparing proactive  versus reactive travel-based interventions during emerging outbreaks. We model global disease spread on a metapopulation mobility network, in which geographic areas (subpopulations) are connected by empirically travel flows. Within each subpopulation, transmission dynamics follow an SLIR compartmental model, while individuals move between subpopulations along network edges according to mobility data. We evaluate six travel and border-control intervention strategies spanning two policy approaches: reactive measures, in which controls are implemented only after an epidemiological trigger is reached and are applied to travel from the outbreak source, and proactive measures, in which controls are implemented early and reduce mobility more broadly across the network (Fig. 1A & B). Within each category, we consider three interventions: (i) border-control measures only (mobility reduction), (ii) border-control measures combined with targeted mitigation that reduces transmission at the source, and (iii) border-control measures combined with global mitigation that reduces transmission across all locations. Using stochastic numerical simulations on both theoretical random networks and the data-driven Global Epidemic and Mobility (GLEAM) metapopulation model, we systematically vary implementation timing and the intensity of mobility reduction.  Results (Fig. 1C) highlight the limitations of reactive, source-focused border measures, which are generally implemented too late to substantially alter international dissemination. In contrast, proactive, early border-control strategies, especially when paired with measures that reduce transmission (global mitigation), provide markedly stronger control of global spread across a wide range of timings and intensities, and can significantly delay or even successfully contain outbreaks. Overall, we offer a general framework to quantify the trade-offs between proactive versus reactive travel restrictions and border control in a globally connected system during the earliest stages of an emerging outbreak. These insights can help inform timely policy design and strengthen preparedness for future emerging infectious disease threats.

column9: Party Time: A Temporal Network Dataset of a Social Celebration and its Bursty Dynamics
column13: Human proximity networks from conferences, classrooms, hospitals, and workplaces have consistently exhibited bursty interaction dynamics [1]. However, many of these contexts involved scheduled interactions of different lengths and participants with different formal roles. Is burstiness an inherent feature of organic social interaction, or limited to settings with heterogeneous types of interactions? Do the temporal statistics of human interaction observed in professional, academic, and public gatherings extend to a private social celebration?  We collected high-resolution proximity data from a cocktail hour of a wedding in a Chicago suburb. Ninety-three consenting wedding guests wore Ultra-Wideband (UWB) proximity badges that detected when other badge-wearers were within 1.5m (± 0.1 m, 5s bins), supplemented by coarse location estimates and pre– and post–event surveys on personality and self-reported conversations. Participants self-identified their wedding party affiliation (among friend/family groups), enabling direct social group-level mixing analysis instead of demographic proxies relied upon for previous group-mixing studies (e.g., [2]). We are preparing a de-identified public release of the resulting temporal network, contributing a novel “private party” setting to the public corpus of face-to-face interaction temporal networks.  Preliminary comparisons to one-hour windows from SocioPatterns collections [3] (conferences, schools, office, hospital) show similarly robust bursty dynamics in the party context, though with systematic differences. As seen in Figure 1, contact rate (edge weights of the integrated network) distributions agree closely; contact duration distribution remains comparably broad but exhibit an earlier cut-off; the inter-arrival time distribution is steeper yet exhibits a stronger power-law trend than the SocioPatterns contexts. Using the self-identified groups, we are investigating if differences between within-group and cross-group interaction timing contributes to the overall burstiness. Once released, this data collection will enable more empirically grounded modeling of social events, whether for contact tracing simulations or cultural studies, in addition to refining the universality of face-to-face interaction burstiness.   [1] Barrat, A., Cattuto, C., “Temporal Networks of Face-to-Face Human Interactions” [2] M. Oliveira, et al., “Group mixing drives inequality in face-to-face gatherings” [3] https://www.sociopatterns.org/

column9: When PageRank Feeds Back: Fixed Points of Personalized Centrality in Complex Networks
column13: PageRank is one of the most influential centrality measures in network science, originally introduced for ranking web pages and later generalized to a wide range of applications in social, biological, economic, and technological networks. While classical PageRank theory focuses on the existence and uniqueness of a stationary distribution for a fixed personalization vector, less attention has been given to PageRank as a functional operator acting on the space of personalization vectors itself. This presentation studies PageRank from this functional perspective. The central aim of the poster is to provide a complete characterization of existence, uniqueness, and structure of fixed points of PageRank functional $PR_\lambda$ in terms of the network’s strongly connected components. Specifically, it is analytically demonstrated that if $\mathcal{G}$ is a strongly connected network, then $PR_\lambda$ admits a unique fixed point, which can be analytically determined. Conversely, when $\mathcal{G}$ is not strongly connected, existence of fixed points is still guaranteed, while uniqueness depends on the structure of the strongly connected components (sinks).   Beyond their theoretical significance, these results hold practical implications for dynamic and temporal networks, where the underlying topology evolves over time. In such contexts, the personalization vector itself may vary dynamically, raising the natural question of how to select teleportation distributions that reflect intrinsic structural properties of the network. For example, in web graphs, one could adopt a feedback mechanism in which teleportation probabilities at a given time step are determined by the PageRank distribution from the previous time step. The steady state of such a process, if it exists, corresponds precisely to the fixed point of the operator $PR_\lambda$. Hence, by adopting a functional operator perspective, this work establishes a rigorous analytical framework for PageRank in complex networks, elucidating both the mathematical structure of the operator and its potential for modeling adaptive and temporally evolving systems.

column9: Bridging contacts as epidemic bottlenecks in a city-scale mobility network
column11: Zambrano, Marlli*; Thampi, Ashish; Jarynowski, Andrzej ; Rincon, Alejandra; Schulz, Steven ; Belik, Vitaly
column12: marlli.a.zambrano.z@outlook.com*; ashish.thampi@netcheck.de; a.jarynowski@fu-berlin.de; alejandra.rincon@netcheck.de; steven.schulz@netcheck.de; vitaly.belik@fu-berlin.de
column13: Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) such as lockdowns and movement restrictions aim to reduce close-range en- counters that can transmit airborne infections. Yet contacts are not equally consequential, their epidemiological impact depends on where they sit in the larger network of human encounters. Here we ask whether a small set of structurally “bridging” contacts can act as transmission bottlenecks and therefore provide high-leverage targets for prevention. We analyze opt-in, anonymized geo-location data from 14 430 Berlin residents with persistent identifiers collected from June to August 2023. From individual trajectories, we reconstruct city-wide mobility and contact networks. A contact is defined by co-location of two individuals within 8 m for at least 2 min, yielding 12 048 observed contacts. Using Louvain community detection on the resulting encounter network, we identify loosely connected mesoscale units and quantify how community structure relates to urban boundaries. Visitation and mixing patterns still align with Berlin’s former east–west division and with current district borders (boundary alignment p << 0.01), indicating that historical and administrative structure continues to shape present-day encounter networks. Classifying edges by community membership shows a near- even split between within-community (6 379) and between-community (5 669) contacts. However, within-community contacts are about 5 x more likely to recur between the same partners, while between-community contacts are more tran- sient. To evaluate intervention leverage, we run SIR-type outbreak simulations and compare edge-removal strategies at a fixed “contact reduction budget.” Removing 30% of edges produces strongly strategy-dependent outcomes: selectively removing between-community edges reduces total infections far more than random deletion of the same size. Relative to the no-removal baseline, the attack rate drops to 0.33 ± 0.05 under targeted inter-community removal versus 0.58 ± 0.08 under random removal, corresponding to 43% fewer infections than random suppression for the same reduction in contacts. These results highlight bridging links between communities as disproportionate drivers of urban transmission and suggest that network-aware policies that selectively limit cross-community mixing could achieve substantial epidemic control with less disruption than uniform restrictions.

column9: Rising inequality and a 'power shift' from the core to a parasitic periphery are precursors of collapse in a model of evolving networks
column13: Understanding why collapses occur in complex systems is important for forecasting and response planning. Here, we study collapses in a mathematical model of an evolving directed graph of $S \gg 1$ nodes. In the model, the eigenvector centrality $X_i$ of node $i$ is considered to be the `strength' of the node. The network evolves one node at a time by replacing the weakest node by a randomly and sparsely connected node (having a connection probability $p$ with other nodes such that $pS < 1$) [1]. The model exhibits spontaneous growth, stasis and collapse wherein the number of nodes with a nonzero strength first grows from order unity to reach its maximum possible value, $S$, remains there for a certain time, and then suddenly drops by a significant fraction of $S$ in a single time step. Previous studies have identified proximate causes of collapse in the model [2–4]. In particular, they have shown that at a collapse, the network is `fragile' in the sense that the number of redundant positive feedback pathways in the largest strong component that is the core of the graph becomes small. However, the long-term dynamics that causes this fragility to arise remains unclear. Here, we compute the Gini coefficient (used as a measure of wealth inequality in economics) of the distribution of node strengths $X_i$ in the model as a function of time. We find that the inequality in node strengths rises as the network approaches collapse. Further, the average strength of periphery nodes (which are parasites in the sense that they do not feed back into the core that sustains them) becomes larger than the average strength of core nodes as a collapse is approached. We refer to this phenomenon as a `power shift' from the core to the periphery. Thus we identify rising inequality and power shift as two novel early warning signals of impending collapse in the model. We also find that a few periphery nodes that acquire a lot of strength are the source of rising inequality. These lessons from the model could be relevant for social systems.

column9: Randomized spectral node embeddings for graph kernel approximation
column11: de Bassompierre, Valentin*; Jacques, Laurent; Delvenne, Jean-Charles
column13: Node embeddings provide a powerful representation of networks by mapping graph vertices into low-dimensional Euclidean spaces while preserving structural information. Such embeddings are now central to a wide range of applications, including node classification, link prediction, community detection, and signal reconstruction. A common objective is to design embeddings whose inner products reflect meaningful notions of node similarity derived from the underlying graph structure. Signal processing on graphs and spectral graph theory offer a principled framework for constructing such embeddings. By exploiting the eigenspectrum of the graph Laplacian, spectral methods define embeddings through filtering operations that encode multi-scale structural information [1, 2]. These approaches connect naturally to classical tools in harmonic analysis, while remaining well adapted to irregular network domains. In this work, we focus on the problem of computing node embeddings with explicit kernel approximation guarantees. Graph kernels—defined as functions of the graph Laplacian provide a flexible and theoretically grounded way to measure node similarity, but their direct computation is often prohibitively expensive for large networks. Inspired by random feature methods for kernel approximation in Euclidean spaces, we introduce randomized spectral embeddings on graphs whose dot products yield low-rank approximations of Laplacian-based graph kernels. In practice, we implement this using the efficient graph wavelet formalism [3] applied to a series of random signals. We present theoretical and empirical results demonstrating that our embeddings achieve more accurate kernel approximations than existing methods [4], particularly when the target kernel is localized in the spectral domain. Moreover, we highlight connections between our approach and randomized SVD, a well-established algorithm in numerical linear algebra. These findings underscore the advantages of randomized spectral constructions for scalable and principled graph representation learning.

column9: Topological Deep Learning for Behavioral Classification of Satellite Networks
column13: Groups of satellites are often networked together in the form of constellations. Within a constellation, satellites configure themselves into complementary orbits for a variety of reasons, such as maximizing visibility of their targets such as ships and other objects, and can be said to maintain baseline shape(s). Other reasons for constellation configuration may include when new satellites are launched, which will cause the constellation to adapt its shape to make room for a new member. There are a variety of such behaviors that are reflected in the changing shapes of a constellation. We can analyze this idea of changing network shape via topological tools such as persistent homology. In persistent homology, we seek to analyze the topology of a network or point cloud by keeping track of the number of topological features such as connected components and loops (or voids) that are present, and the extent of their duration or persistence throughout different spatial scales of the global network structure. These topological features are typically captured within a specific persistent homology representation called a barcode plot. As such, persistent homology functions as a useful way of capturing the underlying behavioral changes of a constellation of satellites as distilled through its topological features captured by a barcode plot.  While the application of these methods towards analyzing satellite constellation behavior is still relatively new, these methods still fall under the traditional approach of topological data analysis. We go a step further and develop an approach where we use these persistent homology representations such as barcode plots as topological embeddings.  These topological embeddings can then be further used as input into a neural network architecture for topological deep learning for purposes such as inference and classification of network behavior. Overall, we explore the application of persistent homology tools towards the classification of satellite constellation behavior, our set of developed topological methods, and review our data analysis pipeline for topological deep learning on networks.

column9: The Role of Homophily in Misperception on Social Networks
column13: Misperception refers to the mismatch between individuals’ beliefs about a population-level opinion and the true level of that opinion. An example arises in the context of climate change. Despite climate change being a polarizing issue in the United States, many climate change mitigation policies enjoy support from large public majorities. However, most Americans substantially underestimate this public support, often by 20 percentage points or more. Such widespread misperception may influence legislative outcomes. Motivated by this, we consider a mathematical expression for misperception as a network-based quantity. We examine how homophily, the tendency of individuals to interact with like-minded others, influences the extent of misperception that can arise. We consider an undirected network of $n$ individuals, $ G = (V,E)$, where nodes are partitioned into supporters of an opinion, $S \subset V $, and opponents of an opinion, $ O = V \setminus S $ . The probability of an edge between two individuals depends only on whether they belong to the same group or to different groups, yielding a stochastic block model representation of interaction.   Using graphon theory and concentration inequalities, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of misperception as the network size grows. We first consider a continuum of agents interacting according to a graphon representation of a stochastic block model and define the corresponding continuum misperception score. We then show that, with probability one, the misperception score of the finite network converges to its continuum counterpart as the number of agents increases. This framework allows us to derive explicit expressions for overall misperception, as well as for group-specific misperception, thereby isolating the role of homophily in generating misperception in large networks with community structure. Notably, overall misperception is highest when supporter homophily is low and opponent homophily is high.

column9: Unveiling the main forces of social polarization in multipolar systems
column11: Benito, Rosa*;  Martín-Gutiérrez, Samuel; Borondo, Javier; Losada, Juan Carlos
column13: Social polarization is a growing concern worldwide, as it strains social relations, erodes trust in institutions, and thus hurts democratic societies. Polarization has been traditionally studied in binary conflicts where two groups support opposite ideas. However, in many social systems, such as multi-party democracies, political conflicts involve multiple dissenting factions. Despite the prevalence of multipolar systems, there is still a lack of suitable analytical tools to study their polarization patterns. In this presentation, we introduce new polarization metrics for multidimensional scenarios and develop a methodology that extracts the ideological structure of multipolar contexts from social networks. We propose the trace of the covariance matrix (the total variation) of the multipolar opinion distribution as a measure of global polarization, and its eigendecomposition to identify the directions of maximum polarization. Instead of using a pre-conceived opinion space (conservative vs progressive, liberal vs authoritarian, etc.), our framework reveals the natural ideological axes of the system. We apply our methodology to tripolar, quadripolar and pentapolar real-world democratic processes, finding non-trivial ideological structures with clear connections to the underlying social context that unveil the main forces leading to political polarization. Our framework opens new avenues for understanding multilateral social tensions and facing the challenges of polarization in a unified way. References 1.Morales AJ, Borondo J, Losada JC, Benito RM. column9: Diffusion on Hierarchical Multilayer Networks
column13: In many contexts, especially biomedical research, the networks used to represent real-world systems are complex. Nodes and edges often differ from one another by the categories of one or more grouping variables (e.g., molecular type, interaction type, or timepoint). Multilayer networks offer a convenient way to incorporate this discrete node- or edge-level information by distinguishing sets of nodes and edges by grouping variables, each of which contains one or more categories that stratify the nodes and edges into distinct sets called layers. The grouping variables and their corresponding categories may have a hierarchical relation to each other. This is evident in biology where, for example, proteins are nested within cells nested within tissue. For diffusion processes on multilayer networks where layers are related hierarchically (Figure 1), the hierarchical structure should inform diffusion dynamics. This serves as motivation for the present work, which is a method for creating a transition matrix from a hierarchical multilayer network, such that transition probabilities between layers located closer together in the hierarchy offer less resistance. Furthermore, the relative strengths of transition probabilities between layers can be controlled at each level of the hierarchy by parameters associated with nodes of the hierarchy. We represent the categories of grouping variables as a hierarchy whose leaves correspond to layers, and define inter-layer transition weights by multiplicatively applying category- and level-specific scaling parameters along the path connecting two layers in this hierarchy, so that layers that diverge higher incur greater attenuation. This transition matrix can be used in downstream diffusion processes such as random walks. In the context of biomedical research, this hierarchical multilayer framework allows for the integration of data from multi-omic, multi-tissue, and longitudinal experiments into a single connected network, wherein inter-layer relationships and diffusion dynamics are governed by the network hierarchy that is set by the user to be most appropriate for the experimental design. This enables a wide range of network diffusion methods to be applied to complex, multi-modal experiments, thus facilitating a holistic, systems-level approach to biomedical research.

column9: Percolation and Criticality in Hyperuniform Networks
column11: Wang, Yongyi*; Kim, Jaeuk; Jiao, Yang; Stuhl, Izabella; Torquato, Salvatore; Albert, Reka
column12: ypw5466@psu.edu*; phy000.kim@gmail.com; yjiao13@asu.edu; ius68@psu.edu; torquato@electron.princeton.edu; rza1@psu.edu
column13: Hyperuniform many-particle systems, which encompass crystals, quasicrystals and certain exotic disordered systems, exhibit an anomalous suppression of density fluctuations on macroscopic length scales relative to those of conventional disordered systems [1]. These systems are well studied in Euclidean space. We propose that networks derived from hyperuniform point configurations show distinctive critical behaviors. In this study, we construct Delaunay triangulation networks of 2D point configurations, in which the points become the vertices and the edges are weighted by Euclidean distance.   We investigate the percolation behaviors of networks derived from disordered stealthy hyperuniform systems, which are an important subclass that exhibits a tunable degree of local order via the parameter $\chi$ [2]. We compare them with those constructed from Poisson (uncorrelated) point configurations. We investigate a distance-based bond percolation process in which shorter edges in the triangulation network are assigned higher occupation probabilities according to a tuning parameter $z$.   We estimate the percolation thresholds $z_c$ and critical exponents of the networks via finite-size scaling and the Newman–Ziff Monte Carlo algorithm. We find that stealthy hyperuniform networks exhibit lower percolation thresholds than Poisson networks. The higher the value of $\chi$, the lower the percolation threshold, suggesting enhanced connectivity and transport efficiency in networks with hyperuniform spatial embeddings, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:configs}. Moreover, we show that stealthy hyperuniform systems with large $\chi$ belong to the lattice universality class, while the critical exponents of the Poisson and low-$\chi$ systems exhibit consistent shifts.   Recent attempts have illustrated the challenges of classifying statistically homogeneous disordered planar networks using classical network centrality measures [3]. Our distance-based percolation method is able to identify and distinguish these networks with suppressed density fluctuations through their emergent clustering properties.  [1] S. Torquato and F. H. Stillinger, “Local density fluctuations, hyperuniformity, and order metrics,” Phys. Rev. E, vol. 68, no. 4, p. 041113, 2003.  [2] S. Torquato, “Hyperuniform states of matter,” Phys. Rep., vol. 745, pp. 1–95, 2018.  [3] E. Newby, W. Shi, Y. Jiao, S. Torquato and R. Albert, "From point patterns to networks: to what extent does the Delaunay triangulation reproduce key spatial and density information?" Journal of Complex Networks, vol. 13, no. 6, 2025.

column9: Time-varying differential network analysis from tumor-educated platelet transcriptome to capture mechanisms of tumor progression
column11: Vessi, Santiago; Rughetti, Aurelia; Filetti, Marco; Farina, Lorenzo; Petti, Manuela*
column13: Differential network analysis has been designed to highlight network changes between conditions: in network biology, this approach can capture tissue-selective processes and identify critical signaling pathways altered during tumor transformation and progression [1]. In oncology, the most appropriate tumor surveillance strategy remains an unsolved issue. Indeed, the typical approach (based on solid biopsies and resource-demanding follow-up programs) has limitations in terms of invasiveness, time resolution and accessibility of molecular data. To date, blood-based liquid biopsies represent a promising source of biomarkers to detect and monitor cancer without invasive procedures. The latest developments in isolating and characterizing various elements in blood, including tumor-educated platelet (TEP) RNA, make it possible to identify cancer-specific genomic and transcriptomic abnormalities in blood. In particular, TEPs are circulating blood cells with a distinct tumor-driven phenotype and act as carriers and protectors of metastases. Some recent studies have shown that the TEPs transcriptome can be used for cancer diagnosis [2]. However, these works are only based on differential expression analysis.  The objective of this work is to propose Differential Network Analysis (DNA) to study longitudinal TEPs transcriptomic data. In particular, we applied the Time-varying DNA (tDNA, [3]) to investigate gene network rewiring during glioblastoma (GBM) progression.  We downloaded mRNA sequencing data of TEPs from the GEO database under accession number 156902 [4] and we selected GBM samples. Longitudinal data were available for 55 patients, although for a subset of 13 patients a complete set of measurements from time 0 to time 3 was available. Given the K=4 time points, the tDNA approach jointly estimated K-1=3 differential networks ∆, enabling the identification of both consistent and time-specific rewiring patterns driven by key genes. These genes were classified as either common (shared across time points) or time-specific critical nodes. Across the three obtained differential networks, we identified 14 common and 134, 80, and 72 time-specific key genes for ∆_(0-1), ∆_(1-2) and ∆_(2-3), respectively. KEGG enrichment analysis of the identified nodes revealed convergence on immune and inflammatory signaling pathways, including IL-17 signaling (adj-p=0.005), Toll-like receptor signaling (adj-p=0.008), and Herpes simplex virus 1 infection (adj-p=0.01), largely driven by time-specific genes from each differential network. These findings highlight processes associated with tumor progression and immune modulation in glioblastoma [5]. To validate the findings obtained with tDNA, we compared them with DiffCorr approach [6], developed to compare pairs of experimental conditions. This alternative method identified 101, 120, and 102 critical nodes in the three differential networks, selected by intersecting the top 10% of genes ranked by degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality. Seventy-one genes overlapped with those identified by tDNA, including 4 classified as common hubs. However, KEGG enrichment analysis did not highlight significant pathways. In conclusion, these results demonstrate that critical nodes identified in time-varying differential networks obtained from longitudinal TEPs transcriptomic data can detect molecular mechanisms of disease progression with potential clinical impact in tumor monitoring.
