column9: Evidence of Gender-based Network Biases in Respondent-driven Sampling Data
column13: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is a network-based method for studying hidden populations, such as people who inject drugs (PWID) (Heckathorn, 1997; Gile et al., 2010). Statistical inference using RDS relies on modeling recruitment as a random walk on the network, assuming participants accurately report their network composition and recruit peers approximately at random (Heckathorn, 1997; Volz and Heckathorn, 2008). In practice, reported networks may not fully reflect the true network structure, and some subgroups may face barriers to participation, potentially biasing statistical inference. Using a uniquely rich RDS dataset (Akiyama et al., 2025) spanning multiple sites and several types of network data, we investigate gender differences in network structure, reporting, and participation, and assess potential biases impacting inference. We analyze RDS data from 3,152 PWID across 17 sites in Kenya, collected as an extension of the TLC-IDU study (NCT01557998), focusing on the reported gender composition of participants’ social networks. Our analysis evaluates whether the observed proportion of women in the sample is consistent with expectations of random recruitment and the observed gender–degree structure of the sample. We further compare gender differences in reported 30-day networks, close contact data, and observed network ties. Population estimates were calculated using standard RDS methods (Volz and Heckathorn, 2008), and network simulation tests were used to assess discrepancies in participation and reporting. Results indicate that participants report more women in their networks than expected, suggesting potential over-reporting or under-participation of women. Across multiple sites, results were more nuanced, but indicate that women report more women in their 30-day networks, close contacts, and observed ties compared to men. These discrepancies highlight challenges in creating valid inferences from reported social network data and provide insight into the complexity of designing targeted interventions for PWID.

column9: Community-aware hyperbolic embeddings: methodology and application on the FlyWire FAFB dataset
column13: Hyperbolic geometry offers a superior latent space for embedding hierarchical complex networks, yet existing methods frequently overlook the utility of efficient community detection methods. We present CLOVE (Cluster Level Optimized Vertex Embedding), a recently published approach that maps networks to the hyperbolic disk by using community structure to dictate angular sectors —optimized via a Traveling Salesman Problem heuristic. We apply this framework to the massive FlyWire Drosophila FAFB connectome, benchmarking the results against ground-truth physical coordinates. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating community priors generates resource-efficient embeddings that successfully capture the topological organization of large-scale biological neural networks.

column9: Community detection and Higher-order Link Prediction
column13: Community detection problem, which intuitively represents decomposition of a network into distinct, potentially overlapping modules, still stays without a precise definition and represents one of the main research fields in the world of complex networks. Community detection algorithms use as input data, graphs representing networks, which are often not complete. Networks are evolving over the time, and it is in our best interest to be able to predict future links. Good example for it would be epidemics spreading, where having this type of knowledge, could help us save lives. Standard approach would be to look at the dyadic nature of links, since that is the view that graph framework offers to us and try to guess future edges. Being part of a large system, means as well multiple interactions, which this link paradigm doesn't present clearly. The idea of this paper to use higher-order link prediction to get robust results concerning community detection problem.

column9: The Impact of Network Structure and Prior Assumptions on Network Reconstructability
column11: Glover, Cory*; Weis, Erik; Kumar, Sagar; Ehlert, Joey; Klein, Brennan
column13: Many real-world systems from biology to financial markets are governed by complex networks of interactions where the network structures are either directly unobservable or must be inferred from data [1]. Often, researchers perform this network reconstruction task by using time series recordings of node-level dynamics in the system.   When reconstructing a network from N node-level time series, there are O(N^2) possible edges to infer. With so many possible edges, any practical network reconstruction method requires regularization to avoid overfitting and yield acceptable results [2]. Regularization, however, can impose structural preferences, producing biases in the network reconstruction. Despite the ubiquity of network reconstruction, these induced structural biases are rarely characterized [3,4].  While there are many techniques for reconstructing networks from time series data, we focus on a nonparametric Bayesian method based on the minimum description length [3]. We use this approach due to its: 1) clear and explicit statistical biases that can be readily interpreted, 2) lack of hyperparameters, the values of which are generally unknown in practical settings, 3) broad applications for a large class of networks, and 4) asymptotic recoverability of the true data-generating model, which is contained within the model class. This last condition ensures that if we record node states for an infinite number of time steps, we are guaranteed to recover the true network exactly, so long as the dynamical process satisfies certain properties [2]. On the contrary, in the case of limited data, our reconstruction will be more heavily influenced by the model’s prior assumptions.  In this work, we simulate Ising model dynamics on a range of synthetic networks, and we investigate the following: given a particular choice of statistical bias, how does reconstruction error vary with the class of network in question? While such questions have been considered in the case where network properties are directly conditioned on the prior [3,4], we instead focus on the case when no network statistics are known a priori, which is a realistic scenario in many practical applications with real data. We find that in the low data regime: 1) dense networks are systematically reconstructed as more sparse (Fig. 1a), 2) networks with high clustering are not reconstructed as such (Fig. 1b), and 3) networks with heterogeneous degree are harder to recover (Fig. 1c). This last finding contrasts with recent work [3], highlighting the utility (and perhaps fragility) of strong assumptions in improving reconstruction accuracy. Overall, our results suggest that, in scenarios with limited data, even well-motivated nonparametric priors may not provide sufficiently strong inductive biases to recover the corrected network.  [1] Oliver M Cliff et al. Unifying pairwise interactions in complex dynamics. Nature Computational Science (2023). [2] Charles Murphy et al. Duality between predictability and reconstructability in complex systems. Nature Communications (2024). [3] Tiago P Peixoto. Network reconstruction via the minimum description length principle. Physical Review X (2025). [4] Jia-Jie Qin and Gang Yan. High Reconstructability of Degree-Heterogeneous Networks. Physical Review Letters (2025).

column9: The Hidden Organization of Online Communities: Reddit through the Lens of Stochastic Block Models and Neural Embeddings
column13: Over the past two decades, online platforms have staged major and challenging events, including the spread of (mis)information, the amplification of unrepresentative voices, toxic public discourse, and coordinated collective action. The exposure and exchange networks they enable provide the structural conditions through which social friction and change emerge. Understanding these networks is therefore crucial for explaining how collective dynamics allow the propagation of news, behavior cascades, norms are enforced, and the coordination of collective action efforts. However, uncovering community structure from observed behavior depends critically on the computational tools employed, which can yield markedly different representations and thus constrain our theories of online collective dynamics. Here, we examine these differences by comparing higher-order communities identified using neural embeddings (NEs) and stochastic block models (SBMs) applied to 13 years of Reddit data from the Pushshift API, comprising approximately 5B comments and 3M users.  Our network-based approach reveals a more complex structure of political discussion on Reddit than that identified by previous work using NE representations. Using different SBM configurations, both fixing the number of communities to 30 and inferring it from the data, we find that the traditional “Political” cluster breaks down into 18 and 112 communities, respectively, while absorbing thousands of additional subreddits and thereby losing thematic coherence. Finally, applying a Hierarchical SBM (hSBM) uncovers the intrinsic nestedness of those communities of interest: it iteratively performs community inference and groups the communities present at lower levels into larger blocks as we move up in the hierarchy. This hierarchical approach uncovers self-organization across multiple resolution levels and identifies information corridors through which content moves as users cross-post across communities. Notably, it shows that some non-political subreddits occupy structural positions equivalent to political communities, highlighting organizational dynamics and generative mechanisms that are concealed in neural embedding representations.  Overall, we show that network-based methods reveal richer and more nuanced patterns of online political structure than previously identified, underscoring the importance of methodological choices in studies of social media networks.

column9: A continuum limit for dense spatial networks
column13: Many physical systems---such as optical waveguide lattices and dense neuronal or vascular networks---can be modeled by metric graphs, where slender ``wires'' (edges) support wave or diffusion equations subject to Kirchhoff boundary conditions at the nodes. We propose a continuum-limit framework which replaces edgewise differential equations with a coarse-grained partial differential equation (PDE) defined on the continuous space occupied by the network. The derivation naturally introduces an edge-conductivity tensor, an edge-capacity function, and a vertex number density to encode how each microscopic patch of the graph contributes to the macroscopic phenomena. These results have interesting similarities and differences with the Riemannian Laplace-Beltrami operator. We calculate all macroscopic parameters from first principles via a systematic discrete-to-continuous local homogenization, finding an anomalous effective embedding dimension resulting from a homogenized diffusivity. Numerical examples---including periodic lattices, random graphs, and quasiperiodic monotiles---demonstrate that each finite model converges to its corresponding PDE (posed on different manifolds like tori, disks, and spheres) in the limit of increasing vertex density. These high-density networks encode emergent material and functional properties. They reflect the ability of many real-world, space-filling networks to function simultaneously at multiple scales using the continuum as a feature.

column9: Saturation Phenomena in Social Media Information Diffusion
column11: Losada, Juan Carlos; Benito, Rosa*; Martínez-Atienza , Julia
column13: In online social networks, the dynamics of information spread are shaped by both individual behaviors and cognitive constraints. A key limiting factor in this diffusion is saturation effect, where users are exposed to more content than they can process, reducing their probability of further propagation. This work builds on recent empirical studies on Twitter to quantify the impact of saturation on retweet behavior. We propose a predictive model in which the probability that a user retweets decays with their information load, which is proportional to their number of followers. We analyze three case studies, global climate protests, national elections in Spain, and 2020 US elections, and simulate diffusion dynamics using real follower networks. In addition, we explore the temporal dimension of these cascades, measuring the evolution of spreading activity in time. Our results show that saturation-induced inattention significantly alters network-wide information propagation and shapes the temporal profile of message virality.

column9: Bridging Simple and Complex Contagions in Belief Dynamics: A Voter Model Extension
column11: Franco, João*; Robinette, Michael; Lipfert, Jackson; Lovato, Juniper; 	Hébert-Dufresne, Laurent
column13: The standard voter model of belief dynamics [1] – how beliefs form and evolve – assumes that individuals consistently express their internal beliefs and that these beliefs can change from one period to another. However, social norms and conformity pressures often lead individuals to either withhold beliefs or express beliefs that are contrary to their own [2], while internally held beliefs may exhibit inertia due to psychological mechanisms such as social hysteresis.   Our extension of the voter model (Figure 1 (a)) distinguishes between expressed beliefs, following simple contagion dynamics, and internal beliefs, that update through complex contagion mechanisms. Individuals hold binary beliefs on a given topic (a = “Against,” f = “in Favour”) but may express the opposite (af = holding “Against” but expressing “In Favour”). Expressed beliefs update through simple contagion based on the beliefs expressed by neighbors in the previous period, with contagion strength mediated by alignment with one’s internal belief (c when aligned and c′ when misaligned), reflecting the potential burden of expressing beliefs contrary to those internally held. Internal beliefs update based on neighbors’ expressed beliefs but follow a q-voter model, capturing complex contagion dynamics and belief inertia.  Mean-field approximations reveal that when individuals face higher contagion pressure to express beliefs contrary to their internal ones (c′ > c), the symmetry typical of voter models breaks down, enabling minority beliefs to persist at higher proportions than their initial frequency in the long term (Figure 1 (b)). These effects are robust across a range of initial conditions. Future work will explore how network structure and belief withholding shape the interplay between simple and complex contagion in real-world contexts.

column9: Modeling Varying Aggregations of Social Networks with Applications to Wealth Dynamics
column11: Weltz, Justin*; Aguiar, Izabel; Redhead, Daniel
column13: Relationships often influence how people accumulate and maintain wealth. Consequently, social  and economic networks capture aggregated notions of interconnected welfare. Data on these networks are primarily collected by querying individuals on their ties to other individuals. However, relationships that affect wealth often involve aggregates of individuals because resources are commonly shared among household members. We offer new statistical methodology that bridges the gap between individual level network data and the reality of wealth dynamics.

column9: Time Series Analysis of Global Earthquakes From Statistical Studies of Complex Networks of Interactions
column13: Abstract: Earthquakes are one the most prominent natural phenomena that can be classified as complex systems. They are inherently unpredictable and potentially destructive, often resulting in significant human and economic losses.   In this study, we obtained data from the World Catalog of Earthquakes of the Advanced National Seismic System (ANSS), which comprise seismic events recorded between 2000 and 2024. The records were classified into shallow earthquakes (i.e., events with depths up to 70 km) and deep earthquakes (i.e., events occurring at depths greater than 70 km). Both sets show good agreement with the Gutenberg–Richter law for minimum magnitudes of 4.5 and 5.1, respectively. The analyzed sample consists of 137,018 shallow events and 5,787 deep events.  First, following the approach in [1] but applied on a global scale, we defined a correlation metric n_ij, which represents the expected number of events between two sequential natural seismic events i and j, with magnitudes within the interval delta m around m_i (the magnitude of event i), occurring within a distance l and separated by a time interval t. This quantity is given by n_ij  = C* t* l^d_f*delta m*10^(-b*m_i), where C is a constant reflecting the regional seismicity. Following this definition, the correlation c_ij between any two earthquakes i and j is inversely proportional to n_ij and is given by c_ij = 1/ n_ij. Furthermore, the distribution of the correlation metric was observed to follow a scale-free behavior.  Building on the earthquake sequence, we constructed two distinct correlation-based networks: one for shallow and one for deep events. Each new earthquake j forms a directed link to a single preceding event, its extremal predecessor i* (the one that maximizes the correlation coefficient c_ij or, equivalently, minimizes the metric n_ij). The weight of this link is defined as n_j*. Low values of n_j* indicate a strong spatio-temporal correlation between the predecessor i* and the target event j, while high values correspond to weaker links, implying that no preceding event was sufficiently significant or proximal to form a meaningful connection with j.   From this extremal events network, we then derived a geographic network where edges are established between the square cells of size L = 20 km representing the epicenters of connected events. Each cell is assigned based on the latitude phi_E and longitude lambda_E of its epicenter, normalized relative to a reference point at phi_0 = 0 and lambda_0 = 0 for simplicity.   Subsequently, we estimated network measures, which revealed scale-free behaviors, thereby reinforcing the universality of the patterns observed in seismic systems. These findings are consistent with the view that seismological events are complex systems, as they exhibit a range of distinctive properties, including long-range spatiotemporal correlations, power-law distributions, critical behavior, and the emergence of nonlinear patterns.  [1] BAIESI, M., PACZUSKI, M., 2004, “Scale-free networks of earthquakes and aftershocks”, Physical Review E—Statistical, Nonlinear, and Soft Matter Physics, v. 69, n. 6, pp. 066106.

column9: Spatial barriers reshape residents’ emotional experiences in urban China
column13: Emotion is a fundamental human physiological process with well-documented associations across a spectrum of life outcomes—from economic success and career advancement to physical health and longevity. Urban spatial structures profoundly shape residents' emotional experiences in their daily movements. While behavioral barriers—visible obstacles like highways and rivers, as well as invisible ones rooted in socioeconomic segregation and uneven amenity access—have been documented[1], how they relate to emotional experiences remains under-explored. This study investigates whether behavioral barriers shape residents' emotional expressions and how economic conditions, infrastructure availability, and urban density moderate this relationship across cities of different scales and regions. We analyzed 75 million geo-tagged social media posts (Weibo, Chinese version of Twitter) from a cleaned dataset of over 2 million residents' check-ins and textual expressions at POI (Point of Interest) level across 60 Chinese cities. This integrated dataset uniquely enables examination of emotional patterns at both neighborhood and inter-regional scales. Our approach combines: (1) mobility neural embeddings to identify behavioral barriers from observed movement patterns, capturing both visible and invisible constraints that traditional geographic analysis misses[1]; (2) sentiment analysis to quantify emotional divergence; and (3) multivariate regression to examine barrier-emotion relationships across city types. Overall, this study integrates emotional wellbeing, place, and human mobility to reveal how spatial segregation shapes not just physical movement but also residents' psychological experiences[2] and wellbeing[3]. By providing fine-grained spatial evidence, we offer actionable insights for designing healthier urban environments.

column9: Moral Signaling and Network Centrality in Online Opioid Recovery Communities
column13: Online communities can play an important role in supporting recovery from opioid use disorder (OUD), particularly for people who lack access to supportive offline networks. While prior work has examined the content of recovery-related discourse, less is known about how moral language is structured within networks of interaction and how it relates to actor prominence and engagement. We study four large Reddit communities focused on OUD recovery and harm reduction, modeling each community as a directed interaction network in which nodes represent authors and edges represent reply relationships.  Using supervised large language models trained to detect ten moral foundations proposed in Moral Foundations Theory (Care, Harm, Fairness, Cheating, Authority, Subversion, Loyalty, Betrayal, Purity, and Degradation), we annotate over half a million posts and comments with moral attributes and enrich network edges with the moral content expressed in interactions. We analyze how moral signaling varies across communities with different recovery philosophies, how moral content relates to engagement, and how it is distributed among central versus peripheral actors.  Across all communities, moral language is common within interaction networks. Distinct moral profiles emerge at the community level, reflecting differing norms and treatment orientations. Central actors, those with both high indegree and outdegree, are are more likely to be morally expressive than less connected participants and engage not only in virtue-oriented discourse (e.g., Care), but also in vice-oriented moral language (Degradation, Cheating) often associated with stigma and shame. Rather than suppressing such discourse, central actors may express negative morality as part of community norm negotiation and as a way of engaging with shared experiences of stigmatizing and dehumanizing moral judgments.  These findings demonstrate how moral sentiment functions as a relational signal within recovery networks and highlight the value of integrating moral content with network analysis to understand community dynamics. More broadly, the work illustrates how moral signaling and network position jointly shape participation and engagement in online support communities.

column9: Knowledge Graph-Based Analysis of Curriculum-Industry Alignment: A Case Study
column11: Yang, Bonan; Banu, Syeda Zunehra; Ercal, Gunes*
column13: This study proposes a knowledge graph-based framework to analyze curriculum-industry alignment. Using a U.S. university's Computer Science program as a case study, we construct a three-layer heterogeneous knowledge graph linking courses, skills, and jobs. Results show that the curriculum covers programming and database skills well, with strong foundations in algorithms, theory, and AI. However, industrial-level skills such as cloud platforms and DevOps are absent, and emerging roles have lower accessibility than traditional ones. The framework is generalizable to other disciplines and institutions.

column9: GRNage: An epigenetic clock based on gene regulatory network features
column11: Shutta, Katherine*; Wu, Helena; DeMeo, Dawn; Quackenbush, John
column13: Epigenetic clocks are models that measure biological aging. The divergence of biological age from chronological age is a hallmark of many complex diseases, including cancer. Epigenetic clocks are typically trained to select a set of DNA methylation loci (CpGs) that are predictive of chronological age or other aging phenotypes in a healthy cohort. A limitation of this approach is the lack of interpretability of the selected model components.  Sets of CpGs that are predictive of the training outcome may not directly participate in underlying biological mechanisms that are drivers of aging or disease progression.  Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are bipartite graphs connecting transcription factors (TFs) to the genes that they regulate. GRNs encode functional regulatory processes within a network structure. We hypothesized that an aging clock based on GRN network features could provide interpretable functional insight into dysregulated biological aging in cancer. To this end, we introduce GRNage, the first gene regulatory network-based aging clock. GRNage models biological age as a linear combination of GRN properties (TF out-degree; target gene in-degree). The input to GRNage is a GRN estimated with the PANDA algorithm ; the output is an estimated biological age (see Figure).  GRNage is trained to select a set of TFs and genes whose degrees are predictive of epigenetic age acceleration as estimated by the Horvath epigenetic clock As gene regulatory processes have been demonstrated to be highly tissue-specific  , GRNage is also tissue-specific. Here, we present a skin-based GRNage clock trained in 451 subcutaneous melanoma (SKCM) samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).  We tested the relevance of SKCM GRNage in biological context by calculating GRNage of four different tumor metastasis classifications.  In the training dataset, the mean GRNage was significantly higher in the regional metastases than the primary tumor (p=0.048 for regional cutaneous/subcutaneous metastases vs. primary, p=0.017 for lymph node metastases vs. primary), while no significant difference was observed between GRNage of the primary tumor and the distant metastasis (p=0.82 for distant vs. primary). In the testing dataset, this pattern was preserved between the primary tumor and regional cutaneous/subcutaneous metastases (p=0.046) GRNage represents a new network-based paradigm in aging research: patterns of epigenetic age can be captured by changes in gene regulatory networks. Importantly, GRNage does not require DNA methylation data, but can be built using only transcriptomic data, which are more widely available. Thus, GRNage opens potential for widespread analysis of epigenetic aging patterns in a range of previously published transcriptomic datasets. Future analyses of the biological context of the features driving GRNage may reveal novel changes in gene regulation associated with accelerated aging in cancer and complex diseases.

column9: Credibility Shapes Sentiment Diffusion in Cryptocurrency Discourse Networks
column13: Online discussions surrounding cryptocurrencies exhibit extreme volatility, rapid attention shifts, and a heterogeneous population of actors ranging from institutional experts to anonymous and automated accounts. While prior work has linked aggregate online sentiment to market dynamics, less is known about how the \emph{credibility} of actors conditions the propagation, amplification, and persistence of sentiment within these networks.  Here we study large-scale cryptocurrency discourse networks constructed from social media interactions, including mentions, replies, and reposts. Nodes represent accounts and directed edges encode information flow. Each actor is assigned a continuous credibility score derived from structural position, interaction stability, and behavioral signals. Message-level sentiment is aggregated to the actor level, enabling a joint analysis of network topology, credibility, and expressed sentiment.  We find that sentiment diffusion is strongly stratified by credibility. High-credibility actors occupy central positions in the interaction backbone and disproportionately shape sentiment flows, even after controlling for activity volume. A credibility mixing analysis reveals pronounced assortativity, with high-credibility actors preferentially interacting with one another while serving as dominant sources of sentiment to lower-credibility regions of the network. Event-aligned analyses around major market-relevant shocks further show that high-credibility actors exhibit earlier, more coherent sentiment shifts, consistent with a leading role in narrative formation rather than reactive participation.  Together, these results demonstrate that credibility is a critical and underexplored dimension governing sentiment dynamics in crypto-related communication networks. Beyond cryptocurrency markets, our framework provides a generalizable approach for studying how trust, reputation, and perceived authority shape diffusion processes in complex socio-technical systems.

column9: A Network of Warring States: Antagonism and the Emergence of Stability in Medieval Japan
column11: Ghasemian, Amir*; Shirado, Hirokazu; Christakis, Nicholas
column13: Negative relationships significantly influence the structure and dynamics of social networks, even possibly serving a role in stabilizing an otherwise unstable system across time. These connections make a significant contribution to conflict management, facilitate the diffusion of information, and alleviate ideological polarization; however, their role in the stabilization of human social networks remains somewhat ambiguous. We explore this idea by analyzing unique historical data from the Warring States period of medieval Japan, where 2,222 clans engaged in 2,889 battles over 133 years. Our network analysis reveals a temporal shift in the topological location of battles and warring actors. Specifically, we delineate a fragmentation phase (1467–1566), characterized by instability and decentralized conflict, followed by a unification phase (1566–1600), distinguished by centralized conflict. By extending classical balance theory to state-like actors, these findings provide insights into the role of negative ties in long-term social destabilization and stabilization cycles.

column9: The Triple Lock: Geometric Obstructions to Partial Information Decomposition
column13: Synergy—information emergent in the whole but invisible to the parts—is a defining signature of complex networks. While Partial Information Decomposition (PID) [1] formalizes this structure via a redundancy lattice, the field remains deadlocked by the lack of a canonical measure. A promising recent inquiry attempts to resolve this ambiguity through Riemannian Information Geometry, defining redundancy as the orthogonal projection of a joint distribution onto a split-independence submanifold [2, 4].  In this work, we prove a No-Go Theorem for Riemannian PID. We demonstrate that the pure Riemannian geometry of the probability simplex is mathematically insufficient to support a consistent decomposition. We identify three irreducible structural obstructions, termed the "Triple Lock":  Rank-Width Mismatch: The tangent space spanned by marginal constraints scales linearly with system size n, whereas the PID lattice scales super-exponentially (Dedekind numbers). We deduce that for n ≥ 3, the tangent bundle lacks sufficient rank to linearly encode the full combinatorial complexity of higher-order redundancies, creating an irreducible bottleneck for purely vector-based decompositions.  The Work Obstruction (Holonomy): Information measures must be state functions (path-independent). However, the non-vanishing curvature of the Fisher metric implies non-trivial holonomy. We show that integrating local informational updates (gradients of redundancy) is path-dependent; the computed value varies with the trajectory through distribution space, rendering the decomposition ill-defined without an auxiliary flat connection.  Möbius Sign Failure: Even effectively freezing the path, geometric projections (m-projections) onto split-independence submanifolds do not guarantee order-preservation on the lattice. This geometric misalignment can structurally force the creation of negative atoms (negative synergy) upon Möbius inversion, putting the Riemannian formulation in direct conflict with the non-negativity axiom of information.  These findings compel a fundamental re-evaluation of how we measure informational decompositional structures. For network scientists seeking to disentangle synergy from redundancy. Whether in neural connectomes or social hypergraphs, our results demonstrate that standard metric-based approaches are structurally flawed. We argue that a rigorous calculus of interaction must abandon purely Riemannian methods in favor of the dually flat affine geometry of the exponential family [3], or pivot to purely combinatorial foundations to consistently capture the rich lattice structure of multivariate dependencies.  References: [1] P. L. Williams and R. D. Beer, Nonnegative decomposition of multivariate information, arXiv:1004.2515 (2010). [2] X. Niu and C. J. Quinn, A Measure of Synergy, Redundancy, and Unique Information Using Information Geometry, Proc. IEEE ISIT (2019). [3] S. Amari, Information Geometry and Its Applications, Springer (2016). [4] J. W. Kay, A Partial Information Decomposition for Multivariate Gaussian Systems, Entropy 26(7) (2024).

column9: Structural Holes in the Bioconductor Dependency Network
column13: Dependency networks have been studied extensively in open-source ecosystems, but remain underexplored in scientific software [1,2]. We investigate structural holes [3] in Bioconductor, a curated repository of over 2,200 R packages for computational biology [4]. To do so, we make use of Bioconductor's hierarchical biocViews classification that maps software packages and biological subdomains (genomics, proteomics, single-cell analysis). Using BiocPkgTools [5], we construct the biocViews-level dependency network and compute brokerage metrics including Burt's network constraint and betweenness centrality. We identify categories of Bioconductor packages that suggest structural holes (e.g. Figure 1). We find that infrastructure categories of software (e.g. annotation packages) occupy high-brokerage positions, and bridge domain-specific biology clusters. Packages in bridging categories also show higher download volumes, as well as indicators of maintenance burden [6]. These findings are consistent with findings on brokerage costs in open-source networks. We also characterize categories of packages as being either net ``importers'' or ``exporters'' of software functionality [7], and find that genomics and single-cell analysis are strong exporters, and clinical and pathway domains are net importers. In short, our findings demonstrate that structural hole theory [8] can be useful to understand how computational tools mediate knowledge exchange between scientific communities.

column9: Locality In Complex Networks and Dynamical Processes
column13: The ability to predict the dynamical behavior of network systems is a problem relevant to many technological, biological, and social systems. However, as the network size increases, these predictions come at increasing computational cost.  Off-diagonal matrix decay, as a generalization of matrix sparsity, has proven useful to approximate matrix computations through dimensionality reduction, with applications in linear algebra [1], condensed matter physics [2], and control theory [3]. Here, we extend the analysis to dynamical processes on networks by exploring the notion of network locality [3-4]. We show that locality is characterized by an information metric induced by the network’s coupling matrix, and that in localized networks, propagation of a disturbance is necessarily concentrated in induced information neighborhoods around the perturbed nodes. This allows us to develop a localized algorithm to approximate dynamical responses, which incurs computational costs orders of magnitude lower than traditional methods. Finally, we survey a large corpus of empirical networks to show that many networks across various disciplines are localized, showing that our results are widely applicable in practice.  [1] Curtain R. (2011). Riccati equations on noncommutative banach algebras. SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization, 49(6), 2542-2557. [2] Benzi, M., Boito, P., \& Razouk, N. (2013). Decay properties of spectral projectors with applications to electronic structure. SIAM Review, 55(1), 3-64.  [3] Duan, C., Nishikawa, T., \& Motter, A. E. (2022). Prevalence and scalable control of localized networks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 119(32), e2122566119. [4] Haber A., Molnar F., \& Motter A.E. (2024). Global network control from local information. Chaos, 24, 123166

column9: How Network Topology Links to Growth and Stagnation in Online Hate Communities
column11: Nefriana, Rr.*; Yan, Muheng; Hwa, Rebecca; Lin, Yu-Ru
column13: While online hate speech is frequently analyzed through content lenses, the structural architecture of extremist networks remains under-researched. This study investigates how these network properties link to future engagement patterns across distinct hate ideologies related to the Israel-Palestine conflict. We analyzed a ten year longitudinal dataset of Facebook activity by hate groups. Monthly networks were constructed where nodes represent unique groups and edges represent shared users (those posting in multiple groups). We employed negative binomial regression modeling to determine how group degree (inter-group connectivity), homophily index (ideological similarity), and the proportion of multi-group users predict next month engagement (likes, comments, and shares). Regression results demonstrate that group degree significantly and positively predicts future engagement for Anti-Semitic and Other-Hate groups, but remains non-significant for Islamophobic groups. Homophily negatively predicts engagement in Anti-Semitic groups, suggesting that insularity leads to activity stagnation. This provides a potential explanation for the distinct structural profiles revealed in our baseline analysis: while Islamophobic groups are highly homophilic, Anti-Semitic groups maintain a balanced structure, a configuration that mitigates the engagement penalties associated with high insularity. A high proportion of posts from multi-group users is associated with lower subsequent engagement across all categories, with the pattern most pronounced in Islamophobic silos. These findings suggest hate groups exhibit distinct survival patterns, calling for tailored interventions. Islamophobic groups are self-sustaining yet fragile to internal dilution; disrupting homophilic echoes, such as via nudges toward alternative perspectives, may be effective. Anti-Semitic groups are more networked and less insular, with a risk of backfire effects from hostile interactions; targeting bridging nodes might help contain their spread, though future research is needed to confirm this.

column9: Robust Community Detection in Signed Temporal Networks
column13: Many real-world relations can be represented by signed networks with positive and negative links \cite{tang2016survey}. For example, in social networks, signed networks can represent relations among online users where positive links indicate friendships, trust, and like, while negative links indicate foes, distrust, and dislike \cite{leskovec2010signed}. Similarly, in geopolitical and military intelligence networks, nodes may represent countries or military units, with positive edges corresponding to alliances or cooperative relationships and negative edges corresponding to adversarial or hostile relationships. An important task in the analysis of signed networks is to partition the network into cohesive subgraphs, i.e., communities. Motivated by social balance theory \cite{harary1953notion,davis1967clustering}, the community detection problem in signed networks reduces to finding antagonistic clusters such that entities within the same cluster have a positive relationship with each other and entities between different clusters have a negative relationship with each other.   While the different definitions of graph cut and modularity have been successfully adopted for signed graphs, they are all limited to single layer graphs where the nodes are connected to each other by a single, static edge. In many contemporary applications, this relatively simple structure cannot capture the diverse nature of the networks. For example, the relationships between people in a social network may change over time resulting in a signed temporal network. In this case, one is interested in both determining the community structure at each time point and tracking the changes across time.   In this paper, we define temporally smoothed quality functions for simultaneously detecting the community structure of signed temporal graphs and tracking the changes across time.  In particular, we introduce a robust community detection framework for signed temporal networks, where we first decompose the positive part of the observed adjacency matrix into low-rank and sparse components and then detect the community structure at each time point such that the balance of the signed network is preserved at each time point while ensuring temporal smoothness of the community structure across time. The resulting formulation is equivalent to a regularized robust principal component analysis of the observed adjacency matrix at each time point. The proposed approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real world networks.

column9: Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer to repurpose drugs for the treatment of Nipah virus infectious disease
column13: Nipah virus (NiV) is a bat-borne pathogen whose infection in humans causes disease with a very high observed mortality rate, with the NiV-M lineage (identified in Malaysia) having a case fatality of 39% while NiV-B lineage (identified in Bangladesh and India) reporting a much higher mortality range of 60% to 100% in different outbreaks. Since the identification of the first cases of NiV infection in humans in Malaysia in 1998, several outbreaks have occurred in South East Asia. Due to its high mortality rate and lack of effective therapies or vaccines, it is currently listed as a select biological agent by both the US Dept. of Health and Human Services and US Dept. of Agriculture. Therefore, it is crucial to develop treatments for care of infectious cases in order to reduce the health impacts and public health concerns. In this work we leverage a heterogeneous graph transformer model in order to repurpose drugs for the treatment of NiV infectious disease. By using the model in a heterogeneous Knowledge Graph (KG) we hope to harness different varied forms of interactions between different biological entities - such as interactions between drugs and gene/proteins, diseases and gene/proteins, diseases and effect/phenotype (symptoms), drugs and effect/phenotype, etc - in order to predict novel indications between already existing, approved drugs and the disease from NiV infection. This KG based drug repurposing capitalizes on the known heterogeneous interactions between relevant biological entities to overcome the time and costs associated with drug development. Our goal is the attention mechanism will extrapolate from newly-observed genes affected by the NiV infectious disease to perform link-prediction on the KG, by learning from the existing topology of relations in the KG and how these predict existing indications. Previous similar methods for drug repurposing by link-prediction on biological networks mostly relied on simplified homogeneous networks, e.g. similarity-matrix based collapses of heterogeneous data into homogeneous versions, thus missing some information. By utilizing an attention mechanism that is able to process a graph with different types of interactions, and between different types of nodes, our link-prediction model exploits the full breath of available information.

column9: Complex Networks Analysis in Mexican Nationalist Music
column13: This research introduces a methodological framework for music analysis from the perspective of complexity science. Musical scores are modeled as complex networks, wherein nodes represent pitches, and weighted edges denote their temporal succession. This formalism is applied to a corpus of four representative works from the late 19th century and the first half of the 20th century Mexican Musical Nationalism.  By calculating network metrics such as degree distribution, betweenness centrality, and modularity, the topological properties of the compositions are quantified. The analysis focuses on identifying structurally central nodes, which correspond to tonal centers or recurrent melodic motifs, and on community detection, which reveals the segmentation of the work into cohesive musical phrases or sections.  The results demonstrate that the analyzed works exhibit non-trivial network topologies, featuring small-world properties and a pronounced modular structure. These structural properties enable a quantitative characterization of the Mexican nationalist style, potentially distinguishing it from other musical genres. This approach not only provides a new tool for computational musicology and stylistic analysis but also lays the groundwork for exploring the cognitive correlations of musical structure.

column9: Posterior Inference of Network Growth Mechanism Mixtures
column13: Real-world networks are often shaped by a mixture of multiple growth mechanisms, yet inference is typically performed from a single observed snapshot with no access to growth trajectories. We address this challenge by formulating posterior inference over mixtures of network growth mechanisms directly from a network snapshot, treating the underlying growth process as latent. By marginalizing over possible growth explanations, we infer a posterior distribution over mechanism mixtures rather than selecting a single best-fitting model.  We visualize this posterior as an energy landscape over the simplex of mixture weights, revealing how uncertainty and trade-offs between mechanisms depend on the underlying generative process. Using simulations, we show that the inferred posterior geometry captures transitions between mixed and near-pure generative regimes. Even without edge-formation information, the snapshot-based posterior preserves the overall structure of the baseline landscape. These results suggest that posterior geometry provides a way to analyze the joint operations of different mechanisms and shed light on the underlying generative process from limited network observations.

column9: Figures as Interfaces: Toward LLM-Native Artifacts for Scientific Discovery
column11: Wang, Yifang*; Cao, Nan; Wang, Dashun
column13: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming scientific workflows, not only through their generative capabilities but also through their emerging ability to use tools, reason about data, and coordinate complex analytical tasks.  Yet in most human-AI collaborations, the primary outputs--figures--are still treated as static visual summaries: once rendered, they are handled by both humans and multimodal LLMs as images to be re-interpreted from pixels or captions.  The emergent capabilities of LLMs open an opportunity to fundamentally rethink this paradigm.  In this paper, we introduce the concept of LLM-native figures: data-driven artifacts that are simultaneously human-legible and machine-addressable.  Unlike traditional plots, each artifact embeds complete provenance: the data subset, analytical operations and code, and visualization specification used to generate it.  As a result, an LLM can ``see through'' the figure--tracing selections back to their sources, generating code to extend analyses, and orchestrating new visualizations through natural-language instructions or direct manipulation.  We implement this concept through a hybrid language–visual interface that integrates LLM agents with a bidirectional mapping between figures and underlying data.  Using the science-of-science domain as a testbed, we demonstrate that LLM-native figures can accelerate discovery, improve reproducibility, and make reasoning transparent across agents and users.  More broadly, this work establishes a general framework for embedding provenance, interactivity, and explainability into the artifacts of modern research, redefining the figure not as an end product, but as an interface for discovery.

column9: Predicting Human Trafficking Patterns Using Multilayer Graph Neural Networks: Con- fronting Extreme Data Scarcity in Anti-Trafficking Surveillance
column13: Human trafficking represents a critical global challenge affecting millions of individuals, yet systematic prediction and surveillance remain severely hampered by fundamental data scarcity. Unlike traditional criminal activities with established reporting mechanisms, trafficking operates in hidden networks where victim identification rates remain extremely low, estimated at less than 1% globally. This work develops a Graph Neural Network approach to predict trafficking burden across countries and years by integrating heterogeneous data sources within a multilayer network framework. While our current analysis focuses on the 81 country-year observations with available ground truth data, the ultimate objective is expanding predictions to all 3,980 country-years spanning global coverage from 2001-2024. Achieving this expansion requires explicitly confronting the reality that ground truth labels exist for only 2% of contexts, developing methods that can leverage sparse supervision to enable comprehensive worldwide trafficking surveillance. We construct a comprehensive trafficking surveillance network incorporating 3,980 country-year nodes spanning 2001- 2024, derived from U.S. State Department Trafficking in Persons reports. The multilayer architecture captures four critical dimensions of trafficking dynamics: temporal edges connecting countries across years to model policy evolution and trend persistence; geographic edges linking spatially proximate nations reflecting regional trafficking patterns and migration corridors; similarity edges joining countries with comparable anti-trafficking policy profiles based on prose- cution, protection, prevention, and partnership indicators extracted from narrative reports; and trafficking flow edges representing documented victim movements between source and destination countries from the Counter-Trafficking Data Collaborative dataset. This structure yields approximately 5.3 million edges with a mean node degree of 1,336, creating dense connectivity that enables message passing across diverse trafficking contexts. The prediction task confronts severe label scarcity characteristic of anti-trafficking work. Only 81 country-year observations possess ground truth victim counts from CTDC data, concentrated within 2002-2018 and representing merely 2% of network nodes. This extreme imbalance reflects the operational reality of trafficking surveillance: most countries lack systematic victim identification infrastructure, reporting mechanisms remain inconsistent, and many victims never enter official statistics. Traditional supervised learning approaches fail under such constraints, as models cannot learn meaningful patterns from dozens of samples across thousands of potential contexts. Our empirical investigation reveals critical insights about data utilization strategies for trafficking prediction. A baseline configuration trains on 41 labeled samples embedded within the full 3,980-node graph, achieving R2 = −0.23 and F1 = 0.63 for trafficking burden classification. The negative R2 indicates that predictions perform worse than simply using the mean, reflecting the fundamental challenge of extracting signal from keyword-based policy features. Counterintuitively, expanding to all 81 available labels while filtering the graph to labeled-only nodes degrades performance to R2 = −0.70 and F1 = 0.57. This paradox emerges because filtering eliminates network structure: the reduced graph contains only 81 nodes with 577 edges (mean degree 7.1), destroying the temporal, geographic, and similarity context that enables GNNs to propagate information across trafficking corridors and policy regimes. The finding illuminates a crucial principle for trafficking prediction under data scarcity: network topology provides more predictive information than marginal increases in labeled samples when underlying features remain weak. The full graph architecture, despite 98% unlabeled nodes, enables each labeled observation to benefit from multi-hop connections to diverse trafficking contexts. A country’s predicted burden in 2015 leverages not only its own historical trajectory but also patterns from geographically proximate nations, countries with similar policy profiles, and documented victim flow networks. The sparse filtered graph severs these connections, isolating labeled nodes within a narrow temporal window and eliminating the structural scaffolding that encodes global trafficking dynamics. These results demonstrate that effective trafficking prediction requires maintaining comprehensive network structure while acknowledging label limitations, rather than filtering to artificially clean datasets. Current negative R2 values across both configurations reveal that the fundamental bottleneck lies in feature quality: keyword-based extraction from policy documents fails to capture the nuanced mechanisms driving trafficking patterns. Addressing this bottleneck is critical for our ultimate goal of expanding predictions from the current 81 labeled observations to comprehensive global coverage across all 3,980 country-years. Future work must focus on sophisticated semantic feature extraction from narrative reports using large language models to generate rich representations of anti-trafficking capacity, organizational infrastructure, and enforcement mechanisms. Combined with the full multilayer graph architecture preserving critical network context, such approaches offer a path toward actionable trafficking prediction at global scale that can inform resource allocation, identify emerging hotspots across all countries regardless of current data availability, and evaluate intervention effectiveness. This expansion from sparse supervision to comprehensive coverage represents a crucial step toward systematic worldwide trafficking surveillance, transforming the current paradigm where predictions remain confined to data-rich contexts into a framework capable of illuminating trafficking patterns in precisely those regions where ground truth data collection remains most constrained by the hidden nature of the crime itself.

column9: Estimating network clustering with a latent space model from Respondent-Driven Sampling data
column11: Jiang, Yun*; Gile, Krista; Nyakowa, Mercy; Fedha, Daniel; Manley, Hannah; Riback, Lindsey; Akiyama, Matthew
column12: yunjiang@umass.edu*; gile@umass.edu; nyakowamercy@gmail.com; mfedha@gmail.com; hannah.manley@einsteinmed.edu; lindsey.riback@einsteinmed.edu; matthew.akiyama@einsteinmed.edu
column13: The social network structure of hidden and hard-to-reach populations can have important implications for understanding risk and planning interventions in epidemiology and public health. Collecting full or even moderately dense network data from such populations is often infeasible due to the absence of a sampling frame, privacy concerns, and resource constraints. Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS) is a popular chain-referral sampling method designed for such areas, which relies on a dual-incentive strategy, providing compensation to both participants and recruiters for successful referrals. Despite its broad application, conventional RDS primarily captures partially observed recruitment trees and offers limited insight into the underlying network structures. To address this challenge, we first incorporated a recently developed token-based strategy which supplements limited recruitment coupon distribution with token distribution, creating richer data on social network structure (see Figure 1). Inspired by the work using aggregated relational data (ARD), with information from RDS data and token ties, we propose a latent space model to effectively describe the network structure. The model is mathematically determined through a series of equations derived from the method of moment estimators. The performance of model construction from RDS and token data is verified through simulation. The developed model is also employed to estimate unobserved network structures and obtain network statistics from RDS data. Systematical assessments on the effectiveness of our model are presented, especially in describing network clustering, which has high practical relevance but is impossible to infer from standard RDS data.

column9: Latent Variable Models for Estimating Feature Interaction Networks
column11: Nemati, Mohammadreza; Huang, Zhipeng; Xu, Kevin*
column13: Many types of complex systems, particularly biological systems, involve relationships between entities that are often not directly observed. These relationships can be modeled by networks where nodes denote entities of interest and edges are constructed by indirect means, usually by estimating them from non-relational data. One common type of estimated network is a correlation network, where each node has a vector of measurements or features, and an edge between two nodes is constructed by taking the correlation coefficient between the feature vectors for the two nodes.  We consider another type of estimated network, which we call a feature interaction network (FIN). A FIN represents the set of all pairwise interaction coefficients in a generalized linear model (GLM) with pairwise interaction terms between all pairs of the p features. The interaction coefficients can be arranged in a p × p interaction coefficient matrix Θ, where entry θ_jk denotes the coefficient for the interaction term x_j x_k. This matrix can be viewed as a weighted and signed adjacency matrix for the estimated network, where the nodes correspond to the features.  Treating feature interactions as a network allows us to estimate different interaction coefficients θ_jk jointly by considering the estimates of the other interaction coefficients θ_j′k′ , which may be related. Conventional regularization methods such as the lasso (ℓ1 penalty) or elastic net (combined ℓ2, ℓ1 penalty), and even methods specifically targeted to interaction terms such as the hierarchical lasso, do not consider the dependencies between edges (interaction terms) because they do not consider the network structure.  We propose a structured regularization approach for estimating the interaction coefficients using an approximate low-dimensional structure in addition to conventional regularization techniques such as the elastic net. We call our proposed approach LIT-LVM, denoting linear and interaction terms with a latent variable model and can be used with many types of latent structures including low rank and latent distance models.  Our proposed structured regularization for the interaction coefficients offers two main benefits. First, it improves estimation accuracy for the interaction coefficients, leading to better predictive accuracy, especially as p grows relative to the number of samples n, which we demonstrate in simulation experiments and across many real datasets. Second, it provides low-dimensional latent representations of the features that are useful for visualizing and analyzing their relationships, which we demonstrate in an application for modeling donor-recipient compatibility in kidney transplantation.

column9: Disorder-promoted stability in network systems
column13: In network systems, emergent collective behaviors—ranging from synchronization and opinion polarization to species coexistence and memory attractors—are traditionally modeled by describing each interacting agent or node through a single first-order equation of motion. This modeling approach, while convenient for analytical treatment, has inadvertently reinforced the prevailing assumption that homogeneity among nodes facilitates stability in collective dynamics. However, recent literature provided evidence that this assumption is not always correct. Here, we show that this assumption is fundamentally false when the nodal dynamics follow second-order equations of motion or involve additional degrees of freedom. For a broad class of network systems, we establish that heterogeneity among nodes can, in fact, promote stability, even when parameters are randomly sampled from suitable distributions and are therefore disordered. Our theory identifies the mixing of network modes as the key mechanism through which disorder promotes stability. The proposed framework allows us to systematically characterize the existence and prevalence of this phenomenon across a broad range of collective dynamics within network systems, reframing disorder not as a limitation, but as a resource for network stability.

column9: Transient network-mediated propagation patterns in time-varying brain networks
column11: Mutnuri, Srikar*; Adiga, Aniruddha; Venkatramanan, Srinivasan; Marathe, Madhav V.; Carlson, Andrew P.
column13: Many real-world networks are spatially embedded and support propagation processes that are often modeled as local or diffusive [1]. In brain networks, however, neural activity unfolds on top of structured, directed, and time-varying connectivity [2,3], raising the possibility that rare or extreme dynamical episodes, such as abrupt neural state transitions or large-amplitude activity events, may exhibit propagation patterns whose event-related latencies and activation ordering across recording sites are not well explained by spatial distance alone. Detecting such effects in time-varying directed brain networks remains an open challenge, particularly when spatial embedding and temporal variability confound standard graph-theoretic measures.  Here, we articulate a network-science perspective on propagation in temporal directed networks, with particular emphasis on applications to large-scale brain dynamics. The central hypothesis is that, during specific neural state transitions or high-amplitude activity episodes, , relative to typically lower-amplitude baseline activity, observed propagation patterns across nodes may be better explained by distances defined on directed functional networks than by spatial distance alone [1]. We propose a method based on event-related node-wise latencies, activation ordering, and path-dependent delays, in which observed propagation patterns are compared against predictions derived from spatial distance and from directed network distance under spatially and temporally randomized null models [4,5]. This perspective emphasizes time-resolved analysis, enabling comparisons between baseline neural dynamics and rare event-driven regimes within the same network.  Our approach aims to assess whether network-based representations provide systematically improved explanations of propagation timing and ordering compared to spatial baselines, beyond what is expected from stochastic fluctuations or static connectivity effects [2,4]. Initially, we plan to validate the method using synthetic excitable-network simulations and publicly available electrophysiological and temporal network benchmarks.  More broadly, this work motivates a general approach for comparing alternative descriptions of propagation in time-varying directed networks. In network neuroscience, rare large-scale events such as spreading depolarization (SD) [6] motivate comparison between spatially ordered and baseline neural propagation on structured cortical networks. While inspired by such neural phenomena, the ideas discussed here are applicable to a wide range of systems in which rare propagation events play a disproportionate role, including biological, infrastructural, and environmental networks.

column9: From Ultra-Processed Foods to Processing Pathways: A Network-Aware Inference Framework
column11: Ispirova, Gordana*; Aldana, Andres; Menichetti, Giulia
column13: Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are consistently associated with an increased risk of metabolic, cardiovascular, hepatic, and inflammatory diseases. However, dominant frameworks for characterizing food processing rely on qualitative and descriptive criteria that collapse highly heterogeneous industrial practices into coarse categorical labels. Foods that differ markedly in ingredients, nutrient profiles, and industrial processing steps and sequences are therefore treated as equivalent, obscuring meaningful variation and potentially masking differential disease risk. Moreover, large-scale product-level analyzes, including our study of more than 70,000 U.S. grocery products, show that food processing information is often incomplete or inconsistently annotated, underscoring the need for systematic methods that can infer fine-grained processing steps. To address these limitations, we constructed a harmonized food-processing database comprising more than 62,000 foods annotated with LanguaL-derived processing descriptors, nutrient profiles, and food-group information aggregated from heterogeneous international sources. Processing annotations are inherently relational and sparse: each food is associated with multiple semantically related descriptors reflecting combinations and sequences of operations, while many plausible food–process associations remain unobserved. This structure naturally induces a bipartite network linking foods and processing descriptors, where observed edges encode partial processing pathways and missing edges represent absent or latent operations. Inferring food processing, therefore, becomes a network learning problem under extreme label sparsity, with the central challenge of distinguishing true absences from missing annotations—a limitation that fundamentally constrains feature-based classifiers lacking access to relational structure. Here, we present a unified inference pipeline that integrates network-aware models with top-k multilabel classification baselines trained on BERT-derived embeddings from curated food metadata. By leveraging network topology, the proposed framework substantially improves recovery of known food–process associations by reducing confusion between absent and unobserved processing operations. The best-performing model achieves Top-5 and Top-10 accuracies of 88.3% and 94.4%, respectively, and a Top-10 recall of 70.9%, despite foods being annotated with only ~5 labels on average out of 269 possible descriptors—corresponding to an 8–15X improvement over random ranking. By reframing food processing as a problem of missing-edge inference in hierarchical bipartite networks, this framework moves beyond coarse UPF categories and enables systematic identification of fine-grained processing steps within and across food groups, informing targeted interventions in food formulation and public health policy. More broadly, it illustrates how network topology can be leveraged to recover latent relational structure from sparse, incomplete annotations, a setting common to many large-scale data integration problems in network science.

column9: Collective Dynamics of Pinned Spirals in a Chemical Reaction-Diffusion System
column13: Collective behaviors of oscillators have drawn great attention in recent years. Study on synchronization becomes necessary to understand the human brain, cardiac activity, etc. We have examined pinned spiral rotors in the Belousov- Zhabotinsky (BZ) chemical reaction-diffusion system. We showed that the two counter-rotating pinned rotors with different frequencies attain phase and frequency synchronization behavior (1). With increasing the network size, we found rich dynamics from cluster formation to chimera states. We moved to look at the collective phenomena of corotating pinned spirals and found that they also synchronize but lack complete phase synchronization (2), as we observed in the case of counterrotating. Experimental observations are reproduced in the numerical simulations.  [1] Physical review. E, 01 Sep 2022, 106(3-1):034201 [2] Eur. Phys. J. Spec. Top. 233, 787–795 (2024)

column9: Omnivory decouples optimal predator fitness from network robustness
column13: The principle of maximum output power is as old as the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model. This principle posits that under competition, those system configurations are most likely to prevail that can capture and transform usable energy at higher rates. While Lotka–Volterra dynamics and species abundances are now standard tools in ecology, explicitly using energy fluxes as the primary currency in ecological models has received much less attention. Here, we revisit predator–prey systems from a network perspective, using a Lotka–Volterra–type model formulated in terms of energy fluxes between interacting species. We define the output power of a food web as the total energy flux through one or more focal top predators, and study how output power depends on the encounter rates (interaction strengths) along the network’s feeding links. For a broad class of network structures without omnivory, we find that encounter rates that maximize output power also maximize feasibility, understood as the fraction of intrinsic growth-rate vectors that yield positive, coexistence equilibria. In these cases, optimal predator fitness and network robustness converge — changing the interaction strength(s) toward the maximum-power state simultaneously expands the feasibility domain. This qualitative picture is reversed when the network exhibits omnivory, i.e. when at least one predator feeds on both a basal and a non-basal species. Omnivory motifs appear as feed-forward loops in ecological networks [2]. For such motifs, the encounter rates that maximize output power lie near geometric bottlenecks or boundaries of the feasibility domain, so that maximizing predator power systematically reduces feasibility. This result holds even when omnivory is realized through species other than the focal top predator. Our analysis shows that omnivory introduces a structural tension between individual-level optimization (maximum output power of predators) and network-level robustness (feasibility), leading to divergent optimal outcomes at the scales of species and ecological networks.

column9: Networked Dynamics of Toxicity in Reddit Gaming Communities
column11: Smith, Serafina; David, Glen; Brunn, Lizzy; Nguyen, Vy; Choi, Eun Cheol*; Luceri, Luca
column12: smithser@usc.edu; gpdavid@usc.edu; lbrunn@usc.edu; vynguyen@usc.edu; euncheol@usc.edu*; lluceri@isi.edu
column13:
Online gaming communities are among the most active and socially complex online spaces, yet they remain persistently affected by toxic behavior such as harassment, aggression, and abusive language, which harms user well-being and discourages participation [1]. While prior work has examined toxicity at the content level, across game genres, or through network dynamics [1,2,3], it remains unclear how community type in terms of game genre and developer scale and user interaction structure jointly shape the prevalence, diffusion, and concentration of toxicity.  We present a comparative, network-based analysis of toxicity across Reddit gaming communities using a 2 × 2 framework that crosses game genre (MMORPG vs. Soulslike) with developer scale (AAA/AA vs. indie). We analyze 550,641 posts and comments from nine gaming subreddits, including a general gaming baseline (r/gaming). Each post and comment is scored using two independent automated toxicity detection systems (OpenAI’s omni-moderation model and Detoxify). Using these scores, we construct thread-level reply trees and directed user-reply networks to examine toxicity across multiple levels of social organization.  	extbf{At the community level}, we compare average toxicity prevalence, severity, and category composition across the 2 × 2 design. Soulslike communities and AAA/AA titles exhibit modestly higher average toxicity than MMORPG and indie communities, driven primarily by conflict-oriented language such as insults, obscenity, and violence-related terms [2]. 	extbf{At the thread level}, we observe robust local contagion across all communities: replies to toxic comments are consistently more toxic, and more toxic threads tend to be larger, deeper, and more structurally viral (Figure 1, left). These patterns align with prior work on toxicity contagion and conversational cascades in online discussion networks [3]. We find no systematic differences in these dynamics across genre or developer scale, indicating that toxicity propagation reflects general properties of online conversational structure rather than community-specific cultures or norms. 	extbf{At the user level}, toxicity is both assortative and structurally concentrated (Figure 1, right). Users with similar toxicity levels preferentially interact, and more central users both produce and receive more toxicity, with network centrality differentiating exposure from expression.  Taken together, these findings show that toxicity in gaming communities is shaped less by genre or developer scale alone and more by interaction structure and network position. Rather than treating specific communities or genres as inherently toxic, the results highlight the importance of network-aware moderation strategies that focus on early conversational contexts and structurally influential users. More broadly, this study provides a comparative, network-based benchmark for understanding harmful behavior in large-scale online interaction systems.   igskip {\small
