column9: A Novel Spatial Representation of Sustainable Transportation Travel Times
column13: Every day, thousands of people commute to and from central business districts in cities throughout the world, forming a complex network of public transit. Urban planners have traditionally built isochrone maps with various free and professional tools to easily conceptualize “accessibility” (distance one can travel in a set time), by various discrete transport modes [1,2]. These maps have enabled the assessment of the health and performance of traffic and public transit networks while informing transportation strategy. With a growing movement in cities to reduce vehicle traffic in central business districts, there is a need to directly compare the travel time of sustainable transport modes with driving. We achieve this by identifying where travel to important destinations is faster by sustainable modes than by car. Focusing on four Canadian cities, New York City, and Berlin, the maps were created using travel time data from Google Maps at a 0.5 km resolution. We observe that neighborhoods as far away as outer suburbs are reachable faster by bicycle in most cities, while transit is faster in well served areas. We compare network centrality statistics between these 6 cities in an effort to provide network theory driven insights to urban planners. This new perspective on urban transportation networks highlights an untapped potential for time savings, safety, environmental, and economic benefits in cities when barriers to sustainable transportation are reduced. Finally, in revealing the neighborhoods where alternative transport modes have superior travel times, municipal leaders can be confident that traffic calming implementations will not significantly reduce accessibility for residents.

column9: The Global Network of Resource Flows from Lithosphere to Technosphere
column11: Kaye, Maxwell*; Galbraith, Eric; Al Faisal, Abduallah
column13: Anthropogenic material fluxes now rival natural geological processes yet are rarely studied within the Earth system framework. Here we present a new approach, global ‘technogeochemical’ flows, and apply it to the roughly 2 Gt/y anthropogenic flows of iron and other critical materials. Using the SESAME-Human Earth Atlas [1], we synthesize disparate data sources to show how critical minerals flow from a few extraction sites, via a few refining plants, to widely distributed in-use stocks. We apply our spatiotemporal approach to other critical materials including copper, lithium, aluminum, lithium, phosphate, and even food production to understand how industrial economic processes are physically embedded in the Earth system.  [1]     Faisal, A. A., Kaye, M., Ahmed, M., Galbraith, E. D. (2025). The SESAME Human-Earth Atlas. Scientific Data, 12(1), 775.

column9: Scale invariance and statistical significance in complex weighted networks
column11: Nascimento Silva, Filipi*; Kojaku, Sadamori; Flammini, Alessandro; Radicchi, Filippo; Fortunato, Santo
column13: Weighted networks appear in a wide range of social, biological, technological, and information systems. Determining whether observed structural patterns are statistically significant in weighted networks requires suitable null models (Fig. A). The most widely adopted choice is the Weighted Configuration Model (WCM), which extends the configuration model by interpreting weights as bundles of unit edges and preserving node strengths in the randomized ensemble.  In many applications, the scale used to express weights is arbitrary (e.g., seconds vs. minutes, or thousands vs. millions of dollars), while standard weighted measures such as the Onnela weighted clustering coefficient, weighted eigenvector centrality, and weighted modularity are themselves scale invariant. This leads to a natural expectation: p-values obtained by comparing empirical scores to their corresponding null distributions should be independent of the chosen weight units.  Here we show that this expectation is violated by the WCM: statistical significance under this model is scale dependent. The origin of this behavior lies in the multi-edge interpretation of weights, which induces distribution fluctuations whose standard deviation grows sublinearly with the rescaling factor A, causing the null distribution to shrink asymptotically as A⁻¹ᐟ². As a result, in the large-A limit, essentially any deviation becomes statistically significant, making inference depend on an arbitrary unit choice (Fig. B: WCM), as previously hinted by studies of scale effects in weighted null models.  To restore scale invariance while preserving network sparsity, we adopt a separable two-step construction inspired by network-reconstruction frameworks. In this approach, topology is first randomized using a degree-based configuration model, and weights are then assigned to realized edges from a scale-invariant maximum-entropy (exponential) distribution, with means chosen to preserve node strengths in expectation. Across representative weighted networks from distinct domains and for key measures (maximum modularity, maximum L2-normalized eigenvector centrality, and weighted clustering), this two-step null model yields scale-flat distributions (Fig. B: CReMb) and thus scale-invariant p-values, enabling unbiased significance testing in complex weighted networks (Fig. C).  Figure caption: (A) Schematic of the hypothesis-testing procedure: a network statistic is measured on the empirical network and compared to its distribution under a null model to obtain a p-value. (B) Standard deviation of null distributions for three weighted measures: maximum modularity, maximum eigenvector centrality, and weighted clustering coefficient, as a function of the rescaling factor A. Under the WCM, the null width decreases approximately as A⁻¹ᐟ², implying scale-dependent significance. In contrast, the separable two-step null (CReMb variant) yields approximately constant variance, indicating scale invariance. (C) Resulting p-values for a few networks under the WCM (dots) and the CReMb variant model (crosses).

column9: Social network structure can invert human microbiome patterns
column13: The network structure of social interactions strongly influences the composition of individuals’ microbiomes. Analysis of a dataset of over 3000 individuals across 18 villages in Honduras reveals that although individuals are more likely to interact with members of their own sex (homophily), friends of the opposite sex (non-romantic) have more similar microbiomes compared to friends of the same sex (non-romantic). We develop a mathematical theory to demonstrate that this counterintuitive pattern can attributed to the higher-order structure of social interactions. Our results show how human social dynamics can invert expected patterns in the human microbiome.

column9: Scientific Consumption in the Era of Large Language Models
column11: Li, Bingsong*; Ginsparg, Paul; Yin, Yian
column13: Large Language Models (LLMs) with Retrieval Augmented Generation capabilities have the potential to significantly reshape the discovery and consumption of the latest science, yet little is known about the real-world impact of LLM use on online scientific consumption. Many have recognized the potential of LLMs to synthesize and mine existing literature and automate workflows in science. At the same time, there are concerns that LLMs may reinforce existing social biases and create scientific monocultures that reduce innovation and intellectual diversity. Here we present the first large-scale analysis of scientific consumption in the era of Large Language Models, using unique log data from a leading preprint server covering 913M referred web visits to 2.84M preprints during a two-year period (Oct 2023 – Sep 2025).  Our analysis uncovers three stylized facts. First, there has been a rapid increase in LLM usage for discovering and accessing scientific literature. Referral traffic from ChatGPT to scientific papers increased fivefold from the release of ChatGPT Search in October 2024 to May 2025, followed by a period of saturation. We observe a similar increase from other GenAI sources such as Gemini and Perplexity, although on a much smaller absolute scale. Second, by linking web traffic logs with bibliometric data from Semantic Scholar, we find LLMs largely equalize the attention received by papers. Compared with traditional web sources, LLM-referred traffic disproportionately points to papers with relatively low citation impact. Third, this equalization of scientific attention extends to the individual researcher level. Analyzing the demographic features of accessed articles, we find that traffic from LLMs is associated with a higher representation of gender and racial minority groups. Compared with traditional web sources, ChatGPT allocated 13.0, 29.6, and 37.9 more percentage points of attention to female, Black, and Hispanic authors, respectively. In sum, despite growing concerns about the homogenizing effect of LLMs, our results highlight that LLMs can also allocate scientific attention more broadly and equitably than traditional search engines.

column9: Beyond the CEO Life Cycle: The Influences of Top Management Team and Middle Man- agers from a Faultline Perspective
column11: Yang, Biying*; Tsai, Chou-Yu; Eckardt, Rory; Dionne, Shelley; Weng, David
column13: CEOs’ strategic paradigms are crucial in shaping organizational performance by influencing direction, resource alloca- tion, and competitive positioning. The CEO life cycle framework introduces a longitudinal lens by suggesting that CEOs’ strategic paradigms generally follow an exploration-exploitation-obsolescence pattern, resulting in an inverted U-shaped performance trajectory. This reflects initial performance improvement followed by stagnation and ultimate decline [1]. We extend this framework beyond the sole focus on CEOs’ influence to examine the impacts of faultlines formed between CEOs and top management team (TMT) members, as well as between CEOs and middle managers (MMs), given the critical roles these agents play in strategic formulation and implementation. Drawing on Campbell et al.’s (2023) classification, we conceptualize faultlines based on observable and unobservable attributes shared by CEO and other strategic agents. We propose that while strong faultlines of observable attributes strengthen performance gains during the exploration phase, strong faultlines of unobservable attributes sustain high performance for a longer time during exploitation and attenuate the decline associated with obsolescence. We use a multiplex network approach [2] to model the strength of these faultlines and conduct random coefficient multilevel growth modeling, supplemented by tangent slope analysis, to specify performance trajectory and its changing rates. Hypotheses are tested using longitudinal data gathered from the U.S. higher education context between 2000 to 2022, with university presidents proxying as CEOs, provosts as the TMT members, and deans as MMs. The sample includes 28 presidents, 63 provosts, and 574 deans, yielding 293 year-performance pairs. Performance is assessed across three dimensions: total revenues (financial), operating efficiency (operational), and research salary (innovation). The results provide a more nuanced perspective on the myth of CEO “solo act” performance. Although total revenues show insignificant curvilinear or moderating effects, operating efficiency is significantly enhanced by stronger faultlines of CEO-TMT and CEO-MM unobservable attribute. Specifically, under stronger unobservable attribute faultlines, efficiency increases at a diminishing rate during the initial years of CEO life cycle; conversely, weaker faultlines of unobservable attribute lead performance to enter a plateau stage directly without a salient initial increase. For research salary, this innovation-related dimension increases more rapidly when CEO-MM observable attribute faultline is weaker, suggesting that diversity among MMs may drive early-stage research growth. These findings demonstrate that organizational per- formance is a multidimensional and collective outcome shaped by temporal dynamics, the joint effects of strategic agents at different hierarchical levels, and perceptual changes among those strategic agents.

column9: Tabular Embedding: A Network Representation for High-Performance Computing Applications
column11: Hasanzadeh Fard, Sanaz*; Dolson, Emily; Andres Moreno, Matthew; Zaman, Luis
column13: Recently, multiple computational hardware platforms, such as the Cerebras Wafer Scale Engine (WSE), have combined a vast number of lower-powered processors to achieve overall high throughput. These platforms offer the potential to dramatically scale up applications that are conducive to being run on them. Here, we propose that bipartite network modeling is such an application and present a technique (tabular embedding) for translating it to computational substrates such as the WSE. We present an application in the context of epidemiology, but see no reason that our technique should not generalize. The primary obstacle to be overcome is enabling efficient communication across the WSE's grid of processors.  We achieve an efficient solution to this problem by conceptualizing our epidemiological network as containing two types of nodes: residences and institutions (i.e. school or work). Edges between these nodes indicate the presence of people who live at a given residence and regularly attend a given institution, enabling disease transmission between the two sites. We then develop a tabular layout in which some table cells (which correspond to processors) correspond to houses, some to institutions, and others to edges between houses and institutions (i.e. people). We present an efficient algorithm for modeling disease transmission along networks represented by these layouts.

column9: Characterizing academic collaborations by prestige and discipline composition
column11: Aoki-Sherwood, Benyoshi; Barnes, Kate; Chavez-Ruelas, Carolina*
column13: Social and systemic factors have been shown to structure how scientists collaborate with each other. As is the case with sociodemographic homophily in collaboration [1], many of these factors reflect existing social inequalities that operate in the scientific ecosystem and reinforce existing hierarchies [2]. For instance, controlling for quality, a scientific idea spreads at a higher rate if it originates from a higher prestige institution than from a lower prestige institution [3]. However, academic collaborations are not restricted to the same institutional prestige or discipline, and it remains unclear the degree to which this occurs in the system. In this project, we aim to characterize prestige homophily and cross-disciplinary collaboration rates across five fields to understand how these boundaries structure academic co-authorship.  We linked faculty profiles in a census of U.S. faculty from the Academic Analytics Research Center (AARC) to publication data from OpenAlex and applied the SpringRank network embedding algorithm to generate institutional prestige scores based on faculty placement patterns [4]. From these data, we created undirected co-authorship multigraphs in which nodes are faculty from the AARC census, and an edge connects two individuals for each of their co-authored publications. We compared the within-field prestige homophily for the fields of computer science, mathematics, physics, sociology, and philosophy using a measure of network assortativity for continuous node features [5]. We chose these fields because they represent diverse collaboration paradigms and scholastic traditions. We excluded collaborations within the same institution because they likely reflect proximity rather than prestige homophily.  The five fields exhibit substantial variation in the prestige homophily of within-field collaborations, ranging from 0.14 in physics to 0.31 in math (Fig. 1). Similarly, rates of interdisciplinary collaboration also vary widely between fields. Almost half of co-authorship pairs involving faculty in philosophy are interdisciplinary. For sociology, this fraction falls to 14% (Fig. 1). Mathematics has both the highest prestige homophily and the second-highest interdisciplinary collaboration rate while philosophy has the highest interdisciplinary collaboration rate but the second-lowest prestige homophily, suggesting a complex relationship between these two lenses on scientific collaboration. Our future work will measure these quantities across a more complete set of fields and examine possible covariates for both prestige homophily and interdisciplinary collaboration. For example, we will test whether prestige homophily is more or less prevalent in interdisciplinary collaborations, clarifying the complex way in which institutional prestige influences who collaborates with whom.

column9: Early Rules Cast Long Shadows: Dependency Dynamics in Wikipedia’s Regulatory Network
column11: Bhattacharya, Shambhobi*; Youn, Hyejin ; Yoon , Jisung
column13: Do rules have their own dynamics? Administrative codes in universities grow slowly as problems get absorbed, shift with leadership, and respond to external shocks [1]. But rules do not exist in isolation. In legal codes, manuals, and online platforms, rules reference each other for justification or exception. These cross-references create dependencies: a rule’s meaning is incomplete without the rules it cites. Prior work showed that Wikipedia’s regulatory pages form exactly such a network, with early rules occupying central positions [2]. Why do some rules become foundational while others remain peripheral? Here we trace the temporal evolution of Wikipedia’s regulatory dependency network to understand how this hierarchy forms and stabilizes. We construct a directed network where nodes are Wikipedia regulatory pages (policies, guidelines, etc.) and edges are cross-references in the text. Figure 1a illustrates this: the Neutral Point of View (NPOV) policy contains links like “please read [[WP:NOT]]” and “content should be [[WP:V]] verifiable.” Each link creates a directed edge. We reconstruct it yearly from 2001 to 2016. Figure 1b shows that the network grows rapidly until 2008, then saturates, consistent with problem absorption [1,2]. The inset shows that in-degree inequality (Gini) rises from 0.59 to 0.81 by 2008, then stabilizes [2]. This reflects cumulative advantage: early rules gain visibility, attract citations, and become difficult to displace. Once formed, the hierarchy persists. Figure 1c traces how this hierarchy forms. In 2001, the emerging core was dominated by NPOV and What Wikipedia Is Not (NOT). By 2003, Verifiability (V) and No Original Research (NOR) emerged, operationalizing neutrality by specifying how to achieve it. By 2008, NPOV was cited by 309 pages, and this core remained stable even as the network grew from 30 to 1,294 pages. Figure 1d reveals the dependency structure. There are asymmetric connections: some rules have far more in-degree than out-degree. This asymmetry indicates hierarchy among rules [3]. Rules with high in-degree but low out-degree are foundational: others depend on them, but they depend on few. NPOV has 452 incoming and 34 outgoing citations (13:1). All four fall below the diagonal, anchoring the network while other rules elaborate on them. Together, foundational rules established in the first two years remain central, making them costly to change. New rules do not displace existing foundations; they attach to them. Wikipedia offers a lens to trace how regulatory hierarchy emerges and persists: what drives this lock-in, is it universal, and what happens when foundations must change?

column9: Reservoir computers as digital twins for brain dynamics
column11: Chepuri, Ravi*; Hunt, Brian; Pecora, Lou; Girvan, Michelle
column13: The brain is a complex network dynamical system, and faithful representations of its dynamics would enable new ways to analyze and predict brain activity using tools from dynamical systems and network science. In this context, a digital twin is a secondary dynamical system coupled to neural measurements that evolves in synchrony with the brain. Such a twin must synchronize to the underlying dynamics, infer unmeasured variables, forecast short-term activity, and capture longer-term patterns of behavior. Together, these capabilities support the study of individual-specific brain dynamics and, in the longer term, the exploration of how targeted interventions might influence neural evolution toward desired regimes.  We adopt reservoir computing (RC) as the core modeling framework for these digital twins. RC offers an efficient approach to learning dynamical systems in which a fixed recurrent network evolves in response to input signals, while training is restricted to a linear readout. Because computation arises from the reservoir’s intrinsic dynamics, RC is well suited to modeling continuous-time, nonlinear systems. This architecture enables fast training, low data requirements, and robustness to noise and nonstationarity, while allowing reservoirs to be designed with interpretable network structure such as sparsity, heterogeneity, and symmetry.  Here, we report early progress toward establishing the feasibility and interpretability of RC-based digital twins of brain dynamics. Using high-density EEG time-series data, we show that these models can synchronize to observed brain activity, infer latent dynamical variables, and generate stable short-term forecasts. Preliminary analyses further indicate that RCs can reproduce longer-term statistical features of the dynamics, suggesting the ability to capture aspects of the brain’s dynamical “climate.” While the present work focuses on modeling and prediction, it lays groundwork for future control-oriented studies and extensions to additional neural data modalities.  From a network science perspective, this framework treats the digital twin itself as a dynamical network coupled to another complex network—the brain. This view enables the application of concepts such as synchronization, observability, and controllability to assess when a learned twin can reliably track and predict brain dynamics. Moreover, the explicit network structure of the reservoir allows systematic investigation of how connectivity, heterogeneity, and symmetry shape dynamical inference and stability, positioning reservoir computing as a natural bridge between data-driven modeling and network science.

column9: A nonparametric model for multiple categorical node features with arbitrary correlations
column13: Many observable complex networks produce data that is both compositional (properties of nodes) and relational (network edges). However, the development of flexible network models that effectively use both of these data sources simultaneously remains a challenge. The existing standard for nonparametric network inference with metadata involves representing metadata as additional layers of a multilayered stochastic block model (SBM). When the node features are correlated, this approach leads to erroneous structure in the inferred node partition, as well as simultaneous overfitting and underfitting. After addressing the limitations of a "naive" solution to the correlated layer problem based on combining layers, we introduce a microcanonical model that avoids these issues, providing a method that is more suitable for the inferential task at hand while achieving improved data compression. Using synthetic and empirical data, we demonstrate how our model can be used alongside existing community detection methods for joint inference of latent node features, without a priori assumptions about the correlation between these data sources.

column9: Covariate-assisted graph matching in academic genealogy and collaboration networks
column11: Arroyo, Jesus*; Dawn, Trisha; Authur, Adam
column13: Data integration is essential across diverse domains, from historical records to biomedical research, facilitating joint statistical inference. A crucial initial step in this process involves merging multiple data sources based on matching individual records, often in the absence of unique identifiers. When the datasets are networks, this problem is typically addressed through {graph matching} methodologies. For such cases, auxiliary features or covariates associated with nodes or edges can be instrumental in achieving improved accuracy. However, most existing graph matching techniques do not incorporate this information, limiting their performance against non-identifiable and erroneous matches. To overcome these limitations, we first propose two novel covariate-assisted seeded graph matching methods, where a partial alignment for a set of nodes, called seeds, is known. The first one solves a quadratic assignment problem (QAP) over the whole graph, while the second one only leverages the local neighborhood structure of seed nodes for computational scalability. Both methods are grounded in a conditional modeling framework, where elements of one graph's adjacency matrix are modeled using a generalized linear model (GLM), given the other graph and the available covariates. We establish theoretical guarantees for our methodology, including a model estimation error rate for the parameters, conditions to establish exact recovery of the solution of the graph matching problem with covariates, and an application to the correlated Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi model with covariates.   The methodology is illustrated in an application to analyze the statistics academic genealogy obtained from the Mathematics Genealogy Project and the co-authorship network between statisticians. By leveraging covariates such as graduation year, institution and academic family, we achieve improved alignment accuracy. Moreover, our model yields interpretable results on the influence of these features. We further extend this model to incorporate community structure and understand the association between academic families and collaboration in the field of statistics.

column9: Percolation in Growing Stochastic Block Models
column11: Pieleanu, Luca; Sabhahit, Narayan*; Laber, Moritz; Krioukov, Dmitri
column13:
The stochastic block model (SBM) [1,2] is a paradigmatic random graph model used extensively in Network Science for inference and community detection, as it naturally accommodates community structure. Despite its broad applicability, some of its most fundamental properties remain poorly understood: rigorous results for the percolation transition (the emergence of the giant connected component (GCC)) are only known in a limited set of special cases, all involving a fixed number of communities [3,4]. Some important regimes---most notably with a growing number of blocks---have remained largely unexplored.  Here, we provide a thorough theoretical analysis of a general class of SBMs, including the special case of the sparse SBM with a growing number of communities. This case is particularly significant since these models are very close to soft random geometric graphs [5], whose percolation properties have so far been analytically intractable [6]. We consider an SBM with $N$ vertices, partitioned into $B_{N}$ blocks of sizes $\{n_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B_{N}}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{B_{N}} n_i= N$, where $p_{ij}$ denotes the connection probability between nodes belonging to communities $i$ and $j$. column9: Predicting Scientific Subfield Adoption in Collaboration Networks: The Role of Exposure Timing and Collaborator Composition
column13: Understanding how collaboration networks are associated with researchers’ entry into new scientific subfields has implications for research policy and scientific innovation. While diffusion theories often assume that greater cumulative exposure to adopting peers increases adoption likelihood [1], empirical evidence remains mixed, particularly when individuals are embedded in environments composed of collaborators at different stages of subfield engagement [2]. We investigate how exposure timing, accumulation, and composition of collaboration networks jointly predict adoption across five scientific fields.  Using longitudinal co-authorship networks from SciSciNet [3], we analyze five subfields that experienced substantial growth between 2015-2019: Computer Engineering, Physical Geography, Demographic Economics, Evolutionary Biology, and Combinatorial Chemistry. We define three researcher roles based on adoption: Alices, recent adopters who first published during the growth period; Bobs, at-risk researchers who collaborated with Alices but have not yet adopted; and Charlies, established researchers who entered the subfield before 2015. For each Bob, we track yearly changes in their local collaboration neighborhood and predict whether they publish in the subfield in a given year. For each Bob–year observation, we construct network-derived features capturing (i) the timing of first exposure to Alice, (ii) cumulative and newly accruing exposure to Alice collaborators, and (iii) exposure to Charlie collaborators, reflecting embeddedness in an established collaborator environment. Using gradient-boosted decision tree models with an expanding-window temporal cross-validation approach, we evaluate predictive performance using the AUC-ROC metric and assess interpretability through SHAP analyses and grouped ablations.  Across all fields, early exposure to recent adopters (Alices) is positively associated with adoption, while the incremental effect of additional exposure diminishes with prolonged exposure. In contrast, exposure to established collaborators (Charlies) is consistently negatively associated with adoption. Ablation tests support this asymmetry: removing exposure to Charlies produces the largest drop in predictive performance across the fields (mean ΔAUC ≈ −0.08 to −0.10), followed by removal of the timing of first-exposure to Alices (mean ΔAUC ≈ −0.06), while cumulative exposure contributes little once timing and neighborhood composition are accounted for.  Together, these findings challenge cumulative diffusion models that focus solely on exposure accumulation. Instead, subfield adoption in scientific collaboration networks depends on when exposure occurs and the structural composition of collaboration networks. By demonstrating the cross-subfield invariance of these temporal and inhibitory network effects, our work highlights the need for diffusion models that incorporate network roles, timing, and competing social signals in the study of scientific adoption. column9: From feature interactions to taxa networks: SHAP-interaction graphs for CRC risk models
column11: Novielli, Pierfrancesco*; Romano, Donato; Magarelli, Michele; Di Bitonto, Pierpaolo; Tangaro, Sabina
column13: Gut microbiome signatures are increasingly used for colorectal cancer (CRC) risk stratification and early detection [1].  Most current pipelines still report ranked taxa. That view is incomplete: dysbiosis is not only a shift in abundance, but a change in how microbial components act together in a host context. Distinct CRC carcinogenic pathways also map to distinct microbiome patterns, reinforcing the need for models that capture heterogeneity rather than a single “average” signature [3].  We propose a network-first interpretation of explainable machine learning for microbiome-based risk models. Starting from a supervised CRC risk predictor trained on gut microbial profiles and validated across cohorts [2], we treat feature interactions as the primary object of analysis. SHAP interaction values quantify how pairs of taxa jointly influence risk predictions beyond their separate contributions.  Aggregating these interactions yields a weighted taxa network where edges represent model-inferred dependencies relevant to the clinical task, not co-occurrence correlations.  This construction exposes microbial hubs and interaction neighborhoods that define “high-risk configurations” in the model’s decision logic.    The second element is stratification at the patient level. By embedding individual explanation vectors (SHAP values) and clustering subjects with adenoma, we identify groups with distinct predicted CRC risk profiles [2].  When we rebuild taxa interaction networks within these adenoma clusters, the graph topology changes: different hubs dominate in different risk groups, and the interaction patterns diverge in ways consistent with heterogeneous dysbiosis pathways.    This is a step toward network medicine and health: models do not only assign a score, they define measurable sub-networks that can be compared across cohorts, monitored over time, and linked to mechanistic and interventional hypotheses.

column9: From networks of data to networks of care: multilayer network thinking for clinical medicine
column11: Novielli, Pierfrancesco*; Bellotti, Roberto; Khalil, Mohamad; Portincasa, Piero; Tangaro, Sabina
column13: Clinical medicine is accumulating layers of information—imaging, clinical variables, and multiple omic readouts—often processed as parallel pipelines [1]. The result is high-dimensional output with limited clinical coherence: signals remain domain-specific, and responsibility for integration is pushed downstream to the clinician.  We argue that the missing layer is not another model, but an explicit network representation of the patient. This is the operational step from network medicine as a concept to network medicine as a clinical workflow: disease is framed as a shift in the patient’s ‘diseasome’ connectivity rather than a single causal factor [2]. Multilayer networks keep within-domain structure while encoding cross-domain couplings (e.g., diet–microbe–metabolite–inflammation), making the integration problem inspectable rather than implicit. In this view, machine learning is a tool that operates on networks, but the clinical product is the trace: which nodes and interactions support a decision, and how that trace changes across contexts and time [3].  We present a point of view that reframes “AI in healthcare” as a shift from fragmented data layers to networks of care [3]: network structures that link data modalities, clinical tasks, and human actors. We outline three actionable principles—network-first integration, explanation as a clinical object, and patient-centered workflows—and discuss how network science can evaluate them through stability of network traces, comparability across sites, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

column9: Discover network dynamics with neural symbolic regression
column11: Yu, Zihan; Ding, Jingtao*; Li, Yong
column13: Network dynamics are theoretical foundation for studying complex systems. Despite observational data accumulated across many domains, mathematical models exist only in a few areas with relatively clear underlying principles. Here we show that a neural symbolic regression approach can bridge this gap by automatically formatting dynamics formulas from data. It reduces searches on high-dimensional networks into equivalent one-dimensional systems and uses a pre-trained neural network to guide accurate formula discovery. Applied to ten benchmark systems, it recovers the correct forms and parameters of dynamics. In two empirical natural systems, it corrects existing models of gene regulation and microbial communities, reducing root mean squared error by 59.68% and 55.94%. In epidemic transmission across human mobility networks of various scales, it discovers dynamics showing consistent power-law correlations across spatial scales and revealing country-level differences in intervention effects. These results demonstrate that machine-driven discovery of network dynamics can enhance understanding of complex systems and promote the development of complexity science.

column9: Coordination through Reply Chains in Information Operation Campaigns
column11: Narain, Stuti*; Narain, Shradha; Kaushal, Rishabh; Iamnitchi, Adriana
column13: Social media platforms are exploited in a well calibrated, orchestrated manner by malicious coordinated groups [1], referred to as Information Operations (IOs) or Coordinated Campaigns (CC). The objectives are to garner support or to influence people through misleading information.  IOs pose serious threats to organic dissemination of information. Particularly during election times, IOs can potentially disrupt free and fair democratic processes.   In this work we focus on how malicious actors try to assert influence artificially through replies to the original posts. We present a network-based framework that investigates reply posts involved in IOs. Specifically, we study coordinated replies on social media platforms using IO datasets which comprise 26 IO campaigns consisting of IO posts from different state actors (eg. Russia, China, etc.) identified by platform through their transparency website and control posts, curated by Seckin et al. [2]) .   We restrict ourselves to reply posts and construct a reply graph for each campaign. Each reply post is categorized as belonging to IO campaign or control. Due to space limitations, we focus on two contrasting campaigns [2] from China (large reply network) and Armenia (small reply network). Further, we consider only those replies whose corresponding original posts are present in the dataset. Reply networks are trees rooted in the original posts, where the rest of the nodes are replies to the original posts or to other replies present either in star or chain formation as depicted in Fig~\ref{fig:chain_patterns}. Table~\ref{tbl:stats} shows reply graph statistics with respect to chains, the average delay (in minutes) between original post and direct reply as well as the last reply, and distinct user accounts engaged in these interactions. In the IOs from China, 33\% of chains (3,750 out of 11,204) have IO replies, as compared to Armenia with only 5\% (16 out of 307). The Chinese campaign has 39 mixed reply chains containing both IO and control replies while no such mixed chains were found for Armenia. IO reply chains are shorter, both on average and in terms of maximum chain length, than control reply chains in both campaigns.   In addition, IO reply chains have much higher out-degree and lower in-degree when compared with control reply chains. Temporally, we measure average delay (in terms of minutes) of direct reply and last reply to the original post. IO replies in the Chinese campaign are exceedingly marked with large delays when compared to control replies, a trend which is reversed in Armenian campaign.  Lastly, the Chinese campaigns employ more distinct user accounts than the Armenian campaigns. To conclude, this study investigates signatures in foreign information campaigns on social media that can be shown using reply chains. Such signatures could be used for detecting campaigns in real time.   \label{tbl:stats} \begin{tabular}{cccccc} \hline Metric & \multicolumn{3}{c}{China} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Armenia} \\ \hline Nodes & \multicolumn{3}{c}{26,285}  & \multicolumn{2}{c}{739} \\ Edges & \multicolumn{3}{c}{17,137} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{463} \\ \hline & IO & Ctrl & Mix & IO & Ctrl \\ \hline Number of Chains & 3750 & 7415 & 39 & 16 & 291\\ Avg Chain Length & 2.42 & 2.68 & 4.08 & 2 & 2.66 \\ Min Chain Length & 2 & 2 & 3 & 2 & 2 \\ Max Chain Length & 17 & 99 & 14 & 2 & 21 \\ Max Out-Degree & 151 & 84 & 2 & 14 & 2 \\ Avg Out-Degree & 3.61 & 2.34 & 0.84 & 6.19 & 0.68 \\ Avg In-Degree & 0.59 & 0.63 & 0.75 & 0.50 & 0.62 \\ \hline Avg Delay Direct Reply & 2094 & 25 & - & 25 & 50 \\ Avg Delay Last Reply & 2151 & 33 & 229 & 25 & 61 \\ \hline Max Distinct Accounts & 6 & 3 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ Avg Distinct Accounts & 1.46 & 1.1 & 2 & 1.06 & 1.04 \\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{wraptable}

column9: The Social or the Media: Platform Mediation of Pan-Africanist Telegram Networks
column13: This study examines how Telegram’s platform infrastructure shapes visibility and authority within francophone Pan-Africanist networks. Drawing on postcolonial theory, we compare algorithmic channel recommendations with user-driven mentions to understand how influence is constructed in marginalized digital spaces. Using 7,394 messages collected from three Pan-Africanist influencers (2024–2025), we build and analyze two networks: Telegram-recommended channels and explicitly mentioned channels. Our findings reveal a clear divergence between algorithmic and organic structures. Telegram’s recommendations amplify established, predominantly francophone voices and favor homogeneity, while user mentions point to larger, more multilingual, and decentralized networks. The complete disjunction between recommended and mentioned channels suggests that algorithmic visibility does not reflect grassroots engagement. Overall, the results highlight how Telegram’s opaque recommendation logic may reinforce echo chambers, while user practices foster more diverse transnational connections within Pan-Africanist digital activism.

column9: Synergistic Motifs in Gaussian Systems
column11: Caprioglio, Enrico*; Mediano, Pedro; Berthouze, Luc
column13: High-order interdependencies are central features of complex systems, yet a mechanistic explanation for their emergence remains elusive. Currently, it is unknown under what conditions high-order interdependencies, quantified by the information-theoretic construct of synergy, arise in systems governed by pairwise interactions. We solve this problem by providing precise sufficient and necessary conditions for when synergy prevails over low-order interdependencies in the weak interactions regime, namely, we prove that antibalanced (highly frustrated) correlational structures in Gaussian systems are sufficient for synergy-dominance and that antibalanced interaction motifs in Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes are necessary for synergy-dominance. We validate the applicability of these analytical insights beyond the weak interactions regime, as well as in Ising, oscillatory, and empirical networks from multiple domains. Our results demonstrate that pairwise interactions can give rise to synergistic information in the absence of explicit high-order mechanisms, and highlight structural balance theory as an instrumental conceptual framework to study high-order interdependencies.

column9: Examining Peer Influence on Research Risk-Taking Through Co-author Networks
column13: At the outset of a new project, when a scientist must decide which research problem they would like to tackle next, they must grapple with a wide range of options and incentives [1]. Specifically, scientists’ findings must be relevant enough to publish, and novel enough to garner citations [2]. In this way, scientists face competing career incentives: they must choose problems where publication is likely in the end, but non-trivial. Seminal work examines the value of novelty and striking the right balance between uncommon recombination and building from disciplinary tradition [3]. However, it is not yet understood how the attributes of a scientist’s collaborators and their professional networks shapes their research strategy. There is reason to believe that the nature of scientific collaborations influences the qualities of the resulting work, as shown by a key study on the relationship between team size and disruptiveness [4].  Accordingly, in this work, we examine the factors that led computer scientists in the AI/ML space to produce work that was highly similar to the articles that work cited. Using arXiv data from the last ten years and joining to OpenAlex data, we scored each pre-print on its similarity to its own cited articles and aggregated the measure at the author level for prolific computer scientists (method details in Figure 1). To examine potential predictors of high similarity, we constructed the co-author network between scientists in our dataset, and built an Autologistic Actor Attribute Model [5], with author-level average max-similarity as the dependent variable. Instead of modeling network ties based on node attributes, ALAAM models node attributes based on other node attributes and network ties (going beyond pure logistic regression). We were therefore able to look for any contagion effects of high similarity scores in peers, and the role of other network structural variables, in driving scientists to produce papers similar to their cited work.  We modeled the contribution of a number of conceivably relevant variables which we thought may increase likelihood of being a similar-article producer. These included positive contagion effect, where scientists with co-author ties producing highly-similar work may also produce similar work; scientists working with larger teams, those with low h-index per article scores (production over impact), those with higher network constraint (ties are ties of each other), among others. Surprisingly, we found no evidence of contagion; however, preliminary results found the variable with the strongest effect was percentile in total citations. The odds ratio of 1.35x suggests a 1SD increase in average citation percentile across authored papers made an author 1.35x more likely to be above the median in terms of average maximum article similarity. This work contributes to a growing literature that marshals transformer-based tools to interrogate digital trace data; here, we apply a network-based inferential model to uncover the role of peer attributes and network structure in shaping scientists’ risk/benefit tradeoffs in choices of research direction. Figure 1: 1) arXiv papers from post-2015 are matched on OpenAlex. 2) Titles and abstracts are embedded with all-MiniLM-L12-v2, and their references are gathered from OpenAlex. 3) Cosine similarity is computed between the article and its references. The max similarity is the article’s score. 4) At the author level, for each prolific author (10+ articles in dataset), a weighted mean of the maximum-similarity-scores of their papers is computed, weighting based on author position as in [6]. 5) A co-author network is computed. ALAAM outputs coefficients and significance data for covariates.

column9: Tracing Burdens: Online Community Networks of Parents of Children with Disabilities
column11: Martinelli, Mauro; Balsamo, Duilio*; Melegaro, Alessia; Balbo, Nicoletta
column13: Parents of children with disabilities often experience substantial emotional, economic, and coordination burdens that remain only partially visible in surveys and administrative data. We use Reddit data to identify these parents and reconstruct a weighted co-affiliation network of the online communities they engage with. Applying noise-corrected backboning and hierarchical stochastic block modeling, we uncover a structured ecology of disability-related, parenting, mental health, and everyday-life communities. The resulting network reveals both a dense core of disability-specific support spaces and a broader separation between emotional–economic concern domains and general parenting and leisure domains. These findings highlight how online community engagement exposes clusters of needs and spillover effects that are largely hidden in traditional data sources.

column9: Human–AI Collaboration in Science at Scale: A Large-scale Randomized Field Experiment
column11: Wang, Binglu*; Liang, Weixin; Xue, Jiahui; Zhang, Yuhui; Cao, Hancheng; Wang, Dashun; Yin, Yian
column12: binglu.wang@kellogg.northwestern.edu*; wxliang@cs.stanford.edu; jiahui.xue@kellogg.northwestern.edu; yuhuiz@stanford.edu; hanchcao@stanford.edu; dashun.wang@kellogg.northwestern.edu; yy994@cornell.edu
column13: Collaboration is the defining mode of modern science, yet its core mechanism—feedback—remains hard to observe, difficult to scale, and unequally distributed. Here we test whether large language models (LLMs) can contribute to this hidden but vital practice. In a large-scale randomized field experiment, we delivered customized LLM-generated feedback for over 34,000 arXiv preprints across 8 STEM domains and 131 geographic regions. Relative to controls, authors who received feedback had a significantly higher likelihood of revising their manuscripts, corresponding to a 12.5% relative increase over the baseline revision rate. These effects nearly doubled among authors based outside English-dominant research regions, consistent with the idea that AI feedback provides the greatest benefit where access to timely critique is otherwise limited. These revisions extended beyond language polishing: treated authors in these settings were significantly more likely to strengthen theoretical soundness and improve novelty. Further heterogeneity analyses reveal a non-linear pattern by intellectual proximity to AI: effects peak at moderate distance, indicating impact is maximized where relevance is high but redundancy is low. Importantly, exposure also increased subsequent adoption of LLM tools in authors’ later papers, suggesting longer-run shifts in scientific practice. Together, these results provide causal evidence that AI can participate in a central collaborative practice of science, expand access to critique for scholars working in feedback-scarce contexts, and accelerate the diffusion of new tools, carrying broad implications for scientists, their collaborators, and the institutions and policymakers that shape the increasingly AI-integrated global research ecosystem.

column9: Recent Advances in Population-scale Social Network Analysis
column13: Over the past five years, population-scale social network analysis has substantially advanced research in network science aimed at understanding the structure and dynamics of large-scale social systems [1]. These developments have been driven primarily by the increasing availability of linkable administrative microdata derived from official government registers covering the complete population of a nation. Such data sources typically include civil population registries, household and family register, employer-employee data, education records, and longitudinal residential histories.  The availability of these data has enabled a shift away from single-layer, incomplete "who-knows-whom" reconstructions often based on surveys or online social media data.  Instead, we rely on multiplex and temporal population-scale graphs that represent multiple dimensions of social connectedness across the entire population [3,8]. This shift has made it possible to revisit longstanding questions across disciplines at an unprecedented scale, e.g., for the complete country of the Netherlands covering 18 million people and hundreds of millions of edges [1].  Recent works cover the analysis of life-course trajectories [10], nation-scale measurement of social segregation [5], the role of network structure in shaping opportunities for upward mobility [7], and the influence of social networks on opinion formation [6]. At the same time, register-based population networks have opened new avenues for addressing fundamental problems in network science itself, such as assessing the community structure of complete populations [8] and understanding time-varying connectivity patterns that govern diffusion processes, including disease spread [2].  In this talk, we present recent advances and insights from population-scale social networks, as well as first steps of cross-country comparative analyses between the Netherlands, Denmark and Sweden [1,3,9]. All of the works described above critically depend on secure data access frameworks operated by national statistical institutes and related authorities. Accordingly, alongside substantive insights for network science, the social sciences, and economics, the talk also highlights recent methodological developments that integrate privacy-enhancing technologies as part of newly funded national research infrastructure projects, with the goal of broadening analytical access to these data while preserving the anonymity of individuals in the data [4].   Looking ahead, continued expansion of cross-national data availability, methodological innovation, and secure research infrastructures positions population-scale social network analysis as a foundational, network-driven approach for understanding societally important problems such as inequality, mobility, diffusion, and social change at nation-scale in the years to come.

column9: Heterophily as a local mechanism for self-organized synergistic interdependencies
column13: Understanding how and which causal dynamical rules generate collective phenomena is a central challenge in complexity science. So far, studies have been limited to which causal dynamics on fixed, finely-tuned networks of interactions lead to synergistic high-order interdependencies. Yet, real-world complex information-processing systems---such as social and ecological systems---are adaptive, with interactions that change in time. Here, we propose heterophily--the tendency to strengthen ties with dissimilar elements as opposed to similar ones---as a simple pairwise (local) adaptive mechanism for the emergence of synergistic (non-local) interdependencies. We study a paradigmatic spin-glass-like model with co-evolving couplings and show how heterophilous adaptation weakens pairwise correlations while simultaneously inducing irreducible high-order constraints, thereby generating robust synergistic interdependencies without fine-tuning. We solve the minimal N=3 case, revealing precisely how these high-order constraints emerge, and numerically validate these results in large systems. In an opinion-dynamics variant with heterogeneous agents and local updates, we demonstrate that heterophilous agents disrupt polarization by enabling the synergistic exchange of opinions. Our results offer a parsimonious route to self-organized high-order information processing in complex adaptive systems with potential applications in computational social sciences, neuroscience, and biology.

column9: From Topological to Functional Resilience in Interdependent Networks
column11: Ahuja, Akanksha *; Herzberg, Sam N.; Rafel, Albert; Lord, Andrew; Zapata, Alejandra B.; Savory, Seb J.
column12: akanksha.ahuja99@gmail.com*; snn26@cam.ac.uk; albert.2.rafel@bt.com; andrew.lord@bt.com; alejandra.l.zapata@bt.com; sjs1001@cam.ac.uk
column13: For decades, network science has treated structural percolation as the foundational heuristic for resilience [1,2,3]. While mathematically elegant, this approach is insufficient for critical infrastructure because it conflates the means of connectivity (physical topology) with the ends (service delivery). Classical percolation implicitly assumes an isomorphism between topological and functional layers. While valid for homogeneous random networks, this equivalence breaks down in spatially embedded systems characterized by functional heterogeneity, such as communication backbones, power grids, transport, water and gas, and brain networks [4]. Consequently, standard structural metrics can become poor proxies for service viability in heterogeneous spatial infrastructures, indicating collapse while functional sub-graphs persist [5,6].  We model such systems as physical–functional interdependent networks, where functional placement is a latent, operator-configurable control parameter. Functions (e.g., routing, storage, peering) are assigned weights based on criticality and deployed under centralized (hub-concentrated) and distributed (regionally replicated) policies onto the physical topology.  We simulate disruption cycles on three national optical backbones [7] using biased site percolation followed by hub-prioritized restoration. To quantify resilience, we introduce Service Continuity as the fraction of nodes retaining access to a function and Service Coverage as the fraction of geographic regions with active service presence.   Are structural percolation metrics reliable indicators of service resilience? We identify a systematic premature-collapse bias in topological metrics. At the point where Service Continuity degrades to 0.8, algebraic connectivity exhibits 9-17 times lower values and the largest connected component 4-7 times lower values across the three networks, prematurely signaling system failure while services persist (Figure 1). Can function placement increase resilience without rewiring? On the same physical topologies, distributed placement yields 13–30% higher resilience for both service metrics. This is quantified by the area under the resilience curve as nodes are sequentially removed. As a result, we show resilience can be engineered through intelligent functional reconfiguration without structural modification to the underlying topology.  Is there a universally optimal placement across attack and recovery? We observe a resilience-recovery asymmetry wherein distributed placement exhibits superior resistance during degradation, while centralized placement facilitates steeper restoration. This trade-off implies that no single configuration optimizes performance across both phases, with distributed architectures acting as shields during attack and centralized architectures acting as springs during recovery. This suggests that optimal architecture is phase-dependent, requiring adaptive reconfigurations to maximize resilience.  [1] C. M. column9: Materials discovery: the role of Networks and AI
column11: Moi, Jacopo; Spallarossa, Davide*; Raju, Avinash; Tyner, Alexander; Balatsky, Alexander; Bonetti, Stefano; Burioni, Raffaella; Panaccione, Giancarlo; Caldarelli, Guido
column12: jacopo.moi@unive.it; davide.spallarossa@unive.it*; avinashraj316@gmail.com; alextyner@gmail.com; alexander.balatsky@uconn.edu; stefano.bonetti@unive.it; raffaella.burioni@unipr.it; panaccione@iom.cnr.it; guido.caldarelli@unive.it
column13: The discovery and optimization of novel materials underpin advances across energy, catalysis, electronics, and struc- tural applications. However, the vastness of materials chemical space and the complex, often nonlinear relationships between composition, structure, processing, and properties severely limit traditional trial-and-error and purely descriptor- driven approaches. In response, recent developments in network science and artificial intelligence (AI) have introduced powerful paradigms for representing, exploring, and learning from high-dimensional materials spaces. Thisreviewsurveyshowmaterialscanbesystematicallyrepresentedasnetworks, wherenodescorrespondtomolecules, crystals, surfaces, or complex materials, and links encode similarity, transformation pathways, or shared structural and functional attributes. We discuss the construction of such networks from diverse descriptors—ranging from composition- based and structural features to physically grounded properties derived from experiments and simulations—and examine how choices of similarity metrics, thresholds, and network topology shape the resulting materials landscapes. Different classes of materials networks, including molecular, crystalline, catalytic, knowledge-based, and multilayer representations, are introduced. We then focus on how network-based methods enable the exploration of materials space beyond conventional cluster- ing, highlighting their ability to identify underexplored regions, interpolate between known materials, detect novelty, and propagate information through similarity relations. Building on this foundation, the review examines the integration of machine learning with materials networks, from classical learning on fixed graphs to modern graph neural networks that learn representations directly from atomic and relational structure. Hybrid frameworks that combine physical graphs, similarity networks, multiplex representations, and attention mechanisms are discussed as emerging tools for adaptive, data-efficient materials discovery. Finally, we outline how these network–AI approaches support property prediction, active learning, and generative modeling for inverse materials design, offering a unifying perspective on data-driven exploration and optimization of materials chemical space. By connecting network representations with modern AI techniques, this review aims to clarify conceptual foundations, methodological choices, and future directions for network-driven materials discovery.

column9: Social Interaction, Campus Engagement, and Academic Outcomes: A Data-Driven Study
column13: This study investigates the role of students’ on-campus presence and social networks in academic performance, using real-time Wi-Fi connectivity data and student career records from the University of Parma, Italy. We observe higher academic performance among students who spend more time on campus, particularly those who attend more lessons. In addition, students within tightly connected groups—identified through co-presence across multiple buildings and synchronous movements—tend to exhibit similar academic outcomes, as well as similar degree programmes and attempted exams, all of which are consistent with peer effect. Interestingly, not all groups deliver academic benefits, and small and highly interactive networks display significant variability in achievements. Among them, focused study groups—students attempting the same exams—demonstrate a clear advantage in results, while less focused groups tend to achieve worse results than the average student. These two categories of groups are mainly characterized by spending most of their campus time attending classes, in the case of focused groups, and by devoting a large share of their campus time to activities outside class hours, in the case of less focused groups. Nevertheless, class attendance generally encourages extra time on campus. This analysis provides novel insights into how creating space and opportunities on campus for students to develop social interactions influence academic performances. It also offers valuable guidance for institutions seeking to improve student retention and achievements through data-driven strategies.

column9: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Modelling Progression of Hepatosplenic Multimorbidity Related to Schistosomiasis
column11: Zhi, Yin-Cong*; Anguajibi, Victor; Oryema, John; Nabatte, Betty; Opio, Christopher; Kabatereine, Narcis; Chami, Goylette
column12: yin-cong.zhi@ndph.ox.ac.uk*; anguajibi@gmail.com; joryema3@gmail.com; bettieful@gmail.com; opiokc@gmail.com; vcdmoh@gmail.com; goylette.chami@ndph.ox.ac.uk
column13: Multimorbidity, which is the existence of two or more chronic conditions within an individual, is poorly understood in low-middle income countries. Schistosomiasis—caused by a parasitic flatworm—is a major cause of liver and spleen multimorbidity. No timelines and risk factors for the progression of schistosomiasis-related hepatosplenic multimorbidity have been previously studied due to the lack of methods to handle complex condition interactions and insufficient data. Here we studied 35 liver and spleen conditions related to severe illness of portal hypertension as dynamic graphical processes using Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). Point-of-care B-mode ultrasound was used to examine 4330 individuals (aged five and older) from 52 rural villages across Uganda within the SchistoTrack Cohort [1] over the period 2022-2025. 54% of participants were found to be multimorbid. We used DBNs, built on top of Bayesian networks, to introduce temporal modelling by learning two time-slice directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and with stationarity assumptions, generalized to represent the transitions to over > 2 year. A DBN with intra- and inter-time edges was learned on our participants to reveal clinically accurate disease progression pathways, while through simulations, we obtained forecasts of the evolution of condition risks over time. Covariates as previously deemed important for cross-sectional analyses of hepatosplenic multimorbidity were incorporated to assess key risk factors in hepatosplenic disease progression, to answer further questions on the long-term efficacy of the treatment. As an example, Fig. 1 shows the dynamics between conditions related to periportal fibrosis (diverse types of liver fibrosis concentrated around the main portal vein related to schistosomiasis), where transitions inferred by the DBN indicated that severe periportal fibrosis typically takes two years to progress from when mild liver fibrosis is first observed. During the two year progression period, individuals would also have higher probabilities of developing hypersplenism (enlarged spleen) and a thickened gall bladder wall. Having both would lead to the highest probability of subsequently developing gastro-oesophageal varices, a life-threatening complication of severe portal hypertension. Hypersplenism was additionally associated with increased risk of splenic varices, splenorenal shunts, and cirrhosis. In contrast, praziquantel treatment showed no measurable influence on the temporal progression of hepatosplenic conditions, suggesting the only available treatment for schistosome infection does not reliably affect the downstream evolution of hepatosplenic pathology. More broadly, this work demonstrates the usefulness of DBNs as a temporal tool for understanding complex disease progression and supporting clinical decision-making. column9: Uncovering Unique, Redundant, and Synergistic Granger-Causal Effects in Networks of Random Processes via Partial Information Decomposition
column13: Understanding how complex, system-wide dynamics emerge from the interactions among the units of a distributed network is still a challenging research field in Network Science. Partial Information Decomposition (PID) represents a well established framework decomposing the mutual information (MI) that a target random variable shares with a set of source variables to highlight how it is distributed among the sources, i.e., the unique information exclusively available from each source, the redundant information that can be obtained from at least two different sources, and the synergistic information that is revealed only when multiple sources are considered simultaneously [1]. Since it is formulated for random variables, PID cannot directly quantify causal information among random processes, despite causality being essential for identifying driver–response relationships within complex networks. To overcome this limitation, we exploit the PID framework to decompose Granger causality (GC) from N source random processes {S1, ...SN } to a target process T into unique, redundant and synergistic information flows. (FS→T ) [2]. In this case the PID decomposes the overall information transferred to a target as: FS→T = F R S→T + F S S→T + N i=1 F U Si →T , where F R S→T and F S S→T are the redundant and the synergistic GC from all drivers to the target, and F U Si →T is the unique GC from the ith driver to the target. Exploiting the formalism of state-space models [2] we provide a joint time and frequency domain formulation which highlights distinct high-order behaviors of Granger causal interactions. In a simulated network of vector autoregressive random processes (Fig. 1), we show that varying the coupling parameter c strongly affects redundant and synergistic causal contributions, localized at 35 Hz and 10 Hz and associated with chain-mediated and common-child structures, respectively (Fig. 1 (c,b)). When c = 0, the dynamics are dominated by a single direct interaction, with only the unique contribution FS1 →T present at 10 Hz, reflecting a causal interaction from S1 toward T (Fig. 1(a,d)). Conversely, for c = 1 the unique contribution arises exclusively from the direct causal effect S2 → T , while redundancy emerges at 35 Hz due to information flowing along the chain S3 → S2 → T (Fig. 1(a,d)). Pure synergistic causal interactions are observed only for intermediate values of c, where the causal influences of S1 and S2 on the target are simultaneously present at 10 Hz.

column9: Recreational boating networks before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic: iterating upon Minnesota aquatic invasive species management tools
column13: In Minnesota, USA, there are over 10,000 lakes and more than 800,000 registered boats, creating a highly dynamic and complex network of boat activity. Given that approximately 6.5% of Minnesota lakes are infested with aquatic invasive species known to be spread by biofouled boats and boating equipment, preventing further spread through this pathway to the thousands of nearby uninfested lakes presents both a management challenge and priority. A thorough understanding of boat movements and associated risk factors has led to the development of innovative network-based tools to understand introduction risk, develop optimal inspection plans, and identify collaboration networks. However, current tools risk becoming out of date as boater movement patterns are dynamic and existing models may no longer represent this dynamic pathway. Here, we advance our understanding of boater connectivity networks by building upon past work and evaluating the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. To predict boater-mediated lake connectivity between 9,233 lakes across three time-periods we developed networks using data from the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources’ watercraft inspection program from 2018 to 2023 and XGBoost machine learning algorithm. We integrated adjustments to account for observation bias in the input data. Analyses suggest stable networks and an increase in connectivity during the peak-pandemic and decrease in the two years following. This approach combines high-performing predictive methods and existing management efforts to expand data-driven resources and leverage collaboration among managers, scientists, and stakeholders to support decision-making and strategic innovation across regions with patchy data availability.

column9: Dynamical analysis of a parameter-aware reservoir computer
column13: Despite the widespread success of reservoir computing (RC) in time-series prediction and forecasting, a mechanistic understanding of how RC learns and reproduces dynamical transitions remains largely unexplored. In particular, existing studies have focused primarily on predictive performance, with almost no systematic investigation of dynamical transitions; especially discontinuous transitions such as crises. We first addressed this gap for continuous transitions by showing that when the reservoir is trained to predict systems undergoing Hopf bifurcations, it itself undergoes a Neimark–Sacker bifurcation, with its critical point lying in close proximity to that of the original system. This demonstrated that RC internalizes phase-space structure rather than acting as a black-box predictor [1]. Building on this foundation, we provided the first mechanistic explanation of how RC reproduces discontinuous transitions. By analyzing the internal dynamics of trained reservoirs, we showed that RC faithfully reproduces boundary and attractor- merging crises, undergoing the same crisis mechanisms and exhibiting identical scaling exponents as the target systems, despite its high dimensionality and distinct dynamics [2]. Together, these results establish a unified dynamical-systems framework for understanding how reservoir computing learns both continuous and discontinuous critical transitions.

column9: Coupled dynamics on hypergraphs: Impact of random architecture on unstable fixed points
column13: Building upon previous finite-size analyses of globally coupled oscillator systems, we investigate the dynamics of a finite population of Kuramoto oscillators in which pairwise interactions are defined on an Erd˝ os–R´ enyi (ER) random graph, while higher-order interactions are globally (all-to-all) coupled. The higher-order coupling contributes exclusively to the backward transition, thereby generating a bistable (hysteretic) regime. The global nature of the higher-order interaction facilitates analytical treatment and reduces numerical complexity. We demonstrate, through a combination of numerical simulations and analytical arguments, that finite-size fluctu- ations induce a transition to the synchronized state in ER networks. In contrast, analysis in the thermodynamic limit predicts the absence of a forward synchronization transition, reflected in the divergence of the critical coupling as the system size tends to infinity. To elucidate this behavior, we develop a numerical procedure to determine unstable fixed points for network-based interactions. The structure of these unstable solutions explains the indeterminate nature of the forward critical coupling in ER networks and supports the absence (presence) of a forward transition in the infinite-size (finite-size) regime. We further characterize finite-size effects by systematically varying the average degree, connection probability of the ER network, and the higher-order coupling strength. The resulting distributions of the critical coupling exhibit qualitatively distinct features compared to the globally coupled case, consistent with the behavior of the corresponding unstable fixed points.
